chunks.title: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts.
# Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts
 Time: about 16 minutes. You will finish with: one 4-5 second image-to-video clip with a deliberate camera move, tested at the right motion strength.
---

chunks.title: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts / Before you start.
Beginners get a slideshow with slight Ken Burns effects, and a vague prompt like "the camera moves fast" makes models morph bodies or smear the background. Video models think in pixel displacement over time, not camera operators, so you control them with three tools: first-frame conditioning (your storyboard frame), cinematography keywords (dolly, pan, tilt) and motion strength. Formula: Start Frame (Storyboard) + Camera Direction Prompt + Motion Slider = Cinematic Shot. You will need a storyboard frame from lesson 2 (Storyboarding & Shot Planning), the library templates/motion-prompt-library.md, the reference templates/cinematography-cheat-sheet.md, and SmartVideo GO AI's Video Studio (image-to-video).

chunks.title: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts / Step by step.
### 1. Pick your start frame
Choose one static storyboard image from lesson 2 at your target aspect ratio (16:9 or 2.39:1) and upload it to the image-to-video input in Video Studio. Menus move; follow the current screen.
You should see: your image shown as the start frame.
If not: if the aspect ratio is wrong, regenerate the still in Image Studio at the target ratio first.
### 2. Choose a camera move
Open templates/motion-prompt-library.md and pick the move that matches the shot's emotional goal. Put the camera phrase at the very beginning of the prompt:
text
Slow dolly in, camera slowly pushes toward the astronaut's face, Arri Alexa cinematic style, 24fps.
You should see: a prompt that starts with the camera movement.
If not: if you only have vague words like "moves fast," swap them for dolly, pan, tilt, crane or track.
### 3. Set the motion strength
If your generator has a motion strength slider, choose by shot type:
1. Low (1-3): dialogue or subtle scenes, which prevents face warping while allowing blinks and head tilts.
2. Medium (4-6): camera pans, walking, panning b-roll.
3. High (7-9): fast action, running, driving.
You should see: a value set that fits your shot.
If not: if there is no slider, express the speed in the prompt ("slow, deliberate motion").
### 4. Render a 4-5 second clip and review

chunks.title: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts / Step by step.
Generate the clip (the worked example used 16:9, 5 seconds). Watch for the morphing zone: bent background objects, extra fingers, clothing changes mid-shot. Also check pacing: smooth or jarring?
You should see: a clip where the face and costume stay consistent with the start frame.
If not: if it glitches, lower motion strength and re-render. If it is too static, rewrite the prompt so the camera direction is at the very start.
### 5. (Optional) Add a last frame
If you need a precise end point, upload a second storyboard image to the Last-Frame Input and describe the move between them:
text
Camera pans left from the cockpit window to focus on the radar screen
You should see: a clip that begins on your first image and arrives at your second.
If not: if your generator has no last-frame input, skip this step; it is optional.

chunks.title: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts / Check yourself.
 [ ] I used a storyboard frame as the start frame.
 [ ] My prompt begins with a proper camera term.
 [ ] I chose a motion strength that matches the shot type.
 [ ] I reviewed the clip for morphing and fixed or accepted it.

chunks.title: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts / Common mistakes.
 Using vague motion words instead of dolly, pan, tilt or crane.
 Burying the camera direction at the end of the prompt.
 Too much motion strength on faces, which warps them.
 Skipping the review and building the edit on glitchy clips.

chunks.title: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts / Go further.
Worked example: Shot 1.2 of "The Last Signal." Input: the static astronaut portrait. Prompt: "Slow cinematic dolly in, camera pushes past glowing green console panels to focus on the tired eyes of the astronaut. Slow, deliberate motion, photorealistic film grain, 24fps." Settings: 16:9, 5 seconds. Result: 0.0-1.5s the camera slides forward and panels leave frame, giving depth; 1.5-3.0s he blinks naturally and shadows match his face; 3.0-5.0s the camera rests on a tight close-up, face and suit consistent with the start frame. Cost: $0.50 (1x Seedance 2 image-to-video fast call). Clip: templates/examples/astronaut-clip.mp4.
Exercises
1. Easy: animate one landscape with three prompts (pan left, tilt up, dolly zoom) and note the pixel warping.
2. Medium: render one close-up at motion strength 2, 5 and 8 and log where features start to break down.
3. Hard: build a scene transition with first and last frame (indoor to outdoor), a continuous camera pass through a door.

chunks.title: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts / Go further.
Compare tools. Seedance 2 (via muapi): outstanding character and costume preservation using omnireference first-frame conditioning, about $0.50 per 5-second clip, best for narrative continuity. Kling 3.0 / Luma Dream Machine: excellent camera tracking and micro-expressions, about $0.75-$0.80 per clip, for client work needing emotional realism. Runway Gen-3 Alpha: camera brush tools to paint direction vectors; subscription, credits burn fast. Local ComfyUI (LTX 2.3 / AnimateDiff): high control through nodes but heavy setup; free after GPU purchase, good for b-roll. Use API models like Seedance 2 for characters and local models for atmospheric b-roll.
Launch it. Package b-roll libraries (drone tracking over futuristic cities, macro pans, light rays) and sell on Adobe Stock, Shutterstock or Gumroad for $15-$30 per pack, or sell tested camera prompt packs for $10-$25 on Whop or Gumroad. Buyers: stock sites, indie game developers and other AI creators.
Templates: templates/motion-prompt-library.md, templates/cinematography-cheat-sheet.md.
Next: Assembling a Short Film.

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film, part 2
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film, part 2.
# Assembling a Short Film, part 2
 Time: about 14 minutes. You will finish with: a finished, graded 24fps export with Foley, music and a unified color look.
---

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film, part 2 — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film, part 2 / Before you start.
In part 1 you cut the clips and added narration and ambience. Now you finish the sound hierarchy with Foley/SFX and music, then fix color drift between generations with a LUT (Look-Up Table) applied over the whole timeline, so separate generations blend into a single visual style. You will need your timeline from part 1 and templates/sound-design-checklist.md for levels.

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film, part 2 / Step by step.
### 1. Add Foley and SFX on A3
Scroll through the video frame by frame. Wherever a physical event happens (a screen flickers, a head turns, boots hit pavement), place a matching effect on A3 and align the audio peak with the visual moment. In the worked example, "Electric spark & CRT monitor flicker hum" lands at 0:08-0:09 as Shot 1.3 cuts in, at -6dB.
You should see: each visible event has a sound that lands exactly on it.
If not: if it feels late or early, slide the effect a few frames and listen again.
### 2. Add the music score on A4
Place your background music on A4 and set it low, around -18dB to -24dB (the example used -20dB with a slow, tense ambient synthesizer pad).
You should see: music present but never covering the narration.
If not: if you cannot hear the voice clearly, lower the music more.
### 3. Enable audio ducking
Turn on Audio Ducking so the music drops by an additional 6dB whenever the voice track A1 is active (the example ducks to -26dB during John's line).
You should see: music dipping under each voice line and returning afterward.
If not: if your editor has no ducking, draw volume keyframes on A4 by hand around each line.
### 4. Apply a unified color grade
Select all clips on V1, add an adjustment layer over the whole timeline and apply a film emulation LUT (for example a Kodak 2383 style). The worked example used a "Teal & Orange" LUT at 70% opacity.

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film, part 2 / Step by step.
You should see: highlights and shadows that match across all clips.
If not: if the look is too strong, lower the LUT opacity; if clips still differ, tweak them individually before the LUT.
### 5. Export at 24fps
Export the finished project at 24fps, then watch it once from start to end with headphones.
You should see: a single video file with picture and all four audio layers.
If not: if the export plays at the wrong speed, check that the timeline and export settings are both 24fps.

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film, part 2 — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film, part 2 / Check yourself.
 [ ] Foley lands exactly on the visual events.
 [ ] Music sits around -18dB to -24dB and ducks 6dB under the voice.
 [ ] A LUT unifies the color across clips.
 [ ] I exported at 24fps and watched the whole film.

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film, part 2 — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film, part 2 / Common mistakes.
 Music loud enough to fight the narration.
 Placing sound effects slightly off the visual impact.
 Grading each clip differently instead of applying one shared look.
 Not watching the export in full before delivering.

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film, part 2 — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film, part 2 / Go further.
Result of the worked example: the screen-flicker sound hides the hard visual cut to the static screen, and the continuous spaceship hum holds the atmosphere together across cuts. Levels used: A1 -3dB, A2 -18dB, A3 -6dB, A4 -20dB ducking to -26dB.
Exercise. Hard: color-match 3 clips generated by different video models (different lighting) with color match wheels or a shared LUT so they look filmed in the same room on the same camera.
Templates: templates/sound-design-checklist.md.
Next: Selling Short-Form Films.

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film.
# Assembling a Short Film
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: your clips cut together on a timeline, with a narration track and a continuous ambience track.
---

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film / Before you start.
Raw silent clips played back to back feel jarring: one has a green tint, the next a warm yellow, motion speeds differ, and the silence reveals the artificial footage. The film is made in the editor. Because AI clips are silent, you build sound from scratch in a hierarchy: dialogue/narration, ambience/room tone, Foley/SFX and music. This part covers the cuts, narration and ambience; part 2 adds Foley, music, the color grade and export. You will need your clips from lesson 3 (Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts), your script from lesson 1, an NLE (non-linear editor, a program that arranges and cuts clips on a timeline) such as DaVinci Resolve, Premiere Pro or CapCut, a text-to-speech or voice tool such as ElevenLabs, and the checklist templates/sound-design-checklist.md. SmartVideo GO AI's Audio and Lip-Sync Studio can also produce voice; follow the current screen.

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film / Step by step.
### 1. Lay out the clips on V1
Import your generated clips into your editor and place them in order on the main video track (V1). Trim glitches at the very start or end of a clip, because models often dissolve or warp in the final half-second.
You should see: your shots in order on V1, with clean first and last frames.
If not: if a clip warps at the end, trim a few frames more or re-render that shot.
### 2. Generate the voiceover
In ElevenLabs or another high-quality TTS or voice tool, paste your script lines from lesson 1. Add line breaks or punctuation (commas, ellipses) to force natural pauses. Download the audio.
You should see: an audio file where the pauses sound natural.
If not: if the voice rushes, add more commas or ellipses, or shorten the line.
### 3. Place the narration on A1
Import the audio onto track A1 and sync the start of each line with the character's visual entrance (in the worked example, the voice line begins at 0:05). Settings used there: centered mono channel, volume -3dB.
You should see: narration lined up with the right shots.
If not: if it drifts, nudge the audio clip, or trim the picture length to match the line.
### 4. Add the ambient soundscape on A2

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film / Step by step.
Find or generate a continuous background track that matches your brief (for example a spaceship drone or rain). Place it on A2, fade it in at the first frame and let it run continuously under all the cuts, which unifies them. The worked example used volume -18dB.
You should see: a sound bed that never drops out between shots.
If not: if you hear a gap at a cut, extend the ambience clip across the whole timeline.

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film / Check yourself.
 [ ] My clips are ordered and trimmed on V1.
 [ ] The narration is on A1 and starts at the right moment.
 [ ] One ambience track runs under the whole timeline.
 [ ] I know what Foley, music and grade come next.

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film / Common mistakes.
 Judging clips in silence and skipping sound.
 Keeping the warped last half-second of generated clips.
 Cutting the ambience track at each shot instead of letting it run continuously.

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film / Go further.
Worked example, first 12 seconds of "The Last Signal" Scene 1: V1 holds Shot 1.1 (wide cockpit, 0:00-0:04), Shot 1.2 (astronaut slow dolly-in, 0:04-0:08) and Shot 1.3 (close-up of static screen, 0:08-0:12). A1: JOHN (V.O.) "No one has answered in six months." from 0:05 to 0:08. A2: continuous loop of "Low spaceship drone hum with computer static" for 0:00-0:12. Part 2 completes the A3, A4 and grade layers.
Exercise. Easy: import 3 random silent clips, add a continuous ambience and a simple music track. Medium: take a silent 4-second clip of a character speaking, generate a line in ElevenLabs, import it and edit the clip's visual duration to match the audio exactly.
Compare tools. DaVinci Resolve / Premiere Pro: professional multi-track editing, ducking and LUT grading, high setup effort, for widescreen films and festival entries. CapCut Desktop: lightweight, auto-captions, built-in sound effects, low effort, best for vertical micro-dramas and fast social formats. ElevenLabs: best voice cloning and natural emotional inflection, plus text-prompted SFX; low setup. Use CapCut for high-volume vertical series and DaVinci Resolve for narrative shorts.
Automation reference. The Open-AI-Micro-Drama-Generator app maps dialogue transcripts to video durations and builds combined assets programmatically.

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film / Go further.
Launch it. Offer "Assembly and Sound Design Packages" at $100-$300 per finished minute, or edit 1-minute vertical drama episodes at $150-$350 per episode. Cold pitch AI influencers who post silent loops, with a 10-second sample of their footage edited with voiceover and effects.
Templates: templates/sound-design-checklist.md.
Next: Assembling a Short Film, part 2.

chunks.title: Selling Short-Form Films
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling Short-Form Films.
# Selling Short-Form Films
 Time: about 17 minutes. You will finish with: a delivery pack list, a sponsorship pitch draft, a festival target and a licensing terms sheet draft.
---

chunks.title: Selling Short-Form Films — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling Short-Form Films / Before you start.
Most AI short films get a few hundred views and earn $0, because makers treat them as hobby art. Meanwhile brands want cost-effective storytelling, vertical drama platforms license short episodes, and AI film festivals pay cash prizes. Three routes: AI film festivals (prestige, low predictability, cash prizes of $1K-$20K), brand sponsorships (moderate predictability, high margins, $300-$1.5K for product placement) and platform licensing (highest predictability, volume-driven, $150-$500 per episode). You will need a finished film from lesson 4 (Assembling a Short Film), your storyboard frames from lesson 2, and the templates templates/sponsorship-pitch-template.md and templates/licensing-agreement-sheet.md. SmartVideo GO AI's Image Studio and Video Studio can make key art and teaser clips, and its Thumbnail studio can help with preview images; follow the current screen.

chunks.title: Selling Short-Form Films — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling Short-Form Films / Step by step.
### 1. Package your deliverables
Prepare three files:
1. Master cut: widescreen 16:9 or 2.39:1, high resolution.
2. Vertical cut: 9:16 for mobile feeds.
3. Clean master: with sound effects and music but no voice track, so platforms can dub it into other languages.
You should see: three clearly named export files.
If not: if you have only a single mix, re-export from your editor with the voice track muted.
### 2. Build a visual pitch outline
Open templates/sponsorship-pitch-template.md and outline your concept. Include your static storyboard frames from lesson 2 to show the visual quality.
You should see: a one-page outline with concept, frames and your name.
If not: if you have no strong frames, generate a key art image in Image Studio.
### 3. Draft a brand sponsorship pitch
List mid-sized brands whose look matches your film (sci-fi: premium desk accessories or software; drama: fashion or skincare). Offer seamless product integration in your story world and quote an upfront fee, $300-$1,000 for initial campaigns (a 5-second placement in a 1-minute clip is $300-$800). Send only to real people you have researched, and no secrets or private data.
You should see: a short pitch email ready to send to a named brand.
If not: if you cannot find brands, look at who advertises heavily on social media (Meta Ad Library) but lacks high-production video.
### 4. Choose festivals

chunks.title: Selling Short-Form Films — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling Short-Form Films / Step by step.
Set up a profile on FilmFreeway, search for "AI Film Festivals" and shortlist a few. Submissions are often free or low-cost. The original lesson names Runway AIFF and muapi Creator Awards as examples; check current deadlines and rules on each page.
You should see: a shortlist with deadlines.
If not: if the "AI Film" filter is missing, search for the festival names directly.
### 5. Draft a licensing terms sheet
Open templates/licensing-agreement-sheet.md and fill in a multi-episode mini-series pitch for vertical drama apps: exclusivity, upfront fee per episode and royalty split. Pitch 10-20 episode packages at $150-$350 per episode, or a lower upfront fee for a higher revenue share (20-30%). For anything binding, get proper legal advice.
You should see: a terms sheet with all three items filled in.
If not: compare with the worked example below.

chunks.title: Selling Short-Form Films — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling Short-Form Films / Check yourself.
 [ ] I have a master cut, a vertical cut and a voice-less clean master.
 [ ] I have a pitch outline using my storyboard frames.
 [ ] I drafted one sponsor pitch with an upfront fee.
 [ ] I have a festival shortlist and a licensing terms sheet draft.

chunks.title: Selling Short-Form Films — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling Short-Form Films / Common mistakes.
 Making films with no delivery pack ready.
 Pitching with no visuals.
 Treating festivals as the only income instead of a credibility channel.
 Sending the same generic pitch to every brand.

chunks.title: Selling Short-Form Films — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling Short-Form Films / Go further.
Worked example, licensing "The Last Signal" to a mobile app. Deal: 5-episode vertical mini-series, 1 minute each. Terms: exclusive mobile app license for 12 months, non-exclusive for your portfolio; $300 per episode ($1,500 upfront); 15% of net pay-per-view revenue; credit line "Created by [Your Name] using muapi models." Math: $25 in video generation credits (Kling/Luma), 15 hours editing, net upfront profit $1,475 (about $98/hour), plus a passive tail from royalties.
Exercises
1. Easy: draft a 1-page pitch deck outline for an AI sci-fi short with target sponsors.
2. Medium: write a cold pitch email to a real watch or tech gear brand for a 5-second integration in a travel-themed short.
3. Hard: draft a licensing term sheet for a 10-episode vertical drama, with regional exclusivity, payment milestones and revenue share.
Compare tools. FilmFreeway: central festival directory with AI Film filters, for credentials, prizes and press. Direct brand outreach (email/LinkedIn): reach marketing managers for short-term cash. Whop / Gumroad: sell templates, visual assets or LUT packs to other creators. Use outreach and licensing for predictable income and festivals as a marketing channel to justify higher rates.
Templates: templates/sponsorship-pitch-template.md, templates/licensing-agreement-sheet.md.

# Cinematography Cheat Sheet
 SmartVideo GO AI Academy — A reusable template from the SmartVideo GO AI course library. Fill it in, then launch it from the matching SmartVideo GO AI studio or Create-With-AI recipe.
A quick-reference sheet for framing, lighting, camera lensing, and style descriptors for prompt engineering.
---

chunks.title: Cinematography Cheat Sheet — 1. Camera Framing Terms
chunks.text:
Academy template: Cinematography Cheat Sheet / 1. Camera Framing Terms.
 Extreme Wide Shot (EWS): Environment is the subject; character is tiny or not visible.
 Wide Shot (WS): Full body of the character is visible; details of the location are clear.
 Medium Wide Shot (MWS): Knee-up framing.
 Medium Shot (MS): Waist-up framing.
 Close-up (CU): Chest/shoulders-up framing.
 Extreme Close-up (ECU): Focuses on eyes, a clock face, a phone screen, or a lock.

chunks.title: Cinematography Cheat Sheet — 2. Camera Lenses & Aperture Descriptors
chunks.text:
Academy template: Cinematography Cheat Sheet / 2. Camera Lenses & Aperture Descriptors.
Inject these terms to force a realistic photographic lens rendering:
 "Anamorphic lens, widescreen bokeh, subtle horizontal blue lens flares" (Best for cinematic/sci-fi films)
 "35mm prime lens, f/1.8 aperture, shallow depth of field, soft out-of-focus background" (Best for close-ups and dramatic portraits)
 "85mm lens, portrait lighting, high detail" (Best for character introduction shots)
 "24mm wide-angle lens, deep depth of field" (Best for establishing landscape or interior room shots)

chunks.title: Cinematography Cheat Sheet — 3. Film Stock & Camera Bodies
chunks.text:
Academy template: Cinematography Cheat Sheet / 3. Film Stock & Camera Bodies.
Forces the AI to simulate specific camera sensor and film characteristics:
 Digital Cinema: Arri Alexa Mini LF, RED V-Raptor, Sony Venice 2
 Analog Film Stock: Kodak Portra 400, Kodak Vision3 500T, Fujifilm Superia, 35mm film grain
 Vintage/Documentary: 16mm film grain, Bolex H16, vintage color grading

chunks.title: Cinematography Cheat Sheet — 4. Lighting & Atmosphere Keys
chunks.text:
Academy template: Cinematography Cheat Sheet / 4. Lighting & Atmosphere Keys.
 Golden Hour: Warm, soft, low-angle sunlight, long shadows.
 Blue Hour: Mood, cool light, soft shadows, right after sunset.
 Chiaroscuro / Film Noir: High contrast between light and dark, sharp shadow lines.
 Volumetric lighting: Light rays visible through smoke, dust, or fog.
 Backlit / Rim light: Highlights the silhouette of the character from behind.

chunks.title: Motion Prompt Library — 1. Dolly & Tracking Shots
chunks.text:
Academy template: Motion Prompt Library / 1. Dolly & Tracking Shots.
Move the camera physically closer, further, or alongside the character.
 Dolly In / Push-in:
 "Slow cinematic dolly in, camera slowly pushes toward the character's face, high quality, 24fps."
 Dolly Out / Pull-back:
 "Cinematic dolly out, camera pulls back to reveal the surrounding environment, wide shot."

 Tilt Up/Down:
 "Slow camera tilt up, starting from the boots on the wet ground up to the character's face."
 Dutch Angle / Roll:

chunks.title: Motion Prompt Library — 3. Advanced Cinematography Actions
chunks.text:

chunks.title: Sound Design Checklist — 1. Dialogue / Narration Layer
chunks.text:
Academy template: Sound Design Checklist / 1. Dialogue / Narration Layer.
- [ ] Clean Dialogue: Ensure the generated voice (TTS/Voice Clone) is free of digital artifacts or slurring.
- [ ] Room Tone: Add a very quiet ambient layer matching the environment under the dry voice clip so the speaker doesn't sound like they are in a vacuum.
- [ ] Pacing & Pauses: Add artificial pauses (0.5 to 1.5 seconds) between sentences. Real people breathe and pause; AI TTS often runs sentences together.

chunks.title: Sound Design Checklist — 2. Ambient Soundscape (Background)
chunks.text:
Academy template: Sound Design Checklist / 2. Ambient Soundscape (Background).
- [ ] Primary Environment Ambience: Layer continuous background sound matching the location (e.g., wind rustle for forest, low rumble for spaceship interior, city traffic chatter).
- [ ] Transitions: Fade ambience in/out during scene changes to smooth out cuts.

chunks.title: Sound Design Checklist — 3. Foley & Sound Effects (SFX)
chunks.text:
Academy template: Sound Design Checklist / 3. Foley & Sound Effects (SFX).
- [ ] Action Syncing: Add synchronized sound effects for physical actions shown on screen (e.g., doors opening, footsteps, coffee cups clinking, keyboard clicks).
- [ ] Audio Sweeps: Use riser or whoosh sounds to match rapid camera pans or transitions.

chunks.title: Sound Design Checklist — 4. Music & Score
chunks.text:
Academy template: Sound Design Checklist / 4. Music & Score.
- [ ] Tone Alignment: Match the music genre to the film's genre.
- [ ] Dynamic Level: Duck the music volume by 6dB to 12dB whenever dialogue is playing.
- [ ] Key Syncing: Sync visual cuts to the beat or transition points in the music track where possible.

chunks.title: Sound Design Checklist — 5. Master Output Check
chunks.text:
Academy template: Sound Design Checklist / 5. Master Output Check.
- [ ] Level Balance: Dialogue should be clearly audible, music secondary, SFX tertiary.
- [ ] No Clipping: Ensure the audio master meter never peaks into the red (above 0dB).

chunks.title: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline, part 2
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline, part 2.
# Niche Selection & Script Pipeline, part 2
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a finished, read-aloud-tested 60-second script of under 180 words, written in a conversational, visually paced format.
---

chunks.title: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline, part 2 — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline, part 2 / Before you start.
Platform recommendation systems (YouTube, TikTok, Reels) prioritize Average Percentage Viewed (retention). Most viewers leave in the first 5-10 seconds, so the script must lead with a hook (fear or desire), then the problem, a step-by-step solve, and a pattern interrupt (a visual change or audio SFX) every 3-5 seconds to restart attention.
You will need: your chosen niche and video topic from part 1, templates/retention-script-template.md, and a text LLM such as Claude or Gemini. Do not paste any password or secret key into the chat. In SmartVideo GO AI you can later lay the finished script out in Storyboard / Campaign Planner.

chunks.title: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline, part 2 / Step by step.
### 1. Lay out the five-part structure
In your retention template, create five blocks with these timings:
 0-10s Hook: the immediate value or shock factor. No generic greetings like "Welcome back to my channel".
 10-25s Problem: why the standard method is failing.
 25-45s Solve: the step-by-step blueprint.
 45-50s Pattern interrupt: a surprising statistic or change in pacing.
 55-60s CTA: send them to the link in your description.
You should see: five empty, labelled blocks.
If not: copy the list above into your document as headings.
### 2. Generate a first draft with a system prompt
In Claude or Gemini, paste this prompt, replacing [Topic] with your topic:
text
You are a professional YouTube Shorts scriptwriter. Write a 60-second script about [Topic]. Keep the tone conversational, informal, and visual. Avoid high-level marketing words. Write short sentences. Every 5 seconds, insert a [Visual transition] instruction. Ensure the total word count is exactly 150-160 words.
You should see: a script with short sentences and a [Visual transition] note about every 5 seconds.
If not: if the script opens with "Are you tired of..." or a greeting, reply asking for a hook that states a specific pain point and a number instead.
### 3. Check the word count
Paste the spoken text into a word counter. Keep it under 180 words for 60 seconds; the prompt targets 150-160.

chunks.title: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline, part 2 / Step by step.
You should see: a count at or under 180.
If not: cut the longest sentences first, or ask the LLM to shorten to 155 words.
### 4. Fit the draft into the five blocks
Move the draft into your template so each block matches its time window, with a visual direction every 5-10 seconds.
You should see: a hook that names a pain point and a time or money cost in the first sentence.
If not: rewrite only the first sentence until it does, as the worked example does ("throwing away five hours a week").
### 5. Run the read-aloud audit
Read the script out loud. Rewrite any sentence you stumble on or that sounds formal. Use active verbs, contractions ("you'll", not "you will") and direct address ("you").
You should see: a script you can read without stumbling.
If not: break any sentence that needs a breath in the middle into two.

chunks.title: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline, part 2 — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline, part 2 / Check yourself.
 [ ] My script is under 180 words.
 [ ] It has all five parts: hook, problem, solve, pattern interrupt, CTA.
 [ ] The first sentence has no greeting and names a specific pain point.
 [ ] I read it aloud and fixed every stumble.

chunks.title: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline, part 2 — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline, part 2 / Common mistakes.
 Writing like a Wikipedia article. Viewers click away in the first seconds.
 Skipping the read-aloud. Text-to-speech also stumbles on formal sentences.
 A script over 180 words. It forces fast, artificial narration.

chunks.title: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline, part 2 — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline, part 2 / Go further.
Worked example excerpt ("Automate Smarter", 158 words).
markdown
[0-5s Hook]
"If you're still manually copying invoices into your accounting software, you are throwing away five hours a week. [Visual: Screen recording of a user typing fast on a spreadsheet, overlay red X]"
[5-15s Problem]
"Most freelancers think they have to pay a virtual assistant to do this. But assistant costs scale up, and copy-paste errors eventually lead to tax discrepancies. [Visual: close-up of calculator showing error screen]"
[15-40s Solve]
"Here is the automated fix. You connect your billing email to Zapier, run it through muapi's document parser, and auto-populate your invoices. Setup takes 10 minutes. [Visual: Clean flowchart animation showing email icon moving to folder]"
Why it holds retention: an immediate hook with a time penalty, a visual change every 5-10 seconds, and short sentences that a TTS model reads naturally.
Exercises. Medium: adapt a dry technical post into a script under 160 words using the five parts. Hard: add three pattern interrupts and say where each goes.
Compare tools. Frontier LLMs (Claude/Gemini) are the best pipeline option; custom system instructions can output the voiceover text and video prompt keys in one run.
Next: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing.

chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline.
# Niche Selection & Script Pipeline
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a graded shortlist of three niches, one chosen niche, and a filled-in script plan for your first video.
---

chunks.title: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline / Before you start.
If your niche has low CPM, your view count does not matter; if your script has low retention, platforms will not show it to anyone. Generic niches such as scary campfire stories or motivational quotes often pay an RPM under $0.50 per 1,000 views, so $1,000 needs about 2 million views. The formula is Earnings = (Views / 1000) RPM + Direct Conversions. In a high-CPM niche (business software, SaaS, banking, real estate, luxury travel) RPM can reach $10-$30, so at $20 RPM you need only 50,000 views to make $1,000. This part picks the niche and plans one video. Part 2 writes and audits the script.
You will need: the two templates linked in the steps, a browser, and about 15 minutes. You will use SmartVideo GO AI's Storyboard / Campaign Planner later to lay out the script; this part needs only the templates.

chunks.title: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline / Step by step.
### 1. Pick three candidate niches
Write down three niches you could talk about for months. Favor industries that sell high-priced products (SaaS, banking, real estate, business software, luxury travel).
You should see: a list of three niche names.
If not: if you only have ideas like "funny moments" or "quote compilations", add at least one business or software angle, because those are the low-CPM traps.
### 2. Open the Niche Evaluation Matrix
Open templates/niche-evaluation-matrix.md and list your three niches in it.
You should see: the score sheet with one row or column per niche.
If not: copy the template contents into a document of your own and use that.
### 3. Check advertiser density for each niche
For each niche, search its key terms in the Meta Ad Library or Google Keyword Planner. High Cost-Per-Click (CPC) bids, or dozens of brands running paid social ads for the keyword, mean advertisers are bidding heavily, so your RPM will be high.
You should see: a clear difference between niches: some keywords with many advertisers or high bids, some with few.
If not: menus move; follow the current screen. If Keyword Planner asks for setup you do not want to do, use the Meta Ad Library alone.
### 4. Score the niches and choose one
Fill in the scores in the matrix and select the niche with the highest score.

chunks.title: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline / Step by step.
You should see: one winning niche. (For comparison, the worked example "Automate Smarter" in SaaS automation scored 22/25.)
If not: if two niches tie, pick the one with software affiliate programs, because those become your main income while you wait for the YouTube Partner Program.
### 5. Plan one video concept
Open templates/retention-script-template.md. Choose a single target problem, for example "how to automate your business bookkeeping" rather than the broad "introduction to accounting". Write the topic at the top of the template.
You should see: one narrow topic written in the template.
If not: if your topic sounds like a school subject, narrow it until it names one problem and one result.

chunks.title: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline — Common mistakes

Academy lesson: Niche Selection & Script Pipeline / Common mistakes.

Compare tools for scripting. Claude 3.5 Sonnet or Gemini 1.5 Pro: excellent at formatting scripts, a natural tone and strict word counts, best for drafting. ChatGPT Plus (GPT-4o): good for topic brainstorming, but tends toward cheesy hooks such as "Are you tired of...". Traditional script editors suit long linear narratives, not short-form hooks.

chunks.title: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing, part 2
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing, part 2.
# Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing, part 2
 Time: about 14 minutes. You will finish with: a timeline where narration runs gap-free on A1 and every visual cut lands on an audio boundary.
---

chunks.title: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing, part 2 — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing, part 2 / Before you start.
The audio track is the spine of the timeline. Once your narration is generated and logged (part 1), you assemble in a fixed order: audio first, then visuals cut to the audio boundaries. This is what removes dead air and resets the viewer's attention at each cut.
You will need: your numbered audio files, your filled-in templates/narration-duration-log.md, the visuals you planned (generated clips or stills, for example from SmartVideo GO AI's Video Studio and Image Studio), and an editor such as CapCut or Premiere.

chunks.title: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing, part 2 / Step by step.
### 1. Set up a clean project folder
Create this structure on your computer:
text
[project-folder]/
├── audio/ # Narrations and voiceovers
├── visuals/ # Generated b-roll and graphics
├── projectfiles/ # Saved CapCut/Premiere project
└── exports/ # Completed renders
You should see: four empty folders; put your audio files in audio/.
If not: any equivalent folder layout works; just keep audio, visuals and exports separate.
### 2. Batch-generate the visuals
With the log open, generate all the backgrounds in one session and save them in visuals/. Doing audio first, then all visuals, keeps you in one mindset at a time.
You should see: one visual per logged line, each at least as long as its audio line.
If not: if a generated clip is shorter than its line, plan to slow it slightly or choose a still with a zoom instead.
### 3. Lay the narration on track A1
Place all narration files back-to-back on audio track A1. Trim blank noise or silence at the start and end of each clip so the voice flows without gaps.
You should see: a continuous voice line with no gaps and a total length close to your sum of logged durations.
If not: if there are small gaps, nudge each clip left until it touches the previous one.
### 4. Place visuals on V1 and cut to the audio

chunks.title: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing, part 2 / Step by step.
Put each visual on video track V1 and cut it exactly to the audio file boundaries. Trim extra frames from clips (a 5.0 s clip for a 4.2 s line loses its last 0.8 s). Stretch stills to the full line length.
You should see: each visual changing at the exact moment the narrator finishes a line.
If not: zoom into the timeline and snap clip edges to the audio edges.
### 5. Add subtle motion to stills
Add a slow scale animation (about a 10% zoom-in) or a pan to static images so the screen stays dynamic.
You should see: gentle movement on every still, and a visual change every 2.5-4.0 seconds.
If not: if the zoom feels distracting, reduce it; it should be barely noticeable.
### 6. Play it back and export a draft
Watch the whole timeline once, then export to exports/.
You should see: narration that feels natural, with no dead air and no rushed lines.
If not: if a line sounds rushed, the visual needs to be longer, not the audio faster; regenerate the line, update the log and re-cut.

chunks.title: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing, part 2 — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing, part 2 / Check yourself.
 [ ] The narration sits back-to-back on A1 with no silences at clip edges.
 [ ] Every visual cut matches an audio boundary.
 [ ] No visual stays on screen longer than about 4 seconds.
 [ ] I exported a draft into exports/.

chunks.title: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing, part 2 — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing, part 2 / Common mistakes.
 Leaving trailing pauses and silent frames, which break the pacing.
 Cutting visuals by eye instead of snapping to the audio.
 Editing before the audio is locked.

chunks.title: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing, part 2 — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing, part 2 / Go further.
Exercise. Take your 6-line script from part 1 and assemble all six visuals to their clips to the frame.
Compare tools. For a single channel, manual editing in CapCut is the fastest way to good pacing. For a network of 5+ channels, a programmatic pipeline like AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator saves editing hours.
Next: Honest RPM & Earnings Math.

chunks.title: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing.
# Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing
 Time: about 14 minutes. You will finish with: a numbered set of narration audio files and a duration log with a visual plan matched to each line.
---

chunks.title: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing / Before you start.
Visuals tell the story, but the audio duration controls the edit. If you make b-roll first and fit a voiceover to it, the narrator has to rush or pause awkwardly. Instead use Narration-First Assembly: Script Text, Voice Generation, Duration Logging, Video Clipping/Gen, Timeline Sync. At about 150 words per minute each word takes roughly 0.4 seconds, so a 10-word sentence needs a 4-second clip, and short-form needs a visual change every 2.5 to 4.0 seconds.
You will need: the finished script from Niche Selection & Script Pipeline, a text-to-speech tool (for example ElevenLabs), and templates/narration-duration-log.md. In SmartVideo GO AI, the Audio studio can generate the voice. This part covers audio and planning; part 2 assembles the timeline.

chunks.title: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing / Step by step.
### 1. Split the script into lines
Divide your script into individual sentences or short thought blocks. Aim for each to be roughly 10 words or fewer so it fits one visual.
You should see: a numbered list of short lines.
If not: split any line longer than one breath at its natural pause.
### 2. Generate the narration for each line
Batch-generate the lines with a premium TTS model (for example ElevenLabs). Save each file with a sequential number, such as 01hook.mp3 and 02problem.mp3.
You should see: one audio file per line, named in order.
If not: if a voice sounds rushed or flat, regenerate just that line; do not stretch the audio.
### 3. Measure each duration
Import the files into your editor or a utility script and read each file's duration to one decimal place. For example, 01hook.mp3 = 4.2 seconds.
You should see: a number like 4.2 for every file.
If not: if your tool shows only whole seconds, switch to the editor's clip properties or timeline readout.
### 4. Log the durations
Open templates/narration-duration-log.md and enter each file name and its duration.
You should see: a complete log with one row per audio file.
If not: copy the template into your own document if you cannot edit it in place.
### 5. Plan the visual for each line

chunks.title: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing / Step by step.
Next to each logged line, note the visual needed. A 4.2-second line needs a visual that shows for exactly 4.2 seconds. Generated video usually comes in 4- or 5-second clips, so plan to trim the extra frames.
You should see: every row of the log has a visual idea and a duration.
If not: if a line is under about 2.5 seconds or over 4.0, merge it with a neighbour or split it so visuals change every 2.5-4.0 seconds.

chunks.title: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing / Check yourself.
 [ ] My audio files are numbered in script order.
 [ ] Every duration is logged to one decimal place.
 [ ] Every line has a planned visual.
 [ ] No visual would stay on screen longer than about 4 seconds.

chunks.title: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing / Common mistakes.
 Generating video first and fitting the voice to it.
 Logging rounded durations. The cut should land on the end of the voice file.
 Forgetting that video clips are 4-5 seconds, so they need trimming.

chunks.title: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing — Go further
chunks.text: Academy lesson: Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing / Go further. Worked example: "Automate Smarter", first 10 seconds. 01hook.mp3 is 4.2 s and 02problem.mp3 is 3.8 s. Visual 1 (0:00-0:04.2) is a generated clip of a person typing, 5.0 s long, with the last 0.8 s cut. Visual 2 (0:04.2-0:08.0) is a still of a calculator with an error screen stretched to 3.8 s.

chunks.title: Honest RPM & Earnings Math
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Honest RPM & Earnings Math.
# Honest RPM & Earnings Math
 Time: about 17 minutes. You will finish with: a filled-in Channel Profitability Calculator showing your cost per video, expected earnings and net monthly profit.
---

chunks.title: Honest RPM & Earnings Math — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Honest RPM & Earnings Math / Before you start.
Views are vanity; profit margins are sanity. A channel can get 1 million views a month and earn only $50 from AdSense in a low-value niche, while subscriptions of $120 mean it runs at a loss. CPM is what advertisers pay per 1,000 views; RPM is what you receive per 1,000 views after the platform's cut (YouTube takes 45% of long-form ad revenue and 55% of Shorts ad revenue). Long-form videos over 8 minutes allow mid-roll ads and RPMs of $5-$25; Shorts draw from a shared pool at about $0.02-$0.06 RPM. Cost per Video = LLM Script Cost + TTS Audio Cost + Video Generator Credit Cost.
You will need: templates/channel-profitability-calculator.md, your chosen niche, a list of your monthly subscriptions, and Google Keyword Planner. Your usage records in SmartVideo GO AI and your TTS tool give you real production costs.

chunks.title: Honest RPM & Earnings Math — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Honest RPM & Earnings Math / Step by step.
### 1. Research CPC bids for your niche
In Google Keyword Planner, type keywords for your niche and read the "Top of Page Bid" range. High bids (for example $5.00+ CPC for "Business Liability Insurance") mean high CPM; low bids (for example $0.10 for "Funny cats") mean low CPM.
You should see: a bid range for at least three keywords.
If not: menus move; follow the current screen. If Keyword Planner is not available to you, use the advertiser check from lesson 1 as a rougher guide.
### 2. List your monthly operating budget
Open templates/channel-profitability-calculator.md. List every recurring subscription and API credit package. Keep the stack lean while you start.
You should see: a total monthly expense number in the calculator.
If not: if you are unsure of a cost, use the last invoice or your account's billing page.
### 3. Calculate production cost per video
For a 60-second video, use your actual consumption. The example figures are: script (LLM) about 0.05 credits, narration (ElevenLabs, about 1,000 characters) about $0.15, video generation (muapi credits, for example Seedance 2) about $0.50, so total cost per video is $0.70.
You should see: a per-video cost entered in the calculator.
If not: if your numbers differ, use yours; the example is only a reference.
### 4. Test a Short against its cost

chunks.title: Honest RPM & Earnings Math — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Honest RPM & Earnings Math / Step by step.
Check: a Short that costs $0.50 and gets 5,000 views at $0.04 RPM earns 5,000 / 1000 0.04 = $0.20, a loss of $0.30. Do the same with your own numbers.
You should see: whether one video of yours earns more than it costs from AdSense alone.
If not: a loss is normal for Shorts. That is why the next step matters.
### 5. Map views to direct sales
If 0.1% of viewers become email subscribers (1 in 1,000 views) and 2% of subscribers buy a $27 product (1 in 50), every 50,000 views yields one $27 sale plus AdSense. Enter your own conversion assumptions in the calculator.
You should see: an estimated number of sales and income from direct conversions.
If not: if the result is zero, raise views or conversion assumptions only if you can justify them; do not guess optimistically.
### 6. Compute net monthly profit
Enter views, RPM, direct sales and expenses. Net profit = AdSense + direct sales - expenses.
You should see: a single net monthly number, positive or negative.
If not: if it is negative, look at the Scenario B example in Go further: fewer views with a funnel beat many views with none.

chunks.title: Honest RPM & Earnings Math — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Honest RPM & Earnings Math / Check yourself.
 [ ] I know my niche's rough CPC range.
 [ ] I know my cost per video.
 [ ] My calculator includes direct sales, not only AdSense.
 [ ] I know my net monthly profit or loss.

chunks.title: Honest RPM & Earnings Math — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Honest RPM & Earnings Math / Common mistakes.
 Chasing views in a low-RPM niche.
 Counting Shorts as if they paid long-form RPM.
 Ignoring tool subscriptions and API credits.
 Skipping affiliate disclosures in descriptions.

chunks.title: Honest RPM & Earnings Math — Go further
chunks.text: Academy lesson: Honest RPM & Earnings Math / Go further. Worked example.

chunks.title: Honest RPM & Earnings Math — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Honest RPM & Earnings Math / Go further.
Exercises. Easy: compare CPC bids for three Finance keywords and three Humour/Meme keywords. Medium: fill the calculator for 50,000 views, 15 videos a month and one $47 product. Hard: project a move from Shorts-only to 2 long-form videos and 15 Shorts a month and see how RPM changes net profit.
Template. templates/channel-profitability-calculator.md.
Next: Scaling to Multiple Channels.

chunks.title: Scaling to Multiple Channels, part 2
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling to Multiple Channels, part 2.
# Scaling to Multiple Channels, part 2
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: finished vertical videos scheduled across YouTube, TikTok and Instagram with a safe posting plan.
---

chunks.title: Scaling to Multiple Channels, part 2 — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling to Multiple Channels, part 2 / Before you start.
With scripts and voices done (part 1), the rest of the batch is visuals, editing and scheduling. A 9:16 vertical video can go to YouTube Shorts (AdSense pool, subscribers), TikTok (Creator Rewards Program) and Instagram Reels (brand sponsorship reach, visual discovery) with zero extra production cost. If you also make long-form videos (8+ minutes), you can extract 5-10 short highlights from them.
You will need: your scripts and audio from part 1, a way to generate visuals (SmartVideo GO AI's Image Studio and Video Studio), an editor such as CapCut, and logins for YouTube Studio, TikTok Studio and Instagram Creator Studio. If you do this with a single video first, it takes the time stated; a full batch of five takes longer.

chunks.title: Scaling to Multiple Channels, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling to Multiple Channels, part 2 / Step by step.
### 1. Batch-render the visuals
Open your image generators and queue prompts for all videos in one session. Save results in folders labelled [Video1], [Video2] and so on.
You should see: a folder per video filled with its visuals.
If not: if a generation fails, re-run only that prompt and keep the folder naming.
### 2. Import audio and visuals into your editor
Import all audio tracks and visual folders into CapCut or your editor.
You should see: every video's assets available in one project.
If not: if files look missing, re-import from the folder rather than the download list.
### 3. Edit all videos in one sitting
Edit the videos back to back, copy-pasting caption styles and audio settings between them, then export the finished files.
You should see: finished 9:16 files, auto-captioned.
If not: if caption styles do not carry over, save one as a preset and reuse it.
### 4. Upload and schedule on each platform
Upload to YouTube Studio, TikTok Studio and Instagram Creator Studio, and use the built-in schedulers to set release times days in advance.
You should see: each video listed as scheduled on each platform.
If not: menus move; follow the current screen. If scheduling is not offered for an account, post at your planned time instead.
### 5. Apply the safety rules

chunks.title: Scaling to Multiple Channels, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling to Multiple Channels, part 2 / Step by step.
Post no more than 1 upload per day per platform, and never upload the exact same video file to two different channels on the same platform.
You should see: a posting calendar with at most one upload per day per platform and distinct content per channel.
If not: spread extra videos to later days and change the content for a second channel.

chunks.title: Scaling to Multiple Channels, part 2 — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling to Multiple Channels, part 2 / Check yourself.
 [ ] My videos are exported as 9:16 files.
 [ ] They are scheduled on all three platforms using native schedulers.
 [ ] No platform gets more than 1 upload a day.
 [ ] No identical file goes to two channels on the same platform.

chunks.title: Scaling to Multiple Channels, part 2 — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling to Multiple Channels, part 2 / Common mistakes.
 Spam uploading, such as 10 videos a day on a new account, which triggers spam filters and tanks views.
 Uploading the same file to two channels. Platforms check video hashes and flag repetitive content.
 Using third-party schedulers for creator channels, which can restrict trending audio.

chunks.title: Scaling to Multiple Channels, part 2 — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling to Multiple Channels, part 2 / Go further.
Compare tools. Native schedulers (YouTube Studio, TikTok web): free, safe, support custom thumbnails; the default choice. Programmatic clipping (ai-clipping-generator): detects speech pauses and cuts long videos into highlights. Third-party schedulers (Buffer/Later): one dashboard, but may restrict custom music or carousel formats.
Exercises. Medium: schedule a 5-day posting calendar with the native schedulers and log dates and times. Hard: use ai-clipping-generator to cut a 10-minute speech into three short clips and write a hook line for each.
Next: Monetization Ladder.

chunks.title: Scaling to Multiple Channels
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling to Multiple Channels.
# Scaling to Multiple Channels
 Time: about 14 minutes. You will finish with: a weekly batch calendar, isolated browser profiles for each channel, and a batch of five scripts with voice files.
---

chunks.title: Scaling to Multiple Channels — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling to Multiple Channels / Before you start.
One channel is a job; three channels is a system. Producing one video at a time takes about 2 hours, so three channels would take 6 hours a day and break your upload consistency. Temporal batching fixes this: write all 5 scripts on Monday, generate all 5 audio files on Tuesday, render clips on Wednesday, edit and schedule after that. This part sets up the calendar and profiles and runs the script and voice batch. Part 2 does visuals, editing and scheduling.
You will need: templates/production-schedule-tracker.md, your retention script template, a TTS tool such as ElevenLabs, and a browser such as Google Chrome.

chunks.title: Scaling to Multiple Channels — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling to Multiple Channels / Step by step.
### 1. Lock in your weekly calendar
Open templates/production-schedule-tracker.md and set batch milestones: Monday scripting, Tuesday voiceovers, Wednesday visuals, Thursday editing, Friday scheduling. Never write a script on edit day.
You should see: a week with one task assigned to each day.
If not: if your week is different, keep the order (scripts, voices, visuals, edit, schedule) and move the days.
### 2. Create browser profiles per channel
If you run more than two channels, create a separate Google Chrome profile (or browser profile) for each channel identity and sign in to that channel's YouTube, affiliate dashboard and email in its own profile.
You should see: one profile per channel, each signed in to its own accounts.
If not: if you see the wrong channel in a profile, sign out there and sign in again with the right account.
### 3. Write the batch of scripts
In one block of time, write 5 scripts using your retention templates, each under 160 words. Do not do any other task during this block.
You should see: 5 finished scripts.
If not: if you are stuck on hooks, reuse the system prompt from lesson 1 for each topic.
### 4. Generate the voices in one run
Feed the scripts into ElevenLabs one after another and download the audio files into your organized project folders.
You should see: audio files for all 5 videos, named in order.

chunks.title: Scaling to Multiple Channels — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling to Multiple Channels / Step by step.
If not: if a voice sounds off, regenerate only that file.

chunks.title: Scaling to Multiple Channels — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling to Multiple Channels / Check yourself.
 [ ] My week has a fixed task for each day.
 [ ] Each channel has its own browser profile.
 [ ] I have 5 scripts and their audio files.
 [ ] I did not mix tasks during the batch.

chunks.title: Scaling to Multiple Channels — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling to Multiple Channels / Common mistakes.
 Switching between scripting, voice and editing multiple times a day.
 Sharing one browser profile across channels, causing login confusion.
 Writing a script on edit day.

chunks.title: Scaling to Multiple Channels — Go further
chunks.text: Academy lesson: Scaling to Multiple Channels / Go further. Worked example: a 2-channel batch (about 6 hours a week). Channel 1 is "Automate Smarter" (Tech SaaS, 3 uploads/week); Channel 2 is "Crypto Blueprint" (Finance, 2 uploads/week).

chunks.title: Monetization Ladder, part 2
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Monetization Ladder, part 2.
# Monetization Ladder, part 2
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: an affiliate pitch sent, a three-email automated sequence drafted, and a pinned-comment call to action.
---

chunks.title: Monetization Ladder, part 2 — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Monetization Ladder, part 2 / Before you start.
With a lead magnet, landing page and checkout in place (part 1), the money comes from the ladder above them: affiliate commissions from software you already recommend, and the digital product, both sold through automated email. A worked example: "Automate Smarter" at 2,500 subscribers and 60,000 monthly Shorts views, not yet in AdSense, converts 0.5% to 300 signups; 3% buy a $49/mo tool at 30% recurring commission ($14.70 each) for 9 sales = $132.30/month; 2% buy a $29 template for 6 sales = $174.00/month; total $306.30/month against $8.40 of production cost (12 videos at $0.70).
You will need: templates/affiliate-pitch-template.md, templates/funnel-setup-checklist.md, your landing page, and an email tool such as ConvertKit or MailerLite.

chunks.title: Monetization Ladder, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Monetization Ladder, part 2 / Step by step.
### 1. List the software you recommend
Write down the tools you show or recommend in your videos.
You should see: a short list of tools, ideally ones with affiliate programs (typically 20-30% recurring monthly).
If not: if none has a program, check each tool's website for "partners" or "affiliates".
### 2. Send affiliate pitches
Use templates/affiliate-pitch-template.md to pitch for custom referral rates, then generate your tracking links.
You should see: at least one pitch sent and, once approved, a tracking link.
If not: if there is no reply, sign up for the standard program and pitch again later with your numbers.
### 3. Draft email 1 (Day 0)
In your email tool, create the automation and write Email 1 to deliver the free lead magnet.
You should see: an email with the lead magnet link.
If not: menus move; follow the current screen. Send the email to yourself to test the link.
### 4. Draft emails 2 and 3
 Email 2 (Day 2): a high-value tip or case study related to the magnet.
 Email 3 (Day 4): introduce the premium product, showing before/after results.
Keep the tone helpful and non-spammy.
You should see: three emails scheduled at Day 0, Day 2 and Day 4.
If not: if the email reads like an ad, remove adjectives and add one concrete result.
### 5. Write the pinned comment and the in-video line

chunks.title: Monetization Ladder, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Monetization Ladder, part 2 / Step by step.
Pin a comment such as "Get the free budget sheet template here: [link]". In the video, do not spend 20 seconds selling; just say "I put the template in the comments below."
You should see: a pinned comment with your landing page link.
If not: if you cannot pin, add the link as the first line of the description.
### 6. Add the disclosure and test the funnel
Where you use affiliate links, add the disclosure from lesson 3. Then sign up through your own landing page and check the email arrives.
You should see: the lead magnet email in your inbox shortly after sign-up.
If not: check the form is connected to the right list or automation.

chunks.title: Monetization Ladder, part 2 — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Monetization Ladder, part 2 / Check yourself.
 [ ] I sent at least one affiliate pitch.
 [ ] My three-email sequence is set for Day 0, 2 and 4.
 [ ] My pinned comment and bio link point to the landing page.
 [ ] I tested the funnel from sign-up to email.

chunks.title: Monetization Ladder, part 2 — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Monetization Ladder, part 2 / Common mistakes.
 Hard-selling in the video. Let the email sequence sell.
 Hiding the link at the bottom of the description (a pinned comment gets about 3x more clicks).
 Forgetting affiliate disclosures.

chunks.text: Academy lesson: Monetization Ladder, part 2 / Go further.

chunks.title: Monetization Ladder
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Monetization Ladder.
# Monetization Ladder
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a lead magnet idea, a live opt-in landing page and a checkout set up for your first paid offer.
---

chunks.title: Monetization Ladder — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Monetization Ladder / Before you start.
Don't wait for a million views; build a ladder to sell to the first thousand. The YouTube Partner Program needs 1,000 subscribers and 4,000 watch hours (or 10 million Shorts views), which can take 6 to 12 months, and the payouts are small (a video with 20,000 views might make $2.00 on Shorts). The ladder matches products to audience size: Tier 1 Lead Magnet & Email (0+ subs), Tier 2 High-Value Affiliates (100+ subs), Tier 3 Digital Products (1K+ subs, $10-$49), Tier 4 Paid Community (5K+ subs, $47-$97/mo). You lead with a free lead magnet and sell the rest by email, where conversion is about 10x higher than in video descriptions.
You will need: templates/funnel-setup-checklist.md, your niche, and free accounts with a page builder (for example Carrd) and a checkout (Gumroad, Whop or Stripe). SmartVideo GO AI's Image Studio can make the cover image for your lead magnet. This part builds Tier 1 and the checkout; part 2 adds affiliates and the email sequence.

chunks.title: Monetization Ladder — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Monetization Ladder / Step by step.
### 1. Design the lead magnet
Find the single biggest friction point in your niche and make a simple tool to solve it. SaaS niche: a pre-built automation template or a checklist of tools. Finance niche: a basic Google Sheets budget calculator. It must be easy to deliver digitally as a link or PDF.
You should see: one sentence describing your lead magnet and how it is delivered.
If not: if you cannot name one friction point, re-read your best-performing script's "Problem" section.
### 2. Open the funnel checklist
Open templates/funnel-setup-checklist.md and fill in the lead magnet name and delivery link.
You should see: the first rows of the checklist completed.
If not: copy the checklist into your own document.
### 3. Build the opt-in landing page
Create a one-page site with a free builder such as Carrd. Keep it clean: a bold title, 3 bullet points of benefits and an email entry form.
You should see: a published page with a title, three benefits and a form.
If not: menus move; follow the current screen. If the form will not connect, check which email tool you will use in part 2.
### 4. Place the link where viewers look
Put the page link in your channel bio, video descriptions and pinned comments.
You should see: the link live in all three places.
If not: if a platform strips links, check its link rules and use the bio link instead.
### 5. Set up the checkout

# Narration Duration Log
 SmartVideo GO AI Academy — A reusable template from the SmartVideo GO AI course library. Fill it in, then launch it from the matching SmartVideo GO AI studio or Create-With-AI recipe.
Use this log during editing to map out your audio spine. Measure each dialogue file's duration in seconds, then plan the exact visual clips to match.
---
Project Title:
Voice Profile: [e.g., ElevenLabs Adam - Deep Narrative]
| Section | Dialogue Sentence / Script Text | Audio File Name | Duration (s) | Target Visual / B-Roll Asset | Cut Frame (Timeline) |
|:---:|---|:---:|:---:|---|:---:|
| Hook | "This single chart explains why most SaaS startups fail in their first week..." | 01hook.mp3 | 4.2s | Zooming graph screenshot | 0:00 - 0:04.2 |
| Problem | "They build before validating. They assume the customer is there..." | 02problem.mp3 | 6.5s | Darkened programmer coding loop | 0:04.2 - 0:10.7 |
| Solve | "Instead, you need to set up a landing page before writing code." | 03solve.mp3 | 5.1s | Fast mockup scroll | 0:10.7 - 0:15.8 |
| | | | | | |
| | | | | | |
| | | | | | |
---
### Editing Guidelines:
 The Audio Spine Rule: Never generate video clips first and stretch audio to fit. Lay down the narration, trim the pauses, and crop the video to the audio boundaries.
 Cut Pacing: A visual transition should occur every 2 to 4 seconds in short-form video to prevent drop-off.

chunks.title: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline, part 2 — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline, part 2 / Before you start.
Part 1 gave you folders, a locked script and a trimmed voiceover. Now you run the last stations: visuals, edit and polish, and the specs check. Exports are checked against strict parameters before delivery so you avoid revision loops.
You will need your part 1 batch folder, an editor (CapCut is the agency standard), and access to the SmartVideo GO AI Image Studio and Video Studio (the worked example used nano-banana-2 for images and seedance-2 for clips).

chunks.title: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline, part 2 / Step by step.
### 1. Generate the visuals before editing
Using your logged audio duration, generate or download background visuals to cover it. The example made 4 widescreen background clips. Keep them in 03assets/ in a subfolder per video number. Do not open the editor yet.
You should see: enough clips to cover the audio length, sorted in subfolders.
If not: if a clip is off-style, regenerate it now; changing visuals after editing breaks the one-way flow.
### 2. Import everything into the editor
Open your editor, import the audio and visuals, and save the project in 04edit/.
You should see: the audio on the timeline with your clips ready to place.
If not: if files are missing, relink from 02audio/ and 03assets/.
### 3. Cut visuals to the audio
Cut the visual clips to the exact audio milestones.
You should see: visuals changing in time with the narration.
If not: if cuts feel late, nudge them to the start of the spoken phrase.
### 4. Polish: captions and color
Apply a text caption template and a LUT color profile.
You should see: readable captions and a consistent look across clips.
If not: if captions are hard to read, raise contrast before exporting.
### 5. Run the specs check
Open templates/asset-specs-checklist.md and verify:
 Aspect ratio is correct (9:16 for vertical, 16:9 for widescreen).
 Peak audio volume sits at -3dB to -1dB.
 The file name contains the primary target keyword.

chunks.title: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline, part 2 — Step by step

Academy lesson: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline.
# The Multi-Step Production Pipeline
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a factory folder set up, a locked script, and a logged voiceover, ready for the visuals in part 2.
---

chunks.title: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline / Before you start.
A single 60-second video can eat an afternoon when you jump between writing, images, voice and editing. At $50 per video and 4 hours of work, you earn $12.50 an hour. A factory fixes this by splitting the work into stations where assets only move forward: Idea, Script, Voiceover, Visuals, Assembly, Polish, Schedule. You never edit a script after the voiceover exists, and never generate visuals after editing starts.
You will need a folder on your computer, a video idea, and a voice tool (the worked example used ElevenLabs). In SmartVideo GO AI you can use the Storyboard / Campaign Planner for scripts and batch briefs. Part 2 covers visuals, editing and export.

chunks.title: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline / Step by step.
### 1. Create the factory folders
On your hard drive, create this structure:
text
[FactoryBatch01]/
├── 01scripts/ # Locked script drafts
├── 02audio/ # Voiceover narrations (.mp3/.wav)
├── 03assets/ # Visual clips, overlays, and screens
├── 04edit/ # Timeline project files (CapCut/Premiere)
└── 05exports/ # Completed masters checked against specs
You should see: five numbered folders inside one batch folder.
If not: if your system sorts them oddly, keep the number prefixes exactly; they enforce the order.
### 2. Pick one idea and write the script
Choose one angle (the worked example used "How physical grocery stores use AI cameras to count inventory"). Draft a script under 180 words for short-form, following a hook structure. Save it in 01scripts/.
You should see: a script file under 180 words (the worked example was 140).
If not: if it runs over, cut the weakest sentences rather than speeding up the voice.
### 3. Lock the script
Read it once, fix it, then call it locked. From now on, no script changes after voiceover is generated.
You should see: a final script you will not touch again.
If not: if you want to change it later, delete the voiceover and redo this station; do not patch backward.
### 4. Generate the voiceover
Feed the locked script into your voice tool (the example used a warm narration voice profile). Save the file in 02audio/.

chunks.title: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline / Step by step.
You should see: one audio file for the script, in .mp3 or .wav.
If not: if the tool rejects the length, check the script is within your plan's limit.
### 5. Cut silences and log the duration
Cut starting and trailing silence from the audio. Write the final duration in your narration log (a simple note or the pipeline template: templates/pipeline-flowchart-template.md).
You should see: a trimmed file and a duration logged next to its name.
If not: if you cannot tell where silence ends, zoom the waveform in your editor until the speech edge is clear.

chunks.title: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline / Check yourself.
 [ ] My folders mirror the five stations.
 [ ] My script is under 180 words and locked.
 [ ] My voiceover is trimmed and its duration is logged.
 [ ] I know the one-way flow: Idea, Script, Voiceover, Visuals, Assembly, Polish, Schedule.

chunks.title: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline / Common mistakes.
 Editing the script after voiceover exists.
 Opening the video editor before audio and visuals are finished.
 Skipping the duration log, which you need to time visuals.

chunks.title: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: The Multi-Step Production Pipeline / Go further.
Worked example, "AI in Retail" explainer (widescreen): Idea 2 min, Script 140 words 6 min, Voice 3 min, Visuals 8 min (4 widescreen clips with nano-banana-2 and seedance-2), Edit and polish 10 min, Export check 2 min. Total: 31 minutes from blank page to finished export.
Compare tools: Manual CapCut editing is medium speed (about 30 mins/video) with high quality, best for client work. Programmatic rendering (AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator) is fast (about 5 mins/video) with medium quality, best for faceless channels. Premiere/DaVinci is slow (60+ mins/video) with ultra-high quality. CapCut is the agency standard; past 3 channels, consider programmatic generators.
Monetize: a Pipeline Audit Service (audit a business's workflow and design a flowchart for $500-$1,000), or hire freelance assistants to run single stations while you keep scripting and editing.
Exercises: Easy: set up the folder structure with mock files. Medium: write your current workflow and rewrite it as strictly one-way. Hard: build a 60-second video with a stopwatch, time each of the 6 stations, and plan to fix the slowest.
Templates: templates/pipeline-flowchart-template.md, templates/asset-specs-checklist.md.
