chunks.title: Building a TikTok/Reels Factory
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a TikTok/Reels Factory.
# Building a TikTok/Reels Factory
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: a vertical 9:16 clip with moving visuals, micro-word captions inside the safe zone, and a pattern interrupt.
---

chunks.title: Building a TikTok/Reels Factory — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a TikTok/Reels Factory / Before you start.
Viewers decide to watch or swipe in under 0.5 seconds. Slow fades, logos, static images, tiny captions and text hidden under platform buttons all lose them. Three things drive retention: a kinetic cut (never leave a still static), micro-word captions (1 to 3 words at a time), and safe-zone placement.
You will need a short voiceover or clip (about 30 seconds), a few background images, and an editor such as CapCut. In SmartVideo GO AI, make backgrounds in Image Studio and motion in Video Studio. Finish lesson 1 first.

chunks.title: Building a TikTok/Reels Factory — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a TikTok/Reels Factory / Step by step.
### 1. Set up the vertical canvas
In your editor, set the project to 9:16 (1080 x 1920 pixels). Place your background assets so they cover the full height.
You should see: a tall canvas with no black bars at top or bottom.
If not: scale or crop the asset until it fills the frame.
### 2. Generate the captions
Run the auto-captioning utility so text tracks appear. Then set captions to show 1 to 3 words at a time.
You should see: short caption chunks following the voice.
If not: if captions are full sentences, lower the words-per-line setting.
### 3. Style the captions
Select all captions and apply:
 Font: Montserrat Bold or Impact.
 Color: White (#FFFFFF) with a black outline/stroke (width: 8).
You should see: bold white text with a heavy black outline.
If not: if the stroke is missing, look for an outline or stroke toggle in the text panel.
### 4. Highlight the keywords
Scan the timeline and change the color of action verbs or key words (for example "WIN", "DANGER") to Yellow (#FFD700) or Green (#00FF00).
You should see: a few highlighted words, not whole lines.
If not: if everything is colored, undo most of it; highlights only work when rare.
### 5. Position inside the safe zone
Center the caption track, then set the Y value so text sits slightly below center but well above the username area: Y = -120 to -150 pixels on a 1080x1920 grid.

chunks.title: Building a TikTok/Reels Factory — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a TikTok/Reels Factory / Step by step.
You should see: captions mid-screen, clear of the right-side icons and bottom account name.
If not: turn on your editor's safe-zone guide if it has one; menus move, so follow the current screen.
### 6. Apply pacing and motion
Follow templates/tiktok-reels-editor-preset.md: first visual cut at exactly 1.5 seconds, then a cut every 2.5 to 3.0 seconds. Add a slow scale-up from 100% to 108% over 3 seconds on every still.
You should see: a cut at 1.5s and constant gentle movement on every clip.
If not: if a still looks frozen, check the scale animation has start and end keyframes.
### 7. Add a pattern interrupt
At the 15-second or 30-second mark, add a sudden zoom-in to 120% with a subtle low "whoosh" or "swish" sound.
You should see: a noticeable but short jolt at that mark.
If not: if the sound is loud, lower its volume so it supports rather than distracts.

chunks.title: Building a TikTok/Reels Factory — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a TikTok/Reels Factory / Check yourself.
 [ ] Canvas is 9:16 (1080 x 1920) with no black bars.
 [ ] Captions are 1-3 words, bold, outlined, with a few highlighted keywords.
 [ ] Text sits within the safe zone (Y = -120 to -150).
 [ ] First cut at 1.5s, later cuts every 2.5-3.0s, 100% to 108% motion on stills.

chunks.title: Building a TikTok/Reels Factory — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a TikTok/Reels Factory / Common mistakes.
 Leaving still images static.
 Tiny bottom captions, or text under platform buttons.
 Starting with a slow fade, a logo, or "Hello guys".

chunks.title: Building a TikTok/Reels Factory — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a TikTok/Reels Factory / Go further.
Worked example, "Peak Performance" (fitness): 0.0-1.5s runner at sunrise (100% to 105% scale-up); 1.5s sharp cut to running shoes on asphalt; 3.5s silhouette athlete doing pull-ups with slow zoom-in. Voiceover "If you want progress, stop looking for comfort." Captions: [If you want] (0.0-0.8s), [PROGRESS] (0.8-1.5s, green), [stop looking] (1.5-2.5s), [for comfort] (2.5-3.5s). Sound: fast-tempo atmospheric synth, plus a low sub-bass drop on the 1.5s cut. Result: instant hook, eye drawn to the highlight, fast pacing.
Compare tools: CapCut Desktop is fast with excellent caption styles and built-in safe-zone guides. Premiere Pro is medium speed, needs manual preset and safe-zone setup. In-app editors (TikTok/Reels) are slow with basic fonts and are best used only to add trending audio at posting.
Monetize: Batch UGC Packs (15 vertical reels for local gyms, cafes or beauty brands, $500-$800), or Creator Captain Services (cut a creator's long videos into 10 clips and schedule them for a $1,000/month retainer).
Exercises: Easy: fit a widescreen image to 9:16. Medium: caption a 30-second audio with Montserrat Bold, 2 words per screen, and 3 highlighted keywords. Hard: a 30-second vertical video with cuts every 2 seconds, 100% to 108% scale on all backgrounds, and text strictly in safe zones.
Template: templates/tiktok-reels-editor-preset.md.
Next: Building a YouTube Shorts Factory.

chunks.title: Building a YouTube Shorts Factory
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a YouTube Shorts Factory.
# Building a YouTube Shorts Factory
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: a Short whose ending flows straight back into its start, with no silence, no fades and matching first and last frames.
---

chunks.title: Building a YouTube Shorts Factory — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a YouTube Shorts Factory / Before you start.
YouTube Shorts rewards Retention Percentage. If a viewer watches to the end and stays into the first 3 seconds of the replay, retention is recorded as 105%, and enough of those push a Short onto the Shorts shelf. Most creators kill it with "Thanks for watching", a subscribe button, or a 2-second music fade. The fix is a seamless loop: the final half-sentence connects to the opening, audio never fades, and the first and last visuals match.
You will need a short script, a voice tool, an editor (CapCut works), and lessons 1 and 2. In SmartVideo GO AI use Image Studio for a 9:16 anchor image and Video Studio to animate it.

chunks.title: Building a YouTube Shorts Factory — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a YouTube Shorts Factory / Step by step.
### 1. Draft the loop hook
Open templates/shorts-looping-blueprint.md. Write the end line unfinished and the start line completing it. Example:
text
Ending text: The best secret to high productivity is...
Starting text: ...this simple time-management trick.
You should see: the two lines read as one sentence when joined: "The best secret to high productivity is... this simple time-management trick."
If not: reword the opener until the grammar flows from the ending.
### 2. Generate the audio in two parts
Generate the script with your voice tool. Output the ending phrase and the starting phrase as separate files, so the voice does not drop its pitch the way it does at the end of a sentence.
You should see: separate ending and starting audio files, with the ending still sounding "open".
If not: if the pitch still falls, add a connecting word in the prompt or regenerate the ending alone.
### 3. Trim the audio tail
Place the audio on your timeline and zoom to frame level. Find the exact frame where the voice stops, then slice and delete all trailing silence. Leave not even a 0.1-second gap.
You should see: the timeline ends exactly on the last spoken word.
If not: if you hear a click, shift the cut a frame or two earlier or later.
### 4. Lock the music

chunks.title: Building a YouTube Shorts Factory — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a YouTube Shorts Factory / Step by step.
Put background music on A2. Cut it exactly at the video end. Lock its level (for example -18dB) from start to finish, with no fade-in or fade-out at the edges.
You should see: a flat music level and no fade at either edge.
If not: delete any default fade handles your editor added.
### 5. Match the first and last frames
Compare the first and last frame. If the first is dark, make the last dark too. Apply a constant pan-right or slow zoom-out to both edges so motion flows across the loop.
You should see: a replay with no visual flash or jump.
If not: adjust color grading or framing on the last clip until it matches the first.
### 6. Preview the loop
Set playback to loop and watch three passes.
You should see: the join is hard to spot, and the sentence reads on from the end into the start.
If not: note whether the problem is audio (silence, pop) or visual (flash), and revisit step 3, 4 or 5.

chunks.title: Building a YouTube Shorts Factory — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a YouTube Shorts Factory / Check yourself.
 [ ] Ending half-sentence completes with the opening line.
 [ ] No trailing silence, not even 0.1 seconds.
 [ ] Music is locked at one level with no fades.
 [ ] First and last frames match in tone and motion.

chunks.title: Building a YouTube Shorts Factory — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a YouTube Shorts Factory / Common mistakes.
 "Thanks for watching" or a subscribe button at the end.
 Fading music out over a blank screen.
 One audio file for the whole script, so the voice drops pitch at the end.

chunks.title: Building a YouTube Shorts Factory — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a YouTube Shorts Factory / Go further.
Worked example, "Focus Blueprint" (productivity): Start (0:00-0:03.0) glowing digital clock, caption [is this simple rule.] (0.0-1.5s) then [If you want focus,] (1.5-3.0s). Body (0:03.0-0:56.0) explains the 90-minute focus block. End (0:56.0-0:59.0) glowing clock, caption [The best hack for work]. Narration ends on "work" at exactly 0:59.00, timeline length exactly 0:59.00, and on loop the voice goes straight to "is this simple rule." The viewer hears "...The best hack for work... is this simple rule. If you want focus..."
How the example clip was made: anchor image via nano-banana-2 (text-to-image, $0.06/image, 9:16); uploaded with muapi's uploadfile endpoint; fed to seedance-2-image-to-video-fast (image-to-video, $0.50/clip) on imageslist with a vertical aspect ratio and a camera-zoom prompt; the .mp4 was converted to a silent GIF with ffmpeg.
Compare tools: manual CapCut editing gives high loop precision for custom loops; programmatic automation (AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator, repo) cuts silence automatically, good for mass production; phone apps have low precision. For volume, programmatic loop audio ensures zero tail silence.
Launch tips: pin a comment that completes the loop or asks "Did you catch the loop?"; keep titles under 40 characters (for example "Automate your invoices in 10 mins").

chunks.title: Building a YouTube Shorts Factory — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a YouTube Shorts Factory / Go further.
Exercises: Easy: write a 3-sentence script whose last sentence connects to the first, and read it aloud. Medium: trim a voiceover's silent tail to the millisecond. Hard: export a 15-second loop, upload to a test channel, and check for stutter or audio pop.
Template: templates/shorts-looping-blueprint.md.
Next: AI Thumbnail Design.

chunks.title: AI Thumbnail Design
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Thumbnail Design.
# AI Thumbnail Design
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a 1280 x 720 thumbnail that stays readable at coin size.
---

chunks.title: AI Thumbnail Design — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Thumbnail Design / Before you start.
You can spend 20 hours on a video, but a weak thumbnail kills it. Platforms measure Click-Through Rate (CTR), and under 3% they stop showing the video to new audiences. Good thumbnails follow three rules: one clear subject with at most 3 words of text (understood in 3 seconds); high contrast against the feed; and the subject on one third of the frame with text on the opposite third, keeping the bottom-right corner clean for the duration stamp.
You will need an image editor (Canva or Photoshop) and the SmartVideo GO AI Image Studio, using nano-banana-2. Finish lesson 1 first.

chunks.title: AI Thumbnail Design — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Thumbnail Design / Step by step.
### 1. Generate the background
Pick a prompt pattern from templates/thumbnail-prompt-library.md. In Image Studio run nano-banana-2 with aspect ratio 16:9 (use 1:1 for square feeds). Example prompt:
text
A modern glowing green digital bar chart floating in a minimalist luxury office.
You should see: a widescreen image with one clear glowing subject.
If not: if it is cluttered, add "minimalist" or simplify the scene and regenerate.
### 2. Set up the canvas
Open your editor, set the canvas to 1280 x 720 pixels, and drop in the image.
You should see: the image filling the canvas.
If not: scale it up until there are no empty edges.
### 3. Boost contrast and saturation
Apply: Contrast +15%, Saturation +12%, and a slight Gaussian blur (size 5) on the background to separate the subject.
You should see: deeper shadows, brighter colors, and a subject that pops.
If not: if the blur softens the subject too, apply it to the background layer only.
### 4. Place the subject and text
Put the main subject on the left or right third and the text on the opposite third. Write at most 3 words (do not repeat your video title). Use an ultra-bold sans-serif such as Archivo Black, in White (#FFFFFF) or Yellow (#FFD700), with a thick black stroke or drop shadow (width: 12).
You should see: a clearly readable phrase facing the subject, with the bottom-right corner empty.

chunks.title: AI Thumbnail Design — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Thumbnail Design / Step by step.
If not: if text blends in, thicken the stroke.
### 5. Run the coin-size audit
Zoom the editor out until the thumbnail is about 10% scale, the size of a coin.
You should see: you can still read the words and recognize the subject.
If not: remove background detail and enlarge the subject, then check again.
### 6. Export
Export the image at 1280 x 720.
You should see: a finished thumbnail file.
If not: if the file is rejected for size, export at a slightly lower quality setting.

chunks.title: AI Thumbnail Design — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Thumbnail Design / Check yourself.
 [ ] One clear subject, 3 words or fewer.
 [ ] Contrast +15% and saturation +12% applied.
 [ ] Subject and text on opposite thirds, bottom-right clear.
 [ ] Readable at coin size.

chunks.title: AI Thumbnail Design — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Thumbnail Design / Common mistakes.
 Packing in 10 words, several logos, or low-contrast backgrounds.
 Repeating the video title as thumbnail text.
 Putting key details in the bottom-right corner.

chunks.title: AI Thumbnail Design — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Thumbnail Design / Go further.
Worked example, "Get Rich Automated": nano-banana-2 via muapi, prompt "A shining silver key glowing with blue light, unlocking a physical lock." Text "AUTOMATE THIS" in Montserrat Extra-Bold yellow with a thick black outline on the left third; glowing blue lock on the right third; bottom-right left clear. Made with a 16:9 nano-banana-2 image ($0.06/image), then Python Pillow overlaid the text with a black shadow stroke.
Compare tools: nano-banana-2 via muapi is high quality and fast (under 15 seconds) and can be scripted alongside your runs; Midjourney v6 is ultra-high quality but slower, via Discord; local Stable Diffusion needs a strong GPU but is very customizable (ControlNet).
Launch tips: The 24-Hour Swap: if CTR is below 3% after 24 hours, swap in a new thumbnail with a different color scheme instead of deleting the video. Keep a Canva template folder of styled text boxes so designs take under 3 minutes.
Exercises: Easy: generate an image and boost contrast 15% and saturation 10%. Medium: design a 1280x720 layout with a subject on the right third and a 2-word text overlay on the left with a thick drop shadow. Hard: audit three competitor thumbnails at small scale and write two readability changes for each.
Template: templates/thumbnail-prompt-library.md.

chunks.title: Batching & Scheduling at Volume
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batching & Scheduling at Volume.
# Batching & Scheduling at Volume
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a filled-in 30-day release calendar and a batch plan that runs one station at a time.
---

chunks.title: Batching & Scheduling at Volume — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batching & Scheduling at Volume / Before you start.
Algorithms reward consistency: a channel posting once a day at the same hour beats one that posts five videos in a day and then vanishes. The answer is to separate production from publishing and build a 30-day queue: Batch Production Week, 30 Scheduled Videos, Daily Auto-Release. You batch one station at a time, schedule in native platform tools, and can repurpose long videos with clipping tools such as ai-clipping-generator.
You will need the pipeline from lesson 1 and a list of sub-topics. This lesson plans the batch and schedule; the full 30-video run takes about 15 hours, so you do the production in your own sessions. SmartVideo GO AI's Storyboard / Campaign Planner can hold batch matrices and briefs.

chunks.title: Batching & Scheduling at Volume — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batching & Scheduling at Volume / Step by step.
### 1. Set your release calendar
Open templates/30-day-production-calendar.md and mark your upload frequency (for example 1 post per day at 12:00 PM).
You should see: a calendar with one release slot per day.
If not: if one daily post is too much, choose a frequency you can sustain; consistency matters more than volume.
### 2. Plan the scripting batch (Days 1-5)
List 30 scripts grouped by sub-topic, for example 10 on Invoice Parsing, 10 on Lead Generation and 10 on Database Syncing.
You should see: 30 numbered topics in three groups.
If not: if you run short, add angles to the strongest group.
### 3. Plan voice and visuals (Days 6-12)
Write the naming rule: audio files named 01.mp3 to 30.mp3, trimmed of pauses (Days 6-8). For visuals (Days 9-12), write one uniform prompt format to keep a consistent style across all 30.
You should see: a naming rule and one reusable prompt pattern in your plan.
If not: if styles vary, tighten the prompt format before generating.
### 4. Plan assembly and export (Days 13-17)
Note one master project file that imports all audio and visual folders, then edit and export all 30 files in bulk.
You should see: a dated block for editing in the calendar.
If not: do not start editing until scripts, voices and visuals are all locked.
### 5. Plan native scheduling (Days 18-20)

chunks.title: Batching & Scheduling at Volume — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batching & Scheduling at Volume / Step by step.
Add the upload block: YouTube Studio Web, TikTok Studio Web and Instagram Creator Studio, with optimized titles and descriptions and a Schedule date and time per video (Day 1 at 12:00 PM, Day 2 at 12:00 PM, and so on).
You should see: every day of the month has a scheduled slot.
If not: menus move; follow the current screen in each studio.
### 6. Choose your release hour
Check your analytics ("When your viewers are on YouTube") for peak time. Schedule 2 hours before the peak. If you cross-post, stagger platforms (YouTube 12:00 PM, TikTok 12:30 PM, Reels 1:00 PM).
You should see: one release time per platform in your calendar.
If not: with no analytics yet, start with 12:00 PM and adjust after a few weeks.

chunks.title: Batching & Scheduling at Volume — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batching & Scheduling at Volume / Check yourself.
 [ ] My calendar shows a release slot every day for 30 days.
 [ ] Each station (scripts, voice, visuals, edit, schedule) has its own block of days.
 [ ] Files use a sequential naming rule.
 [ ] Cross-posts are staggered, not simultaneous.

chunks.title: Batching & Scheduling at Volume — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batching & Scheduling at Volume / Common mistakes.
 Editing a video before all scripts and voiceovers are locked.
 Posting in bursts and then going silent.
 Posting to every platform at exactly the same minute.

chunks.title: Batching & Scheduling at Volume — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batching & Scheduling at Volume / Go further.
Worked example, 30-Shorts run (15 hours): scripting 30 scripts in Claude, 3 hours; audio 30 ElevenLabs generations, 1 hour; visuals 150 image prompts via muapi, 4 hours; editing in CapCut, 5 hours; scheduling across YT Shorts, TikTok and Reels, 2 hours. Result: 90 posts (30 videos on 3 platforms) from 15 hours of work.
Compare tools: native web studios (high bulk capability, free, reliable, precise hours); Buffer / Later (medium, some API upload limits, better for brand updates); clipping automation ai-clipping-generator (fast clip extraction from long videos). Prefer native schedulers for high-traffic channels.
Exercises: Easy: fill a 7-day schedule. Medium: write 5 scripts, generate 5 audio files and trim them in one session, logging your time. Hard: feed a 10-minute video to ai-clipping-generator, extract 5 clips and schedule them daily on a test channel.
Template: templates/30-day-production-calendar.md.

chunks.title: Selling Content-Factory Output as a Service
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling Content-Factory Output as a Service.
# Selling Content-Factory Output as a Service
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a priced package, a recurring-payment plan, and a ready-to-send retainer proposal.
---

chunks.title: Selling Content-Factory Output as a Service — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling Content-Factory Output as a Service / Before you start.
Selling "per video" or "per hour" keeps your income at zero between jobs, and clients order three videos, pause, then ask for revisions weeks later. A monthly retainer locks in predictable income and weekly batch delivery (for example 7 videos every Friday). Costs are low: a $1,500 retainer costing about $30 in API credits is a 98% net profit margin.
You will need your pipeline and calendar from lessons 1 and 5, and a payment tool (Stripe, PayPal or Whop). Use your own accounts and never paste secret keys into any chat. You can produce sample work in SmartVideo GO AI's Image Studio and Video Studio.

chunks.title: Selling Content-Factory Output as a Service — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling Content-Factory Output as a Service / Step by step.
### 1. Define your tiers
Open templates/bulk-pricing-sheet.md and pick your packages:
text
Growth Factory ($1,500/mo): 30 vertical videos, custom thumbnails, SEO tagging.
Syndication Network ($2,800/mo): 60 vertical videos, scheduled across YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram.
You should see: at least one named package with a price and deliverables.
If not: start with one tier; add a second later.
### 2. Set up recurring billing
Open a merchant account (Stripe, PayPal or Whop) and create a subscription product matching your package price. Bill upfront at the start of each 30-day cycle. Never produce before the invoice is paid.
You should see: a subscription product with a payment link.
If not: if setup needs identity checks, finish them in the tool itself; menus move, so follow the current screen.
### 3. Choose target clients
List 10 prospects from: professional services (real estate brokers, law firms, accountants, private clinics), high-ticket consultants, business coaches and software founders, and e-commerce brand owners.
You should see: a list of prospects with high marketing budgets and little time.
If not: narrow to one niche you know best.
### 4. Write the proposal
Fill in templates/agency-retainer-proposal.md: deliverables, delivery schedule (weekly batches) and upfront price. Add that revisions must be requested in a single batch within 48 hours of delivery.

chunks.title: Selling Content-Factory Output as a Service — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling Content-Factory Output as a Service / Step by step.
You should see: a one-page proposal with scope, schedule, price and revision cap.
If not: keep it simple; cut anything that is not deliverables, schedule or price.
### 5. Prepare onboarding
Plan a shared folder (Google Drive or Dropbox) with [RawAssetsFromClient] for logos, color books and reference images, and [WeeklyDeliveries] for the weekly batch of 7 videos.
You should see: the two folders named and ready to share after payment.
If not: create them empty now; share only after the first payment clears.

chunks.title: Selling Content-Factory Output as a Service — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling Content-Factory Output as a Service / Check yourself.
 [ ] I have a package with a price and clear deliverables.
 [ ] Billing is upfront and recurring.
 [ ] My proposal states schedule and a 48-hour single-batch revision rule.
 [ ] Onboarding folders are planned.

chunks.title: Selling Content-Factory Output as a Service — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling Content-Factory Output as a Service / Common mistakes.
 Selling per video or per hour.
 Producing before the invoice is settled.
 Allowing revisions to drag on for weeks.

chunks.title: Selling Content-Factory Output as a Service — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling Content-Factory Output as a Service / Go further.
Worked example, "Apex Bookkeeping": local accounting firm, $1,500/month for 30 short-form videos, 7 uploaded every Friday. Time: 4 hours scripting and 4 hours editing and captioning, so 8 hours/month. API expense 30 videos at $0.70 = $21.00/month. Net $1,479.00/month, about $184.87/hour, roughly a 98% margin.
Compare tools: Stripe Billing (professional invoices, auto-collection, multiple currencies, auto-renewing subscriptions); Whop (affiliate tracking, access links, good for creators); DocuSign / PandaDoc (legally binding signatures for high-value contracts). Send your PDF proposal with a Stripe subscription link, then automate a welcome email on payment.
Scale up: sell a posting and scheduling add-on for an extra $300/month.
Exercises: Easy: draft your pricing sheet. Medium: fill the proposal with a mock client and weekly batch deliverables. Hard: find three local service sites with empty social feeds and draft a cold email offering a 10-video test batch.
Templates: templates/agency-retainer-proposal.md, templates/bulk-pricing-sheet.md.

chunks.title: Shorts Looping Blueprint
chunks.text:
Academy template: Shorts Looping Blueprint.
# Shorts Looping Blueprint
 SmartVideo GO AI Academy — A reusable template from the SmartVideo GO AI course library. Fill it in, then launch it from the matching SmartVideo GO AI studio or Create-With-AI recipe.
YouTube Shorts loop infinitely. If you construct your script so that the final sentence leads seamlessly back to your opening sentence, viewers will watch the first 2-3 seconds of the video twice before realizing it looped. This pushes your retention rate above 100%, triggering the Shorts algorithm to distribute your video.
---

chunks.title: Shorts Looping Blueprint — The Loop Construction Formula
chunks.text:
Academy template: Shorts Looping Blueprint / The Loop Construction Formula.
[Final Half-Sentence (End of Video)] ──► (Zero Pause Cut) ──► [First Half-Sentence (Start of Video)]
### Script Example Structure:
 Opening Hook (Start of Script):
 "...is this simple automation blueprint." (Wait, this is the end of the sentence. The actual video starts here).
 Opening Explanation (First 5 seconds):
 "If you want to save five hours a week, all you need..."
 Body of Video:
 [Explain the steps: connect Zapier, parse invoice, auto-save data]
 Transition Out (End of Script):
 "The easiest way to set this up..."
### Complete Loop Audio Read-out:
When the video finishes and loops, the viewer hears:
 "...The easiest way to set this up... is this simple automation blueprint. If you want to save five hours a week, all you need..."
---

chunks.title: Shorts Looping Blueprint — Timeline Editing Rules for Loops:
chunks.text:
Academy template: Shorts Looping Blueprint / Timeline Editing Rules for Loops:.
- [ ] No Music Fade-Out: Keep the background music track at a constant volume up to the last frame. Cut the music track sharply at the end so it matches the starting frame's music.
- [ ] Zero Tail Silence: Crop the ending voice file to the exact frame the speaker finishes talking. Do not leave a 0.5-second gap of silence at the end of the timeline.
- [ ] Continuous Motion: If the final clip has a panning camera motion, the starting clip should have a similar motion direction (e.g. pan-right to pan-right) to keep the visual flow continuous.

chunks.title: Building a Consistent AI Character
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a Consistent AI Character.
# Building a Consistent AI Character
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: a locked master portrait of your character, one face-swapped scene render, and a plan for a 9-post launch batch.
---

chunks.title: Building a Consistent AI Character — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a Consistent AI Character / Before you start.
A virtual influencer lives or dies on face drift. If you prompt a character in a bedroom and again in an office, text-to-image models give you two different people: hair length, facial symmetry and clothing all change. Audiences do not bond with a face that keeps changing, and you cannot sell sponsorships to an account that looks like several different accounts. The fix is three anchors: a description anchor (the same face and hair tokens in every prompt), a wardrobe anchor (one or two clothing tags that never change) and a master face projected onto every new scene with a face swap.
Master Face Portrait ──► New Scene Generation ──► Face Swap Layer ──► Consistent Render
You need: the character style guide template, and these SmartVideo GO AI studios: Image Studio (anchors, character sheets) and AI Influencer Studio (consistent recurring characters). No prerequisites.

chunks.title: Building a Consistent AI Character — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a Consistent AI Character / Step by step.
### 1. Define your character profile
1. Open templates/character-style-guide.md.
2. Write down the face, hair, clothing style and signature colors. Use unique tokens, for example: textured crop brown hair, oval face, green eyes, slight freckles. Pick one or two wardrobe tags, for example: a dark blue crewneck sweater.
You should see: a filled-in profile with a face description, hair, and a wardrobe line you will not change.
If not: if the description is vague ("a beautiful woman"), add concrete details until two people would picture the same face.
### 2. Generate the master portrait
1. In Image Studio, use nano-banana-2 with aspect ratio 1:1.
2. Paste this example prompt (swap in your own description):
text
Front portrait of Emma, a 28-year-old female influencer with a short textured brown bob, oval face, slight freckles on her nose, looking at the camera. Soft neutral studio lighting, clean gray background, photorealistic, 8k.
3. Generate a few and save the best as your Master Reference Face, for example emma-master.jpg.
You should see: a clean, front-facing, evenly lit headshot with a plain background.
If not: if the face is turned away or the lighting is dramatic, regenerate; the master must be neutral and front-facing.
### 3. Generate a new scene with identical tokens
Keep face, hair and wardrobe wording 100% identical to the master prompt and change only the location:
text

chunks.title: Building a Consistent AI Character — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a Consistent AI Character / Step by step.
Emma, a 28-year-old female influencer with a short textured brown bob, oval face, slight freckles, wearing a dark blue crewneck sweater, sitting at a wooden cafe table holding a coffee cup. Minimalist cafe background, warm morning light, photorealistic, 8k.
You should see: a cafe scene with someone who looks similar to your master, possibly with small differences.
If not: if the clothing or hair changed a lot, compare your prompt to the master line by line and restore the exact tokens.
### 4. Run the face swap
If the face drifted, use the /z-image-p (or InsightFace face swap) endpoint, or ai-image-face-swap:
1. Source Image (Reference): upload emma-master.jpg.
2. Target Image: upload your new cafe generation.
3. Run it. The engine keeps the target's lighting and head angle while locking in the master's nose, eyes and cheek structure.
You should see: the cafe scene with the master's exact facial features.
If not: if the result looks pasted or the angle is extreme, regenerate the scene with a more frontal pose and swap again.
### 5. Compare against the master
Put the master and the swapped render side by side.
You should see: the same nose, eyes, freckles, hair and sweater in both.
If not: if any feature differs, swap again, or generate a new scene with the anchor tokens repeated word for word.
### 6. Plan the launch batch

chunks.title: Building a Consistent AI Character — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a Consistent AI Character / Step by step.
Create dedicated Instagram and TikTok accounts for the character. Write a normal, humanized bio (for example: "Sharing automation hacks and tech reviews"); do not label it "AI Generated" in the main bio header. Then list 9 scene prompts (office, home, studio, cafe, and so on), all reusing your anchors, so the grid looks cohesive when a new viewer lands on the profile.
You should see: a list of at least 9 scene prompts, each starting with the same character description and wardrobe tag.
If not: if you are short of ideas, vary only location and lighting.

chunks.text:

chunks.text:

 Changing the outfit in every scene.

 Publishing before there are at least 9 consistent posts.

chunks.title: Building a Consistent AI Character — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a Consistent AI Character / Go further.
Worked example, "Emma" (tech influencer): master profile is a 28-year-old with a short textured brown bob, oval face, freckles, dark blue crewneck sweater. Scene 1 office desk, Scene 2 modern living room, Scene 3 studio with professional microphones; each is face-swapped with the master. Across three scenes with different lighting, face, hair and sweater stay consistent. Reference images: master, consistent cafe render, motion clip.
How the real example was made via muapi: master 1:1 with nano-banana-2 ($0.06/image); 9:16 cafe scene with nano-banana-2 using identical tokens; both uploaded to ai-image-face-swap ($0.03/swap).
Compare tools:
| Tool | Consistency | Cost | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| muapi /ai-image-face-swap | High, any angle or lighting | ~$0.03 per swap | Fast, bulk face swaps for image feeds |
| Midjourney --cref | High; can struggle with precise clothing | Subscription | Background variations and poses |
| Stable Diffusion (IP-Adapter) | Ultra-high, full control | Free (local GPU) | Agencies building custom models |
Fastest starter pipeline: Midjourney or nano-banana-2 for the scene, then a muapi face swap.
Exercises:
1. Easy: write a detailed physical description, generate three headshots, pick the master.
2. Medium: generate two scene variations (walking in a city, sitting in a park) with identical anchors.

# Character to Content Pipeline, part 2
 Time: about 12 minutes. You will finish with: a talking-head edit that cuts between the avatar and b-roll so viewers stay engaged.
---

chunks.title: Character to Content Pipeline, part 2 — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character to Content Pipeline, part 2 / Before you start.
A talking head on screen for a full 60 seconds loses viewers. Pros cut away from the avatar every 4-5 seconds to b-roll (screenshots, charts, slides) while the voice track keeps playing. That keeps engagement high and also keeps rendering cost low, because you only lip-sync the parts where the face is visible.
You need: the lip-sync clip from part 1, b-roll (screen recordings, product shots), and an editor such as CapCut. In SmartVideo GO AI, Video Studio can supply extra clips.

chunks.title: Character to Content Pipeline, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character to Content Pipeline, part 2 / Step by step.
### 1. Import and place the hook
Import the talking-head video into CapCut. Keep the avatar on screen for 0.0 - 3.0s to establish the human hook.
You should see: the avatar speaking on the timeline for the first 3 seconds.
If not: if the clip is silent, check that the audio track imported with it.
### 2. Cut away to b-roll
From 3.0 - 15.0s, cut to high-contrast b-roll while the voiceover continues on A1.
You should see: b-roll on the video track with the narration still playing underneath.
If not: if the voice stops, you cut the audio too; extend the voice track so it runs under the whole b-roll section.
### 3. Cut back to the avatar
From 15.0 - 18.0s, cut back to the avatar's face to re-establish connection.
You should see: avatar, then b-roll, then avatar, with no gaps.
If not: close any gaps by dragging clips together.
### 4. Polish with chroma key and light
 If you generated your master portrait on a solid green background, use the editor's Chroma Key tool to remove it and place the talking head over any video clip.
 Add an adjustment layer with a soft amber or teal overlay at 5% opacity so the face blends into the background lighting.
You should see: an avatar that looks integrated with the background.
If not: if green edges remain, increase the chroma key tolerance slightly; if the tint is obvious, lower it below 5%.

chunks.text:

 [ ] The avatar is on screen for the first 3 seconds.

chunks.title: Character to Content Pipeline, part 2 — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character to Content Pipeline, part 2 / Common mistakes.
 Leaving the talking head on screen for the whole video.
 Cutting the voice track together with the b-roll.
 Making the color overlay too strong.

chunks.title: Character to Content Pipeline, part 2 — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character to Content Pipeline, part 2 / Go further.
Worked example timeline (Emma, 60-second Short plan): 0.0 - 4.5s Emma speaks to the audience with text captions; 4.5 - 20.0s cut to a screen recording of a Zapier automation workspace with her voiceover continuing; 20.0 - 24.0s cut back to Emma. The video stays dynamic and informative while rendering costs stay low.
Exercise (Hard): produce a 30-second vertical video: avatar speaks for the first 3 seconds, cuts to green-screen b-roll for 20 seconds, and cuts back to the avatar for a 7-second call-to-action.
Next: Voice Cloning & Dialogue.

chunks.title: Character to Content Pipeline
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character to Content Pipeline.
# Character to Content Pipeline
 Time: about 12 minutes. You will finish with: a lip-synced talking-head clip of your character that passes a quality audit.
---

chunks.title: Character to Content Pipeline — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character to Content Pipeline / Before you start.
A still avatar only works on photo grids, but the highest reach and advertiser payments are on video feeds (TikTok, YouTube Shorts, Reels). Run a consistent character through a standard image-to-video model and the face warps as soon as the head moves: hair changes, clothing textures slide, and the uncanny valley drives viewers away. The professional answer is a lip-sync pipeline that animates only the mouth, jaw and eyes:
Static Avatar Portrait + Clean Voice Audio ──► Lip-Sync Engine ──► Talking Head Video
You need: your master portrait from the previous lesson (for example emma-master.jpg), a clean voiceover file (for example 01intro.mp3), the lip-sync spec sheet, and SmartVideo GO AI's Lip-Sync Studio and Video Studio. This lesson covers the render; part 2 covers the edit.

chunks.title: Character to Content Pipeline — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character to Content Pipeline / Step by step.
### 1. Prep your assets
1. Open templates/lipsync-spec-sheet.md.
2. Check that your master portrait (centered face) and your clean narration meet its visual and audio guidelines.
You should see: both files ticked off against the checklist.
If not: fix the failing item (re-crop the face, re-export clean audio) before rendering; bad inputs cost credits.
### 2. Submit to the lip-sync engine
In Lip-Sync Studio, or via the /sync-lipsync (or volcengine lip-sync) endpoint through muapi, provide:
 Audio URL: the public URL of your narration file.
 Image URL: the public URL of your avatar portrait.
 Aspect ratio: 9:16 or 1:1, to match your target feed.
You should see: a render that finishes as an .mp4 of the same length as your audio (a 4.5 second hook gives a 4.5 second clip).
If not: if it rejects the files, check that both URLs are public and the formats match the spec sheet. Menus move; follow the current screen.
### 3. Download and audit the render
Download the .mp4 and play it through, checking two things:
 Mouth warping: the mouth should not stretch unnaturally on fast words.
 Drift: lips should match the syllables.
You should see: natural mouth movement and blinks with the head, hair and clothing unchanged.
If not: if the lips lag slightly, shift the audio track by -50ms to -100ms in your timeline. If the mouth warps badly, re-render with a cleaner, more front-facing portrait.

chunks.title: Character to Content Pipeline — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character to Content Pipeline / Check yourself.
 [ ] My portrait and audio passed the spec sheet.
 [ ] I rendered a lip-sync clip in the right aspect ratio.
 [ ] I audited the clip for mouth warping and sync drift.

chunks.title: Character to Content Pipeline — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character to Content Pipeline / Common mistakes.
 Running the character through plain image-to-video and letting the face warp.
 Rendering before checking the spec sheet, then paying for a bad clip.
 Ignoring a small audio lag instead of nudging the track by -50ms to -100ms.

chunks.title: Character to Content Pipeline — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character to Content Pipeline / Go further.
Worked example, animating "Emma" for a 60-second Short: emma-master.jpg plus 01hook.mp3 ("Hey, it's Emma here. Today we are...", 4.5 seconds) went into /sync-lipsync; the output is 4.5 seconds with natural blink animation. The real motion loop was made from the consistent cafe image with seedance-2-image-to-video-fast (image-to-video, $0.50/clip) on the imageslist param with a vertical aspect ratio and a prompt describing Emma's facial movement; see the clip.
Compare tools:
| Tool | Quality | Cost | Setup |
|---|---|---|---|
| muapi /sync-lipsync | High; keeps background, natural blinking | ~$0.50 per clip | Low (direct API call) |
| HeyGen / Synthesia | Very high; pre-built bodies and gestures | $30-$200/mo | Low |
| Local ComfyUI (LivePortrait) | Ultra-high; tracks a webcam actor | Free | Very high (heavy GPU setup) |
For client content factories, /sync-lipsync scales best: pay per call, no subscription lock-in.
Exercises:
1. Easy: gather one clean front-facing face image and a 5-second audio clip; verify they meet the spec checklist.
2. Medium: submit them to a lip-sync engine, download the video, align the audio and fix any small delay.
3. Hard: see part 2 for the 30-second edit.
Template: templates/lipsync-spec-sheet.md has prep checklists and sync logs.
Next: Character to Content Pipeline, part 2.

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & Dialogue, part 2
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & Dialogue, part 2.
# Voice Cloning & Dialogue, part 2
 Time: about 12 minutes. You will finish with: a script with phonetic fixes and pacing cues, rendered at locked voice settings.
---

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & Dialogue, part 2 — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & Dialogue, part 2 / Before you start.
A cloned voice still mispronounces brand names and acronyms (it may read "SaaS" as "S-A-A-S" or "muapi" as "myoo-api") and reads run-on sentences flat. Two tools fix this. A phonetic dictionary of spelling workarounds ("sass", "moo-ah-pee") forces correct pronunciation. And punctuation works as breathing cues: a comma triggers a short pause, an ellipsis (...) a longer reflective pause, and a dash (-) a sudden shift in flow.
You need: your cloned voice from part 1 (for example EmmaV1) and a short script containing your niche terms.

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & Dialogue, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & Dialogue, part 2 / Step by step.
### 1. Generate a pronunciation test
Write a test sentence with your brand names and acronyms and generate it in ElevenLabs:
text
Automate your invoice parsing using muapi.
You should see: audio you can listen to for each tricky term.
If not: if no audio plays, check that your cloned voice is selected.
### 2. Fix mispronunciations phonetically
Re-spell any wrong term in your script and regenerate:
text
Automate your invoice parsing using moo-ah-pee.
Likewise, "SaaS automation with Zapier." became "Sass automation with Zapier." and was then read as one word.
You should see: the term pronounced correctly with natural flow.
If not: try another spelling and keep a note of each working fix in a phonetic dictionary.
### 3. Add pacing cues
Rewrite long sentences with punctuation cues.
Before:
text
We connect Zapier to the database and then it populates the records automatically which takes ten seconds.
After:
text
We connect Zapier to the database... and within ten seconds... the records populate... automatically.
You should see: a conversational rhythm with audible breaths and pauses.
If not: if it sounds choppy, remove some ellipses and use commas instead.
### 4. Lock your voice settings
Once the sliders sound right, write them down. Standard values are Stability: 40% and Clarity: 75%, which allow an expressive range without digital distortion.

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & Dialogue, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & Dialogue, part 2 / Step by step.
You should see: your settings recorded in your voice checklist.
If not: if the voice sounds distorted, move back toward those standard values.
### 5. Batch your generations
Generate all script lines for the month in one session so volume, tone and pacing stay consistent across the batch.
You should see: a set of audio files with matching loudness and tone.
If not: if one file differs, regenerate it at the locked settings.

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & Dialogue, part 2 — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & Dialogue, part 2 / Check yourself.
 [ ] I fixed any mispronounced term with a phonetic spelling.
 [ ] My script uses commas, ellipses and dashes for pacing.
 [ ] I wrote down Stability 40% and Clarity 75% (or my tuned values).
 [ ] I generated my lines in one batch.

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & Dialogue, part 2 — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & Dialogue, part 2 / Common mistakes.
 Trusting the default spelling of acronyms and brand names.
 Writing long run-on sentences.
 Changing slider settings between videos.
 Generating lines on different days with different settings.

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & Dialogue, part 2 — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & Dialogue, part 2 / Go further.
Worked example: the draft line "SaaS automation with Zapier." came out as "S-A-A-S"; changing the script to "Sass automation with Zapier." fixed it. The final audio was clear, with natural breathing.
Exercise (Hard): write a script with three brand names or acronyms, generate the voice, audit the pronunciation, design phonetic workarounds for errors and render a clean final audio file.

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & Dialogue
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & Dialogue.
# Voice Cloning & Dialogue
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a cloned voice profile (for example EmmaV1) built from clean training audio.
---

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & Dialogue — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & Dialogue / Before you start.
A photorealistic avatar with a generic computer voice breaks the illusion: cheap text-to-speech lacks breath sounds, natural pauses, rising inflections on questions and varied emphasis, and viewers swipe away. The fix is a custom cloned voice built from real human samples. Quality is capped by the input: background noise, static or room echo gets learned by the model and comes back as a raspy, low-fidelity voice. You need dry, clean, isolated mono recordings.
Clean Audio Samples (Dry/Mono) ──► Cloning Engine (ElevenLabs) ──► High-Fidelity Vocal Profile
You need: a microphone, a quiet carpeted space, a free editor such as Audacity, an ElevenLabs account, and the voice cloning checklist. In SmartVideo GO AI, the Audio and Lip-Sync Studio use the finished voice. Prerequisites: the previous two lessons. Part 2 covers pronunciation and pacing.

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & Dialogue — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & Dialogue / Step by step.
### 1. Read the checklist
Open templates/voice-cloning-checklist.md and note the training audio requirements and noise gate steps.
You should see: a short list of recording requirements you can follow.
If not: if anything is unclear, follow the checklist wording rather than guessing.
### 2. Record training samples
Record speaking samples in a normal, conversational tone. The worked example used 8 minutes of clean reading from a desk USB microphone inside a carpeted closet.
You should see: a recording with no echo or fan hum in a quiet playback.
If not: move to a smaller, softer room (carpet, clothes) and record again.
### 3. Clean and export
1. Import the audio into Audacity (or another free editor).
2. Apply a Noise Gate to strip silent floor noise and background hiss.
3. Export as a mono .wav file.
You should see: a mono .wav with silent gaps clean and speech intact.
If not: if the voice sounds chopped, lower the noise gate strength and redo it.
### 4. Upload to the cloning engine
1. Open ElevenLabs and go to Voices - Add Generative or Cloned Voice (menus move; follow the current screen).
2. Upload your training .wav.
3. Write a clear tone description, for example: "Conversational, professional 20s female voice, warm and clear."
4. Generate the voice profile and name it, for example EmmaV1.
You should see: your named voice in your voice list, ready to generate from.

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & Dialogue — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & Dialogue / Step by step.
If not: if upload fails, check the file format and size limits shown on the current screen.
### 5. Test it with one sentence
Generate a short test line and listen.
You should see: clear audio with natural breathing and no hiss.
If not: if it sounds raspy, the training audio was noisy; clean it again or re-record.

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & Dialogue — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & Dialogue / Check yourself.
 [ ] My training audio is a clean mono .wav.
 [ ] I cloned a named voice profile.
 [ ] A test line sounds clear without hiss or echo.

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & Dialogue — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & Dialogue / Common mistakes.
 Uploading audio with background noise, static or room echo.
 Recording in a hard, echoing room.
 Skipping the checklist.

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & Dialogue — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & Dialogue / Go further.
Worked example, "EmmaV1": 8 minutes recorded with a desk USB mic in a carpeted closet; cleaned in Audacity with a noise gate and hiss removal; cloned in ElevenLabs as EmmaV1.
Compare cloning paths:
| Path | Fidelity | Cost | Setup |
|---|---|---|---|
| ElevenLabs PVC (Professional) | Ultra-high | High (high-tier subscriptions) | High (30+ minutes of audio) |
| ElevenLabs IVC (Instant) | High | Low | Low (1-2 minutes of audio) |
| Local XTTS v2 | Medium | Free (local GPU) | High (Python environment) |
PVC is the industry standard for professional influencers; IVC suits early testing and simple client explainers.
Exercises:
1. Easy: record 2 minutes of speech and clean it in Audacity to remove silent gaps and fan hum.
2. Medium: upload a 2-minute sample to an Instant Voice Cloning tool, generate a 15-second test paragraph and judge the clarity.
Template: templates/voice-cloning-checklist.md covers training audio requirements, noise gates and post-clone validation.
Next: Voice Cloning & Dialogue, part 2.

chunks.title: Monetization Tiers by Follower Count
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Monetization Tiers by Follower Count.
# Monetization Tiers by Follower Count
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: a filled-in sponsor media kit, a bundled offer and a ready-to-send brand pitch.
---

chunks.title: Monetization Tiers by Follower Count — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Monetization Tiers by Follower Count / Before you start.
Famous virtual influencers such as Lil Miquela (millions of followers, $8,000+ per post) make creators assume they cannot earn until 100k followers. In reality B2B virtual influencers can monetize under 10,000 followers: software buyers, accountants and developers are high-value audiences, so a tech channel with 5,000 targeted followers can command rates that entertainment channels need 100,000 for. Potential grows in three tiers:
Tier 3: Brand Ambassador (25K+ followers) ──► Corporate Retainers ($1,000 - $3,000/mo)
Tier 2: Dedicated Integrations (5K - 25K followers) ──► Sponsored Video Batches ($300 - $800)
Tier 1: Affiliate & SaaS referral (0 - 5K followers) ──► High-Ticket recurring commissions
Brands do not buy views; they buy access to demographics. They also like avatars: zero real-world PR risk, precise brief following and revisions in minutes. You need: the sponsor media kit template, your character, and SmartVideo GO AI's AI Influencer Studio and Storyboard / Campaign Planner later for production.

chunks.title: Monetization Tiers by Follower Count — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Monetization Tiers by Follower Count / Step by step.
### 1. Draft your virtual media kit
Open templates/sponsor-media-kit.md. Fill in character profile, niche, follower metrics and target demographics. Keep the style modern and visual.
You should see: a kit that proves your audience matches a brand's buyers.
If not: if you have no real numbers yet, use clearly labelled mock figures for practice, and never present them to a brand as real.
### 2. Find advertisers with budgets
Search your niche keywords on the Meta Ad Library. A software brand running multiple paid social ads has an active marketing budget.
You should see: a list of at least three brands running paid ads in your niche.
If not: try broader or neighbouring keywords.
### 3. Bundle your placements
Do not pitch "one video". Offer The Integration Pack: 3 dedicated reels showing how your avatar uses the software, plus a pinned comment link for 30 days, priced at $400-$600 for micro-channels.
You should see: a package with deliverables and a price written in your media kit.
If not: if the price feels arbitrary, anchor it inside the $400-$600 range above.
### 4. Write the pitch
Find the Partnership Manager's email on LinkedIn or Apollo and adapt this pitch:
text

chunks.title: Monetization Tiers by Follower Count — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Monetization Tiers by Follower Count / Step by step.
Hi [Name], I manage [Avatar Name], a virtual tech creator with over [Number] followers. Our audience is highly targeted around [Niche]. We love [Product Name] and would love to showcase a dashboard walkthrough to our viewers next month. Here is our media kit: [Link]. Are you currently open to short-form integration partnerships?
You should see: a pitch with every bracket replaced by real details.
If not: if you cannot find an email, use direct messaging for smaller founder-led brands, knowing messages often land in spam folders.
### 5. Set up tracking
After a deal, build the video to the brand guidelines and set up a tracking link (for example via Bitly or Rewardful) to measure the traffic your avatar drives.
You should see: a tracking link for the campaign.
If not: if the link shows no clicks, test it yourself before sending it to the brand.
### 6. Plan for renewal
Over-deliver on the first deal: if a brand pays for 3 videos, deliver 4 (about $0.70 more in API credits). Seven days after the campaign ends, send a clean screenshot of views, likes and link clicks.
You should see: a note in your calendar to deliver the extra video and send the report.
If not: if you forget the report, send it late; brands rarely get proactive reporting and it still stands out.

chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Monetization Tiers by Follower Count / Check yourself.
 [ ] My media kit lists niche, metrics, packages and prices.
 [ ] I found three brands running paid ads.
 [ ] My pitch is personalised and links to the kit.
 [ ] I have a tracking and reporting plan.

chunks.title: Monetization Tiers by Follower Count — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Monetization Tiers by Follower Count / Common mistakes.
 Waiting for 100k followers before pitching.
 Pitching "one video" instead of a bundle.
 Pitching brands with no ad activity.
 Not reporting results after the campaign.

chunks.title: Monetization Tiers by Follower Count — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Monetization Tiers by Follower Count / Go further.
Worked example, Emma (tech niche, 8,000 followers) and "TaskFlow AI": a $400 deal for 3 dedicated vertical clips. Production: master portrait face swapped onto a scene with Emma holding a phone, a screen recording overlay of TaskFlow's site, voiceover "Here is how I automate my daily work schedule...". Costs: API credits $2.40; gross $400.00; net $397.60 (99% margin).
Compare tools:
| Tool | Strength | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Bento.me / Linktree dynamic media kits | Fast, mobile-friendly pages with in-app view stats | Showing your avatar's portfolio and stats |
| Apollo.io / Lemlist | Contact sourcing and email sequences; watch bounce rates | Cold outreach to marketing managers at scale |
| Direct social messaging | Direct access but often lands in spam requests | Small founder-led startups |
A free Bento.me link with your best vertical clips and follower stats is a professional portfolio; use Apollo for direct corporate emails rather than DMs.
Exercises:
1. Easy: fill out the media kit with mock follower counts.
2. Medium: find three SaaS companies advertising on the Meta Ad Library and locate a marketing manager's email.
3. Hard: draft a 3-video integration campaign outline recommending a specific software tool, with hooks, script topics and b-roll concepts.

chunks.title: Agency Case Study: Small-Team Economics
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Agency Case Study: Small-Team Economics.
# Agency Case Study: Small-Team Economics
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: a customised agency agreement, a pitch for one niche and a weekly batch plan with a monthly profit estimate.
---

chunks.title: Agency Case Study: Small-Team Economics — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Agency Case Study: Small-Team Economics / Before you start.
Launching your own virtual influencer means a roughly 6-month ramp-up with zero cash flow while subscriptions and API bills keep arriving. A faster route is a Virtual Influencer Agency (VIA): you build, manage and animate virtual spokespeople for existing clients (SaaS startups, law firms, accounting practices) who are too busy or camera-shy to record. The model rests on a management retainer:
Client Retainer ($2,000/mo) ──► Upfront Invoice settled ──► Agency delivers 15 Videos/mo
Industry-standard IP separation: the agency owns the engine files (prompt guides, model seeds, voice clone credentials) and the client owns distribution rights to the finished video exports. You need: the agency agreement template, skills from lessons 1-4, and the SmartVideo GO AI AI Influencer Studio, Lip-Sync Studio and Storyboard / Campaign Planner.

chunks.title: Agency Case Study: Small-Team Economics — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Agency Case Study: Small-Team Economics / Step by step.
### 1. Customise your service contract
Open templates/influencer-agency-agreement.md. Set the monthly fee ($1,500-$2,500/month is standard for micro-agencies) and volume (typically 15 vertical clips per month). State the IP split: you keep engine files, the client gets video distribution rights.
You should see: an agreement with fee, volume, payment schedule and ownership rules filled in.
If not: this is a business document; have it reviewed by a professional before real use.
### 2. Add approval and re-render terms
Write in two rules: once a script is approved it cannot be modified (a lock-in milestone), and a post-approval script change costs a flat $50 re-render fee per video.
You should see: both rules in the agreement.
If not: if a client resists, explain that re-renders cost you API credits and edit time.
### 3. Pick a niche and write the pitch
Choose one: bookkeeping/accounting (tax write-offs), recruiting (interview tips) or local real estate (buying guides). Write one paragraph stressing that they do not need to show their face or record audio.
You should see: a one-paragraph pitch aimed at a single niche.
If not: if it is generic, name a specific video topic from the niche.
### 4. Plan the character briefing

chunks.title: Agency Case Study: Small-Team Economics — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Agency Case Study: Small-Team Economics / Step by step.
Agree on age, look, style and voice with the client, for example: "professional HR advisor in her 30s, warm and clear voice." Record it in the character style guide as your seed guidelines.
You should see: a one-page brief the client can approve.
If not: if the client cannot decide, show two or three options from Image Studio.
### 5. Design the weekly batch station
Plan 4 videos every Friday: (1) write scripts and get approval by email; (2) batch-generate cloned voice audio; (3) run the static avatar and voice tracks through /sync-lipsync; (4) trim, subtitle and color-grade.
You should see: a weekly checklist with those four stages.
If not: if the week overruns, reduce scope before dropping approval.
### 6. Set up delivery
Upload finished files to the client's shared folder and send: "Batch 2 is ready in your folder. Let us know if you need any adjustments by Monday." Send invoices via Stripe and approve scripts by simple email.
You should see: a folder structure and a message template ready to use.
If not: keep communication simple; avoid inviting clients into complex project spaces.
### 7. Project your monthly profit
Fill a P&L using the worked example's numbers below, then replace them with your own.
You should see: a total for income, costs and net profit.
If not: double-check that you multiplied API cost by the number of videos.

chunks.title: Agency Case Study: Small-Team Economics — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Agency Case Study: Small-Team Economics / Check yourself.
 [ ] My agreement states fee, volume and the IP split.
 [ ] I added a lock-in milestone and a $50 re-render fee.
 [ ] I have a niche-specific pitch.
 [ ] I have a weekly batch routine and a P&L.

chunks.title: Agency Case Study: Small-Team Economics — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Agency Case Study: Small-Team Economics / Common mistakes.
 Letting clients change scripts after approval for free.
 Giving the client the engine files (prompts, seeds, voice credentials).
 Over-complicating communication with chat tools and project boards.
 Promising full-time income without costing time.

chunks.title: Agency Case Study: Small-Team Economics — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Agency Case Study: Small-Team Economics / Go further.
Worked example, "HireFast" (recruiting SaaS) with virtual HR consultant "Maya": $2,000/month retainer for 15 vertical tips (such as "how to write a resume"). P&L: retainer $2,000.00; API 15 videos x $0.70 = $10.50; ElevenLabs + CapCut Pro $45.00; net $1,944.50/month (97% margin); about 5 hours per month. One editor could manage up to 4 clients ($8,000/month gross).
Compare tools:
| Tool | Role |
|---|---|
| Stripe Invoicing | Reliable recurring card charges; professional billing terms |
| Google Drive / Dropbox | Folder sharing for large video files and raw client assets |
| ClickUp / Slack | Task assignment and milestones for complex multi-client operations |
For small agencies: Stripe for invoices, email for approvals, a shared Drive folder for files.
Exercises:
1. Easy: fill out the agreement with a mock client and set character ownership rules.
2. Medium: research three local business niches and write a pitch for one.
3. Hard: project the monthly P&L for an agency with 3 client avatars, including all subscriptions and API credits, at 15 videos/month each.
Template: templates/influencer-agency-agreement.md.

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & TTS Basics
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & TTS Basics.
# Voice Cloning & TTS Basics
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: a cleaned mono .wav sample, a cloned voice profile, and a saved stability and clarity setting in your cloning log.
---

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & TTS Basics — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & TTS Basics / Before you start.
Default text-to-speech sounds robotic: static pitch curves, no emotional context, no breathing. Viewers of faceless videos, courses and ads notice and swipe away. A cloned voice profile captures a real speaker's timbre, accent and breaths, so you can generate hours of narration from text. There are two kinds: Instant Voice Cloning (IVC) needs only 1 to 5 minutes of sample audio and is fast and cheap, while Professional Voice Cloning (PVC) needs 30+ minutes of studio-quality speech and is nearly indistinguishable from the speaker. This lesson uses IVC.
You will need: a cardioid condenser microphone, a room with soft furnishings (carpet, curtains), Audacity (free), an ElevenLabs account, and the spec sheet templates/voice-cloning-spec.md. No prerequisites. The studios in SmartVideo GO AI that use a finished voice are Lip-Sync Studio and AI Influencer Studio (see Go further).

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & TTS Basics — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & TTS Basics / Step by step.
### 1. Set up your recording space
Open templates/voice-cloning-spec.md. Place the cardioid condenser microphone 6 inches from your mouth, in a room with carpets or curtains to stop echo.
You should see: a quiet room where a test clap does not ring or echo.
If not: move to a smaller, softer room, or hang blankets on bare walls.
### 2. Record at least 6 minutes of varied speech
Read a mix of texts with different emotional tones: news paragraphs, technical explainers and conversational stories. Keep a consistent volume and do not rush.
You should see: a recording at least 6 minutes long with no long gaps or clipping.
If not: record more passages until you reach 6 minutes. Clip warnings mean you should move back slightly or lower the input gain.
### 3. Clean the audio in Audacity
Import the file into Audacity, then run these in order:
1. Noise Reduction: sample the silent room noise, then apply noise reduction at level 12dB.
2. Noise Gate: set the threshold to -48dB to silence gaps between breaths.
3. Normalize: set peak amplitude to -3.0dB.
You should see: quiet gaps between phrases and a loud, undistorted voice that peaks near -3.0dB.
If not: if word starts are chopped, raise the gate threshold slightly (for example to -50dB, as in the worked example) and rerun on the original file. Menus move; follow the current screen.
### 4. Export as mono WAV

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & TTS Basics — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & TTS Basics / Step by step.
Export the cleaned file as a mono .wav file. Keep your raw originals in a separate local master folder.
You should see: a .wav file that plays as one channel.
If not: set the track to mono (Tracks menu in Audacity) before exporting.
### 5. Upload to the cloning engine
Open ElevenLabs. Go to VoiceLab, then Add Instant Voice. Upload the cleaned .wav files and write the label specification, for example:
text
energetic male, American accent, clear presentation tone
Submit the files for synthesis.
You should see: your new voice listed in your voice library.
If not: the menu names may have moved; follow the current ElevenLabs screen for adding an instant voice clone.
### 6. Generate a 20-second test paragraph
Type or paste a short paragraph of about 20 seconds in your cloned voice and generate it with the default settings.
You should see: audio in a voice recognisably like yours.
If not: if it sounds off, check your sample for noise or too-short length and re-upload more clean audio.
### 7. Tune the sliders and log them
Regenerate the same paragraph while adjusting the two sliders:
1. Stability (target 40% to 45%): lower is more expressive; higher locks a consistent style.
2. Clarity / Similarity (target 75% to 80%): higher enforces exact timbre, but too high can add digital crackles.
Write your best settings in the cloning log from the spec template.

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & TTS Basics — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & TTS Basics / Step by step.
You should see: a version that is expressive, with soft breaths, and no crackle.
If not: monotone means lower Stability; crackle means lower Clarity.

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & TTS Basics — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & TTS Basics / Check yourself.
 [ ] My recording is at least 6 minutes, cleaned, and exported as mono .wav.
 [ ] The gate is at -48dB (or a documented nearby value) and the peak at -3.0dB.
 [ ] My cloned voice reads a test paragraph without sounding robotic.
 [ ] My best Stability and Clarity settings are saved in the cloning log.

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & TTS Basics — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & TTS Basics / Common mistakes.
 Recording in an echoey room or with a laptop microphone.
 Setting Stability and Clarity too high (60% and 90% gave a monotone voice in the worked example).
 Deleting the raw training files; keep them in a master folder so you can retrain.
 Sharing your cloned Voice ID publicly; others could generate audio against your API limits.

chunks.title: Voice Cloning & TTS Basics — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice Cloning & TTS Basics / Go further.
Worked example, "Arthur" (B2B SaaS spokesperson): 7 minutes of clean, dry wav of a SaaS guide, normalized to -3dB peak, gate at -50dB, cloned in ElevenLabs IVC as ArthurB2BV1. Run 1 (Stability 60%, Clarity 90%): clean timbre but monotone, no breath pauses. Run 2 (Stability 40%, Clarity 75%): expressive, soft inhalations at sentence starts, tone shifts on question marks. Result: ready for bulk narration. Demo audio: rachel-vocal-cloned.mp3.
Compare tools:
| Tool | Realism | Settings | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| ElevenLabs IVC / PVC | Ultra-high (breaths, emotional pacing) | Stability, Clarity, Exaggeration | Narrations, ads, spokesperson clones |
| Play.ht (v2.0) | High | Speed and pitch | Customer service avatars, explainers |
| Coqui TTS (local) | Medium | Python integration | Bulk rendering with zero API credits (XTTS v2 also works locally) |
Exercises:
1. Easy: record a 1-minute sample and check the peak level of the silences in a free editor.
2. Medium: upload a 3-minute sample, generate a test script, and find the slider settings where the voice stops sounding robotic.
3. Hard: record 6 minutes, apply noise reduction and a gate below -48dB, export mono wav, and train a profile that passes the similarity test.
Templates: templates/voice-cloning-spec.md has hardware guidelines, gate parameters and stability logs.

 Time: about 16 minutes. You will finish with: a dubbed version of a short video in a second language that keeps the original speaker's voice, plus a pacing audit.
---

chunks.title: AI Dubbing & Translation — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Dubbing & Translation / Before you start.
If you publish only in English you ignore over 80% of the world's internet users, and traditional localization (translators, voice actors, studios, manual alignment) is slow and expensive. Automated dubbing preserves the speaker's timbre and pitch while a translation engine speaks the target language. Different languages take different times: "Automate your billing" becomes "Automatice su facturación" in Spanish, which has more syllables, so the engine compresses speech slightly (for example 1.1x) to fit the original slot.
You will need: a short source video (10 seconds is enough), an ElevenLabs account, an editor with a timeline, and templates/dubbing-translation-checklist.md. Prerequisite: lesson 1, Voice Cloning & TTS Basics. SmartVideo GO AI studios that help: Video Studio and Lip-Sync Studio (see Go further).

chunks.title: AI Dubbing & Translation — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Dubbing & Translation / Step by step.
### 1. Prepare the source dialogue
Open templates/dubbing-translation-checklist.md. Export the text transcript of your source video, remove filler words, and extract timecode logs, for example Line 1: 0:00.00 to 0:04.50.
You should see: a clean transcript where every line has a start and end time.
If not: play the video and note the times by hand in the checklist.
### 2. Configure the dubbing project
Open ElevenLabs and go to the Dubbing tab (or call the /dubbing API route). Set:
1. Source Language: English, or detect automatically.
2. Target Language: Spanish (or German, French, Hindi, etc.).
3. Resolution: "Highest Resolution", to preserve background music isolation.
You should see: a project ready to submit with both languages shown.
If not: menus move; follow the current ElevenLabs screen for dubbing.
### 3. Submit the video
Upload the video file and start the dub. The engine separates dialogue from background music (stem splitting), translates, re-synthesizes the dialogue in the original speaker's cloned voice, and recombines it with the original music.
You should see: a finished dub you can play, in the target language.
If not: if processing fails, try a shorter clip or a supported file format.
### 4. Listen for voice and meaning
Play the dub with the transcript beside it.
You should see: a voice that sounds like the English speaker, with the music still present under it.

chunks.title: AI Dubbing & Translation — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Dubbing & Translation / Step by step.
If not: if the voice differs a lot, retry with cleaner source audio.
### 5. Audit pacing and syllable speed
Zoom in on the timeline in your editor. Check for "chipmunk" speed where the translation was compressed too much for a short slot.
You should see: each dubbed line starting and ending inside its original timecodes.
If not: if a line is clipped at the end, split the background clip and add a 0.5-second freeze frame so the voice can finish.
### 6. Translate the metadata
Translate your title, description and tags using the checklist, so a Spanish audio track does not carry an English title.
You should see: translated metadata recorded in the checklist.
If not: ask a native speaker to check short phrases before publishing.

chunks.title: AI Dubbing & Translation — Check yourself

Worked example (English to Spanish tutorial): original 4.5 seconds: "Here is how to parse your invoice files instantly." Spanish: "Aquí le mostramos cómo analizar sus archivos de facturas al instante." The voice matched the speaker's timbre; the engine auto-compressed speech by 1.12x; audio started at 0:00.00 and ended at 0:04.45, so it sits on the original timeline. Demo: rachel-vocal-dubbed.mp3.
