chunks.title: Podcast Production & Audio Cleaning
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Podcast Production & Audio Cleaning.
# Podcast Production & Audio Cleaning
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a voice track cleaned and mastered to -16 LUFS (stereo) or -19 LUFS (mono), logged in a production sheet.
---

chunks.title: Podcast Production & Audio Cleaning — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Podcast Production & Audio Cleaning / Before you start.
Listeners forgive low video resolution but turn off painful audio within 10 seconds. Raw voice recordings suffer from room echo, low rumble, sibilance (sharp "S" sounds) and volume swings. A standard pipeline fixes them: a high-pass filter cuts rumble (speech has no useful information below 80Hz), a noise gate silences gaps, EQ boosts presence (3kHz to 5kHz) and cuts mud (300Hz to 400Hz), a compressor flattens volume, and loudness normalization targets -16 LUFS for stereo or -19 LUFS for mono. LUFS is the standard way to measure and match loudness across platforms.
You will need: Audacity (or Audition) and a raw voice recording, plus templates/podcast-production-sheet.md. No prerequisites. In SmartVideo GO AI, the Video and Lip-Sync studios use finished audio like this (see Go further).

chunks.title: Podcast Production & Audio Cleaning — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Podcast Production & Audio Cleaning / Step by step.
### 1. Import and note your starting levels
Import your voice file into Audacity. Open templates/podcast-production-sheet.md and write down the initial decibel peak levels.
You should see: a waveform and a filled "before" row in the sheet.
If not: if the file will not import, export it as WAV from the recorder and try again.
### 2. Apply the high-pass filter
Apply a High-Pass Filter at 80Hz for male voices or 100Hz for female voices, with rolloff of 24dB per octave.
You should see: less low rumble and mud, with the voice still full.
If not: if the voice sounds thin, lower the frequency a little.
### 3. Set the noise gate
Apply a Noise Gate with threshold -48dB (slightly higher if your room hums loudly), attack 10ms and release 150ms.
You should see: silent gaps between words and no chopped first or last syllables.
If not: if syllables are cut, lower the threshold or lengthen the release.
### 4. Apply compression
Apply a Compressor: threshold -16dB, ratio 3:1 (conversational dialogue), auto-makeup gain on.
You should see: loud and quiet parts closer in volume.
If not: if it sounds squashed, raise the threshold.
### 5. Normalize to the loudness standard
Run Loudness Normalization: target -16.0 LUFS for stereo or -19.0 LUFS for mono. Set the True Peak Limiter to -1.0 dBTP.
You should see: an output measuring at the target with peaks under -1.0 dBTP.

chunks.title: Podcast Production & Audio Cleaning — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Podcast Production & Audio Cleaning / Step by step.
If not: menus move; follow the current screen, or use a loudness meter effect to check the result.
### 6. Check in mono and log the result
Switch the final mix to mono and listen. Then fill in the "after" row of the production sheet.
You should see: a clear voice that does not fade or cancel.
If not: check for phase problems between the two channels.

chunks.title: Podcast Production & Audio Cleaning — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Podcast Production & Audio Cleaning / Check yourself.
 [ ] The high-pass filter and noise gate are applied and nothing is chopped.
 [ ] Compression uses a 3:1 ratio.
 [ ] The final track hits -16 LUFS stereo or -19 LUFS mono with true peak -1.0 dBTP.
 [ ] I logged before and after values in the production sheet.

chunks.title: Podcast Production & Audio Cleaning — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Podcast Production & Audio Cleaning / Common mistakes.
 Recording with reverb, delay or EQ already applied; capture dry.
 Setting the gate so high it clips word endings.
 Skipping the mono check; many listeners use one earbud.
 Using the stereo target on a mono file.

chunks.title: Podcast Production & Audio Cleaning — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Podcast Production & Audio Cleaning / Go further.
Worked example (home-office interview): USB desk mic with fan noise. High-pass at 90Hz, gate at -45dB, EQ presence +2dB at 4kHz, compressor 3:1 at -18dB threshold, mastered to exactly -16.0 LUFS with true peak -1.0 dBTP. Result: clean, warm, quiet background.
Compare tools:
| Tool | Quality | Control | Setup |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audacity / Audition | High | Ultra-high | Medium (manual) |
| Adobe Enhance API | High, but can add artificial sounds | None | Low (one click) |
| Auphonic / Wavespeed | High | Medium, strong loudness matching | Low (automated) |
Launch ideas: audio cleanup can be offered as a service. The original lesson cites $50 to $150 per episode for a 30-minute episode, or $300 to $500 per month for 4 episodes on retainer. Treat these as examples, not guarantees.
Exercises:
1. Easy: apply a high-pass at 80Hz and log the change in clarity.
2. Medium: adjust a gate until gaps read as -inf dB.
3. Hard: master a 1-minute intro with high-pass, gate, compressor and limiter targeting -16 LUFS.

chunks.title: AI Music & Sound Effects
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Music & Sound Effects.
# AI Music & Sound Effects
 Time: about 16 minutes. You will finish with: a custom instrumental loop, a transition sound effect, and a three-track timeline with music ducked under narration.
---

chunks.title: AI Music & Sound Effects — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Music & Sound Effects / Before you start.
Stock music is expensive, and popular music can get your video muted, demonetized or struck. Even copyright-free tracks must be fitted to your script by hand. Instead, generate your own loops and sound effects (SFX) and automate the mix. Write structured prompts with tempo (BPM), genre, lead instruments and vocal exclusions ("instrumental only") rather than abstract moods. Generate SFX in isolation with no echo. Then duck the music under the voice: -18dB while speaking, -12dB during silence.
You will need: an AI music engine (Suno or Udio), an ElevenLabs account for Sound Effects, a video editor, a voiceover, and templates/audio-prompt-library.md. No prerequisites. SmartVideo GO AI's Video Studio is where the finished soundtrack goes (see Go further).

chunks.title: AI Music & Sound Effects — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Music & Sound Effects / Step by step.
### 1. Pick a prompt formula
Open templates/audio-prompt-library.md and choose a music formula.
You should see: a formula with BPM, genre, instruments and "instrumental only".
If not: use the example in the next step.
### 2. Generate a background loop
Open Suno or Udio and use this prompt:
text
120 BPM, clean corporate tech house loop. Minimalist synthesizer, warm deep bass, soft digital percussion, optimistic mood. Instrumental only, seamless audio loop, high fidelity.
Download the instrumental .mp3.
You should see: a loop with no vocals.
If not: if a voice appears, repeat "no vocals" in the prompt and regenerate.
### 3. Generate a transition SFX
Open ElevenLabs and choose the Sound Effects tool (or call the /sound-effects API). Use:
text
Cinematic sub-bass whoosh transition sound effect, deep low rumble, clean isolated track.
Download the output.
You should see: a short, clean whoosh without background reverb.
If not: add "clean isolated track, no echo" and regenerate.
### 4. Set up three timeline tracks
In your video editor set: A1 voiceover at 0dB, A2 SFX at -6dB, A3 background music at -18dB.
You should see: three labelled audio tracks with your files placed.
If not: drag each file onto its own track.
### 5. Enable auto-ducking

chunks.title: AI Music & Sound Effects — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Music & Sound Effects / Step by step.
If your editor supports it (for example Premiere Pro or CapCut), enable ducking on the music track A3, link it to the voiceover A1, set the ducking amount to -18dB and the fade in/out speed to 0.3 seconds.
You should see: music dipping automatically when the voice speaks.
If not: menus move; follow the current screen.
### 6. Or duck manually with keyframes
Without auto-ducking, place keyframes on A3: -18dB during talking sections and -12dB during visual-only sections.
You should see: a volume line that dips and rises with the narration.
If not: zoom the timeline so keyframes land exactly on speech start and stop.
### 7. Check the final level
Play the mix and confirm the music never exceeds -10dB.
You should see: a clear voice with music underneath.
If not: lower the music; loud music gets compressed by phone speakers and distorts the voiceover.

chunks.title: AI Music & Sound Effects — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Music & Sound Effects / Check yourself.
 [ ] My music prompt included BPM, instruments and "instrumental only".
 [ ] The SFX is clean and isolated.
 [ ] Tracks are A1 0dB, A2 -6dB, A3 -18dB.
 [ ] Music ducks under narration and never exceeds -10dB.

chunks.title: AI Music & Sound Effects — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Music & Sound Effects / Common mistakes.
 Prompting with vague moods like "cool coding music".
 Forgetting "instrumental only", so vocals fight the narrator.
 Music too loud for phone speakers.
 Regenerating common SFX each time instead of reusing a saved vault.

chunks.title: AI Music & Sound Effects — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Music & Sound Effects / Go further.
Worked example (15-second vertical SaaS ad): narrator speaks 0:00 to 0:03, silent 0:03 to 0:06 for the demo, speaks 0:06 to 0:15. Music at -18dB, rises to -12dB during the demo, drops back to -18dB for the call to action. A UI click SFX sits at 0:03.50 when the cursor clicks a button.
Compare tools:
| Tool | Purpose | Control | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Suno / Udio | Songs and loops | Good, supports extension | Unique genre-specific tracks |
| Mubert / Soundraw | Loop-based audio | High, can mute stems | Fast modular B2B tracks (mute the melody, keep drums and bass) |
| ElevenLabs SFX | Isolated effects | Instant, 2-4s clips | Whooshes and button taps |
Organize: keep an SFX vault of reusable files such as whooshfast.wav and clickmodern.wav.
Exercises:
1. Easy: generate a 1-minute loop with "instrumental" and "loop" in the prompt.
2. Medium: keyframe music down 6dB under speech.
3. Hard: generate 3 transition SFX and align them to the frames of a logo reveal or cut.
Templates: templates/audio-prompt-library.md.

chunks.title: Singing Voice Conversion & Vocal Synthesis
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Singing Voice Conversion & Vocal Synthesis.
# Singing Voice Conversion & Vocal Synthesis
 Time: about 16 minutes. You will finish with: a converted singing vocal mixed over an instrumental, with the conversion settings logged in a brief.
---

chunks.title: Singing Voice Conversion & Vocal Synthesis — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Singing Voice Conversion & Vocal Synthesis / Before you start.
You want a theme song or musical ad but cannot sing, and text-to-speech reads lyrics like a lecture. Singing Voice Conversion (SVC) takes your guide vocal and outputs the same melody in another voice. It uses Retrieval-based Voice Conversion (RVC), which looks up a target singer's characteristics from a trained model, to do timbre transfer: swap the voice's colour while keeping pitch and timing. The guide must be dry and isolated; background music in the recording gets converted into screeches. Crossing male to female needs a transpose of +12 semitones (one octave).
You will need: a microphone, an audio editor with a pitch-correction tool (GSnap or Auto-Tune), an RVC interface (or ElevenLabs Voice-to-Voice), a target voice model you have the rights to use, an instrumental track, and templates/vocal-conversion-brief.md. Prerequisite: lesson 1. SmartVideo GO AI's Lip-Sync Studio and AI Influencer Studio can give the voice a face (see Go further).

chunks.title: Singing Voice Conversion & Vocal Synthesis — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Singing Voice Conversion & Vocal Synthesis / Step by step.
### 1. Record a dry guide vocal
In silence, with no music playing, record yourself singing the lyrics. Do not worry if you sound flat.
You should see: a vocal-only recording.
If not: if music bleeds into it, rerecord with headphones and silence the room.
### 2. Snap the pitch
Import the track into your editor and apply a pitch-correction tool (GSnap or Auto-Tune) to snap notes to the key. Save it as guidevocal.wav.
You should see: notes sitting in the chosen key.
If not: check the key setting matches your melody (the worked example used C-Major).
### 3. Upload and choose the target model
Open your RVC interface (or call the /voice-to-voice API) and upload guidevocal.wav. Choose the target model, for example emmasingingv2.
You should see: the file and model both selected.
If not: confirm the model is installed or available to your account.
### 4. Set the transpose
Male guide to female target: +12 semitones. Female guide to male target: -12 semitones. Record this in templates/vocal-conversion-brief.md.
You should see: the pitch shift value in the settings.
If not: if the output is strained, check you did not apply the wrong direction.
### 5. Set the retrieval parameters
1. Feature Retrieval Index Rate: target 0.65 to 0.70. Too high (0.90) sounds robotic; too low (0.40) keeps too much of the guide singer's tone.

chunks.title: Singing Voice Conversion & Vocal Synthesis — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Singing Voice Conversion & Vocal Synthesis / Step by step.
2. Consonant Protection: target 0.33, to stop "s", "t" and "sh" sounding like static.
You should see: both values set in range.
If not: adjust in small steps and re-run.
### 6. Convert and download
Click convert and download the output .wav.
You should see: the melody sung in the target voice.
If not: if it screeches, return to step 1 and check the guide is dry.
### 7. Mix the final vocal
Import the converted vocal into your editor with the instrumental. Add a subtle plate reverb and a stereo delay, and limit the vocal peak to -3dB.
You should see: a vocal that blends with the music without peaking.
If not: lower the reverb wet level (the worked example used 15% wet).

chunks.title: Singing Voice Conversion & Vocal Synthesis — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Singing Voice Conversion & Vocal Synthesis / Check yourself.
 [ ] My guide vocal was dry, with no backing music.
 [ ] Transpose matches the guide and target voices (+12 or -12 semitones).
 [ ] Index rate is about 0.65 to 0.70 and consonant protection 0.33.
 [ ] The final vocal peaks at -3dB and sits over the instrumental.

chunks.title: Singing Voice Conversion & Vocal Synthesis — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Singing Voice Conversion & Vocal Synthesis / Common mistakes.
 Recording the guide with music playing.
 Index rate set too high or too low.
 Using models trained on famous pop stars for commercial work; platforms remove these tracks and legal risk is real.
 Forgetting to transpose across male and female ranges.

chunks.title: Singing Voice Conversion & Vocal Synthesis — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Singing Voice Conversion & Vocal Synthesis / Go further.
Worked example (theme song, male guide to Emma avatar): guide sung "Automate your SaaS...", snapped to C-Major. Target emmasingingv2, pitch +12, index rate 0.68. Output: on-pitch female vocal with Emma's timbre, mixed with a lofi backing, reverb 15% wet, mastered to -16 LUFS.
Compare tools:
| Tool | Quality | Cost | Setup |
|---|---|---|---|
| RVC | High | Free (local GPU) | Medium (WebUI script) |
| ElevenLabs Voice-to-Voice | Ultra-high, keeps breaths | High (per character) | Low (web dashboard) |
| So-Vits-SVC 4.0 | Ultra-high | Free | High (Python training) |
Copyright: train a custom singing model, for example from 20 minutes of scales and songs by a local singer, and lock the IP ownership.
Exercises:
1. Easy: record a 10-second rhythmic sing-song guide.
2. Medium: convert it with +12 semitones and analyze the octave shift.
3. Hard: make a 15-second loop: acapella guide, auto-tune, RVC convert, delay and reverb, mix over an instrumental.
Templates: templates/vocal-conversion-brief.md.
Produce this in SmartVideo GO AI: Lip-Sync Studio (voice plus mouth-sync), AI Influencer Studio (a recurring character), Image Studio and Video Studio for visuals.

Academy lesson: Product Shots Without a Photographer, part 2.
# Product Shots Without a Photographer, part 2
 Time: about 10 minutes. You will finish with: a composited product shot with a contact shadow, a directional shadow and matched colours.
---

chunks.title: Product Shots Without a Photographer, part 2 — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Product Shots Without a Photographer, part 2 / Before you start.
Pasting a product onto an AI background looks fake because the shadows and light colours do not match. Two fixes make it believable: the Double Shadow Technique (a tight contact shadow plus a longer directional shadow) and ambient lighting sync (shifting the product's colour curves to the backdrop's tone). You need the layered file from part 1 open in your photo editor.

chunks.title: Product Shots Without a Photographer, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Product Shots Without a Photographer, part 2 / Step by step.
### 1. Add a shadow layer
Create a new transparent layer between the product and the backdrop. Set the brush to black, opacity 40%, hardness 0%.
You should see: an empty layer sitting under the product layer and above the backdrop.
If not: if the shadow would cover the product, drag the layer below the product layer.
### 2. Paint the contact shadow
Paint a tight, dark, highly softened shadow right beneath the bottom edge of the product, where it touches the stone.
You should see: the product looks grounded, with no gap of light under its base.
If not: if the shadow looks like a hard line, lower hardness to 0% and reduce opacity.
### 3. Paint the directional shadow
On the same layer, paint a larger, lighter shadow stretching to the left, matching the angle of the sunlight in the backdrop. Set the layer blend mode to Multiply.
You should see: a soft shadow falling away from the light, consistent with the backdrop's shadows.
If not: if it points toward the light, redraw it on the opposite side of the product.
### 4. Match the colours
Add a colour balance adjustment layer clipped to the product layer. For a warm golden-hour backdrop, add a slight yellow and red highlight shift. For an overcast beach backdrop, add a subtle blue/cyan midtone shift.
You should see: the product's highlights share the backdrop's light colour.

chunks.title: Product Shots Without a Photographer, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Product Shots Without a Photographer, part 2 / Step by step.
If not: if the product looks tinted overall, reduce the shift until only the highlights change.
### 5. Export and compare
Export the image and view it next to the raw photo from part 1.
You should see: the new image looks like a premium studio shot.
If not: recheck shadow direction and product scale, the two most common giveaways.

chunks.title: Product Shots Without a Photographer, part 2 — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Product Shots Without a Photographer, part 2 / Check yourself.
 [ ] The contact shadow sits directly under the product base.
 [ ] The directional shadow matches the backdrop light angle and uses Multiply.
 [ ] The colour balance layer is clipped to the product only.
 [ ] My result looks clearly better than the raw photo.

chunks.title: Product Shots Without a Photographer, part 2 — Common mistakes
chunks.text:

 Shadows pointing the wrong way relative to the light.
 Colouring the whole image instead of clipping the adjustment to the product.
 A hard-edged brush for shadows.

Worked example: in the aloe gel tube case, a soft contact shadow was painted at the base and colour temperature was warmed by +10 to match golden window sunbeams.

chunks.title: Product Shots Without a Photographer
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Product Shots Without a Photographer.
# Product Shots Without a Photographer
 Time: about 14 minutes. You will finish with: a transparent product cutout and a studio backdrop, composited together and ready for shadows.
---

chunks.title: Product Shots Without a Photographer — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Product Shots Without a Photographer / Before you start.
A premium backdrop shifts your product from cheap to premium. A studio shoot costs thousands of dollars and weeks of coordination, while a phone photo on a cheap background makes customers assume the product is cheap too. The fix is to photograph the real product once, isolate it as a transparent PNG, and build the environment around it, because image generators (like Stable Diffusion or FLUX) cannot render existing labels or logos accurately. The pipeline is: raw photo, background removal, AI backdrop, composite and shadows. This lesson covers the first three parts and the composite; lesson 1, part 2 adds shadows and colour.
You will need: a phone, one product with a clean label, a background remover (Photoroom, Clipdrop or a /remove-background API), an image generator (for example Image Studio in SmartVideo GO AI), a photo editor (Photoshop, Photopea, or a Python Pillow script), and templates/photography-brief-template.md.

chunks.title: Product Shots Without a Photographer — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Product Shots Without a Photographer / Step by step.
### 1. Photograph the product
Use diffused daylight from a window. Do not mix warm yellow house lamps with cool daylight: it creates mixed reflections on the packaging that AI cannot fix later. Make sure the label is clean, in focus and free of extreme glare.
You should see: a sharp photo where every word on the label is readable.
If not: move away from the lamp, turn off overhead lights, and shoot again with the product facing the window.
### 2. Isolate the product
Upload the photo to Photoroom, Clipdrop, or call the /remove-background API. Download the result as a transparent PNG named productmask.png.
You should see: the product on a checkerboard (transparent) background with clean edges and an intact label.
If not: if edges are ragged, retake the photo against a plain, contrasting surface and run the remover again.
### 3. Open your photography brief
Open templates/photography-brief-template.md and fill in the backdrop environment and composition fields before you generate anything.
You should see: a brief that names the surface, light direction and mood you want.
If not: copy the prompt from the next step as your starting backdrop description.
### 4. Generate the studio backdrop
In your image generator, run this prompt:
text

chunks.title: Product Shots Without a Photographer — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Product Shots Without a Photographer / Step by step.
An elegant studio product backdrop. A single rectangular travertine stone slab on a beige concrete surface, soft side golden sunlight, warm shadows, minimalist aesthetic, commercial product setup, high resolution, f/4 lens, depth of field.
Save the best result as backdrop.jpg.
You should see: an empty stone slab with warm side light and no product on it.
If not: if a product or text appears, regenerate. Keep the slab as the only subject.
### 5. Composite the layers
In your photo editor, place backdrop.jpg as the bottom layer and productmask.png as the top layer. Scale the product to sit naturally on the slab. Hold Shift while scaling so the aspect ratio never stretches or warps.
You should see: the product standing on the slab at a believable size, still looking a bit "pasted" (no shadows yet).
If not: if it looks squashed, undo and rescale holding Shift. Save the layered file, since part 2 continues from it.

chunks.title: Product Shots Without a Photographer — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Product Shots Without a Photographer / Check yourself.
 [ ] My product photo used diffused daylight with no mixed lamps.
 [ ] productmask.png has a transparent background and a readable label.
 [ ] backdrop.jpg contains only the empty stone slab scene.
 [ ] I scaled the product proportionally onto the backdrop.

chunks.title: Product Shots Without a Photographer — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Product Shots Without a Photographer / Common mistakes.
 Mixing warm house lamps and cool daylight when photographing.
 Stretching or warping the product PNG to fit the background.
 Asking the generator to draw the product itself, which ruins labels and logos.

chunks.title: Product Shots Without a Photographer — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Product Shots Without a Photographer / Go further.
Worked example: backdrop shift for an organic aloe vera gel tube. Source: a green plastic bottle on a white desk under office lighting. Background removed, keeping only the container. Backdrop prompt:
text
Minimalist bathroom counter, white marble surface, warm sunbeams passing through a window, soft shadows, green eucalyptus leaf casting shadows, high-end organic cosmetic background, 85mm, photorealistic.
The tube was scaled to occupy 70% of the vertical frame. Result: it looks shot in a high-end luxury spa, raising perceived value.
Exercises. Easy: photograph a coffee mug and isolate it as a transparent PNG with a free remover. Medium: generate a wooden-block backdrop with a soft sunset shadow and composite your object onto it. Hard: continue in part 2 with the two-part shadow and colour balance.
Compare tools.
| Tool | Purpose | Control | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| FLUX Dev / Schnell | Backdrop generation | High (responds well to prop and lighting prompts) | Complex, stylized studio settings |
| Photoroom / Clipdrop | Fast background replacement and auto shadows | Instant (template-driven) | Fast batch rendering of basic Amazon listings |
| Magnific AI / Relight | High-resolution detailing and colour matching | High | Premium hero images for luxury sites |

Academy lesson: Product Shots Without a Photographer / Go further.
For standard listings, Photoroom gives a clean white-background shot with auto-shadows in about 5 seconds. For creative banners, FLUX backdrops with manual compositing give the highest quality.

chunks.title: Before/After Conversion Case Studies
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Before/After Conversion Case Studies.
# Before/After Conversion Case Studies
 Time: about 16 minutes. You will finish with: a completed listing audit, a written hypothesis and a configured 50/50 A/B test plan (the test itself runs 14 days).
---

chunks.title: Before/After Conversion Case Studies — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Before/After Conversion Case Studies / Before you start.
Brands update images blindly, assuming "pretty" sells. CRO (Conversion Rate Optimization) is the science of improving how many visitors to a product page actually buy. High traffic but low sales means the gallery images fail to build trust. Low clicks in search means the main image lacks contrast. Two numbers drive this: Click-Through Rate (CTR), helped by the main search image, and Conversion Rate (CVR), helped by gallery and lifestyle images. Never ship new images without a split test: run Variant A (original) and Variant B (AI image) concurrently, 50% of traffic each, until you reach 95% statistical significance.
You need module 1 skills, a product page with real metrics (or a mock one), templates/conversion-audit-checklist.md, and a split-testing tool (VWO, AB Tasty or Shopify's native test features). Image creation uses Image Studio in SmartVideo GO AI.

chunks.title: Before/After Conversion Case Studies — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Before/After Conversion Case Studies / Step by step.
### 1. Audit the bottleneck
Open templates/conversion-audit-checklist.md and record the page's current metrics. If traffic is high but conversion is below 2%, the gallery images are weak: redesign the lifestyle context. If organic traffic is low, redesign the main hero image so it stands out in search results.
You should see: a filled checklist that names one bottleneck: gallery (CVR) or hero (CTR).
If not: if you have no real data, use a mock listing and invent clearly labelled sample numbers.
### 2. Write the visual hypothesis
Name the customer's core objection and write one sentence, for example:
text
Replacing the flat white background of the facial oil listing with a premium marble counter backdrop will increase user trust, boosting CVR by 20%.
You should see: one hypothesis with one change and one expected outcome.
If not: if it mentions two changes (say image and price), cut one. Test one variable at a time.
### 3. Build Variant B
Create the new image using the module 1 rules. Add benefit callouts such as "100% Organic Cold-Pressed" as clean, high-contrast text overlays.
You should see: a Variant B image with a premium backdrop, realistic shadows and readable callouts.
If not: if text is hard to read, enlarge it or raise the contrast.
### 4. Check it on mobile
Over 70% of e-commerce traffic is on mobile. View Variant B on a physical phone screen.

chunks.title: Before/After Conversion Case Studies — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Before/After Conversion Case Studies / Step by step.
You should see: the text readable without pinching and zooming.
If not: increase the font size and re-export.
### 5. Configure the split test
In your testing tool, set Variant A as the control (original images), Variant B as the test page, and split traffic 50% Control / 50% Test.
You should see: two variants listed with an even split.
If not: if the tool offers no even split, look for a "traffic allocation" setting; menus move, so follow the current screen.
### 6. Set your stopping rule
Write down: run at least 14 days (to capture mid-week and weekend behaviour), do not stop early, push Variant B live to 100% only if it shows a lift with more than 95% significance, then log the result in your case study index.
You should see: a written rule with a start date and a decision date.
If not: add the dates to the audit checklist so you cannot forget them.

chunks.title: Before/After Conversion Case Studies — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Before/After Conversion Case Studies / Check yourself.
 [ ] My audit names one bottleneck, CTR or CVR.
 [ ] My hypothesis changes one variable only.
 [ ] Variant B is readable on a phone.
 [ ] The test is set to 50/50 with a 14-day minimum and 95% significance rule.

chunks.title: Before/After Conversion Case Studies — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Before/After Conversion Case Studies / Common mistakes.
 Changing price and image at the same time.
 Stopping the test early when one variant leads.
 Checking images only on a desktop screen.

chunks.title: Before/After Conversion Case Studies — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Before/After Conversion Case Studies / Go further.
Worked example: specialty coffee bag. A $25 bag sold on a flat stock photo at 1.8% CVR. Variant B: a high-contrast angled hero with a long realistic shadow, and a lifestyle composite on a dark slate kitchen bar with soft morning light beams, an espresso cup with glossy crema and scattered roasted beans. Test: 3,000 visitors per variant over 14 days. Variant A 1.8% (54 conversions); Variant B 3.1% (93 conversions). Result: a 72% increase in sales with no extra ad spend.
Exercises. Easy: find a live listing with weak lifestyle photos and note 3 improvements. Medium: audit a mock listing with the checklist and write a hypothesis. Hard: design Variant A (product on white) and Variant B (premium composite on an AI stone base) for a kitchen product, with mobile crops for both.
Compare tools.
| Tool | Purpose | Speed | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| VWO / AB Tasty | Enterprise A/B testing | Medium (tracking scripts) | CRO audits on custom sites |
| Shopify split-testers | Store variant testing | Fast (one-click apps) | Product gallery image tests |
| Hotjar / Clarity | Heatmaps and scroll depth | Fast | Seeing where users leave a page |
VWO also tracks hover times and specific clicks.

chunks.text:

# Selling as a Productized Service
 Time: about 16 minutes. You will finish with: a priced service offer, an intake form plan, a free-sample pitch and a delivery board outline.
---

chunks.title: Selling as a Productized Service — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling as a Productized Service / Before you start.
Agencies that bill by the hour struggle to scale: custom proposals, scope creep and price haggling. Pitch "AI backgrounds" and clients see cheap labour. A Productized Service packages work into a defined scope, fixed price and clear turnaround, pitched around conversion increases. Compare your price with a physical studio shoot (about $3,000 plus shipping and models), not with freelancers: for example, 10 lifestyle photos for $499 in 3 days. Lock scope (e.g. "2 rounds of text edits", defined output formats) and automate onboarding so no sales calls are needed.
You need templates/productized-service-offer.md, a form tool (Typeform or Google Forms), a shared drive (Google Drive or Dropbox), a task board (Asana or Trello), and the module 1 workflow, using Image Studio in SmartVideo GO AI for visuals.

chunks.title: Selling as a Productized Service — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling as a Productized Service / Step by step.
### 1. Define your tiers
Open templates/productized-service-offer.md and customize the packages. Example: Pack A at $499 one-time for listing launch visuals, and Pack B at $999/month for ongoing studio asset testing.
You should see: two packages, each with price, deliverables, turnaround and revision count.
If not: if a package says "unlimited" anything, replace it with a number.
### 2. Build the intake form
Create a form that links to a shared folder. Collect: high-resolution transparent PNG product photos; brand colours, style preference (minimalist, tropical, dark) and logo files; and bounding box guidelines (for example the Amazon 85% fill rule). Never ask clients to send passwords or secret keys.
You should see: a form with those three sections and an upload destination.
If not: if the form cannot take large files, ask for a shared-folder link instead.
### 3. Make the free sample
Find a local Shopify brand with weak product photos. Download one product image, remove the background, composite it onto a premium travertine slab with a soft shadow (module 1), and make a before/after side by side.
You should see: one clear before/after image.
If not: if the product edge looks rough, choose a different product image.
### 4. Write the pitch email
Email the owner the side-by-side. Lead with the result, then the fixed offer.

chunks.title: Selling as a Productized Service — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling as a Productized Service / Step by step.
You should see: a short email with the image, the pack and the price.
If not: cut any sentence about tools; brands care about metrics.
### 5. Set up the delivery board
In Asana or Trello create a card outline with the stages: Intake Received - Backdrop Design - Composite Audit - Final Delivery.
You should see: four columns or stages ready for a new client card.
If not: build them manually; automation can come later.
### 6. Plan delivery and contract basics
Plan to deliver WebP assets within the promised time, include a copy of templates/conversion-audit-checklist.md to encourage split-testing and a retainer upgrade. In your agreement, state that the client owns the final composites, and charge upfront before any design work.
You should see: three written rules: ownership, upfront payment, delivery checklist.
If not: add them to the offer template.

chunks.title: Selling as a Productized Service — Check yourself

Academy lesson: Selling as a Productized Service / Check yourself.

 Selling "AI images" instead of conversion results.
 Leaving scope open, so revisions never end.
 Starting work before payment.
 Booking sales calls instead of using an automated intake.

chunks.text:

Worked example: e-commerce conversion booster. Offer: "E-commerce Conversion Booster Pack, 10 Lifestyle Scenes in 3 Days for $499." Found 50 skincare stores with basic images and emailed personalized before/afters. 8 owners responded, 3 bought the $499 pack, 1 upgraded to the $999/month "Infinite Retainer". About $2,496 billed in under 8 hours of production using templates.
Exercises. Easy: adapt the offer template to a niche such as luxury watches or pet supplies. Medium: build a before/after email pitch for a weak live listing. Hard: set up a mock Stripe checkout link connected to an onboarding questionnaire that creates upload folders.

chunks.title: Batch Workflows for Catalogs, part 2
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batch Workflows for Catalogs, part 2.
# Batch Workflows for Catalogs, part 2
 Time: about 13 minutes. You will finish with: matching, SKU-named WebP catalog images exported to 05finaldeliver/.
---

chunks.title: Batch Workflows for Catalogs, part 2 — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batch Workflows for Catalogs, part 2 / Before you start.
With masks and a locked backdrop from part 1, consistency now comes from one template: every container sits on the same vertical baseline and fills the same relative height, so the grid looks like a brand catalog. Because the lighting is identical, one shadow layer is reused for all products. You need masterbackground.jpg, the PNG masks in 02isolatedmasks/, and Photoshop or a comparable editor.

chunks.title: Batch Workflows for Catalogs, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batch Workflows for Catalogs, part 2 / Step by step.
### 1. Build the alignment template
Open masterbackground.jpg. Pull a horizontal ruler guide to the baseline where product bottoms touch the pedestal. Add side guides for maximum padding. Save as catalogtemplate.psd.
You should see: a PSD with a baseline guide and padding guides.
If not: turn on rulers and guides in the View menu; menus move, so follow the current screen.
### 2. Import the masks
Import each product PNG mask into the template as its own layer group.
You should see: one layer per product, all stacked in the file.
If not: if a mask arrives huge, scale it proportionally (hold Shift).
### 3. Align and scale
Align each mask's base to the baseline guide, and scale each to fill the standard bounding box (for example 80% height).
You should see: every product bottom on the same line and the same height.
If not: compare against the bounding box map in templates/batch-catalog-spec.md.
### 4. Reuse the shadows
Duplicate the shadow layer under each product. Since lighting is identical, the same contact and drop shadow layers work for all files.
You should see: identical shadows under each product.
If not: if a base is wider than the others, nudge the shadow, not the baseline.
### 5. Export as WebP

chunks.title: Batch Workflows for Catalogs, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batch Workflows for Catalogs, part 2 / Step by step.
Toggle each product on one at a time (click the eye icon next to a layer to show or hide it), keeping the backdrop and shadow layers the same. Export each as WebP into 05finaldeliver/, named by SKU such as SKU-BOT-01.webp, at one uniform size such as 2000x2000px square.
You should see: one WebP per product, same size, named by SKU.
If not: mixed shapes break a store grid, so re-export any odd file at the standard size.

chunks.title: Batch Workflows for Catalogs, part 2 — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batch Workflows for Catalogs, part 2 / Check yourself.
 [ ] Every product base sits on the same baseline.
 [ ] All products fill the same bounding box.
 [ ] Shadows and background are identical across files.
 [ ] Files are SKU-named WebP at one uniform size.

chunks.title: Batch Workflows for Catalogs, part 2 — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batch Workflows for Catalogs, part 2 / Common mistakes.
 Mixing square and vertical exports.
 Naming finals without the SKU, which blocks CSV import.
 Re-tuning shadows per product so the set no longer matches.

chunks.title: Batch Workflows for Catalogs, part 2 — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batch Workflows for Catalogs, part 2 / Go further.
Worked example result: 5 matching skincare images with uniform lighting, shadows and sizing in under 10 minutes. SKU names let developers link images to listings through CSV spreadsheets automatically.
Exercise (hard): batch 3 coloured beverage cans on the same ledge, same baseline and shadow layer, and export 3 matching WebP files.

chunks.title: Batch Workflows for Catalogs
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batch Workflows for Catalogs.
# Batch Workflows for Catalogs
 Time: about 14 minutes. You will finish with: a catalog folder structure, isolated product masks and one locked master backdrop.
---

chunks.title: Batch Workflows for Catalogs — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batch Workflows for Catalogs / Before you start.
Brands launch 20, 50 or 200 variations. If each backdrop is prompted from scratch, lighting, shadows and camera angles differ and the catalog looks messy. At 1 hour per product, a 50-item catalog takes about a week. Batch production rests on three ideas: Prompt Pinning (same prompt and seed, one pre-rendered background for all products), Layout Standardization (the same baseline Y-coordinate and relative height) and Batch Masking (remove backgrounds in bulk through folder tools or an API).
You need 3 to 5 raw product shots of one collection, templates/batch-catalog-spec.md, Photoshop (or an API/Python script) for masking, and Image Studio in SmartVideo GO AI for the backdrop.

chunks.title: Batch Workflows for Catalogs — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batch Workflows for Catalogs / Step by step.
### 1. Create the catalog folders
Open templates/batch-catalog-spec.md and create: 01rawassets/, 02isolatedmasks/, 03aibackgrounds/, 04compositedrafts/, 05finaldeliver/.
You should see: five empty folders in order.
If not: match the names exactly so the spec and your scripts agree.
### 2. Add and name the raw shots
Put every raw product shot in 01rawassets/ named by SKU, for example skulavender01.jpg, skurose02.jpg.
You should see: every file starting with its SKU.
If not: rename any file named like IMG2041.jpg now, not later.
### 3. Batch remove backgrounds in Photoshop
Go to File - Scripts - Image Processor (menus move; follow the current screen). Set the source folder to 01rawassets/ and choose "Save as PSD". In the Actions panel record a new action: Select Subject, apply Mask, save as transparent PNG. Run it on the folder, outputting to 02isolatedmasks/.
You should see: one transparent PNG per product in 02isolatedmasks/.
If not: if a mask is poor, rerun that one file. Alternative: run a Python script that sends the folder's files to /remove-background and downloads the results. Never put API keys in chat.
### 4. Lock your master backdrop
Generate backdrops with the module 1 prompt style and choose one. Scale and center the travertine block or pedestal surface, then save it as masterbackground.jpg. Keep the prompt and seed in the brief so it can be regenerated identically.

chunks.title: Batch Workflows for Catalogs — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batch Workflows for Catalogs / Step by step.
You should see: one backdrop file in 03aibackgrounds/ that every product will share.
If not: if you want a different look, change it now; changing it later means redoing every composite.

chunks.title: Batch Workflows for Catalogs — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batch Workflows for Catalogs / Check yourself.
 [ ] All five folders exist with the exact names.
 [ ] Raw files are named by SKU.
 [ ] Every product has a transparent mask in 02isolatedmasks/.
 [ ] I have exactly one masterbackground.jpg.

chunks.title: Batch Workflows for Catalogs — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batch Workflows for Catalogs / Common mistakes.
 Generating a new background for each product.
 Naming files by camera defaults instead of SKU.
 Cleaning masks by hand, pixel by pixel, instead of batching.

chunks.title: Batch Workflows for Catalogs — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batch Workflows for Catalogs / Go further.
Worked example: skincare serum catalog. 5 serum droppers (Rose, Lavender, Cucumber, Tea Tree, Citrus). Master environment: travertine marble ledge against cream stucco. Baseline at Y: 800px on a 1920x1920px square canvas; product height standardized to exactly 1100px. Folder-wide background removal on the 5 raw shots, then all masks imported into one template.
Exercises. Easy: set up the five standard folders. Medium: record a Photoshop Action or write a script that scales an image to 1080x1080px and adds a 10% outer border. Hard: batch process 3 coloured beverage cans on the same ledge at the same baseline with the same shadow layer.
Compare tools.
| Tool | Speed | Suitability | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Photoshop Batch Actions | High (local folders, recorded hotkeys) | Excellent (keeps manual control) | Designers with complex layer adjustments |
| Photoroom Batch API | Ultra-high (cloud, hundreds of files at once) | Good | High-volume stores with simple layouts |
| Python Pillow (PIL) | Ultra-high | Good (needs scripting) | Programmers automating bulk overlays |
For agencies, recorded Photoshop actions plus manual QA on shadows is best. For 500+ items, Photoroom's Batch API is the fastest.

# Batch Catalog Processing Spec
 SmartVideo GO AI Academy — A reusable template from the SmartVideo GO AI course library. Fill it in, then launch it from the matching SmartVideo GO AI studio or Create-With-AI recipe.

chunks.title: Batch Catalog Processing Spec — 1. Directory Structure Blueprint
chunks.text:
Academy template: Batch Catalog Processing Spec / 1. Directory Structure Blueprint.
Configure your project folders:
[project-root]/
├── 01rawassets/ # Raw product photo uploads
├── 02isolatedmasks/ # Output png files after background removal
├── 03aibackgrounds/ # Generated environment backdrop images

chunks.title: Garment Try-on for Fashion E-commerce
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Garment Try-on for Fashion E-commerce.
# Garment Try-on for Fashion E-commerce
 Time: about 16 minutes. You will finish with: one flat garment draped onto a model, checked at high zoom, with a filled try-on spec sheet.
---

chunks.title: Garment Try-on for Fashion E-commerce — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Garment Try-on for Fashion E-commerce / Before you start.
A single fashion shoot with models, hair and makeup, a photographer and a studio can cost over $5,000 and take weeks to edit. Flat-lays and ghost mannequin shots are cheap but look flat, which means low click-through and high returns because shoppers cannot judge the fit. A Virtual Try-On (VTO) pipeline fixes this: it isolates your garment (segmentation), then drapes it onto a model body while preserving about 95% of the original texture, stitching, buttons and patterns.
You will need:
 One photo of a garment, flat-lay or on a mannequin, in focus under clean daylight.
 The spec sheet templates/tryon-spec-sheet.md.
 SmartVideo GO AI: Image Studio for the cut-out and try-on. The tool names below (IDM-TryOn, Kolors VTO, nano-banana-2-edit) come from the original lesson; menus move, so follow the current screen.

chunks.title: Garment Try-on for Fashion E-commerce — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Garment Try-on for Fashion E-commerce / Step by step.
### 1. Cut out the garment
1. Open your garment photo in Image Studio (or any AI subject cutter).
2. Remove the background so only the garment remains, and save it as garmentref.png.
You should see: the garment alone on a transparent background, edges clean, no table or hanger left.
If not: if edges are ragged, re-shoot flatter and in better light, then cut out again.
### 2. Define the model
1. Open templates/tryon-spec-sheet.md.
2. Write the target model's parameters, for example:
text
East Asian male, 28 years old, athletic build, standing in a studio environment.
You should see: the demographic line saved in your spec sheet.
If not: if you are unsure, copy the example above and change one detail at a time.
### 3. Choose the target pose
1. If your try-on tool supports reference models, upload a photo of a model in your pose (Pose A: standing straight, hands at sides).
2. If you use a text-to-image edit model such as nano-banana-2-edit, upload the original mannequin photo, mask the clothing area and paste your model description from step 2.
You should see: a pose image or a masked mannequin photo ready as the body input.
If not: if the tool has no reference-model option, use the mask-and-describe route.
### 4. Run the draping engine

chunks.title: Garment Try-on for Fashion E-commerce — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Garment Try-on for Fashion E-commerce / Step by step.
1. Submit to your try-on engine (such as IDM-TryOn or Kolors VTO API): garmentref.png as the clothing input, the pose image or text as the target body input.
2. Set the draping fitting rate to 0.75, which balances cloth detail with realistic body wrinkles.
3. Generate and download the output .jpg.
You should see: your garment worn by the model, with natural folds.
If not: if details look washed out, check that the garment input is sharp; if the fit looks stiff, keep 0.75 and change only one setting per retry.
### 5. Quality-check at high zoom
Zoom in on the result and inspect three areas:
 Collar and buttons: crisp shapes, not blurred or merged with skin.
 Cuffs and hem: hands pass naturally through cuffs; the hem lies straight.
 Prints and textures: stripes, prints and logos follow the body's curves.
You should see: all three areas pass; record the result under QA checks in the spec sheet.
If not: regenerate, or fix small border bleed in a photo editor.

chunks.title: Garment Try-on for Fashion E-commerce — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Garment Try-on for Fashion E-commerce / Check yourself.
 [ ] I have a clean garmentref.png with a removed background.
 [ ] The model description is in the spec sheet.
 [ ] I used a fitting rate of 0.75.
 [ ] I checked collar, cuffs, hem and prints at high zoom.

chunks.title: Garment Try-on for Fashion E-commerce — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Garment Try-on for Fashion E-commerce / Common mistakes.
 A blurry or tilted garment photo. The model can only preserve detail that exists in the input.
 A different model face on every item. Use the same model face and body across one category page, or the store looks amateur.
 Skipping the zoom check. Errors hide at collars and cuffs.
 Not saving poses. Keep your best model poses in a master folder to speed up batch rendering for the next line.

chunks.title: Garment Try-on for Fashion E-commerce — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Garment Try-on for Fashion E-commerce / Go further.
Worked example, linen shirt mannequin-to-model swap. Input: a ghost mannequin shot of an off-white linen button-down. Target: a 30-year-old Caucasian male model, athletic build. Pipeline: IDM-TryOn API call with garmentimage = linenshirt.png and modelimage = referencemalemodel.jpg. Output: buttons clear, stitching sharp, the cross-hatch linen texture preserved, soft shadow under the collar. The catalog moved from a plastic mannequin to a professional model shot.
Motion loop: templates/examples/linen-shirt-motion.mp4
Compare tools
| Tool | Detail preservation | Pose customization | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| IDM-TryOn | Ultra-high (patterns, textures, stitching) | Medium | High-fidelity catalog photos |
| Kolors Virtual Try-On | High | High | Editorial lookbooks, social graphics |
| Kling AI Image-to-Video | Medium | High | Short walking loops |
IDM-TryOn suits product detail pages (Shopify, Amazon) because logos and textures stay sharp. Kolors suits banner ads with active poses.
Exercises
1. Easy: photograph a t-shirt flat-lay and make a clean clothing PNG with a background cutter.
2. Medium: try the t-shirt on a male and a female model.
3. Hard: run a buttoned jacket from a ghost mannequin shot, review collar and cuff seams at 200% zoom and fix any border bleeding in a photo editor.
Template: templates/tryon-spec-sheet.md.

chunks.title: High-converting Studio Lookbooks
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: High-converting Studio Lookbooks.
# High-converting Studio Lookbooks
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: one lookbook image: a generated backdrop, a model composited with matched shadows, and a colour grade, filled in on your moodboard.
---

chunks.title: High-converting Studio Lookbooks — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: High-converting Studio Lookbooks / Before you start.
Seasonal lookbooks are logistics nightmares (weather, travel, props, changing light), shot in a plain office they look flat, and stock photos look generic. The fix is a cohesive pipeline: pick a theme, build a backdrop with consistent lighting, composite your try-on model, then apply one colour grade (LUT) so every image looks like the same shoot. Use diffused side softbox light with soft neutral shadows; avoid harsh sunbeams unless the collection is high-contrast summer.
You will need:
 A try-on model image from lesson 1 (Garment Try-on).
 templates/lookbook-moodboard.md.
 SmartVideo GO AI Image Studio for the backdrop; a layer editor such as Photoshop or Photopea for compositing and grading (menus move; follow the current screen).

chunks.title: High-converting Studio Lookbooks — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: High-converting Studio Lookbooks / Step by step.
### 1. Lock the moodboard theme
1. Open templates/lookbook-moodboard.md.
2. Choose a visual archetype, colour palette and studio lighting setup. Example: "Nordic Autumn" with taupe, soft sand and slate grey.
You should see: a filled moodboard with theme, palette and lighting.
If not: if you cannot choose, use the Nordic Autumn example and change it later.
### 2. Generate the backdrop
1. In Image Studio (or another image generator), paste this prompt:
text
A high-end fashion studio backdrop. A minimalist light grey textured plaster screen, soft diffused overcast window light casting faint shadows, editorial fashion set, photorealistic, 8k resolution, shot on 85mm lens, f/5.6.
2. Save the result as studiobg01.jpg.
You should see: an empty plaster-style set with soft light and faint shadows.
If not: if the light is harsh or colours drift from your palette, add your palette words to the prompt and regenerate.
### 3. Composite the model
1. Import your lesson 1 model layer over studiobg01.jpg.
2. Position the model centred in the frame.
You should see: the model standing on the backdrop, still floating without shadows.
If not: if edges look cut out, refine the mask edge before continuing.
### 4. Match light and cast shadows
1. Check that highlights on the face and shoulders match the backdrop's light direction (for example key light from top-left).

chunks.title: High-converting Studio Lookbooks — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: High-converting Studio Lookbooks / Step by step.
2. Paint a soft shadow on the screen where shoulders and torso block the light; set the layer to 25% opacity and Multiply blend mode.
3. Paint a soft contact shadow under the shoes at the baseline.
You should see: the model sits in the scene, lit from the same side as the backdrop.
If not: if the shadow looks pasted on, soften the brush and lower the opacity.
### 5. Grade and export
1. Create one global grading layer (gradient map, LUT or Lightroom preset).
2. Shift shadows slightly toward teal and midtones toward warm beige; limit maximum contrast so dark fabrics keep detail.
3. Export as high-quality WebP, at least 2000px vertical so shop zoom stays sharp.
You should see: a finished lookbook image with a unified colour feel.
If not: if skin looks over-smoothed or orange, reduce the grade strength and skip blur filters.

chunks.title: High-converting Studio Lookbooks — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: High-converting Studio Lookbooks / Check yourself.
 [ ] My moodboard names a theme, palette and lighting setup.
 [ ] Backdrop light direction matches the model's light.
 [ ] Shadow layer is 25% Multiply, with a contact shadow at the shoes.
 [ ] One grade is applied, and the export is at least 2000px vertical.

chunks.title: High-converting Studio Lookbooks — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: High-converting Studio Lookbooks / Common mistakes.
 Mixed themes. A sand plaster screen for one model and a concrete warehouse for the next breaks the story.
 Harsh direct light. Stick to diffused side softbox light.
 Over-smoothed skin. Keep natural pores and hair texture; it builds credibility.
 Grading each image by hand. Apply one shared grade across the whole set.

chunks.title: High-converting Studio Lookbooks — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: High-converting Studio Lookbooks / Go further.
Worked example, cashmere collection (Nordic Autumn). Minimalist plaster backdrop, soft side daylight, earth tones. Backdrop: a warm grey stucco wall with a soft window-frame shadow. Model: beige oversized organic cashmere knit sweater. Grading: shadows teal shift +5%, highlights gold shift +8%, 5% digital grain for a film feel. Export 1080x1350px vertical. Result: a 10-page editorial lookbook ready for print and web.

2. Medium: generate 2 backdrops with different prompts but identical palette and lighting angles.
3. Hard: composite a model on your backdrop, apply a custom LUT matching the model's highlights to the backdrop's warm tone, and add a soft grain layer.

chunks.title: Sizing & Layout Consistency
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Sizing & Layout Consistency.
# Sizing & Layout Consistency
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: one model image aligned to a 1080 x 1350px grid (shoulders at Y 400, seam at X 540) and exported as WebP.
---

chunks.title: Sizing & Layout Consistency — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Sizing & Layout Consistency / Before you start.
If head size or shoulder height jumps between product pages, a store looks cheap, and aligning by eye always produces errors. The fix is a standard grid. Three rules: align the shoulder joints to the same Y coordinate on every image; keep margins on a 4:5 vertical canvas (1080x1350px) of 10% at the bottom for the feet and 12% at the top for head clearance; and put the garment's vertical centre seam (zipper or buttons) on the canvas centre X.
You will need:
 A model try-on render (from lesson 1).
 templates/mannequin-alignment-template.md.
 An editor with guides (Photoshop, Photopea). SmartVideo GO AI Image Studio can produce the render; menus move, so follow the current screen.

chunks.title: Sizing & Layout Consistency — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Sizing & Layout Consistency / Step by step.
### 1. Set up the canvas grid
1. Open templates/mannequin-alignment-template.md.
2. In your editor, set canvas size to 1080 x 1350px.
3. Add a vertical guide at X: 540px and horizontal guides: Shoulder Line Y: 400px, Waist Line Y: 750px, Hip Line Y: 950px.
You should see: a blank canvas with one vertical and three horizontal guides.
If not: if guides will not snap, turn on snapping in your editor's View menu.
### 2. Import the model layer
Import your try-on render and place it roughly in the centre.
You should see: the model over the grid, not yet aligned.
If not: if the layer is far too big or small, scale it down or up first before fine alignment.
### 3. Align the shoulders
1. Scale the layer proportionally (hold Shift).
2. Drag until the left and right shoulder seams sit on the Shoulder Line (Y: 400px).
3. Let head and legs scale naturally.
You should see: both shoulder seams touching the 400px guide.
If not: if the shoulders are tilted, check the pose; a tilted source cannot be fixed by scaling.
### 4. Align the centre seam
Move the layer left or right until the collar button or zipper line sits on the vertical guide (X: 540px).
You should see: the seam straight on the centre guide.
If not: if the garment looks tilted, not just offset, regenerate with a straighter pose.
### 5. Check margins and export

chunks.title: Sizing & Layout Consistency — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Sizing & Layout Consistency / Step by step.
1. Make sure the head does not cross the top safety line and hands and sides stay inside the side padding.
2. Hide the grid layers and export as WebP.
3. Repeat for every item in the collection.
You should see: a clean image with no guides, framed with the 12% top and 10% bottom margins.
If not: if the head is clipped, rescale slightly smaller and re-align the shoulders.

chunks.title: Sizing & Layout Consistency — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Sizing & Layout Consistency / Check yourself.
 [ ] The canvas is 1080 x 1350px with guides at X 540 and Y 400 / 750 / 950.
 [ ] Shoulders sit on Y 400 and the seam on X 540.
 [ ] Top and bottom margins are respected.
 [ ] I exported WebP without grid layers.

chunks.title: Sizing & Layout Consistency — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Sizing & Layout Consistency / Common mistakes.
 Aligning by eye. Always snap to guides.
 Changing camera height between shots. Keep the camera at chest level (about 4 feet) so perspective stays the same and baselines align.
 Aligning the head instead of the shoulders. Shoulders are the garment's anchor.
 Undocumented grid settings. Record them in the alignment template and share with your team.

chunks.title: Sizing & Layout Consistency — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Sizing & Layout Consistency / Go further.
Worked example, 5-item windbreaker collection. Catalog 1080x1350px, centre guide X 540, shoulder guide Y 400, waist guide Y 750. Five VTO renders (black, blue, orange, red, grey) were scaled so shoulder seams snapped to Y 400 and zippers were centred. Result: on the catalog page the models stand at the same height and centre, so shoppers compare colours without distraction.
Motion loop: templates/examples/mannequin-grid-clip.mp4
Compare tools
| Tool | Automation | Layout control | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Photoshop / Photopea | Low (manual scaling) | Ultra-high | High-end listing QC |
| Python Pillow (PIL) | Ultra-high (scripted crop and align using keypoints) | Medium | Large catalogs |
| Figma | Low | High | UI mockups, page layout checks |
For 1000+ catalog updates, a script using a keypoint model such as YOLO-pose to detect shoulder joints and auto-crop is the standard way to scale.

chunks.title: Before/After Conversion Cases, part 2 — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Before/After Conversion Cases, part 2 / Before you start.
Part 1 gave you a return rate and new listing images. Now you prove they work. Apparel tests need about 30 days because returns arrive late, so you must measure both conversion rate (CVR) and return rate, then compare net profit after return shipping. The worked example in Go further went from 28.0% returns to 16.5% with the same approach.
You will need:
 The three body-type images with callouts from part 1.
 templates/fashion-cvr-tracker.md and your store's testing app.
 Optional return-tracking and analytics tools (see Go further).

chunks.title: Before/After Conversion Cases, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Before/After Conversion Cases, part 2 / Step by step.
### 1. Define the two variants
1. Control (Variant A): the standard ghost mannequin gallery photos.
2. Test (Variant B): the AI model photos with different body types and measurement callouts.
Write both in the tracker's split-test log.
You should see: two clearly named variants in your log.
If not: change one thing at a time where you can, so results stay readable.
### 2. Start the 50/50 split
Configure your testing app to split incoming traffic 50/50 between A and B, and start the test.
You should see: the test marked as running in your testing app.
If not: testing apps differ and menus move; follow the current screen, or use your platform's help page.
### 3. Record the start date and baselines
In the tracker, write the start date, baseline CVR and baseline return rate for A.
You should see: a dated baseline row.
If not: with no data yet, start recording from day one.
### 4. After 30 days, compare results
1. Check CVR and return rate for both variants.
2. Calculate net profit margin after subtracting return shipping costs.
You should see: a side-by-side table of A and B.
If not: if returns are still arriving, extend a few days before deciding.
### 5. Decide
If Variant B shows fewer returns and more sales, push it live across the entire product category. Otherwise keep A and review your return reasons again.
You should see: a written decision in the tracker.

chunks.title: Before/After Conversion Cases — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Before/After Conversion Cases / Before you start.
Online apparel stores typically see return rates of 20% to 40%, mostly from fit errors ("tighter than it looked", "longer than I realised"), and returns destroy margin. Static mannequin shots also convert poorly. Showing the same garment on several body shapes helps: shoppers who see products on models matching their build are 40% more likely to convert. Pair that with a clear callout of the model's measurements, for example height, build and size worn.
This is part 1 of 2. Here you diagnose and build the assets; in part 2 you run the 30-day test.
You will need:
 Your store's returns data (or mock data) and templates/fashion-cvr-tracker.md.
 The try-on workflow from lesson 1 (Garment Try-on) and a photo editor.
 SmartVideo GO AI Image Studio for the try-ons.

chunks.title: Before/After Conversion Cases — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Before/After Conversion Cases / Step by step.
### 1. Calculate your return rate
1. Open templates/fashion-cvr-tracker.md.
2. Compute return rate: returned units divided by units sold (for example 90 returned of 500 sold is 18%).
You should see: a return rate percentage in your tracker.
If not: if you have no store data, use the mock numbers from the worked example in Go further.
### 2. Read the return reasons
Read the return reason logs. If over 50% of returns mention "too small", "too large" or "poor fit", optimize the model listings.
You should see: a count of fit-related returns against the 50% threshold.
If not: if fit is not the main reason, fix the real reason first; this fix will not help.
### 3. Generate three body-type try-ons
Pick your best-selling garment and, following lesson 1, generate three try-on variations: slim, athletic and curvy.
You should see: the same garment on three clearly different body shapes.
If not: if the garment changes between images, reuse the same garmentref.png and fitting rate 0.75.
### 4. Add a measurement callout
In your photo editor add a clean, low-contrast text bar at the bottom of the listing image, in your brand font:
text
Model is 5'9" (175cm), athletic build, wearing size Small.
Use the model's real height, build and size.
You should see: a legible bar that does not cover the garment.
If not: keep it in the same position on every page, using your lesson 3 layout guidelines.

chunks.title: Before/After Conversion Cases — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Before/After Conversion Cases / Check yourself.
 [ ] I calculated a return rate as returned divided by sold.
 [ ] I know whether more than 50% of returns are fit-related.
 [ ] I have three body-type try-on images of one garment.
 [ ] The callout states the true model height, build and size.

chunks.title: Before/After Conversion Cases — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Before/After Conversion Cases / Common mistakes.
 Lying in the overlay. Listing a model as size Medium when they wear XS raises returns.
 Optimizing without data. Check return reasons first.
 Inconsistent callout placement. Keep it in the same spot on every page.

chunks.title: Before/After Conversion Cases — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Before/After Conversion Cases / Go further.
Worked example, denim brand. Baseline: 28% return rate with flat-lay-only photos. Variant B used three models: Model 1 (5'11", slim, size 26), Model 2 (5'8", curvy, size 30), Model 3 (5'6", petite, size 25), with height and waist tags. 30-day results: return rate 28.0% (280 of 1,000 sold) for A versus 16.5% (165 of 1,000) for B; CVR up 38% (1.8% to 2.5%); $4,600 saved in return shipping and net revenue up $7,000 in one month.

2. Medium: complete the CVR and return log in the tracker with mock data.

# Empty Room → Staged Room Pipeline
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: one staged room photo, staged-living-room.jpg, made from a vacant room with its perspective and floor intact.
---

chunks.title: Empty Room → Staged Room Pipeline — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Empty Room → Staged Room Pipeline / Before you start.
Empty rooms feel smaller and colder, and buyers struggle to picture living there. The National Association of Realtors (NAR) reports that 81% of buyers find it easier to visualize a property as a future home when it is staged, and staged homes sell for up to 20% more. Physical staging costs $2,500 to $5,000+ per month and takes 3 to 7 days. Careless editing makes furniture look flat or floating. This lesson uses perspective-locked, depth-aware inpainting: depth mask, perspective alignment, furniture inpainting, then shadow checking.
You will need: a vacant room photo (your own, or a stock photo of an empty room), basic comfort with image prompts, and Image Studio in SmartVideo GO AI (menus move; follow the current screen). Keep templates/virtual-staging-brief.md open.

chunks.title: Empty Room → Staged Room Pipeline — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Empty Room → Staged Room Pipeline / Step by step.
### 1. Pick the source photograph
1. Choose a high-resolution wide-angle photo of a vacant room. Real estate lenses are 16-24mm.
2. It should be straight (level horizon, vertical walls) and lit by natural daylight.
3. Save it as empty-room-source.jpg.
You should see: a bright, level photo of an empty room with a clear floor and windows.
If not: if walls lean or the horizon tilts, choose another photo. Furniture will look skewed if perspective is off.
### 2. Mask the floor area
1. Open your photo editor or the inpainting interface.
2. Paint a mask over the open floor where furniture will sit, covering 60-70% of the open floor space.
3. Keep windows, fireplaces, support columns and structural walls untouched.
You should see: a mask layer on the floor only, with structural features outside it.
If not: if the mask touches windows or walls, erase those parts. Otherwise the AI may alter them.
### 3. Choose a style from the brief
Open templates/virtual-staging-brief.md. Pick one style preset. Examples:
 Modern Scandinavian: light oak, neutral linen sofas, minimalist coffee tables, potted monstera plants.
 Contemporary Luxury: velvet sectionals, marble coffee tables, brass accent lighting, plush area rugs.
 Coastal Modern: light textiles, rattan accents, soft blues, woven jute rugs, warm natural sunlight.
You should see: one style chosen, with its furniture list in front of you.

chunks.title: Empty Room → Staged Room Pipeline — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Empty Room → Staged Room Pipeline / Step by step.
If not: if unsure, use Contemporary Luxury, which matches the prompt in the next step.
### 4. Paste the staging prompt
Add the prompt in Image Studio. It starts with architectural and lighting anchor words that match the original photo:
text
High-end modern luxury living room virtual staging. A sleek cream fabric L-shaped sectional sofa with plush pillows resting on a soft beige area rug, low-profile oval wood coffee table, potted fiddle-leaf fig in ceramic planter, natural sunlight casting soft shadows, interior design magazine style, 8k photorealistic resolution, perfectly aligned to floor plane.
Then add the negative prompt:
text
warped floor, distorted furniture legs, floating objects, cartoon, low resolution, blurry, altered windows, altered walls, 3d render look, oversaturated.
You should see: both prompts entered in their own fields.
If not: if there is no negative prompt field, look for "avoid" or "exclude"; menus move, so follow the current screen.
### 5. Run the inpainting with depth reference
1. Give the tool empty-room-source.jpg and your mask. Models used in this course include FLUX Inpainting and muapi /nano-banana-2 in inpainting mode.
2. Set ControlNet Depth weight to 0.75 so floor geometry is enforced while the model still builds 3D furniture.
3. Generate.
You should see: a staged image with furniture inside the masked floor area.

chunks.title: Empty Room → Staged Room Pipeline — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Empty Room → Staged Room Pipeline / Step by step.
If not: if furniture floats or warps, raise the depth weight slightly and run again.
### 6. Check contact shadows at 100% zoom
1. Zoom to 100%.
2. Floor contact: sofa and table legs should touch the floor with dark, tight contact shadows (ambient occlusion).
3. Light source: highlights on the furniture should match the window sunlight direction.
You should see: grounded furniture with shadows consistent with the window light.
If not: regenerate. Check that the prompt still says "perfectly aligned to floor plane".
### 7. Save the result
Save the final image as staged-living-room.jpg. Keep it next to empty-room-source.jpg for lessons 2 and 3.
You should see: both files in your folder.
If not: if the export is small, re-export at the highest resolution available.

chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Empty Room → Staged Room Pipeline / Common mistakes.
 Using a tilted photo, which skews furniture.
 Masking windows, doors or walls, which lets the AI alter them.
 Skipping the negative prompt, which allows floating objects and warped floors.
 Judging the result only at thumbnail size instead of 100% zoom.

chunks.text:

Furniture pack: Scandinavian Luxury (cream sectional, oak coffee table, textured rug, indoor botanicals). Settings: denoising strength 0.65, depth weight 0.80, 16:9 aspect ratio to match the camera. Result: 4 minutes processing, $0.06 AI cost versus a $3,200 physical staging quote. # Pricing Against Traditional Staging
 Time: about 16 minutes. You will finish with: a filled pricing sheet, three packages, a margin calculation and a one-page comparison deck outline.
---

chunks.title: Pricing Against Traditional Staging — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing Against Traditional Staging / Before you start.
Beginners fall into a commodity trap, charging $5 to $10 per photo against low-quality editors. Agents spend $2,500 to $6,000 on physical staging, so a $10 offer looks cheap and unfit for high-end MLS listings. The fix is to sell speed and listing ROI: Listing ROI = (Perceived Property Value Increase - Staging Cost) / Days on Market (DOM). Each vacant day costs the seller or realtor mortgage carrying costs, HOA fees and taxes, averaging $100 to $250/day. Anchor against a $3,000 physical quote: a 5-room package at $199 is a 93% cost savings with 95%+ of the visual impact.
You will need: lesson 1 finished (Empty Room → Staged Room Pipeline), templates/realtor-pricing-sheet.md, and Canva or Google Slides for the deck. Image Studio and Video Studio produce the deliverables.

chunks.title: Pricing Against Traditional Staging — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing Against Traditional Staging / Step by step.
### 1. Benchmark local physical staging costs
1. Search physical staging companies in your target city.
2. Note their rates. Typical figures: setup fee $1,500 - $2,500; monthly furniture rental $1,000 - $2,000/month.
3. Enter them in the sales comparison matrix in templates/realtor-pricing-sheet.md.
You should see: a comparison matrix with your local competitor figures.
If not: if you find no local quotes, use the typical figures above and mark them as estimates.
### 2. Set up three productized packages
Write these into your pricing sheet:
text
Essential Package - $99
- 3 Staged Rooms
- 1 Style Revision
- 24h Turnaround
- High-Res MLS Specs
Full House Tier - $199
- 6 Staged Rooms
- 2 Style Variations
- Virtual Twilight Shot
- 24h Turnaround
Luxury Agency Pass - $399
- 8 Staged Rooms
- Virtual Decluttering
- 2 Motion Video Clips
- Same-Day Turnaround
You should see: three clear tiers in your sheet.
If not: if the layout is messy, a simple list per package is fine.
### 3. Price the add-ons
Add these to the sheet:
 Virtual Decluttering / Furniture Removal (removing old tenant furniture before staging): +$25/photo.
 Virtual Twilight Conversion (daytime exterior to dusk): +$30/photo.
 Staging Motion Clips (5-second image-to-video walkthroughs for Reels and TikTok): +$40/clip.
You should see: three add-ons with prices.

chunks.title: Pricing Against Traditional Staging — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing Against Traditional Staging / Step by step.
If not: keep the prices above, then adjust them for your market later.
### 4. Calculate gross margin for the Full House Tier
Work through the unit economics:
1. Generation cost (muapi / FLUX): about $0.06 per room x 6 rooms = $0.36.
2. Storage and delivery: $0.05.
3. Production cost: $0.41 (the 15 minutes of prompting time is about $10 labor equivalent, not counted here).
4. Package revenue $199 - $0.41 = $198.59 gross profit (99.8% margin).
You should see: your sheet showing $198.59 gross profit.
If not: recheck that 6 rooms x $0.06 = $0.36, then add $0.05.
### 5. Build the Staging Comparison Deck
Make a 1-page visual PDF in Canva or Google Slides:
1. Left side: Physical Staging ($3,500, 5-day setup, 1 static style).
2. Right side: your AI Virtual Staging ($199, 24h delivery, 3 style choices: Modern, Scandinavian, Luxury).
3. Add the savings line: $3,301 saved and 4 days faster.
You should see: a one-page two-column comparison.
If not: if it is crowded, cut to the three numbers: price, days, styles.
### 6. Write your negotiation rules
Add two rules to your sheet:
 100% upfront payment. Real estate moves fast; collect card payment (for example via Stripe invoicing) before releasing unwatermarked high-res MLS files.
 Limit revisions. Include 1 free style revision per photo (for example Scandinavian oak to Industrial black metal), then charge $15 per photo.

chunks.title: Selling to Realtors & Agencies — Before you start
