Academy lesson: Selling to Realtors & Agencies / Before you start.
Generic emails like "I do AI virtual staging for $10" get deleted. Agents with active vacant listings that have sat on Redfin or Zillow for 20+ days are losing money and facing seller pressure, so reach them then. The method is the "Active Vacant Listing" Audit: find a vacant listing, make a staged sample, send a personalized email, then close a retainer. The four stages are precision prospecting, a free transformation hook, hyper-personalized outreach, and retainer locking ($499-$1,299/month). This part covers the first three; part 2 covers video audits, the retainer and scaling.
You will need: lessons 1 and 2 (Module 1 Pipeline, Pricing & Packaging), a Zillow or Redfin account view, and templates/agency-outreach-template.md. Image Studio makes the sample.

chunks.title: Selling to Realtors & Agencies — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling to Realtors & Agencies / Step by step.
### 1. Filter for vacant listings
Open Zillow or Redfin and apply:
 Status: For Sale (Active).
 Keywords: "vacant", "empty", "unfurnished", "bring your ideas".
 Days on Zillow: 14+ days.
You should see: a list of active listings with empty rooms in the photos.
If not: filters move between sites; follow the current screen, or widen your search area.
### 2. Record 10 prospects
Extract 10 listing URLs. For each, note the listing agent's name, email and brokerage into templates/agency-outreach-template.md. Prefer listings at 20+ days on market. Tools such as Apollo.io or Hunter.io can help find contact info (free tiers exist).

If not: if agent emails are hidden, check the brokerage website, or fill the rest in later and start with the ones you have.
### 3. Create the proof-of-value sample
1. Download the hero empty living room image from Listing #1.
2. Run it through your Module 1 Pipeline with a sleek Modern Scandinavian theme in Image Studio.
3. Save the before/after asset as sample-staging-listing1.jpg.
You should see: a before/after image of that exact room, furnished.
If not: if furniture warps, redo the mask and depth settings from lesson 1.
### 4. Personalize the email
Copy this email, replace the bracketed parts, and attach or embed the before/after:

chunks.title: Consistent Headshot Generation, part 2 — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Consistent Headshot Generation, part 2 / Before you start.
Part 1 gave you an identity-locked render. Now you keep it believable. Low-end filters destroy natural pores, fine wrinkles and freckles, so you inspect at 100% zoom and keep the identity seed locked while changing clothes. Professional lighting follows a 3-point idea: a key light (softbox at 45 degrees, Rembrandt or Butterfly pattern), a fill light (soft light on the shadow side) and a rim / hair light (backlight separating hair and shoulders).
You will need your render from part 1 and Image Studio. Menus move; follow the current screen.

chunks.title: Consistent Headshot Generation, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Consistent Headshot Generation, part 2 / Step by step.
### 1. Check the 3-point lighting on your render
1. Look for a key light shaping one side of the face, soft fill in the shadow side, and a rim edge on hair and shoulders.
2. If one is missing, add it to the prompt (for example "subtle rim light separating shoulders from background") and regenerate.
You should see: dimension on the face, no harsh dark patches, and a clean edge around hair and shoulders.
If not: add "soft Rembrandt key light" to the prompt and keep the negative prompt "harsh direct flash".
### 2. Swap clothing and background with inpainting
1. If the client wants variations (formal suit versus business casual sweater), run targeted inpainting over the torso area only.
2. Keep the facial identity seed locked so the face does not change.
You should see: new clothing on the same face and the same lighting.
If not: if the face shifts, your mask touched the head. Redraw the mask below the chin.
### 3. Inspect skin and eyes at 100% zoom
1. Zoom to 100%. Confirm visible natural pores and authentic eye catchlights.
2. Apply subtle sharpening to the iris reflections, and use frequency separation in post if skin looks flat.
You should see: realistic skin micro-texture, not a smooth mannequin face.
If not: re-run with denoising strength nearer 0.40 and the negative prompt "plastic skin, smooth mannequin face".
### 4. Save the final file

chunks.title: Consistent Headshot Generation — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Consistent Headshot Generation / Before you start.
Traditional studio headshots cost $250 to $600 per person, take 5 to 7 days for edited proofs, and are nearly impossible to keep consistent across a remote team. Basic face swaps and over-filtered presets look fake: waxy skin, drifting eye colors, rows of artificial teeth, and background light that does not match the face. The fix is a pipeline: casual selfie, then identity lock, then a studio lighting and outfit prompt, then detail and skin-texture checks. Identity-locking models (InstantID / FLUX PuLID) read face landmarks (eye spacing, jawline, nose bridge, skin tone) from 1 to 3 selfies so the result looks like the subject.
You will need 3 to 5 casual photos of one willing subject (yourself is fine), the file templates/headshot-style-guide.md, and access to SmartVideo GO AI Image Studio (use AI Influencer Studio if you want the same face to recur). Menus move; follow the current screen.

chunks.title: Consistent Headshot Generation — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Consistent Headshot Generation / Step by step.
### 1. Collect quality source selfies
1. Gather 3 to 5 casual photos: well lit by window daylight, no heavy filters, no sunglasses, neutral or smiling expression.
2. Make sure they show direct eye contact and varying angles (front-facing and 3/4 turn).
You should see: a small folder of sharp, evenly lit photos where the face is clearly visible.
If not: retake any photo that is dark, filtered or hides the eyes. Weak sources produce weak identity locks.
### 2. Open the style guide and pick a tier
1. Open templates/headshot-style-guide.md.
2. Choose the target tier: Executive Corporate or Creative Tech Founder.
You should see: the lighting, wardrobe and negative prompt entries for your chosen tier.
If not: if the file will not open, use the prompts in the next steps directly.
### 3. Assemble the studio prompt
Copy the prompt for your tier and replace [Identity Anchor] with your subject description. Executive Corporate:
text
Photorealistic 8k corporate studio portrait photograph of [Identity Anchor], confident friendly expression, wearing a tailored charcoal navy blazer and crisp white shirt, soft Rembrandt key light, subtle rim light separating shoulders from background, blurred modern glass office background with soft bokeh, shot on 85mm f/1.8 lens, natural skin pores, studio quality.
Creative Tech Founder:
text

chunks.title: Consistent Headshot Generation — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Consistent Headshot Generation / Step by step.
Photorealistic 8k editorial portrait photograph of [Identity Anchor], warm approachable smile, wearing a stylish dark grey turtleneck, soft warm studio lighting, neutral grey gradient background, crisp focus on eyes, 85mm lens, highly detailed.
Negative prompt (use with either):
text
plastic skin, smooth mannequin face, extra teeth, asymmetric eyes, cartoon, oversaturated, harsh direct flash, warped neck, low resolution, blurry.
You should see: one complete positive prompt plus the negative prompt, with no leftover square brackets.
If not: if a bracket remains, the generator may draw it literally. Replace it with a short description of the subject.
### 4. Run identity-locked inference
1. In Image Studio, add your selfies as the face reference and paste the prompt and negative prompt.
2. Set the aspect ratio to 1:1 for LinkedIn/Slack avatars or 4:5 for executive team pages.
3. Use the settings from the worked example as a starting point: denoising strength 0.45 (keep within 0.40–0.55), identity weight 0.85. Generate.
You should see: a portrait that looks unmistakably like your subject, in studio light with a soft office or gradient background.
If not: if the face drifts, raise identity weight slightly or add a better reference selfie. If the skin looks waxy, lower denoising strength toward 0.40.

chunks.title: Consistent Headshot Generation — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Consistent Headshot Generation / Check yourself.
 [ ] I used 3 to 5 sharp, well-lit selfies with eye contact.
 [ ] My prompt has an identity anchor, lighting, wardrobe, lens and the negative prompt.
 [ ] I rendered at 1:1 or 4:5 with denoising 0.40-0.55.
 [ ] The result looks like the person, not a random face.

chunks.title: Consistent Headshot Generation — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Consistent Headshot Generation / Common mistakes.
 Over-filtered source photos. Filters carry into the render; use plain window daylight.
 Denoising too high. Above about 0.55 the model rewrites skin and identity.
 Skipping the negative prompt. It is what keeps plastic skin and extra teeth away.
 Leaving [Identity Anchor] unfilled.

The consumer AI headshot market is commoditized: apps and Fiverr freelancers sell $5 to $10 packs. At that price, acquisition costs eat margins and refund requests ruin profit. Creative professionals reject bland corporate photography. Keynote speakers and authors want dramatic stage light and dark moody backgrounds; podcasters and music artists want gel accents (neon cyan, warm amber); tech founders and designers want relaxed environmental settings like sunlit lofts and brick walls. Clients like these pay $150 to $350 per custom portrait pack. The pipeline: identity lock, cinematic mood prompt, gel and environment light, then editorial polish. Three styles: Keynote Speaker (dark background, strong key, warm rim), Tech Founder Loft (brick, soft window light, casual attire) and Podcast / Media Creator (magenta key plus cyan rim, dark studio).
You will need a client selfie (lesson 1 standards), templates/headshot-style-guide.md, and SmartVideo GO AI Image Studio. Menus move; follow the current screen.

chunks.title: Designing Sellable AI Art for Merch — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Designing Sellable AI Art for Merch / Before you start.
Raw AI images (1024x1024px) pixelate when stretched across a t-shirt chest print area that needs 4500x5400px at 300 DPI. A solid-background image prints as an ugly box on the shirt, and dark or muddy colors wash out in direct-to-garment (DTG) ink. The fix is a pipeline: isolated vector prompt, then transparent PNG, then 4x upscale, then mockup.
You need access to SmartVideo GO AI Image Studio (generation) and Video Studio (optional showcase motion), a background remover and an AI upscaler (tools below), and the template templates/merch-prompt-brief.md. No prerequisites.

chunks.title: Designing Sellable AI Art for Merch — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Designing Sellable AI Art for Merch / Step by step.
### 1. Open the prompt brief
Open templates/merch-prompt-brief.md and keep it beside Image Studio.
You should see: vector style prompts, DPI specs and negative prompts.
If not: check the Templates list in the track overview for the file.
### 2. Write the vector prompt
Draft this apparel-optimized prompt:
text
Clean vector t-shirt graphic of a cyberpunk samurai cat wearing futuristic glowing neon goggles, Japanese typography, bold outlines, vibrant synthwave colors, isolated on solid black background, high contrast, 8k graphic.
You should see: a single prompt that names subject, style, outlines, colors and an isolated solid background.
If not: add "vector illustration, isolated on white background, clean lines, bold graphic, high contrast, 300 DPI" as the style core.
### 3. Add the negative prompt
Use this negative prompt with it:
text
photograph, realistic skin, complex background, gradient box, blurry lines, low resolution, noise, drop shadow.
You should see: the negative field filled in beside the prompt.
If not: if your tool has no negative field, say "no photograph, no drop shadow, no gradient box" inside the prompt.
### 4. Generate the graphic
Run the prompt with muapi /nano-banana-2.
You should see: a bold graphic with strong outlines on a solid background.
If not: if it looks like a photo or has a busy background, regenerate and keep the negative prompt.

chunks.title: Designing Sellable AI Art for Merch — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Designing Sellable AI Art for Merch / Step by step.
### 5. Isolate the artwork
Pass the output to an AI background remover (Photoroom or Clipdrop) and save merch-graphic-transparent.png.
You should see: the artwork on a checkerboard (transparent) background with no box.
If not: try again from a solid-color background; edges are cleaner when the subject stands out.
### 6. Upscale 4x
Run an AI upscaler (Real-ESRGAN, muapi high-res upscaling, or Vectorizer.ai for vector SVG) at a 4x scale factor.
You should see: the image at least 4500px wide, with crisp, sharp linework.
If not: if it is smaller, run the upscaler again on the result or choose a higher scale; if edges are soft, regenerate with bolder outlines.
### 7. Boost vibrancy
Raise color vibrancy about +15% before exporting, because POD ink absorbs slightly into the fabric. Also check contrast on dark vs. light garments (white linework for black tees, dark linework for white or heather grey).
You should see: punchy colors that still keep detail.
If not: if colors clip or look neon-flat, back off the boost a little.
### 8. Place it on a mockup
Place merch-graphic-transparent.png on a heavy cotton t-shirt mockup in your editor, about 2 inches below the neck collar.
You should see: the graphic sitting cleanly on the shirt with no rectangle behind it.
If not: a visible box means the background was not fully removed; redo step 5.

chunks.title: Print-on-Demand Platform Basics — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Print-on-Demand Platform Basics / Before you start.
Great artwork is half the job. Traditional inventory means buying 100+ shirts upfront in S, M, L and XL, storing boxes and risking unsold stock. Print-on-Demand (POD) removes that risk: when a customer buys, the supplier prints and ships automatically. The flow is: customer orders on Etsy or Shopify, the order auto-syncs to the print supplier (Printify), it is printed and shipped by DTG (Direct-to-Garment, inkjet printing onto fabric one item at a time, no minimum order), and tracking is sent to the customer automatically.
You need your merch-graphic-transparent.png from lesson 1 (Designing Sellable AI Art for Merch), an Etsy or Shopify store, and SmartVideo GO AI Image Studio for lifestyle mockups. Use only your own accounts and sign in through each service's own page; never paste passwords or keys into chat.

chunks.title: Print-on-Demand Platform Basics — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Print-on-Demand Platform Basics / Step by step.
### 1. Create the supplier account
Create a Printify (or Printful) account. Printify has the vendor network and lowest base prices; Printful has in-house print quality.
You should see: your supplier dashboard.
If not: menus move; follow the current screen and the supplier's help page.
### 2. Connect your store
Link the supplier to your Etsy or Shopify store using the OAuth connection (sign in on the store's own page and approve).
You should see: your store listed as connected in the supplier.
If not: allow pop-ups and try again; if it shows the wrong store, disconnect and reconnect.
### 3. Pick a garment
Select a garment such as the Bella+Canvas 3001 Unisex Tee.
You should see: a blank product mockup with a printable area.
If not: search the catalog for the garment name.
### 4. Upload and center the graphic
Upload merch-graphic-transparent.png (300 DPI) and center it on the printable area.
You should see: the artwork on the shirt with no box behind it.
If not: a box means the PNG is not transparent; redo the background removal from lesson 1.
### 5. Make lifestyle mockups
Generate lifestyle product photos with your AI photography pipeline from templates/merch-prompt-brief.md (Image Studio) or use Printify mockup tools.
You should see: the shirt or mug shown in a real-world setting.
If not: simplify the scene prompt; keep the product the hero.
### 6. Turn on automatic fulfillment

chunks.title: Print-on-Demand Platform Basics — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Print-on-Demand Platform Basics / Step by step.
Enable Automatic Fulfillment in your supplier settings so incoming store orders process without manual intervention.
You should see: the setting shown as on.
If not: menus move; check the current screen under order or store settings.
### 7. Set a backup supplier
Set up backup supplier routing in Printify so if one print shop runs out of stock on black L shirts, orders route to a secondary supplier.
You should see: a second print provider listed as fallback.
If not: not every product offers this; note it and check again later.

chunks.title: Building a Catalog Without Repeating Yourself, part 2 — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a Catalog Without Repeating Yourself, part 2 / Before you start.
You have 12 graphics from part 1. Now you turn them into a sellable catalog: isolate and upscale in batch, apply each graphic to 3 high-margin product types, and clear trademark risk. 12 graphics x 3 products = 36 unique store listings.
You need the 12 generated graphics, your connected supplier from lesson 2, a background remover and upscaler from lesson 1, and templates/merch-prompt-brief.md (trademark checklist).

chunks.title: Building a Catalog Without Repeating Yourself, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a Catalog Without Repeating Yourself, part 2 / Step by step.
### 1. Isolate all 12 backgrounds
Run each graphic through your AI background remover and save transparent PNGs.
You should see: 12 transparent PNGs with no boxes.
If not: redo any with leftover background; regenerate if edges stay messy.
### 2. Upscale all 12 in batch
Upscale with a 4x factor to at least 4500px wide at 300 DPI.
You should see: 12 crisp, print-ready files.
If not: rerun any that look soft, as in lesson 1.
### 3. Pick three product types
Choose three high-margin products: T-Shirt, Coffee Mug, Canvas Tote Bag.
You should see: three product templates ready in your supplier.
If not: pick the closest available product.
### 4. Cross-publish
Apply each graphic to each of the 3 products and publish to your store.
You should see: a path to 36 listings (12 x 3).
If not: start with one graphic on all 3 products, confirm it looks right, then repeat.
### 5. Check trademarks
Never use trademarked names (for example Disney, Marvel, Nike) or celebrity likenesses in prompts or store tags. Search the USPTO TESS database before publishing, and use the checklist in templates/merch-prompt-brief.md.
You should see: no protected names in any graphic, title or tag.
If not: remove or rename the listing before it goes live.

chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a Catalog Without Repeating Yourself / Before you start.
Real revenue on Etsy or POD marketplaces needs a catalog of 50 to 200+ listings. Two mistakes sink creators: spamming near-identical designs with tiny color tweaks (flagged as listing spam), and burning hours on one-off prompts. The fix is a Niche Prompt Matrix that expands one core theme across sub-niches and styles, for example Retro Vintage Animals, then Cat / Dog / Owl / Bear, then 80s Synthwave / Japanese Ink / Minimal Line, giving 12 distinct listings.
You need lesson 1 (Designing Sellable AI Art for Merch) and lesson 2 (Print-on-Demand Platform Basics) done, templates/merch-prompt-brief.md, and SmartVideo GO AI Image Studio and Storyboard / Campaign Planner for batch matrices.

chunks.title: Pricing & Passive-Income Math for POD — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Passive-Income Math for POD / Before you start.
Many POD sellers make sales but lose money, because they price a t-shirt at $19.99 and ignore fees: Etsy listing fee ($0.20), transaction fee (6.5%), payment processing (~3% + $0.25), supplier garment cost ($9.50) plus shipping ($4.75), and ad spend ($2 - $5 per sale). Together Etsy fees are roughly 9.5 - 10% of retail, which this model uses. The goal is $7 to $12 net profit per sale.
Net Profit = Retail Price - (Print Supplier Cost + Shipping) - Marketplace Fees - Ad Spend
You need lessons 1 to 3, a spreadsheet (Google Sheets or Excel), and templates/pod-pricing-calculator.md. SmartVideo GO AI Storyboard / Campaign Planner can hold test plans.

chunks.title: Pricing & Passive-Income Math for POD — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Passive-Income Math for POD / Step by step.
### 1. Open the calculator
Open templates/pod-pricing-calculator.md.
You should see: COGS models, margin calculators and fee formulas.
If not: copy its columns into a new spreadsheet.
### 2. Enter T-shirt costs
Bella+Canvas 3001: $9.25 print + $4.75 shipping = $14.00 base.
You should see: $14.00 in your base-cost cell.
If not: recheck the addition.
### 3. Enter mug and hoodie costs
Ceramic Mug (11oz White): $4.50 + $5.00 = $9.50 base. Heavyweight Hoodie (Gildan 18000): $18.50 + $7.50 = $26.00 base.
You should see: three base costs: $14.00, $9.50, $26.00.
If not: use your own supplier's current prices instead and keep the same formula.
### 4. Set retail prices
Set T-Shirt $24.99, Mug $17.99, Hoodie $44.99.
You should see: net profit $8.49 (T-shirt: 24.99 - 9.25 - 4.75 - 2.50 fees), $6.69 (mug) and $14.49 (hoodie).
If not: check that fees are about 10% of retail.
### 5. Check the margin
Target a 35%+ net margin where you can; the sample T-shirt nets 34%.
You should see: each product's margin next to its profit.
If not: raise the price or lower costs.
### 6. Project monthly income
Use 100 active listings, 10,000 monthly visitors, a 2.0% conversion rate (range 1.5% - 2.5%): 200 sales/month. At $8.50 average profit: $1,700 / month.
You should see: 200 sales and $1,700 in your sheet.
If not: multiply visitors x conversion first, then x profit.
### 7. Add ad spend

chunks.title: Pricing & Passive-Income Math for POD — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Passive-Income Math for POD / Step by step.
Subtract ad spend (for example $2 - $5 per sale) and see if profit stays in range.
You should see: profit still near $7 - $12 per sale, or a clear warning.
If not: raise the price; this projection is a model, not a guarantee.

chunks.title: What Actually Sells on Stock Marketplaces — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: What Actually Sells on Stock Marketplaces / Before you start.
Beginners upload thousands of generic AI images (fantasy landscapes, cyber cities, aesthetic portraits) and earn $0.00 in total royalties. Buyers such as ad agencies, news editors and corporate design teams want commercial concepts that illustrate a business problem: a handshake on a deal, a solar farm, healthcare workers discussing charts, a data breach. Images with clean copy space (negative space on the left or top 30% of the frame, for headlines and logos) sell 4x more often than cluttered ones. Stock agencies also reject recognizable brand logos (Apple, Nike, BMW), trademarked architecture and copyrighted artwork.
The pipeline is: Commercial Demand Search, Concept Prompting, Quality Audit and Upscale, IPTC Keywording, Marketplace Submission. IPTC (International Press Telecommunications Council) is the industry-standard schema for embedding titles, keywords and copyright fields inside an image file.
You will need: an Adobe Stock Contributor account (or access to its portal), an IPTC editor such as ExifTool or a stock tagger, and Image Studio in SmartVideo GO AI. Optionally Video Studio for a motion clip.

### 3. Generate the image with copy space
In Image Studio, paste this prompt:

Photorealistic 8k commercial stock photo of two diverse business executives shaking hands across a glass conference table in a sunlit modern corporate office, copy space on left side for text overlay, shot on 35mm lens, neutral corporate color palette, high resolution.
Then add this negative prompt (if your studio has a negative prompt field; otherwise skip it):

 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: a batch of 20 upscaled stock images with a metadata.csv, ready for FTP upload.

chunks.title: Batch-Generating a Licensable Catalog — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batch-Generating a Licensable Catalog / Before you start.
Stock licensing is a volume numbers game. Earning $500 to $2,000+ per month in passive royalties takes a portfolio of 500 to 2,000+ high-quality commercial assets. Doing each image by hand (generate, upscale, keyword, upload) takes about 15 minutes per image, so 500 images would take over 125 hours. A batch pipeline removes that: Batch Prompt Matrix, Automated Generation, 4x Upscale, Auto-CSV Metadata Tagging, FTP Batch Upload.
The three pillars: batch API generation (calling /nano-banana-2 from a Python script, 50 images per run), bulk AI upscaling from raw 1024px to 4000px+ (12+ Megapixels) as agencies require, and CSV metadata files (filename, title, keywords, category) that Adobe Stock and Freepik accept, so you skip manual text entry.
You will need: lesson 1 finished, a working generation script (or Image Studio in SmartVideo GO AI for generation), an AI upscaler, an Adobe Stock Contributor account with FTP details from the portal (never paste passwords into chat), and templates/stock-metadata-template.md.

chunks.title: Batch-Generating a Licensable Catalog — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batch-Generating a Licensable Catalog / Step by step.
### 1. Open the template and define the matrix
Open templates/stock-metadata-template.md for the batch CSV schemas, keyword libraries and FTP guides. Then write down this prompt pattern:
text
Photorealistic 8k commercial stock photo of [TECHCONCEPT], blue fiber optic illumination, clean high-tech server room background, widescreen 16:9, copy space.
You should see: a prompt with one [TECHCONCEPT] placeholder.
If not: copy the prompt again exactly, including the square brackets.
### 2. Fill the placeholder list
Substitute [TECHCONCEPT] with each of: AI cloud data server, biometric facial scanner, cyber security firewall node, quantum computer processor. That gives 4 concepts to repeat across the batch.
You should see: 4 finished prompts, one per concept.
If not: make sure each prompt keeps "copy space" and "no logos" style framing from lesson 1.
### 3. Run the batch generation
Run your generation script (calling /nano-banana-2) to output 20 high-res stock images into an outputraw/ directory. You can also generate the same prompts one by one in Image Studio.
You should see: 20 image files in outputraw/.
If not: check your script's prompt list and output folder path; run a single prompt first to find the problem.
### 4. Upscale the batch
Pass all images through an AI upscaler to reach 4000px+ resolution (12+ Megapixels).

chunks.title: Batch-Generating a Licensable Catalog — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Batch-Generating a Licensable Catalog / Step by step.
You should see: each file measuring 4000px or more on the long edge.
If not: re-run the upscaler on the files that stayed small; agencies reject low-resolution files.
### 5. Inspect and filter
Open each upscaled image at 100% zoom. Delete any render with visual glitches, noise artifacts or hand distortions. Aim to keep your approval rate above 80% on Adobe Stock.
You should see: only clean images left in your upload folder.
If not: when more than a fifth fail, adjust the prompt and regenerate rather than keeping weak images.
### 6. Build metadata.csv
Create a metadata.csv with the columns filename, title, keywords, category, with a title and 30 keywords for each file.
You should see: one CSV row per surviving image, each with about 30 keywords.
If not: compare your columns with the CSV schema in the template and check that no filename is misspelled.
### 7. Upload via FTP
Upload the batch and the CSV via FTP to the Adobe Stock Contributor Portal using the FTP details the portal gives you. Enter credentials only in your FTP client, never in chat. Tick the "Created using Generative AI tools" option when the portal asks.
You should see: your files appearing in the portal's pending uploads.
If not: menus move; follow the current screen and recheck the FTP host and login in the portal.

Academy lesson: Licensing Models & Realistic Passive-Income Expectations.

 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: non-exclusive contributor accounts, extended licensing enabled, and a written earnings projection for your catalog.

chunks.title: Licensing Models & Realistic Passive-Income Expectations — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Licensing Models & Realistic Passive-Income Expectations / Before you start.
New contributors expect to upload 10 images and earn $1,000/month. When earnings start at $0.33 per download they get discouraged and quit. Others misunderstand licensing types and miss $80 to $250+ single-license payouts when an ad agency uses an image on a billboard or in a broadcast campaign.
Two models exist: Standard Royalty-Free (RF) for digital use (websites, social, blogs, internal slides) at about $0.33 to $1.20 per download, and Extended / Enhanced for physical resale products (book covers, billboards, TV ads, retail packaging) at $25 to $250+ per download. Uploading the same non-exclusive portfolio to several platforms (Adobe Stock, Freepik, Wirestock) is called multi-platform syndication and multiplies one asset pool's reach.
You will need: lessons 1 and 2 finished, a few images ready to upload, and templates/stock-licensing-calculator.md. Studios are only needed if you generate more assets: Image Studio and Video Studio in SmartVideo GO AI.

chunks.title: Licensing Models & Realistic Passive-Income Expectations — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Licensing Models & Realistic Passive-Income Expectations / Step by step.
### 1. Register non-exclusive accounts
Register non-exclusive contributor profiles on Adobe Stock and Freepik. Non-exclusive status lets you syndicate the exact same portfolio across several portals.
You should see: two contributor dashboards, both showing non-exclusive status.
If not: menus move; follow the current screen, and read each portal's contributor terms before choosing a status.
### 2. Enable extended licensing
In your contributor settings, check the "Allow Extended / Commercial Licensing" box so your assets qualify for high-ticket commercial downloads.
You should see: the option saved as enabled.
If not: look through the account or portfolio settings; the option may sit under a differently named heading.
### 3. Open the calculator
Open templates/stock-licensing-calculator.md, which holds royalty calculators, syndication trackers and portfolio growth models.
You should see: the calculator ready to take your numbers.
If not: check the link path as written, then use any spreadsheet if needed.
### 4. Project your earnings
Use RPA (Revenue Per Asset), benchmarked at about $0.50 to $1.50 per image per year, and these portfolio benchmarks:
1. 500 images: about 50 to 100 downloads/month = $150 to $350/month.
2. 2,000 images: about 200 to 400 downloads/month = $600 to $1,400/month.
Enter your own catalog size and write down a low and a high monthly figure.

chunks.title: Licensing Models & Realistic Passive-Income Expectations — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Licensing Models & Realistic Passive-Income Expectations / Step by step.
You should see: a low and a high monthly estimate for your catalog.
If not: if the numbers look far above the benchmarks, recheck your downloads per asset assumption.
### 5. Compare Standard against Extended
Calculate the revenue gap between 100 Standard RF downloads and 5 Extended Commercial downloads, using the ranges above ($0.33 to $1.20 per RF download, $25 to $250+ per Extended).
You should see: a few Extended licenses can rival or beat many standard downloads.
If not: multiply each count by the matching per-download range and compare low to low, high to high.
### 6. Syndicate a batch
Upload a 20-image commercial batch to both portals (optionally through a distributor such as Wirestock). Then write a reinvestment plan: put early earnings into API compute credits to grow the catalog from 100 to 1,000+ assets over 6 months.
You should see: the batch pending or live on two portals, and a written growth plan.
If not: check each portal's rejection notes, and fix and resubmit the flagged images.

chunks.title: Image Models — Which One for Which Use Case — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Image Models — Which One for Which Use Case / Before you start.
Many creators use one image tool for everything. Midjourney gives garbled text on typography jobs, and DALL-E 3 gives over-saturated, plastic-looking skin on corporate headshots. Matching the model to the requirement saves you from fighting its limits. The four dimensions to judge are: photorealism and texture (lead: FLUX 1.1 Pro / FLUX Schnell), typography (Ideogram v2 / FLUX), prompt adherence on spatial layouts (DALL-E 3 / FLUX), and artistic style (Midjourney v6).
You will need a client brief or a made-up one (for example a headshot, a logo and a banner), and the template templates/image-model-selection-guide.md. In SmartVideo GO AI you will use Image Studio, with Storyboard / Campaign Planner for the plan.

chunks.title: Image Models — Which One for Which Use Case — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Image Models — Which One for Which Use Case / Step by step.
### 1. Open the selection guide
Open templates/image-model-selection-guide.md next to your brief.
You should see: comparison matrices, prompt adherence rules and resolution benchmarks.
If not: check the link path as written; if the file will not open, use the Compare Tools table in Go further below.
### 2. Name the primary constraint
Read your brief and pick the one thing that matters most:
1. Photorealistic headshots or products need skin pores and sub-surface scattering: FLUX 1.1 Pro / muapi /nano-banana-2.
2. Graphic typography and merch quotes need perfect spelling: Ideogram v2 / FLUX.
3. Cinematic concept art and storyboards need painterly lighting defaults: Midjourney v6.
You should see: one model (or pair) written next to each part of your brief.
If not: if a brief has two constraints, split it into two assets and choose per asset.
### 3. Set the model parameters
Note the settings for each chosen model:
1. FLUX models: guidance scale 3.5, steps 28 to 40.
2. Midjourney v6: --stylize 100-250 for photorealism, or --stylize 500+ for artistic flair.
You should see: a settings line beside each model choice.
If not: menus and setting names move between tools; follow the current screen and use the nearest equivalent.
### 4. Generate the asset in Image Studio

chunks.title: Image Models — Which One for Which Use Case — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Image Models — Which One for Which Use Case / Step by step.
Open Image Studio in SmartVideo GO AI and generate the asset with your chosen model and settings. Add explicit lighting words to the prompt, because FLUX needs explicit lighting prompts.
You should see: a finished image for your main constraint.
If not: if the result is flat, add a lighting description and run it again.
### 5. Audit at 100% zoom
Zoom to 100% and inspect edges, text legibility and finger geometry.
You should see: clean edges, correctly spelled text and natural fingers.
If not: if text or skin fails, go back to step 2 and switch to the model that leads that dimension.
### 6. Plan a multi-model pipeline
Write one line for each stage: FLUX for the base asset, Ideogram for text overlays, Midjourney for artistic atmosphere exploration.
You should see: a short pipeline note you can reuse on the next brief.
If not: if one stage has no job in your brief, leave it out.

chunks.title: Image Models — Which One for Which Use Case — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Image Models — Which One for Which Use Case / Common mistakes.
 Using Midjourney for complex typography, which gives garbled text.
 Using DALL-E 3 for photorealistic headshots, which gives plastic skin.

chunks.title: Image Models — Which One for Which Use Case — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Image Models — Which One for Which Use Case / Go further.
Worked example: "High-Fashion Apparel Campaign." Requirement: 8k studio product shot with legible brand typography on a black hoodie. DALL-E 3 had great text spelling but waxy, plastic skin. FLUX 1.1 Pro (via muapi) gave perfect skin pores, crisp fabric weave and exact spelling. Final selection: FLUX 1.1 Pro, with 100% client approval. Visuals: templates/examples/model-benchmark-comparison.jpg and templates/examples/tools-workflow-motion.mp4.
| Model | Strengths | Weaknesses | Best use case |
|---|---|---|---|
| FLUX 1.1 Pro / Schnell | Photorealistic skin, top-tier text rendering, high prompt adherence | Requires explicit lighting prompts | Corporate headshots, POD merch, stock content |
| Midjourney v6 | Superior out-of-the-box aesthetics, cinematic color defaults | Text spelling can drift, proprietary Discord interface | Concept art, film storyboards, social creative |
| Ideogram v2 | Unrivaled vector typography and logo layout | Lower photorealism on human skin | Posters, apparel text designs, badges |
| DALL-E 3 | High prompt adherence for simple concepts | Over-saturated, cartoonish skin texture | Fast conceptual brainstorming |

1. Easy: generate a 1-word logo graphic in Ideogram v2 vs. Midjourney v6 and compare spelling accuracy.
2. Medium: render a corporate portrait with FLUX 1.1 Pro and inspect skin micro-textures at 100% crop.

# Video Models — Which One for Which Use Case
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a video model chosen for your scene, a camera motion prompt and a motion strength setting.
---

chunks.title: Video Models — Which One for Which Use Case — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Video Models — Which One for Which Use Case / Before you start.
Video credits cost $0.25 to $1.50 per 5-second generation, so the wrong model wastes money. High-motion models on subtle pans cause morphing distortion, low-motion models on action give frozen frames, and Text-to-Video (T2V) instead of Image-to-Video (I2V) breaks consistency across scenes. Judge models on four factors: I2V fidelity (Kling 1.5 / Seedance 2 I2V), camera controls (Runway Gen-3 Alpha / Luma Dream Machine), physics and fluid motion (Kling 1.5 / Sora), and speed (Seedance 2 I2V Fast via muapi, about 10-30 seconds).
You will need a source image (finish lesson 1 first) and the template templates/video-audio-stack-matrix.md. In SmartVideo GO AI you will use Video Studio.

chunks.title: Video Models — Which One for Which Use Case — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Video Models — Which One for Which Use Case / Step by step.
### 1. Open the motion matrix
Open templates/video-audio-stack-matrix.md.
You should see: motion control parameters, camera movement guides and model speed benchmarks.
If not: check the link path as written, or use the Compare Tools table in Go further.
### 2. Map your scene to a model
Pick the line that matches your scene:
1. Subtle slow architectural pan or product rotation needs high I2V stability: Kling 1.5 / Seedance 2 I2V.
2. Dramatic cinematic zoom or fly-through needs keyframe camera control: Runway Gen-3 Alpha.
3. Complex fluids such as water splashes or explosions need advanced physics: Kling 1.5 / Sora.
You should see: one model written down for your scene.
If not: if the scene mixes needs, split it into separate shots.
### 3. Start from an image
Choose or generate your source image first (see lesson 1). Always begin with I2V, never T2V, for commercial work.
You should see: one pristine keyframe image ready to animate.
If not: if the image has flaws, fix them in Image Studio first; video will amplify them.
### 4. Write the motion prompt
Add explicit camera movement words. Use this as a model:
text
Camera slowly pans right across the modern living room, soft sunlight streaming through windows, 24fps film grain, photorealistic.
You should see: a prompt naming the camera move, the light and the look.

chunks.title: Video Models — Which One for Which Use Case — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Video Models — Which One for Which Use Case / Step by step.
If not: if the prompt names no camera move, add one (pan, push-in or orbit).
### 5. Set the motion strength
Set the scale: low motion (2 - 4) for portraits, headshots and real estate; high motion (6 - 8) for action, sports and vehicles.
You should see: a number that fits your scene type.
If not: menus move; follow the current screen and look for a motion or strength control.
### 6. Generate in Video Studio and check
Open Video Studio, upload your image, paste the prompt, set the motion and generate.
You should see: a clip where the subject keeps its shape and lighting.
If not: if the subject morphs, lower the motion strength or switch to the model with better I2V stability.

chunks.text:

chunks.title: Video Models — Which One for Which Use Case — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Video Models — Which One for Which Use Case / Common mistakes.
 Using T2V for commercial work, so the subject changes shape.
 High motion on subtle pans, which morphs the subject.
 Low motion on action, which freezes the frame.
 Animating a flawed image instead of fixing it first.

chunks.title: Video Models — Which One for Which Use Case — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Video Models — Which One for Which Use Case / Go further.
Worked example: "Commercial Car Reel." Requirement: 5-second tracking shot of a sports car on a coastal road at sunset. T2V morphed the car into a different vehicle halfway. I2V with Kling 1.5 / Seedance 2 locked the vehicle geometry from the keyframe and gave smooth chassis reflections. Result: 100% stable motion reel. Visual: templates/examples/camera-motion-matrix.jpg.
| Video model | Camera control | Motion fidelity | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Runway Gen-3 Alpha | Extremely high (keyframe camera controls) | High | Film trailers, dramatic camera moves, advertising |
| Kling 1.5 | High | Superior physics and human motion | Real estate walkthroughs, character motion, I2V stability |
| Luma Dream Machine | Medium | High dynamic camera movement | Fast 3D camera sweeps, conceptual loops |
| Seedance 2 I2V Fast (muapi API) | High | Fastest API inference (about 15s) | High-volume client pipelines, social clips |
Exercises:
1. Easy: animate a static product photo with Seedance 2 I2V and a slow camera zoom prompt.
2. Medium: compare Runway Gen-3 vs. Kling 1.5 camera control on the same keyframe.
3. Hard: produce a 3-shot scene with consistent lighting using I2V keyframes across scenes.

 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: an audio plan with a voice, a music prompt, a transcript step and a mix level for one video.
---

chunks.title: Voice/Audio Models — Which One for Which Use Case — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice/Audio Models — Which One for Which Use Case / Before you start.
Viewers tolerate mediocre resolution but click away from bad audio. Low-end TTS sounds robotic, full songs with vocals bury dialogue when the scene needed ambient instrumentals, and voice cloning without noise-cleaned reference audio gives distorted artifacts. The audio stack keeps speech, music and effects separate: Text Script, then ElevenLabs voice, then a Suno/Udio instrumental, then stem mix and mastering. Three pillars: voice synthesis and cloning (ElevenLabs / Bark), generative music (Suno v3.5 / Udio), and speech-to-text (Whisper).
You will need a short script for a video and the template templates/video-audio-stack-matrix.md. In SmartVideo GO AI you will use Video Studio and Lip-Sync Studio for voice and mouth-sync.

chunks.title: Voice/Audio Models — Which One for Which Use Case — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice/Audio Models — Which One for Which Use Case / Step by step.
### 1. Open the stack matrix
Open templates/video-audio-stack-matrix.md.
You should see: voice parameter setups, music prompt structures and stem mixing checklists.
If not: check the link path as written, or use the Compare Tools table in Go further.
### 2. Map each audio need to a tool
1. Narration and commercial voiceover: ElevenLabs Multilingual v2 (high emotional dynamics, stability 0.45, clarity 0.85).
2. Cinematic score or background beat: Suno v3.5 (instrumental prompt mode) or Udio.
3. Subtitles and transcripts: OpenAI Whisper (Large-v3 model).
You should see: three lines, one tool per need.
If not: if your video has no narration, skip line 1.
### 3. Set the voice parameters
In ElevenLabs set Stability to 0.40 - 0.50 for expressive, natural modulation and Clarity + Similarity Boost to 0.80 for clean studio presence.
You should see: both values noted, then a voiceover generated from your script.
If not: if the voice sounds monotone, lower stability slightly within the range. Menus move; follow the current screen.
### 4. Write the music prompt
Ask for an instrumental, not a song with vocals. Use this as a model:
text
Ambient corporate piano, warm uplifting strings, 110 bpm
You should see: a background track with no vocals that fits your voiceover tempo.
If not: if vocals appear, switch to instrumental prompt mode.
### 5. Plan the transcript

chunks.title: Voice/Audio Models — Which One for Which Use Case — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Voice/Audio Models — Which One for Which Use Case / Step by step.
Run the finished voiceover through OpenAI Whisper to get timestamped subtitles (an SRT file).
You should see: a transcript with timestamps.
If not: if words are wrong, check the voiceover for background noise and re-run.
### 6. Mix the stems
In your video editing, duck the background music -14dB below the voiceover track.
You should see: dialogue clearly on top of the music.
If not: if you still strain to hear the speech, lower the music further.
### 7. Note the voice-cloning rule
If you ever clone a client voice, provide at least 3 minutes of background-noise-free, 44.1kHz studio WAV audio.
You should see: a note in your plan about clean reference audio.
If not: without clean reference audio, expect distorted artifacts and do not clone.

chunks.title: Voice/Audio Models — Which One for Which Use Case — Go further
chunks.text:

Worked example: "Commercial Real Estate Ad." Voiceover: ElevenLabs "Adam - Deep Corporate Narrator" (stability 0.45). Score: Suno v3.5 instrumental ("Ambient corporate piano, warm uplifting strings, 110 bpm"). Transcription: Whisper auto-generated SRT subtitles. Production time: 8 minutes. # API vs. Local: A Decision Framework
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a monthly API cost, a payback period for a local GPU and a written hosting decision.
---

chunks.title: API vs. Local: A Decision Framework — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: API vs. Local: A Decision Framework / Before you start.
Buying a $3,500 RTX 4090 workstation for 20 images a week takes years to break even, while 10,000 monthly high-res renders on pay-per-request APIs cost $600+/month. Confidential client assets sent over a public cloud API may also break NDA agreements. Two formulas decide it:
 Monthly Cloud API Cost = Renders per Month x Cost per Render
 Local GPU Amortization Period = GPU Workstation Cost / Monthly Savings vs. API
Cloud APIs (muapi / Replicate) cost $0 upfront and suit low volume ($5-$20/mo); a local GPU (ComfyUI / RTX 4090) costs $1,500 - $4,500 but has $0 marginal cost per render (only electricity) and 100% offline privacy. It also needs Python, VRAM management (VRAM = Video RAM, the dedicated memory on your GPU that holds the AI model during generation) and CUDA drivers (CUDA = NVIDIA's software layer that lets your GPU run AI workloads).
You will need a calculator and the template templates/api-cost-calculator.md. Lessons 1-3 give you your render types.

chunks.title: API vs. Local: A Decision Framework — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: API vs. Local: A Decision Framework / Step by step.
### 1. Open the calculator
Open templates/api-cost-calculator.md.
You should see: API cost formulas, GPU payback calculators and hardware VRAM decision trees.
If not: check the link path as written; the two formulas above are enough to continue.
### 2. Enter your monthly volume
Write down how many renders you make per month and your average cost per render.
You should see: two numbers.
If not: if you do not know your average cost, use $0.06 as in the examples.
### 3. Calculate the API cost
Multiply renders by cost per render. For reference: Scenario A, 300 renders at $0.06 = $18/month. Scenario B, 10,000 renders at $0.06 = $600/month.
You should see: a monthly API cost in dollars.
If not: recheck that both numbers are monthly, not weekly.
### 4. Calculate the payback
Divide the workstation cost by the monthly API cost. Scenario A: a $2,500 machine takes 138 months to break even, so stay on Cloud APIs (muapi). Scenario B: the $2,500 workstation pays for itself in under 4.5 months, so invest in a Local GPU (RTX 4090).
You should see: a payback period in months for your numbers.
If not: if your monthly savings are near zero, the payback is effectively never; stay on the API.
### 5. Apply the privacy test
If you handle NDA corporate headshots or unreleased product prototypes, enforce Local GPU Air-Gapped Rendering regardless of volume.

chunks.title: API vs. Local: A Decision Framework — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: API vs. Local: A Decision Framework / Step by step.
You should see: a yes/no answer on privacy for each client type.
If not: if unsure, check the client contract before sending assets to any cloud service.
### 6. Consider the middle ground
Renting cloud GPUs on RunPod at $0.44/hour gives ComfyUI node control without buying hardware.
You should see: a note on whether renting fits better than buying.
If not: prices change; check the current rate on the provider's page.
### 7. Write your decision
Pick one: Cloud API only, local GPU, rented GPU, or a hybrid. A hybrid uses Cloud APIs for rapid mobile client intake and burst processing, and Local ComfyUI for heavy offline batch fine-tuning and LoRA training.
You should see: a one-paragraph infrastructure plan with the numbers behind it.
If not: if the numbers and privacy point different ways, privacy wins for those clients.

chunks.title: API vs. Local: A Decision Framework — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: API vs. Local: A Decision Framework / Common mistakes.
 Buying hardware early when volume is low.
 Staying on pay-per-request APIs at very high volume.
 Sending NDA assets over a public cloud API.
 Ignoring setup work (Python, VRAM, CUDA drivers) in a local build.

chunks.title: API vs. Local: A Decision Framework — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: API vs. Local: A Decision Framework / Go further.
Worked example: "Scale Studio Rebrand." Output: 6,500 image renders and 200 short video clips per month. Cloud API estimate: $390 image credits + $150 video credits = $540/month. Local build: dual RTX 4090 24GB VRAM rig = $3,800. Payback: $3,800 / $540 = 7.0 months. Outcome: the agency bought the workstation and saved $6,480/year after month 7.
| Hosting option | Flexibility | Scaling speed | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| muapi Cloud API | High (FLUX, Seedance, InstantID via HTTP) | Instant (no VRAM limits) | Startups, freelancers, mobile app backends |
| Local ComfyUI | Unlimited node control | Fixed to GPU VRAM | High-volume agencies, custom LoRA trainers, NDA projects |
| RunPod / Vast.ai (cloud GPU) | High (rent a cloud RTX 4090 per hour) | High | Burst processing 5,000 images over a weekend |
Exercises:
1. Easy: calculate your monthly API spend with the formula in api-cost-calculator.md.
2. Medium: rent a cloud GPU on RunPod and launch a ComfyUI web interface.
3. Hard: build a hybrid plan combining Cloud API mobile submission with local GPU batch processing.

# AI Tool Evaluation Framework Checklist
 SmartVideo GO AI Academy — A reusable template from the SmartVideo GO AI course library. Fill it in, then launch it from the matching SmartVideo GO AI studio or Create-With-AI recipe.
Use this 5-point evaluation framework to test and score new AI models before integrating them into production client workflows.
---

chunks.title: AI Tool Evaluation Framework Checklist — 🔍 5-Point Tool Evaluation Checklist
chunks.text:
Academy template: AI Tool Evaluation Framework Checklist / 🔍 5-Point Tool Evaluation Checklist.
### 1. Photorealism & Micro-Detail Fidelity (Weight: 25%)
- [ ] Skin Pores & Anatomy: Does the model maintain natural skin texture without waxy/plastic smoothing?
- [ ] Lighting Falloff: Do highlights and shadows behave realistically across complex surfaces?
### 2. Prompt Adherence & Spatial Control (Weight: 25%)
- [ ] Multi-Subject Placement: Does the model respect positional instructions (left, right, background, foreground)?
- [ ] Text Legibility: Can the model render clean, un-garbled typography when prompted?
### 3. Identity & Geometry Stability (Weight: 20%)
- [ ] Face Vector Retention: Does identity locking remain consistent across 5 consecutive generations?
- [ ] I2V Temporal Stability: Does Image-to-Video generation prevent morphing distortion?
### 4. API Speed & Developer Experience (Weight: 15%)
- [ ] Inference Speed: Does the render complete within acceptable SLA thresholds (< 30 sec)?
- [ ] API Reliability: Is the uptime and response rate above 99.5%?
### 5. Unit Economics & Pricing Model (Weight: 15%)
- [ ] Margin Protection: Does the cost-per-render allow for at least a 70%+ gross margin on client packages?
- [ ] Commercial Rights: Does the provider grant full commercial licensing for generated assets?
---

chunks.title: Pricing Your Services
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing Your Services.
# Pricing Your Services
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a value-based price, a 3-tier offer and a scope-trade-off reply written for one real service you could sell.
---

chunks.title: Pricing Your Services — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing Your Services / Before you start.
AI makes you many times faster, so hourly billing punishes you for being efficient. In the lesson's example, retouching 50 corporate headshots takes 20 hours by hand (20 x $50 = $1,000) but about 1.5 hours with AI (1.5 x $50 = $75). You would lose $925 for being efficient. The fix is to charge for the business value delivered, not for time spent.
The core formula is: Project Fee = Traditional Market Replacement Cost x (25% - 40%). If traditional production costs the client $28,000, you charge about $7,000 to $11,200. All figures in this lesson are worked examples, not guarantees of what you will earn.
You will need:
 A service you could offer (for example headshots, product images, social video ads).
 A calculator or spreadsheet, and a way to look up what traditional providers charge.
 About 15 minutes.

chunks.title: Pricing Your Services — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing Your Services / Step by step.
### 1. Write down the traditional replacement cost
Pick one service. List what a client would pay a traditional provider to get the same result. The lesson's example for a 100-person company's headshots: photographer day rate $3,500, equipment and lighting $1,200, travel for remote staff $12,500, retouching $120 x 100 = $12,000. Total: $28,700.
You should see: one total number for your own service, built from line items.
If not: search for local production-house or retoucher rates and use a rough range. A labelled estimate is fine.
### 2. Calculate your fee range
1. Multiply your total by 25%.
2. Multiply it by 40%.
3. Pick a flat project fee inside that range.
In the example, $28,700 gives roughly $7,175 to $11,480, and the lesson offers a flat $7,500, which saves the client $21,200 and delivers in 24 hours instead of 4 weeks.
You should see: a low figure, a high figure and one chosen flat fee.
If not: if your fee comes out below $1,500, check step 1 for missing costs, or see step 6 on your floor.
### 3. Check your margin
List your direct costs (COGS): tool or API costs, upscaling compute and any reviewer's time. The lesson's example: 300 images at $0.04 = $12.00, upscaling $5.00, one hour of offshore QA review $15.00, total $32.00. Then: Net Profit = fee - COGS = $7,500 - $32 = $7,468, about a 99.57% gross margin (an example, not a promise).

chunks.title: Pricing Your Services — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing Your Services / Step by step.
You should see: a COGS total and a margin for your own offer.
If not: if your costs are unknown, estimate high and refine after your first project.
### 4. Build three tiers
Never send a single take-it-or-leave-it price. Copy this structure and fill in your own numbers. The lesson's example tiers are:
text
TIER 1: ESSENTIALS - $2,500 (one-time)
- Single asset batch, 25 final 8k renders
- 48-hour turnaround, 2 revision rounds
- Standard commercial license, email support only
TIER 2: PROFESSIONAL (Recommended) - $5,500 (one-time)
- Full multi-format asset suite, 75 final 8k renders
- 24-hour express sync, 3 revision rounds
- Full commercial IP assignment, priority Slack/email support
TIER 3: ENTERPRISE - $9,500 / month
- Unlimited on-demand assets, dedicated custom LoRA model
- 12-hour priority SLA, unlimited revisions
- Full commercial IP transfer, dedicated account manager
You should see: three tiers where the middle one is marked Recommended.
If not: make sure each tier differs in quantity, speed, revisions and support, not only in price.
### 5. Use anchoring on purpose
1. Tier 3 is the high anchor that sets premium positioning.
2. Tier 2 is your target deal, labelled "Most Popular" or "Recommended".
3. Tier 1 is your budget floor; the lesson notes it still keeps a 98%+ margin in its example.
You should see: Tier 2 feels reasonable next to Tier 3.

chunks.title: Pricing Your Services — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing Your Services / Step by step.
If not: if Tier 1 loses money, raise it or trim its contents.
### 6. Set your project floor
Set your minimum contract size to $1,500 and never quote under $1,000. Write this down where you will see it when quoting.
You should see: a written floor number.
If not: if you are tempted to go lower, use the scope trade-off in the next step instead.
### 7. Prepare your negotiation reply
When a client asks for a discount, never reduce price without reducing scope. Copy this script and adjust the numbers to your offer:
text
We would love to work with your $3,000 budget! To fit within that investment level, we can adjust the Professional package from 75 renders down to 30 renders, with a 48-hour turnaround instead of 24 hours. Which set of deliverables would you prefer us to lock in?
You should see: a saved reply that cuts scope in exchange for a lower price.
If not: write the trade-off as a choice for the client, ending in a question.
### 8. Run the numbers in the calculator template
Open templates/agency-pricing-calculator.md in this track and enter your fee, COGS and tiers to confirm gross margin before you send any proposal.
You should see: your margin worked out for each tier.
If not: if a tier shows a thin margin, adjust its scope.

chunks.title: Pricing Your Services — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing Your Services / Check yourself.
 [ ] I can explain why hourly billing loses money when AI makes me faster.
 [ ] I have a replacement-cost total and a fee between 25% and 40% of it.
 [ ] I have three tiers with the middle one recommended.
 [ ] I have a floor and a scope-trade-off reply ready.

chunks.title: Pricing Your Services — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing Your Services / Common mistakes.
 Charging for time. Charge for business value delivered.
 Quoting one price. Always present three tiers.
 Discounting without cutting scope. An unearned discount destroys authority.
 Treating example numbers as promises. Use your own market research.

chunks.title: Pricing Your Services — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing Your Services / Go further.
Retainers. One-off projects create a revenue rollercoaster, so aim to convert clients into monthly retainers (the lesson's range: $3,000 to $10,000 a month). Example models from the lesson (illustrative figures):
| Vertical | Deliverables | Fee | Est. COGS | Net |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E-Commerce Merch | 20 new merch graphics + 5 image-to-video promos | $4,000/mo | $50 | $3,950/mo |
| Real Estate Staging | Virtual staging for 10 properties (80 renders) | $5,500/mo | $65 | $5,435/mo |
| Corporate Branding | Headshot onboarding, up to 30 hires/mo | $3,500/mo | $25 | $3,475/mo |
| Social Video Ads | 12 short-form AI video ads + voiceovers | $7,500/mo | $120 | $7,380/mo |
Exercise. Build your own retainer row with deliverables, fee, estimated COGS and net.
Pitch deck. See the mockup at templates/examples/agency-pricing-deck-mockup.jpg for how a priced proposal can look.
Next: Contracts and scope basics.

chunks.title: Contracts and Scope Basics
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Contracts and Scope Basics.
# Contracts and Scope Basics
 Time: about 16 minutes. You will finish with: a customised contract draft with the five key clauses, a payment schedule and ready replies to common scope-creep requests.
---

chunks.title: Contracts and Scope Basics — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Contracts and Scope Basics / Before you start.
Standard creative contracts assume human labor and slow timelines. With AI work, three gaps appear: clients assume that because AI generates images in seconds they can demand endless variations; clients ask for your prompt libraries, ComfyUI workflows and LoRA weights; and AI copyright is ambiguous (the lesson points to U.S. Copyright Office rulings on AI-generated assets).
Two agreements cover this. The Master Services Agreement (MSA) governs the whole relationship (liability caps, confidentiality, payment terms, governing law) and is signed once per client. A Statement of Work (SOW) is a project-specific addendum with deliverables, milestone dates, revision limits and fees, signed per project.
The clause wording below is example text from the course, not legal advice. Have a qualified lawyer review your final contract.
You will need:
 templates/freelance-client-contract.md from this track.
 A project you might sell, so you can fill in real numbers.
 About 16 minutes.

chunks.title: Contracts and Scope Basics — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Contracts and Scope Basics / Step by step.
### 1. Open the contract template
Open templates/freelance-client-contract.md. Note where the MSA ends and the SOW begins.
You should see: a master agreement section and a per-project statement of work.
If not: copy the template into your own document and mark the two parts yourself.
### 2. Add the revision cap clause
Scope creep is the biggest threat to your profit. Add a clause like this one (adjust the numbers to your offer):
text
Clause 4.2 - Scope of Revisions: The agreed Contract Value includes exactly two (2) rounds of revisions per deliverable. A "Revision" is strictly limited to minor adjustments in color grading, background lighting adjustments, contrast correction, or minor masking fixes. Any request by Client for structural prompt re-engineering, model replacement, pose changes, or fundamental style alterations following sign-off of the initial Brief shall be classified as an Out-of-Scope Change Order, billed at Agency's standard rate of $150.00 per hour.
You should see: your contract defines what counts as a revision and a change order rate.
If not: check the clause names a number of rounds, a list of allowed edits and a rate.
### 3. Set the milestone payment schedule
Never start renders without paid, non-refundable money upfront. Use this structure:
text

chunks.title: Contracts and Scope Basics — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Contracts and Scope Basics / Step by step.
MILESTONE 1: 50% non-refundable deposit upon contract signing. Unlocks compute resources, model selection and initial draft generation.
MILESTONE 2: 25% upon first watermarked draft review. Delivered as low-res watermarked proofs for Client feedback sign-off.
MILESTONE 3: 25% upon final asset handover. Unlocks un-watermarked 8k master files and the commercial usage license.
You should see: three milestones adding up to 100%.
If not: recheck that 50 + 25 + 25 = 100.
### 4. Protect your payment leverage
Add one line to your process: never deliver final un-watermarked master files before 100% payment clears. Send low-resolution watermarked previews before the final milestone.
You should see: a written rule about watermarked proofs and release on full payment.
If not: add it to the SOW delivery section.
### 5. Add the IP and commercial license clause
text

chunks.title: Contracts and Scope Basics — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Contracts and Scope Basics / Step by step.
Clause 8.1 - Intellectual Property & AI Commercial License: Upon receipt of full payment, Agency grants to Client an exclusive, perpetual, worldwide commercial usage license to use, display, distribute, and monetize the final delivered media assets. Client acknowledges that deliverables utilize state-of-the-art Generative AI models (e.g., FLUX, Runway, ElevenLabs) operating under commercial enterprise tier agreements. Agency warrants that its prompt workflows and post-processing methods do not incorporate confidential third-party trade secrets or trademarked visual assets without authorization.
You should see: the license starts only after full payment.
If not: have your lawyer check the warranty wording matches the tools you really use.
### 6. Reserve your background IP
text
Clause 8.4 - Agency Background Technology: Agency retains all right, title, and interest in and to its pre-existing tools, proprietary prompt libraries, ComfyUI node graphs, LoRA model weights, workflow scripts, and background automation technology ("Agency Background IP"). Nothing in this Agreement shall be construed as transferring ownership of Agency Background IP to Client.
You should see: the final outputs go to the client while your workflows stay yours.
If not: confirm Clause 8.4 and Clause 8.1 do not contradict each other.
### 7. Add the client input warranty
text

chunks.title: Contracts and Scope Basics — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Contracts and Scope Basics / Step by step.
Clause 9.3 - Client Data & Input Warranty: Client represents and warrants that all logos, brand guidelines, reference images, trademarks, and employee headshots provided to Agency for AI model input do not infringe upon any third-party intellectual property or privacy rights. Client agrees to defend, indemnify, and hold harmless Agency against any claims arising from Client-provided inputs.
You should see: the client is responsible for the inputs they give you.
If not: compare against the template and add the missing wording.
### 8. Save your three scope-creep replies
Keep these ready in a notes file:
text
Endless variations: We'd love to explore those new variations! As per Clause 4.2 of our SOW, our 2 included revision rounds are complete. I can send over an Out-of-Scope Change Order for $450 to cover 15 additional variations.
text
Workflow source files: Our final 8k deliverables are fully licensed to you upon final payment! However, as outlined in Clause 8.4, our internal ComfyUI node graphs and prompt libraries are proprietary Agency Background IP and are not included in this deliverable.
text
Late payment (Net-60): We completely understand corporate AP cycles! Per our agreement, high-resolution un-watermarked master files are released immediately upon final invoice clearance. Let us know as soon as the wire goes through!

chunks.title: Contracts and Scope Basics — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Contracts and Scope Basics / Step by step.
You should see: three replies that each cite a clause.
If not: change the clause numbers to match your own contract.

chunks.title: Contracts and Scope Basics — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Contracts and Scope Basics / Check yourself.
 [ ] I can explain the difference between an MSA and an SOW.
 [ ] My contract has a revision cap, a 50/25/25 payment schedule, an IP clause, a background IP clause and an input warranty.
 [ ] I will not release un-watermarked masters before full payment.
 [ ] A lawyer will review the final contract before I use it.

chunks.title: Contracts and Scope Basics — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Contracts and Scope Basics / Common mistakes.
 Vague revision wording. Define what a revision is and what is a change order.
 Starting work before the deposit. Compute and time are spent first, then payment is hard to get.
 Transferring your workflows by accident. Separate output licensing from Agency Background IP.
 Copying clauses without legal review. The text is an example to adapt.

chunks.title: Finding and Closing Clients
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Finding and Closing Clients.
# Finding and Closing Clients
 Time: about 17 minutes. You will finish with: a target segment, a 100-name prospect list plan, one personalised cold email, a discovery call plan and three objection replies.
---

chunks.title: Finding and Closing Clients — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Finding and Closing Clients / Before you start.
The biggest early mistake is pitching local consumer businesses (restaurants, salons, gyms) with budgets of roughly $200 to $500. The lesson's advice is to target high-LTV B2B clients, meaning clients with high lifetime value (total revenue across the whole relationship, not just one project), who already spend $20,000+ per quarter on traditional media production.
Cold emails that work are under 100 words, personalised, and ask for one low-friction next step. Budget ranges below are the lesson's examples, not guarantees.
You will need:
 Access to LinkedIn Sales Navigator or Apollo.io (the lesson's tools) or another way to find prospects.
 templates/outreach-and-discovery-script.md from this track.
 About 17 minutes.

chunks.title: Finding and Closing Clients — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Finding and Closing Clients / Step by step.
### 1. Pick one target segment
Choose one from the lesson's matrix:
1. Realtors and brokerages: top 5% producing agents; need virtual staging and promo videos; budget $2,500 to $5,000 a month.
2. Remote SaaS and tech teams: VP of People or HR; need automated team headshots; budget $3,000 to $7,500 a project.
3. E-commerce apparel brands: Head of E-Commerce; need merch mockups and ad content; budget $4,000 to $10,000 a month.
You should see: one segment, one buyer title and one need written down.
If not: choose the segment where you already have a sample or case study.
### 2. Build your prospect list
Use LinkedIn Sales Navigator or Apollo.io to compile 100 targeted leads in that segment. Note for each one a recent trigger event (hiring surge, new listing, product drop).
You should see: a list with name, company, title and one trigger per row.
If not: narrow the filters (company size, role) until the results match your buyer.
### 3. Learn the 4-sentence structure
Every cold email has four sentences: (1) a trigger hook about a recent specific event, (2) the business outcome you deliver, (3) social proof from a similar client, (4) a low-friction ask to send a 30-second personalised sample.
You should see: you can name the four sentences from memory.
If not: reread the headshot template in the next step and label each sentence.
### 4. Write your first email

chunks.title: Finding and Closing Clients — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Finding and Closing Clients / Step by step.
Use the template for your segment. Headshots version:
text
SUBJECT: Quick question re: [Company Name] team headshots
Hi [First Name],
Noticed [Company Name] recently added 18 new team members across engineering and sales on LinkedIn.
We help remote tech companies replace $25,000 physical photo shoots with 8k studio-grade AI headshots generated directly from employee selfies in 24 hours.
We recently delivered a 60-person roster for [Competitor/Similar SaaS] with zero travel costs, saving them over $18,000.
Open to seeing a quick 30-second before/after sample demo built for [Company Name]?
Best,
[Your Name]
Managing Director | [Your Agency Name]
Apparel version:
text
SUBJECT: New asset pipeline for [Brand Name]'s Q3 catalog
Hi [First Name],
Loved your recent summer collection launch on Instagram - the color palette is incredible.
We help growing apparel brands turn flat vector art into 8k lifestyle model mockups and video ads without booking $15k model shoots or renting studio space.
We just helped [Similar Brand] expand their catalog from 10 to 80 SKUs in 48 hours while cutting content production costs by 70%.
Would you be opposed to checking out a 45-second prototype video render of your top-selling tee?
Best,
[Your Name]
[Your Agency Name]
Only use social proof you can truthfully claim; replace the example results with your own real ones.

chunks.title: Finding and Closing Clients — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Finding and Closing Clients / Step by step.
You should see: an email under 100 words with the placeholders filled in.
If not: cut any sentence that is not one of the four.
### 5. Record a personalised prototype
Create a personalised 60-second Loom video walkthrough showing a prototype asset built for one high-value prospect.
You should see: a short video you can link in a follow-up.
If not: start with one prospect and one asset; keep it under a minute.
### 6. Plan the 20-minute discovery call
Use this frame: 0 to 3 min frame and agenda; 3 to 10 min discovery and pain (past production costs and bottlenecks); 10 to 15 min custom solution (show a live before/after demo); 15 to 20 min proposal lock (present 3 tiers and secure a deposit commitment).
You should see: a four-row agenda with minutes.
If not: write the minute marks on a sticky note beside your screen.
### 7. Prepare your discovery questions
text
What was your total expenditure on traditional photo and video shoots over the past 12 months?
How long did it take from booking a photographer to getting final retouched files back for your last campaign?
If we could deliver 8k studio-grade assets in 24 hours at 30% of your traditional shoot cost, what impact would that have on your Q3 roadmap?
You should see: three questions that uncover cost and delay.
If not: swap in your segment's terms (for example listings instead of shoots).
### 8. Save your objection replies
text

chunks.title: Finding and Closing Clients — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Finding and Closing Clients / Step by step.
"Isn't AI media recognizable and cheap-looking?" - You are 100% right - public consumer tools create glossy, fake-looking images. That's why we don't use public tools. We build custom identity locks, Rembrandt lighting control rigs, and 300 DPI print upscaling. Here is a side-by-side comparison of a traditional $5,000 photographer shoot vs. our AI pipeline. Can you tell which one is AI?
text

You aren't paying for a software subscription; you are paying for our identity consistency pipelines, enterprise commercial IP indemnification, 4500px DPI scaling, and guaranteed 24-hour SLA delivery.
text
"We don't have the budget right now." - I completely understand! The main reason companies hire us is actually to save budget. If you have any upcoming content shoots or branding updates planned over the next 6 months, our pipeline typically cuts those planned line-item expenses by 60% to 70%. Should we touch base 30 days before your next planned shoot?
