chunks.title: Scaling from Freelancer to Small Agency
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling from Freelancer to Small Agency.
# Scaling from Freelancer to Small Agency
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: one written SOP, an operator job post, a team cost check and a 2-tier QC checklist.
---

chunks.title: Scaling from Freelancer to Small Agency — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling from Freelancer to Small Agency / Before you start.
The lesson describes a Solo Bottleneck at around $8,000 to $10,000 a month (an example figure): your time goes into execution, outbound sales stops, and revenue flatlines because you cannot take client #6 without working 80 hours a week. To grow toward $25,000 to $50,000 a month (example figures, not guarantees) you shift from Prompt Operator to Creative Director and Account Executive, and delegate through written procedures, not verbal Slack instructions.
You will need:
 A project you will run soon, and a screen recorder such as Loom.
 An Upwork or OnlineJobs.ph account, plus Slack and ClickUp.
 About 15 minutes.

chunks.title: Scaling from Freelancer to Small Agency — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling from Freelancer to Small Agency / Step by step.
### 1. Record your next project
Record your screen with Loom while you execute your next project, speaking your steps aloud.
You should see: a video of one full production run.
If not: record one repeatable part (for example intake to export) instead of everything.
### 2. Write the SOP header
Every SOP starts with an objective, required tools and estimated time. The lesson's example:
text
SOP #HS-04: BATCH CORPORATE HEADSHOT GENERATION & UPSCALING
1. OBJECTIVE: Convert client raw selfie CSV roster into 8k studio headshots.
2. TOOLS REQUIRED: ComfyUI Node Graph #v4.2, FLUX 1.1 Pro API, Topaz Gigapixel
3. ESTIMATED TIME: 3 minutes per employee roster entry.
Replace the content with your own pipeline.
You should see: a numbered header with objective, tools and time.
If not: write one sentence for each of the three parts.
### 3. Write the execution steps
Turn the recording into numbered steps. The example sequence:
text
1. Intake Audit: Open client Google Drive folder 01RawInputs. Verify image resolution is at least 1080p.
2. Crop & Center: Run Python auto-crop script scratch/cropheadshots.py to center facial bounding box at 1:1 ratio.
3. ComfyUI Ingestion: Load JSON workflow workflows/b2bheadshotv4.json. Set seed to -1 and LoRA weight to 0.75.
4. Quality Control Check: Inspect rendered output against the 4 Quality Control Criteria.

chunks.title: Scaling from Freelancer to Small Agency — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling from Freelancer to Small Agency / Step by step.
5. Upscale & Export: Export approved renders into Topaz Gigapixel AI. Upscale 4x to 4500x4500px @ 300 DPI JPEG. Save in 02FinalDelivery.
You should see: each step names a folder, file or setting, so a stranger could follow it.
If not: add the exact file names or values you used.
### 4. Add the QC criteria
The SOP's four quality criteria are: eye reflection symmetry (no distorted pupils), teeth count and alignment, skin texture preservation (no plastic blur), and background lighting contrast.
You should see: four pass/fail checks inside the SOP.
If not: rewrite each as something that can be answered yes or no.
### 5. Set up the 2-tier sign-off
Quality control runs: offshore operator (prompt run), then internal QC audit (pass/fail against the SOP), then Creative Director final sign-off, then client proofing (watermarked HD). Write that order in your SOP. Then copy this checklist:
text
[ ] Facial symmetry and geometry verified.
[ ] Resolution meets 300 DPI print requirement.
[ ] No AI artifacts or distorted hands/fingers.
[ ] Color profile matches client brand guidelines (RGB/CMYK).
You should see: a checklist attached to the SOP.
If not: adapt items to your asset type (video needs motion checks).
### 6. Check the team economics

chunks.title: Scaling from Freelancer to Small Agency — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling from Freelancer to Small Agency / Step by step.
The lesson's example team (illustrative): an offshore AI prompt operator at $12 to $18/hr, 20 hrs/week, about $1,200/mo; a post-production video editor at $15 to $25/hr, 15 hrs/week, about $1,200/mo; a virtual assistant at $8 to $12/hr, 10 hrs/week, about $400/mo. Total about 45 hrs and $2,800/mo against $20,500/mo of revenue, leaving $17,700 net profit (86%). Compute the same for your own planned hires, aiming for a net margin of 80% or more.
You should see: your total monthly cost, revenue and margin percentage.
If not: margin = (revenue - cost) / revenue; recheck the division.
### 7. Post the operator job
Post a listing on Upwork or OnlineJobs.ph for an "AI Media Production Operator". Attach your SOP so applicants can see the work.
You should see: a live listing referencing your SOP.
If not: start with a draft listing and refine it after reading your first applicants.
### 8. Set up your workspace
Create Slack and ClickUp channels: #sales-leads, #active-production, #qc-audit, #client-delivery.
You should see: four channels matching your pipeline stages.
If not: create the channels first and invite people later.

chunks.text:

chunks.title: Scaling from Freelancer to Small Agency — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling from Freelancer to Small Agency / Common mistakes.
 Delegating by chat message. Without written or recorded SOPs, quality drifts.
 Skipping QC. Two sign-offs protect your reputation.
 Hiring before documenting. Write the SOP first.
 Treating example rates as fixed. Rates vary; confirm with real applicants.

chunks.title: Scaling from Freelancer to Small Agency — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Scaling from Freelancer to Small Agency / Go further.
Role map. Creative Director (you) and Account Executive, then AI Prompt Operator ($12 to $18/hr), Video and Audio Editor ($15 to $25/hr) and Client Onboarding and Support virtual assistant ($8 to $12/hr), as example rates.
Exercise. Document your first 3 SOPs, one per production stage.

chunks.title: Building a Portfolio That Sells
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a Portfolio That Sells.
# Building a Portfolio That Sells
 Time: about 14 minutes. You will finish with: one 4-part commercial case study with a metrics table, and a plan for a before/after demo portal.
---

chunks.title: Building a Portfolio That Sells — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a Portfolio That Sells / Before you start.
Many creators build portfolios like art galleries: pretty images with no client or numbers. Corporate buyers (CMOs, VPs of Marketing, E-Commerce Directors) do not buy art; they buy solutions to expensive business problems. A headline like "How We Saved a 120-Person Remote SaaS Team $22,000 and 3 Weeks in Headshot Production" does more than "Check out my cool fantasy renders". Dollar figures here are the lesson's examples; use your own real, truthful numbers.
You will need:
 One past project (with client permission to share) and its numbers.
 templates/case-study-portfolio-template.md from this track.
 About 14 minutes.

chunks.title: Building a Portfolio That Sells — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a Portfolio That Sells / Step by step.
### 1. Pick a project to reframe
Choose your best past project. If you have none, build a clearly labelled sample project instead; never invent a client.
You should see: one project chosen.
If not: pick the one where you can name the problem it solved.
### 2. Open the template and write the Client and Challenge
Part 1 covers the client, traditional costs, slow timelines and pain points.
You should see: a paragraph naming who the client was and what the old way cost or delayed.
If not: ask the client or estimate, labelling estimates.
### 3. Write the AI Pipeline
Part 2 describes your custom prompt architecture and identity locking: what you built and why it beat the traditional method.
You should see: a short description of the pipeline in plain business terms.
If not: explain the result before the tools.
### 4. Build the ROI metrics table
Part 3 is hard numbers. Use this layout (the lesson's sample figures):
text
Metric | Traditional | AI Pipeline | Client benefit
Total Campaign Cost | $24,500 | $6,000 | $18,500 direct savings (75.5%)
Delivery Turnaround | 25 business days | 24 hours | 25x faster
Employee Downtime | 3.5 hours per employee | 2 minutes (selfie upload) | 420 productive hours saved
Usage Rights | 2-year limited license | Full commercial IP transfer | Perpetual global asset rights
Calculate your own exact savings and speed-up numbers.

chunks.title: Building a Portfolio That Sells — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a Portfolio That Sells / Step by step.
You should see: a table with traditional, AI and benefit columns for your project.
If not: savings % = (traditional - AI) / traditional; check against the example (18,500 / 24,500 is about 75.5%).
### 5. Request a testimonial
Part 4 is a verified quote. Ask the client for a 30-second smartphone video testimonial to embed on your site.
You should see: a sent request.
If not: ask for a written quote instead and follow up in a week.
### 6. Plan the demo portal
Build an interactive page (Notion, Webflow, Framer, or simple HTML) with a before/after slider: raw selfie on one side, AI headshot on the other.
You should see: a sketch listing slider, motion clips and sample download.
If not: start with a plain two-image page; add the slider later.
### 7. Add the three portal elements
1. Interactive image sliders between inputs and final renders.
2. Embedded image-to-video loops showing lighting motion and camera pans.
3. A downloadable zip of 5 uncompressed 8k sample files for the client's design team.
You should see: a checklist of the three elements on your portal plan.
If not: include at least the slider first.
### 8. Repeat for three projects
Convert your 3 best projects into case studies using the template.
You should see: a list of three titled case studies.
If not: finish one fully before starting the next.

chunks.title: What Coding Agents Actually Do — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: What Coding Agents Actually Do / Before you start.
Many creators think building tools needs a computer science degree. The barrier used to be that you could not build what you could not write. With coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, you can build anything you can clearly describe: the agent writes, edits, debugs and explains the code, and you direct it. A coding agent reads your project files, writes or edits code, runs it, reads the errors and corrects itself. A chatbot (ChatGPT, Claude.ai on the web) only replies in a chat window and has no file access, and a traditional script is code you must write and debug yourself.
You will need: a computer where you can install software, an empty folder for the project, and a basic comfort with typing one command in a terminal. You do not need any earlier lesson. This lesson is about building tools, so no SmartVideo GO AI studio is required here; the studios come back in Go further.

chunks.title: What Coding Agents Actually Do — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: What Coding Agents Actually Do / Step by step.
### 1. Pick one agent
Choose one of the two most creator-friendly options:
 Claude Code (Anthropic): a terminal-based agent that runs inside any project folder.
 Cursor (cursor.sh): a VS Code-based editor with the agent in a chat sidebar. Pick this if the terminal feels intimidating.
You should see: one choice made. You only need one.
If not: if you cannot decide, pick Cursor; it has the more familiar visual layout.
### 2. Install it and open an empty folder
1. For Claude Code, run this in a terminal (it needs Node.js already installed):
bash
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
2. For Cursor, download the app from cursor.sh, then use it to open a new empty folder.
3. Sign in to the agent with your own account when asked. Never paste a secret key into a chat.
You should see: the agent's prompt in your terminal (Claude Code) or a chat sidebar next to an empty file list (Cursor).
If not: if the npm command is not found, Node.js is not installed yet. Install it first, then run the command again.
### 3. Prime your first session
Open templates/vibe-coding-session-brief.md and read how a session is set up. You will use it properly in lesson 3; for now just see the fields.
You should see: a brief with fields such as tool name, input, output and error handling.
If not: if the link does not open, continue; the next step does not depend on it.

chunks.title: What Coding Agents Actually Do — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: What Coding Agents Actually Do / Step by step.
### 4. Give the agent one clear instruction
Type this single instruction into the agent:
text
Create a Python script called batchpromptrunner.py that reads a list of prompts from a file called prompts.txt (one prompt per line) and prints each one numbered.
You should see: the agent creating the file and confirming it works. It may also create prompts.txt or ask you to.
If not: if the agent asks a question, answer in plain English. If prompts.txt is missing, ask the agent to create it with three sample prompts.
### 5. Run what the agent built
Run the file in your terminal:
bash
python batchpromptrunner.py
You should see: your prompts printed, numbered. This is your first agent-built tool.
If not: if python is not found, tell the agent the exact error message and ask it how to run the script on your system.
### 6. Change it with a plain-English correction
Tell the agent:
text
Now instead of printing, save the output to a file called results.txt.
Run the script again and open results.txt.
You should see: a new results.txt with your numbered prompts. You did not read any code; you only described the change.
If not: if nothing was created, paste the exact error message back to the agent and ask it to fix it.

chunks.title: What Coding Agents Actually Do — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: What Coding Agents Actually Do / Common mistakes.
 Starting with something huge. One small instruction first; ambition comes in lesson 2.
 Describing the change vaguely. Say exactly which file and what output you want.
 Pasting secret keys into the chat. Keys belong in environment variables, never in a prompt.
 Treating the chatbot as an agent. A chat window with no file access cannot run or fix your project.

chunks.title: Building Your First Sellable Micro-Tool — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building Your First Sellable Micro-Tool / Before you start.
Most creators who discover coding agents try to build something huge, such as a full SaaS platform. These projects stall within 48 hours because the scope is too large to describe in one instruction, errors cannot be traced, and weeks pass with nothing to sell. The Micro-Tool Method fixes this: build one tool that does exactly one thing well, small enough for a single 60-minute session. Before you open the agent, answer four questions: what is the exact input, the exact output, the one transformation, and who is the buyer.
You will need: a coding agent from lesson 1 (Claude Code or Cursor) in a new empty folder, an OpenAI API key stored in an environment variable called OPENAIAPIKEY (never pasted into a chat), and 5 real product names. Prerequisite: lesson 1. No SmartVideo GO AI studio is needed to build the tool.

chunks.title: Building Your First Sellable Micro-Tool — Step by step
chunks.text:

Choose one category, or your own in the same style:
| Tool Category | What It Does | Target Buyer | Sell Price |

| Batch Prompt Runner | Sends 50+ prompts to FLUX/muapi in one click | AI image creators | $29 - $49 |
| Etsy SEO Title Generator | Generates 3 title + keyword sets per product from a name list | POD sellers | $19 - $39 |
| Stock Metadata CSV Writer | Reads image filenames and writes 30 IPTC keywords per image | Stock contributors | $29 - $59 |
| Pricing Calculator Widget | Interactive web form that calculates package pricing for a client | Agency freelancers | $19 - $29 |
| YouTube Script Formatter | Reformats a raw script into hook / body / CTA sections with timestamps | Faceless channel creators | $15 - $25 |
The rest of this lesson uses the Etsy SEO Title Generator.
You should see: one tool chosen that solves a task you or a buyer repeats often.
If not: if two tools tempt you, pick the one whose buyer you can name today.
### 2. Fill in the scope definition
Open templates/tool-scope-definition.md and answer the four questions. For the Etsy tool:
 Input: a .txt file named products.txt, one product name per line (for example Cyberpunk Cat Tee, Botanical Wildflower Mug).
 Output: a seotitles.csv with columns Product Name, Title 1, Title 2, Title 3, Keywords.

chunks.title: Building Your First Sellable Micro-Tool — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building Your First Sellable Micro-Tool / Step by step.
 Transformation: call the OpenAI API with a fixed SEO prompt for each product name.
 Buyer: Etsy POD sellers who publish 20+ new designs per month.
You should see: four short, specific answers, each one line.
If not: if an answer needs "and", the tool is doing two things. Cut one.
### 3. Give the agent the instruction
Open your agent in a new empty folder and paste this, adapting it only if you chose another tool:
text
Build a Python script called etsyseogenerator.py that:
1. Reads product names from products.txt (one per line).
2. For each name, calls the OpenAI chat completions API using the model gpt-4o-mini with this system prompt: 'You are an expert Etsy SEO copywriter. Generate 3 optimized Etsy listing title variations and 5 relevant keywords for the given product name. Format your response as JSON: {title1, title2, title3, keywords}.'
3. Writes all results to seotitles.csv with columns: ProductName, Title1, Title2, Title3, Keywords.
4. Reads the OpenAI API key from an environment variable called OPENAIAPIKEY.
You should see: the agent creating etsyseogenerator.py and explaining in plain English what it built.
If not: if the explanation does not match the four points, correct it with one sentence, not a full re-description.
### 4. Test with real data
1. Create products.txt with 5 of your actual product names.
2. Run:
bash
python etsyseogenerator.py

chunks.title: Building Your First Sellable Micro-Tool — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building Your First Sellable Micro-Tool / Step by step.
3. Open seotitles.csv and judge the titles.
You should see: a CSV with 5 rows, each with 3 titles and keywords.
If not: paste the exact error message into the agent. If a title looks weak, tell it:
text
Improve the system prompt to produce more buyer-intent focused titles with emotional hooks.
### 5. Package it for non-technical buyers
Ask the agent:
text
Add a simple README.md explaining how to install and run this tool in plain English for someone who has never used Python. Include the exact terminal commands.
You should see: a README.md with numbered install and run steps.
If not: if it is too technical, ask the agent to rewrite it for a complete beginner and add a sample products.txt.

chunks.title: The Vibe-Coding Workflow: Prompt, Build, Test, Ship — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: The Vibe-Coding Workflow: Prompt, Build, Test, Ship / Before you start.
After a second or third tool, many creators hit a wall: the agent produces a file that crashes, you paste the error back, something else breaks, and after 3 rounds the project is abandoned. Vibe-coding without structure is just random prompting. The fix is a 4-phase loop, Prompt, Build, Test, Ship, which gives you and the agent a clear contract for each phase. Original timing guidance: Prompt about 10 minutes, Build 15-30, Test 10-15, Ship 10. A first run with a small tool can be much faster, which is what this lesson uses.
You will need: Claude Code or Cursor from lesson 1, a small tool idea (the example is a FLUX Batch Prompt Runner), 3 real prompts, and a muapi key stored as the MUAPIKEY environment variable (never typed into chat). Prerequisites: lessons 1 and 2.

chunks.title: The Vibe-Coding Workflow: Prompt, Build, Test, Ship — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: The Vibe-Coding Workflow: Prompt, Build, Test, Ship / Step by step.
### 1. Write the session brief before opening the agent
Open templates/vibe-coding-session-brief.md. A brief needs a one-sentence description, error handling rules and tech constraints. Golden rule: never open the agent without a written brief. Fill it in like this:
text
Tool Name: FLUX Batch Prompt Runner
One-Line Description: Reads prompts from prompts.txt, sends each to muapi /nano-banana-2, saves all output image URLs to results.csv.
Input: prompts.txt - one prompt string per line
Output: results.csv - columns: PromptText, ImageURL, Timestamp
API: muapi (key from MUAPIKEY environment variable)
Error Handling: If an API call fails, log the error to errors.log and continue.
Packages Allowed: requests, csv (standard library)
You should see: a complete brief with every field filled and no blanks.
If not: if you cannot fill a field, the tool is not scoped yet. Revisit lesson 2's four questions.
### 2. Build: paste the whole brief once
Paste the full brief into the agent in a single message and let it finish without interrupting.
You should see: the agent generating the complete first version and explaining it in plain English.
If not: if the agent stops to ask something, answer briefly and let it continue.
### 3. Check the explanation, not the code
Read the agent's plain-English explanation and compare it with your brief.

chunks.title: The Vibe-Coding Workflow: Prompt, Build, Test, Ship — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: The Vibe-Coding Workflow: Prompt, Build, Test, Ship / Step by step.
You should see: an explanation that matches your input, output, API and error handling.
If not: correct it with one targeted sentence, not a full re-description. In the original example the agent used requests.get() instead of requests.post(), and a single sentence fixed it.
### 4. Test on real data
Create a prompts.txt with 3 real prompts you would actually use, then run the script (adapt the file name to what your agent created):
bash
python batchrunner.py
Check three things: is the output format correct, does it handle blank lines, special characters and long strings, and does it finish in under 60 seconds for a typical input?
You should see: a results.csv with 3 rows and working image URLs.
If not: paste the exact error message, not a paraphrase:
text
Running the script gives this error: KeyError: 'title1'. Fix it.
### 5. Ship: generate the packaging files
Ask the agent:
text
Write a plain-English README.md explaining installation and usage. Also create a requirements.txt listing all pip packages needed.
You should see: a README.md and a requirements.txt in the folder.
If not: if packages are missing from requirements.txt, ask the agent to check every import in the script.
### 6. Zip and name it
Zip the folder as [tool-name]-v1.0.zip. Uploading to Gumroad or LemonSqueezy is covered in lesson 4.

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling Tools You Build With Agents — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling Tools You Build With Agents / Before you start.
Many creators undercharge or give their tool away free. They post it on GitHub, get 200 stars and make $0. Others price by gut feel ("$5, it's just a script"). Buyers pay for time saved, not code complexity. A single well-scoped tool can bring $500 to $3,000 in the first 30 days from an audience of a few thousand. The pricing formula is:
Tool Price = Hours Saved Per Month x Buyer's Hourly Rate x 0.10
In plain English: price at roughly 10% of the monthly value the tool saves. If it saves an Etsy seller 8 hours a month at $25/hour, that is $200/month of value, so charge $20 one-time (or $9/month if you have ongoing API costs).
You will need: a finished tool zip from lesson 3 (or a tool idea), and about 14 minutes. Prerequisites: lessons 2 and 3. Part 2 covers the platform setup and launch.

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling Tools You Build With Agents — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling Tools You Build With Agents / Step by step.
### 1. Calculate your price
Plug your own numbers into the formula above. Write down hours saved per month, the buyer's hourly rate and the result.
You should see: one number, for example 8 x $25 x 0.10 = $20.
If not: if you do not know the hours saved, time the manual task once and multiply by how often the buyer does it.
### 2. Choose a pricing model
Pick one:
1. One-time lifetime license (most popular for scripts): single payment, no server costs. Converts at 3-5x the rate of subscriptions for audiences under 10,000 followers.
2. Monthly subscription (for tools with API costs): pass your GPT-4 or muapi costs through with a $9-$29/month plan. LemonSqueezy handles subscription billing.
3. Pay-what-you-want with a minimum: a floor of $9 with a suggested price of $25; Gumroad supports this natively.
You should see: one model chosen that matches whether your tool costs you money on every run.
If not: if it calls a paid API on each run, choose the subscription.
### 3. Write the headline and the pain
Open templates/micro-tool-product-page.md. Lead with the outcome, not the tool name. Write 5 headline variations and keep the strongest. Example:
text
Generate 30 IPTC Keywords for Every Stock Photo in 4 Minutes
Not "Stock Metadata CSV Script v1.2". Then one sentence of pain:
text
Manually tagging 100 stock images takes 25+ hours. This tool does it in 4 minutes.

Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Before you start.
SmartVideo GO AI Academy. This track takes one of the ready-made reseller apps from your own GitHub copy to a live, hosted business, with an AI chat doing the technical work for you through connectors.
Who it is for. You own (or are about to own) one of the 38 reseller apps and you are not a developer. You do not want to learn a framework. You want to be able to say "host this", "add sign-up", "check the payment went through" to a chat and have it done, while you stay in control of what changes and what it costs. If you can create accounts, copy and paste, and read a screen carefully, you can do this track. Every step tells you what you should see when it worked.
What you will build. By the end you will have, for one app of your choice:
1. Free accounts on Netlify, Clerk and Stripe (Stripe in test mode), alongside GitHub.
2. Connectors that let Claude and/or ChatGPT see and use those services with your approval.
3. Your app built and hosted on Netlify from your own GitHub copy, at a netlify.app address.
4. Clerk sign-up and sign-in so real people can create accounts.
5. Stripe test payments that add credits, which you can check by asking the chat.
6. A reusable set of prompts so the next app takes a fraction of the time.

chunks.title: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — The lessons
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / The lessons.
Plan on a weekend for your first app, taking breaks between lessons. The second app will take an afternoon.

chunks.title: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — What the apps already include (and what they do not)
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / What the apps already include (and what they do not).
Be clear about this before you start, because it decides what your assistant has to change.
 Already in the apps: Stripe payments and credit packs, a PostgreSQL database accessed through Prisma, Google sign-in through NextAuth, and the AI calls through your own MuAPI key. Each app's workshop page lists its exact variable names.
 Not in the apps: Netlify hosting settings and Clerk sign-in. Your assistant adds those to your own copy of the code, on a separate branch, and you approve every step.
This is why the track is a build and not a button: you are making two real changes to a real application, safely.

chunks.title: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Step by step: how to use this course
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Step by step: how to use this course.
### 1. Start with lesson 1 and go in order
Each lesson depends on the one before it. Open lesson 1 and finish it before moving on.
You should see: each lesson ends with a Check yourself list and a pointer to the next lesson.
If not: if you skipped ahead and a step does not match your screen, go back to the first lesson you did not finish.
### 2. Stop at the end of any lesson
Every lesson ends at a safe stopping point, and nothing is left half-changed. Take a break there.
You should see: all the boxes in Check yourself ticked before you close the lesson.
If not: if one box will not tick, use that lesson's Common mistakes before you continue.
### 3. Use Module 13 to do the work
The Reseller Setup Walkthrough (/academy/reseller/launch) takes you through Vercel-based deployment, the database, Google sign-in, Stripe and launch for the app you select. Module 13 of that course is the interactive version of this track: Learn, Follow along, Complete and Verify for each lesson, with your selected app's facts shown beside the steps.
You should see: your selected app's facts beside each step.
If not: use this track to understand the whole picture, and follow the written steps here.

chunks.title: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — The rules that keep you safe
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / The rules that keep you safe.
 Sign in to your own accounts only. Never connect a client's or an employer's account to practise.
 Read-only first. Before a chat is allowed to change anything, test it with a question that only reads.
 Never paste a secret key into a chat. Not Stripe keys, not the Clerk secret key, not database addresses, not the MuAPI key. Secrets go into the dashboard settings of Netlify, Clerk and Stripe. The assistant's job is to tell you which variable name to fill in; your job is to paste the value into the dashboard yourself.
 Test mode until lesson 13. Stripe stays in test mode, and Clerk stays on its development instance, until you go live in lesson 13.
 Small steps, explained first. Ask the assistant to say what it will change and why before it changes it. You can undo anything in GitHub.
 Menus change. Claude, ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe all rename and move things. This track teaches the flow and tells you what the result should look like; when a label differs, follow the service's official page.

chunks.title: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — How to use an assistant well
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / How to use an assistant well.
1. Give context once, clearly (lesson 4), then refer back to it.
2. Ask for a plan before a change. "Plan how to... Do not change anything yet."
3. One change at a time. After each, test it before the next.
4. Make it show evidence. "Show me the file you changed." "Read the deploy log and tell me the first error."
5. Keep a note of what worked, because the prompts become your template for every later app.

chunks.title: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Check yourself.
 [ ] I know which app I am taking live.
 [ ] I know the two things the apps do not include: Netlify settings and Clerk sign-in.
 [ ] I can state the safety rules: own accounts, read-only first, no secrets in chat, test mode.
 [ ] I know to start with lesson 1.

chunks.title: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Words you will meet
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Words you will meet.
 Repository (repo): your app's folder of code on GitHub.
 Branch: a separate line of changes you can test without touching the working app.
 Deploy: building the app and putting it online.
 Environment variable: a named setting (like a key) kept in the hosting dashboard, not in the code.
 Webhook: a message Stripe sends your app to say a payment happened.
 Connector (plugin): a switch that lets Claude or ChatGPT use another service for you.
 Test mode: Stripe's practice mode: fake cards, no real money.

chunks.title: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Common mistakes.
 Rushing past a check. Tick every box before the next lesson.
 Pasting a secret to "help" the chat. Secrets go only into dashboards.
 Skipping the plan. Ask for a plan before every change.

chunks.title: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe.
# Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: GitHub, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe accounts, all protected, with Stripe in test mode.
---

chunks.title: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Before you start.
A live app is several services working together. You will open or check four accounts, each with one job, and knowing the job makes every later step make sense.
| Account | Its one job | What you will put in it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GitHub | Stores your own copy of the app's code | The repository for your chosen app |
| Netlify | Builds the code and serves it on the internet | Your site and its environment variables |
| Clerk | Handles sign-up, sign-in and user accounts | Your application and its keys |
| Stripe | Takes payments and reports them | Test keys, a webhook, test payments |
The AI part (MuAPI) and the database (Supabase or Neon) you already set up in Modules 4 and 5 of the Reseller Setup Walkthrough. If you have not done those, finish them first; lesson 6 needs the database address.
All three new services offer a free plan at the time of writing. That does not mean free forever at any size. Free plans have limits (for example on build minutes, bandwidth or monthly active users), and the numbers change. A free plan is more than enough to build and test, and often to take your first customers. Nothing in this track asks you to pay.
You will need:
 Your GitHub account from the Reseller Setup Walkthrough, with your app already forked.
 A business email address and a password manager.

chunks.title: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Before you start.
 About 18 minutes. This is a full lesson with four sign-ups, so go at a calm pace and stop at any step.

chunks.title: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Step by step.
### 1. Check your GitHub copy
1. Sign in to the GitHub account you used in the Reseller Setup Walkthrough.
2. Open your own copy (fork) of the app.
You should see: the app's repository under your account name.
If not: fork the app into your account first, because Netlify deploys from your copy.
### 2. Note each free plan's limits
1. Open the pricing page of Netlify, Clerk and Stripe (menus and prices move; use each service's current page).
2. Find the current free plan and write its main limits in your own notes, with today's date.
You should see: a dated note with limits such as build minutes, bandwidth or monthly active users.
If not: if a service has no free plan today, re-check the page before paying for anything.
### 3. Sign up to Netlify
1. Open Netlify's sign-up page and choose Sign up with GitHub. This lets Netlify read the repositories you choose, which makes lesson 5 easier.
2. When asked, accept the free plan and give your team a name matching your business.
You should see: your team dashboard, a list of projects that is empty for now.
If not: if Netlify cannot see your repo, change which repositories it may read in your GitHub settings under installed applications.
### 4. Create your Clerk application
1. Open Clerk's sign-up page and create an account.
2. Create an application named after your business. This is the name people see on sign-up screens.

chunks.title: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Step by step.
3. Keep the sign-in options Email and Google. Add others later if you want.
You should see: a Clerk development instance, the practice version. It works on netlify.app and preview addresses, and it is where you stay until you have your own domain.
If not: if Clerk asks you to choose a plan, choose the free plan if the current pricing page offers one.
### 5. Find your Clerk API keys
1. In Clerk, open the API keys page.
2. Look at the publishable key and the secret key, but do not copy them anywhere yet.
You should see: both keys listed. Just know where they are; later lessons tell you where each one goes.
If not: menus move, so look for a page named API keys or developers in the dashboard's current layout.
### 6. Put Stripe in test mode
1. Create or sign in to your Stripe account.
2. Check that the dashboard shows a Test mode or Sandbox indicator.
You should see: test mode on. Everything in this track uses test mode. You do not need to activate your account for real payments yet; that is lesson 13 and Module 9.
If not: switch to test mode before doing anything else. There is nothing to gain from live mode before the test purchase works.
### 7. Protect every account
1. For each of the four accounts, turn on two-step sign-in.
2. Save a strong, unique password in your password manager, and make sure each account uses your business email.

chunks.title: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Step by step.
You should see: two-step sign-in listed as on in each account's security settings.
If not: if you used a personal email, change it now; it makes handing the business over harder later. These accounts control your app, your customers' sign-ups and your payments, so treat them like the keys to a shop.

chunks.title: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Check yourself.
 [ ] I can open GitHub, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe dashboards.
 [ ] Stripe shows test mode and Clerk shows a development instance.
 [ ] Two-step sign-in is on for all four.
 [ ] I wrote down each free plan's limits and the date.

chunks.title: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Common mistakes.
 Skipping the pricing pages, then discovering a limit mid-launch.
 Using a personal email, which makes handing the business over harder later.
 Switching Stripe to live too early. Stay in test mode until lesson 13.
 Connecting a client's account to practise. Use your own.
Next: lesson 2, connecting Claude.

chunks.title: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe.
# Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: Claude connected to your three services, proven by a read-only test.
---

chunks.title: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Before you start.
Without connectors, a chat can only talk. It can explain how to deploy a site, but it cannot see your Netlify account. A connector (sometimes called a plugin or an integration) gives the chat a controlled way to use another service as you. You sign in to the service, approve what the chat may do, and from then on you can say:
 "List my Netlify sites and their last deploy."
 "Show my five most recent Stripe test payments."
 "Which Clerk application am I connected to?"
Most connectors are built on an open standard called the Model Context Protocol (MCP). You do not need to understand it. What you do need to understand is the trust model:
1. You sign in to the real service.
2. The service tells you what the chat is asking permission to do.
3. You approve it, and you can remove it any time from the same settings.
The chat never needs your password or your secret keys, because the connector holds the sign-in.
Netlify, Stripe and Clerk each offer a connector for Claude. Availability depends on your Claude plan and on whether your workspace allows connectors, and the names and places of the menus change. So this lesson teaches the flow and what the result looks like; where a label differs on your screen, follow the official page for each service.
You will need:
 Your Netlify, Clerk and Stripe accounts from lesson 1, each signed in to in this browser.
 About 15 minutes.

chunks.title: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Step by step.
### 1. Open the connector settings
1. Open Claude, sign in, and open its settings.
2. Look for the area that manages connectors (or integrations).
You should see: a list of connectors, or a button to add one.
If not: your plan or workspace may restrict connectors. Check the official help page for your plan, or ask your workspace admin.
### 2. Add Netlify
1. Add the Netlify connector. A Netlify sign-in page opens; sign in with the account from lesson 1.
2. When Netlify shows what is being requested, approve access for your own team only.
You should see: Netlify shown as connected back in Claude.
If not: if the window opens and closes without finishing, allow pop-ups for Claude and try again.
### 3. Add Stripe (test mode only)
1. Add the Stripe connector and sign in.
2. Choose your test-mode account when asked, and approve.
You should see: Stripe shown as connected, with the test or sandbox account named. Stripe's documentation describes its connector and what it can do; the page is linked in the Reseller Setup Walkthrough, lesson 13.2.
If not: if it shows a live account, disconnect and reconnect, choosing test mode. Nothing in this course needs live mode before lesson 13.
### 4. Add Clerk
1. Add the Clerk connector and sign in.
2. Select the application you created in lesson 1 and approve.
You should see: Clerk shown as connected with your application's name.

chunks.title: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Step by step.
If not: some connectors need a separate authorization step before their tools appear. If Clerk says it needs authorization, finish that sign-in from the connector's entry in settings.
### 5. Run the read-only test
Open a new chat and paste this:
text
Using your Netlify, Stripe and Clerk connectors, list my Netlify sites, my Clerk application name, and my five most recent Stripe test payments. Do not change anything.
You should see: an answer naming your Clerk application and either "no sites" or the sites you really have. A new account will show zero sites and zero payments. That is fine: you are checking that Claude reaches the right account, not that there is data.
If not: if Claude says it cannot see a service, open that connector's entry in settings and finish any pending authorization. This test should never need you to approve a change.
### 6. Compare the answer with your dashboards
Open the Netlify, Clerk and Stripe dashboards in other tabs and check the answer against them.
You should see: the same Clerk application name, the same (possibly empty) lists, and Stripe in test mode.
If not: a different name or live Stripe data means you signed in with a different account in the browser. Disconnect that connector, sign out of the service, sign in with the right account and reconnect.

chunks.title: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Check yourself.
 [ ] All three connectors show as connected.
 [ ] The read-only test answered with facts from my own accounts.
 [ ] Nothing was changed by the test.
 [ ] I know how to disconnect each connector.

chunks.title: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Keeping it safe
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Keeping it safe.
 Approve narrowly. Choose your own team, your test-mode Stripe account, your one Clerk application.
 Read before write. Until you trust the setup, ask questions before you ask for changes.
 Know how to remove it. Each connector can be disconnected from the same settings, and from inside the service's own "authorized apps" page.

chunks.title: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Common mistakes.
 Pasting a secret key to "help". If the chat asks for a secret key, stop: the connector should not need it. Say: "Do not ask me for secret keys. Tell me which dashboard setting to fill in."
 Assuming it works because it connected. Always run the read-only test.
 Approving a live Stripe account. Test mode only until lesson 13.
 Copying a menu path from an old video. These menus move. Use the official page.
Next: lesson 3, ChatGPT.

chunks.title: Connect ChatGPT the same way
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect ChatGPT the same way.
# Connect ChatGPT the same way
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: ChatGPT connected to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe, or a clear decision to build with Claude instead.
---

chunks.title: Connect ChatGPT the same way — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect ChatGPT the same way / Before you start.
You will connect ChatGPT to the same three services you opened in lesson 1: Netlify (hosting), Clerk (sign-up) and Stripe (payments, in test mode). ChatGPT uses connectors built on the same open standard as Claude, so the safety rules are exactly the ones from lesson 2: sign in to your own accounts, approve only what you understand, and test with a question that only reads.
What is different is whether and where you can add connectors. That depends on your ChatGPT plan, on whether your workspace admin allows third-party connectors, and on menus that OpenAI renames and moves from time to time. So this lesson teaches the flow and tells you what the result should look like. If a label differs on your screen, follow OpenAI's current help page for connectors and apps.
You will need:
 Your Netlify, Clerk and Stripe accounts from lesson 1, each signed in to in this browser.
 About 15 minutes.

chunks.title: Connect ChatGPT the same way — Do you need both assistants?
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect ChatGPT the same way / Do you need both assistants?.
No. Pick one to do the build and stay with it, because one conversation that knows your app is more useful than two that each know half.
 Use the assistant whose connectors worked first time on your plan.
 Keep the other as a second opinion for a stubborn error: paste the error message (never a secret) and ask for an independent explanation.
If you already finished lesson 2 and Claude works for you, you can skip this lesson and come back if you ever want a second opinion.

chunks.title: Connect ChatGPT the same way — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect ChatGPT the same way / Step by step.
### 1. Check whether your plan allows connectors
1. Open ChatGPT and sign in.
2. Open its settings and look for an area called connectors, apps or integrations.
You should see: a list of services you can connect, or a button to add one.
If you do not: your plan or workspace may not allow connectors. Skip to step 7. You have not done anything wrong.
### 2. Add Netlify
1. Choose to add or connect Netlify.
2. Sign in to Netlify when asked, using the account from lesson 1.
3. When Netlify shows what is being requested, approve access for your own team only.
You should see: Netlify listed as connected in ChatGPT.
If not: if a window opens and closes without finishing, allow pop-ups for ChatGPT and try again.
### 3. Add Stripe (test mode only)
1. Choose to add or connect Stripe and sign in.
2. Pick your test-mode account when asked, and approve.
You should see: Stripe listed as connected, and the test or sandbox account named.
If not: if it shows a live account, disconnect it and reconnect, choosing test mode. Nothing in this course needs live mode yet.
### 4. Add Clerk
1. Choose to add or connect Clerk and sign in.
2. Select the application you created in lesson 1 and approve.
You should see: Clerk listed as connected with your application's name.
If not: some connectors need a separate authorization before their tools appear. Open the connector's entry and finish that sign-in.

chunks.title: Connect ChatGPT the same way — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect ChatGPT the same way / Step by step.
### 5. Run the read-only test
Open a new chat and make sure the connectors are switched on for it, if ChatGPT asks you to enable them per chat. Then paste this and send it:
text
Using your Netlify, Stripe and Clerk connectors, list my Netlify sites, my Clerk application name, and my five most recent Stripe test payments. Do not change anything.
You should see: an answer with names from your own accounts. A brand-new account will say it has no sites and no payments. That is a good result: it proves ChatGPT reached your accounts.
If not: if it says it cannot see a service, check that connector is enabled for this chat. If ChatGPT asks to confirm an action, read it carefully. This test should never need you to approve a change.
### 6. Compare the answer with your dashboards
Open the Netlify, Clerk and Stripe dashboards in other tabs and check the answer against them.
You should see: the same Clerk application name, the same (possibly empty) lists, and Stripe in test mode.
If not: a different name or live Stripe data means you connected the wrong account. Disconnect that connector, sign out of that service in your browser, sign in with the right account and connect again.
### 7. If your plan does not allow connectors
You can still finish the whole course:
1. Do the build with Claude (lesson 2), or

chunks.title: Connect ChatGPT the same way — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect ChatGPT the same way / Step by step.
2. Keep using ChatGPT without connectors: ask it to explain each change and to tell you exactly which dashboard to open, and make the dashboard changes yourself.
Either way, the rule does not change: never paste a secret key into the chat.

chunks.title: Connect ChatGPT the same way — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect ChatGPT the same way / Check yourself.
 [ ] I connected ChatGPT to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe, or I confirmed my plan does not allow it and will use Claude.
 [ ] The read-only test returned my real data and changed nothing.
 [ ] Stripe shows test mode.
 [ ] I know how to disconnect each connector.

chunks.title: Connect ChatGPT the same way — Differences worth knowing
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect ChatGPT the same way / Differences worth knowing.
 Some features exist only on certain plans or only in certain modes. If a feature is missing, it is usually the plan, not you.
 Connector tools may need to be switched on in each chat. If the chat says it cannot see Netlify, check that first.
 Actions that change something may ask for confirmation each time. Read it and approve only what you expect.
 You can disconnect a connector from ChatGPT's settings and from the service's own list of authorized apps.

chunks.title: Connect ChatGPT the same way — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect ChatGPT the same way / Common mistakes.
 Copying a menu path from an old video. These menus move. Use the official page.
 Assuming it works because it connected. Always run the read-only test.
 Giving broad access. Approve one team, one application and test mode.
 Pasting a key to "help". The connector signs in for you, so the chat never needs your secret keys.
Next: lesson 4, briefing your assistant on the app.

chunks.title: Brief your assistant on the app
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Brief your assistant on the app.
# Brief your assistant on the app
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: an assistant that has read your app, understands what it already includes, and has agreed to your working rules.
---

chunks.title: Brief your assistant on the app — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Brief your assistant on the app / Before you start.
A new chat knows nothing about your app, even when connectors are working. It does not know what the app is, where its code lives, what it already does or what you want. Most failed AI builds fail here: a vague request ("put my app online") produces vague, sometimes destructive, changes. A good briefing takes about ten minutes and saves hours.
A good briefing has four parts:
1. Where the code is. Your own GitHub repository (the fork from the Reseller Setup Walkthrough), not the original and not someone else's.
2. What the app already includes. Taken from your app's workshop page (the Overview, Accounts, Database and Environment panels, though panel names may differ slightly on your screen):
 Framework: the reseller apps are Next.js applications.
 Database: PostgreSQL through Prisma, with the address in DATABASEURL.
 Sign-in: Google sign-in through NextAuth.
 Payments: Stripe checkout and a webhook that adds credits.
 AI: calls made with your MuAPI key.
3. What you want changed. For this track: host on Netlify, replace sign-in with Clerk, and keep the Stripe credits flow working in test mode.
4. How you want to work. Small steps, explain before changing, a separate branch for risky changes, and never ask for secret keys (the assistant says which dashboard setting to use instead).

chunks.title: Brief your assistant on the app — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Brief your assistant on the app / Before you start.
Your workshop page lists the exact variable names for your app. Names only, never values.
You will need:
 The assistant you chose in lessons 2 or 3, open in a new chat.
 Your fork's GitHub address and your app's workshop page.
 About 18 minutes.

chunks.title: Brief your assistant on the app — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Brief your assistant on the app / Step by step.
### 1. Find your repository address
Open your own fork on GitHub and copy its address from the browser bar.
You should see: an address with your own GitHub username in it.
If not: if the username is not yours, you are on the original repository. Go back to the Reseller Setup Walkthrough and open your fork.
### 2. Note what your app includes
Open your app's workshop page and look at the panels listed above. Write down the app name and the environment variable names (not values).
You should see: Next.js, PostgreSQL with Prisma, NextAuth with Google, Stripe and MuAPI, plus a list of variable names.
If not: if a panel is missing or named differently, look for the same information elsewhere on the page. Do not guess.
### 3. Send the briefing
Copy this, fill in the two placeholders (<APP NAME and <YOUR REPO ADDRESS), and paste it into a new chat:
text

chunks.title: Brief your assistant on the app — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Brief your assistant on the app / Step by step.
I am building my own copy of a reseller app called <APP NAME. My code is in my GitHub repo <YOUR REPO ADDRESS. It already uses Next.js, Prisma with PostgreSQL, Stripe payments and Google sign-in through NextAuth. My goal: host it on Netlify, replace sign-in with Clerk, and keep the existing Stripe credits flow working in test mode. Work in small steps. Before each change, tell me what you will change and why, and wait for my approval. Make risky changes on a new branch. Never ask me to paste secret keys into this chat; tell me which dashboard setting to use instead. Start by reading the repo and summarising: how sign-in works, how payments and credits work, the build command, and every environment variable the code reads (names only).
You should see: the assistant reads the repository and replies with a summary.
If not: if it says it cannot see your repo, use its GitHub connector. Otherwise paste only the specific files it asks for, never anything containing a secret.
### 4. Check the summary against the workshop page
The summary is your first test. Compare it with your panels:
 Does it name the same sign-in system (NextAuth with Google)?
 Does it find the Stripe webhook route and say what it does?
 Does it list the same environment variable names?
 Does it find where users and credits are stored?
You should see: matching answers to all four questions.
If not: go to step 5.

chunks.title: Brief your assistant on the app — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Brief your assistant on the app / Step by step.
### 5. Correct anything it got wrong
Tell it plainly, for example: "the webhook path is actually..." and ask it to summarise again.
You should see: a corrected summary that matches your workshop page.
If not: if it keeps getting something wrong, ask it to show you the file where it found that information. Every later step builds on this understanding, so do not move on with a wrong assumption.
### 6. Send the working rules
Send this:
text
Good. For the rest of this project: always show me a plan first, change one thing at a time, tell me how to test each change, and tell me exactly which dashboard I must visit for anything involving a key or a setting.
You should see: the assistant agrees to those rules.
If not: if it starts changing things without a plan, stop it and send the message again. This one message shapes the whole build.
### 7. Learn to read a change without being a developer
You will be asked to approve code changes. You do not need to understand every line, but check three things each time:
1. Does the explanation match what I asked for? If you asked for Clerk sign-in and it is also rewriting payment code, stop and ask why.
2. Is it on a branch? Risky work belongs on a branch, so the working app is untouched until you merge.
3. Is there a test I can run? Every change should come with "open this page, you should see this".

chunks.title: Brief your assistant on the app — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Brief your assistant on the app / Step by step.
You should see: you can answer all three questions for any proposed change.
If not: say, "Explain that change in plain language and tell me what could go wrong."

chunks.title: Brief your assistant on the app — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Brief your assistant on the app / Check yourself.
 [ ] The assistant correctly summarised my app.
 [ ] It agreed to explain before changing and not to ask for secrets.
 [ ] I corrected anything it got wrong.
 [ ] I know the three checks for approving a change.

chunks.title: Brief your assistant on the app — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Brief your assistant on the app / Common mistakes.
 Pasting secrets "to help". Never. The assistant does not need them to plan or to write code.
 Letting it make many changes at once. One change, one test.
 Skipping the summary check. A wrong assumption now becomes a broken build later.
Next: lesson 5, hosting on Netlify.

chunks.title: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site.
# Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: your app checked for Netlify and a Netlify site connected to your GitHub repo.
---

chunks.title: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site / Before you start.
Netlify connects to your GitHub repository. Every time you push a change, it builds the app (turns the code into something a browser can run) and publishes it. You do not run a server. If a build fails, nothing breaks: the previous working version keeps serving until a new one succeeds.
For a Next.js app, Netlify provides its own support for running Next.js features. Which settings you need (Node version, build command, plugin) can change between versions, so the assistant should check the current Netlify docs for Next.js rather than guess.
You will need:
 The chat from lesson 4, where the assistant already knows your app.
 Your Netlify and GitHub accounts, signed in.
 Your app's workshop page, open in another tab.
 About 18 minutes.

chunks.title: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site / Step by step.
### 1. Ask the assistant to check the app is ready
Send this:
text
Check this Next.js app is ready to deploy on Netlify, using the current Netlify docs for Next.js. List the build command, the Node version needed, and every environment variable the code reads (names only). Tell me about any change needed before I deploy, and wait for my approval before changing anything.
You should see: a build command, a Node version, a list of variable names and any proposed changes.
If not: if it does not mention the Netlify docs or guesses at settings, ask it to check the current Netlify docs for Next.js and answer again.
### 2. Compare the variable list with your workshop page
Open the Environment panel on your workshop page and compare it with the assistant's list.
You should see: the same names.
If not: differences are worth a question: "Why does the code read X when my workshop page does not list it?"
### 3. Put any approved changes on a branch
If the assistant proposes a change (for example a Netlify configuration file or a build setting), ask it to put it on a new branch named something like netlify-setup, and to explain it first.
You should see: a branch with a small configuration file, and no changes to your app's behaviour.
If not: if it wants to change how the app works, stop and ask why. Netlify setup should not change what the app does.
### 4. Choose how to create the site

chunks.title: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site / Step by step.
You have two options:
 Ask the assistant to create the Netlify site from your GitHub repository through the connector, or
 Do it yourself in Netlify. Doing it yourself the first time is a good way to learn where things are.
You should see: you have picked one way and are ready to start.
If not: if the Netlify connector is not working, do it yourself.
### 5. Start a new project from GitHub
If you are doing it yourself, in Netlify choose to add a new project (the button wording may differ) and import from GitHub. If you asked the assistant, read its plan first and approve it.
You should see: Netlify listing your GitHub repositories, or the assistant describing the site it will create.
If not: if your repository is missing, Netlify may need permission to see it. Follow the prompt to grant access to that one repository.
### 6. Pick your repository and branch
Pick your own repository and branch, and accept the build settings the assistant listed in step 1.
You should see: the build command and Node version matching the assistant's list.
If not: if Netlify suggests different settings, ask the assistant which is right according to the current docs.
### 7. Confirm the site exists
Open your site's page in Netlify.
You should see: a site connected to your repository. Its first deploy may not succeed yet, because variables are added in lesson 6. That is expected.

chunks.title: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site / Step by step.
If not: if no site appears, repeat step 5 and check you are in the right Netlify team.

chunks.title: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site / Check yourself.
 [ ] The assistant listed the build command and every variable name, and it matches my workshop page.
 [ ] Any change was on a branch and explained first.
 [ ] A Netlify site exists, connected to my repository.

chunks.title: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site / Common mistakes.
 Accepting changes that alter the app's behaviour. Netlify setup should not change what the app does.
 Skipping the comparison with the workshop page.
Next: lesson 6, add variables, deploy and fix failures.

chunks.title: Add variables, deploy and fix failures
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Add variables, deploy and fix failures.
# Add variables, deploy and fix failures
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: your app live at a netlify.app address, with every secret in Netlify's settings and none in the chat or the code.
---

chunks.title: Add variables, deploy and fix failures — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Add variables, deploy and fix failures / Before you start.
Your app reads secrets (the database address, Stripe keys, the MuAPI key, Clerk keys later) from environment variables. The rule for the whole track:
 The assistant tells you the name of each variable.
 You paste the value into Netlify's environment variable settings.
 Values never go in the chat, the repository, a screenshot or an email.
After you add or change a variable, you must redeploy, because the app only reads variables when it is built or started.
Variables you do not have yet (Clerk keys, the Stripe webhook secret) come in lessons 8 and 10. The app will not be fully working until then; that is expected.
You will need:
 The Netlify site from lesson 5.
 Your workshop page's variable names and the services that own the values (database host, Stripe, MuAPI).
 About 18 minutes.

chunks.title: Add variables, deploy and fix failures — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Add variables, deploy and fix failures / Step by step.
### 1. Open the environment variables area
In your site's settings in Netlify, find the environment variables area (the exact menu name may differ).
You should see: a place to add a variable name and value.
If not: look for a section named variables, environment or build settings. If you cannot find it, ask the assistant to check the current Netlify docs for where it is.
### 2. Add each variable name
For each variable name from your workshop page, add the name exactly as written, including capitals.
You should see: the names listed in Netlify.
If not: a typo in a name is the most common cause of later errors. Compare each name with your workshop page.
### 3. Paste each value from the service that owns it
Paste the value from the service that owns it (database host, Stripe, MuAPI). Mark secrets as secret if Netlify offers the option.
You should see: each variable saved, with secret values hidden.
If not: if you cannot find a value, open the service's own dashboard to get it. Do not ask the assistant to guess it and do not paste it in the chat.
### 4. Check the database address
Use the connection string your database host gives for applications. If your host offers a "pooled" and a "direct" string, your workshop page says which variable takes which.
You should see: DATABASEURL and any other database variable matching what your workshop page says.

chunks.title: Add variables, deploy and fix failures — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Add variables, deploy and fix failures / Step by step.
If not: if you are unsure which string goes where, ask the assistant which variable takes which, and check your answer against the workshop page.
### 5. Deploy
Trigger a deploy and watch the log.
You should see: the deploy ends with a status such as Published.
If not: go to step 6.
### 6. If the deploy fails, ask for the first error
Do not guess. Send this:
text
Read the failed deploy log through the Netlify connector and tell me the first error and what causes it. Do not change anything yet.
You should see: the first error and its cause. The first error is usually the real one; later errors are often consequences.
If not: if the connector cannot read the log, copy the first error line from the log and paste only that (check it contains no secret).
### 7. Fix one error at a time
Fix one error at a time, redeploying after each, until the deploy shows Published.
You should see: the deploy log getting further each time.
If not: if a fix does not help, undo it with the assistant before trying another, so you know which change did what.
### 8. Set the site's public address and redeploy
The variable your app uses for its own URL must match your real netlify.app address. You only know the address after the first deploy, so open the site, copy the address, set that variable in Netlify, then redeploy.

chunks.title: Add variables, deploy and fix failures — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Add variables, deploy and fix failures / Step by step.
You should see: a second deploy that shows Published, and your netlify.app address opening your app's home page.
If not: check the address has no typo and no trailing differences from the one Netlify shows.
### 9. Know what "working" looks like now
 The home page loads.
 Pages that do not need sign-in or payments work.
 Sign-in may not work yet (lessons 7 to 9 replace it) and payments are not connected to your Netlify address yet (lesson 10). That is fine.

chunks.title: Add variables, deploy and fix failures — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Add variables, deploy and fix failures / Check yourself.
 [ ] The deploy shows Published.
 [ ] My netlify.app address opens my app's home page.
 [ ] All variables I have so far are in Netlify, none in the chat or the repository.
 [ ] I redeployed after adding variables.

chunks.title: Add variables, deploy and fix failures — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Add variables, deploy and fix failures / Common mistakes.
 Changing a variable and not redeploying. Nothing changes until the next deploy.
 A typo in a variable name. Names must match exactly, including capitals.
 Putting secrets in a file in the repo. Even a private repo is not the place.
 Fixing several errors at once. You will not know which fix worked.

chunks.title: Add variables, deploy and fix failures — If something is off
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Add variables, deploy and fix failures / If something is off.
 Build fails on a missing variable. The build reads it. Add it in Netlify and redeploy.
 The page loads but data fails. The database address is wrong or the tables were not created. Revisit Module 5 of the Reseller Setup Walkthrough.
 Works locally but not on Netlify. The assistant should compare the Node version and build command with Netlify's settings.
Next: lesson 7, planning the Clerk change.

chunks.title: Plan the Clerk change
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Plan the Clerk change.
# Plan the Clerk change
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a reviewed plan for replacing NextAuth with Clerk that keeps every person's credits.
---

chunks.title: Plan the Clerk change — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Plan the Clerk change / Before you start.
Your app ships with Google sign-in through NextAuth. Clerk replaces it with ready-made sign-up and sign-in screens, email and Google options, and a dashboard where you can see your users. This is a real change to your copy of the code, so we do it carefully, and the plan comes before the code.
What must not break: the link between a person and their credits. Your app stores users and credits in its own database. If Clerk creates a new user identity and the app does not connect it to a user record, every new sign-up will have no credits (or worse, someone sees another person's).
How Clerk works, in plain terms:
 Clerk keeps the account (email, password or Google, sessions).
 Your app asks Clerk, on every request, "who is signed in?" and gets a user ID.
 Your app uses that ID to find, or create, its own user record and its credits.
Clerk gives you two keys:
 A publishable key: safe to be visible in the browser.
 A secret key: private; it goes only in Netlify's environment variables, never in the chat.
Clerk's official docs describe adding it to Next.js and also describe tools for working with AI assistants. Always ask your assistant to follow the current Clerk docs rather than work from memory, because the exact setup changes between versions.
You will need:
 The chat from lessons 4 to 6, where the assistant knows your app.

chunks.title: Plan the Clerk change — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Plan the Clerk change / Before you start.
 About 15 minutes. You will not change any code in this lesson.

chunks.title: Plan the Clerk change — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Plan the Clerk change / Step by step.
### 1. Ask for a plan, not a change
Send this:
text
Plan how to replace NextAuth with Clerk in this app using the current Clerk docs for Next.js. Show me where users and credits are stored, how each Clerk user will map to a user record in our database, what happens to people who already signed in with Google, and the exact files you will change. Do not change anything yet.
You should see: a written plan and no code changes.
If not: if it starts editing files, tell it to stop and undo, then send the prompt again.
### 2. Check the mapping
Look for how a Clerk user ID is stored against a user record, and how a new user gets starting credits (if the app gives any).
You should see: a clear statement of where the Clerk user ID is stored and how credits are attached to it.
If not: ask, "Where exactly will the Clerk user ID be stored, and how does a new user get their credits?"
### 3. Check what happens to existing users
If you already have customers, ask how they keep their credits. A new app with no customers can ignore this.
You should see: a plan that keeps existing people's credits, or you confirming you have no customers yet.
If not: ask, "How will someone who signed in with Google before keep their credits after the change?"
### 4. Check the file list
Read the list of files it will change.

chunks.title: Plan the Clerk change — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Plan the Clerk change / Step by step.
You should see: files about sign-in, middleware and the user lookup, not payments or AI calls.
If not: if the plan touches payment code, ask why before going any further.
### 5. Confirm it follows the current Clerk docs
Ask the assistant to confirm which Clerk documentation it used and to note anything that depends on a version.
You should see: a reference to the current Clerk docs for Next.js.
If not: ask it to check the current Clerk docs again instead of working from memory.
### 6. Approve the plan in words
When you are satisfied, reply that you approve the plan and that the next step is to make the change on a new branch. Do not ask for the keys in the chat; you add them in Netlify in lesson 8.
You should see: the assistant agrees to wait for lesson 8's change, on a branch.
If not: if you are unsure about any point, do not approve yet. Ask for it to be explained in plain language.

chunks.title: Plan the Clerk change — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Plan the Clerk change / Check yourself.
 [ ] I read the plan and it maps Clerk users to user records and credits.
 [ ] It says what happens to existing users (or I have none).
 [ ] The file list is about sign-in and users, not payments or AI calls.
 [ ] No code has been changed yet.

chunks.title: Plan the Clerk change — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Plan the Clerk change / Common mistakes.
 Approving a plan that touches payment code without asking why.
 Skipping the plan and asking for the change directly.
Next: lesson 8, make the change and add the keys.

chunks.title: Make the Clerk change and add the keys
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Make the Clerk change and add the keys.
# Make the Clerk change and add the keys
 Time: about 15 minutes, plus the wait for the preview build. You will finish with: Clerk working on a Netlify preview deploy, with the keys in Netlify only.
---

chunks.title: Make the Clerk change and add the keys — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Make the Clerk change and add the keys / Before you start.
Your plan from lesson 7 is approved. Now the assistant makes the change on a separate branch, so your working site stays untouched, and you add the Clerk keys yourself. The assistant never needs to see them. Netlify keeps them as environment variables and the app reads them when it is built.
Clerk's development instance is for building and testing. It works on netlify.app and preview addresses. A production instance requires your own domain and its own keys, and it is a separate set of users. You will set that up when you go live in lesson 13; do not use it earlier.
You will need:
 The approved plan from lesson 7 and the chat where you made it.
 Your Clerk and Netlify dashboards, signed in to in this browser.
 About 15 minutes. Menu names in Clerk and Netlify change from time to time, so if a label differs, look for the closest match.

chunks.title: Make the Clerk change and add the keys — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Make the Clerk change and add the keys / Step by step.
### 1. Ask for the change on a branch
Paste this into the same chat as your plan and send it:
text
Create a branch called clerk-signup and make the change you described. Explain each file you change. Tell me the exact environment variable names I need to add in Netlify. Do not ask me for secret keys.
You should see: the assistant creating a branch called clerk-signup, explaining each file it changes, and giving you a list of environment variable names.
If not: if it works on your main branch or asks you for a key, stop it and repeat the prompt. Keys never go into the chat.
### 2. Read the explanation of each file
Read what the assistant says about every changed file. Ask about anything you do not follow.
You should see: a plain-language reason for each file, matching the plan you approved.
If not: if it changed files your plan did not mention, ask why before going on.
### 3. Write down the variable names
Copy the exact variable names the assistant gave you into a note. You will type them into Netlify in step 5.
