You should see: a short list of names, typically one for the publishable key and one for the secret key.
If not: ask the assistant to list the names again. Do not guess them.
### 4. Open the API keys page in Clerk
In Clerk, open the API keys page for your development instance.
You should see: a publishable key and a secret key, with the development instance selected.

chunks.title: Make the Clerk change and add the keys — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Make the Clerk change and add the keys / Step by step.
If not: if you see a production instance, switch to development. Use production only in lesson 13.
### 5. Add the keys in Netlify
In Netlify, open your site's environment variable settings. Add each variable name from step 3, pasting the publishable and secret values yourself.
You should see: every variable from your list saved in Netlify.
If not: a mistyped name is the usual cause of failures later. Compare each name against your note, letter by letter.
### 6. Redeploy the branch as a deploy preview
Ask Netlify to build a preview for the clerk-signup branch. Netlify can build a preview for a branch, and a new build is needed because variables are only picked up on the next build.
You should see: a deploy preview for the branch building and then marked as published, with its own preview address.
If not: if the build fails, copy the error text (never a key) into the chat and ask the assistant to explain it. If the build succeeded before you added the keys, trigger it again.

chunks.title: Make the Clerk change and add the keys — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Make the Clerk change and add the keys / Check yourself.
 [ ] The change is on a branch called clerk-signup.
 [ ] Each changed file was explained to me.
 [ ] Clerk keys are in Netlify only.
 [ ] A preview deploy of the branch built successfully.

chunks.title: Make the Clerk change and add the keys — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Make the Clerk change and add the keys / Common mistakes.
 Putting the Clerk secret key in code or chat.
 Forgetting to redeploy after adding the keys.
 Using the production instance too early.
Next: lesson 9, test sign-up and merge.

chunks.title: Test sign-up and merge
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test sign-up and merge.
# Test sign-up and merge
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: Clerk handling sign-up and sign-in, tested with a fresh account, with each person's credits correct, and the branch merged.
---

chunks.title: Test sign-up and merge — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test sign-up and merge / Before you start.
You will test on the preview deploy from lesson 8 and merge the branch only when every check passes. A fresh account matters because your existing sessions can hide problems: an old login may work while a brand-new visitor is stuck.
You will need:
 The preview address of the clerk-signup branch from lesson 8.
 A new test email address (an alias you control is fine).
 Your Clerk dashboard open in another tab.
 About 15 minutes. Menu names in Clerk, Netlify and your code host change from time to time, so look for the closest match.

chunks.title: Test sign-up and merge — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test sign-up and merge / Step by step.
### 1. Sign up with a fresh account
1. Open the preview address in a private window.
2. Use sign-up with a new test email address and complete any email verification Clerk asks for.
You should see: you land in the app, signed in.
If not: if sign-in fails on the preview address, check that you are using the development instance keys and that the allowed addresses in Clerk include your preview address. Ask the assistant to check the current Clerk docs.
### 2. Check the user in Clerk
In Clerk's dashboard, open Users.
You should see: your test user listed.
If not: you may be looking at the wrong Clerk instance. Make sure it is the development instance whose keys you added.
### 3. Check the credits
In the app, check credits.
You should see: a new user has exactly what a new user should have.
If not: if sign-up works but credits are missing, the new Clerk user is not linked to a user record. Ask the assistant to create or look up the record the first time a user is seen, and to show you where.
### 4. Sign out and back in
Sign out, then sign back in with the same test account.
You should see: the same account and the same credits.
If not: if you get a redirect loop, it is often a middleware setting. Ask the assistant to read the middleware and explain which routes are public.
### 5. Test the edge cases
1. Sign in with Google, if you enabled it.

chunks.title: Test sign-up and merge — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test sign-up and merge / Step by step.
2. While signed out, visit a page that needs sign-in.
3. While signed in, visit the sign-in page.
You should see: the Google sign-in works; the protected page sends you to sign-in, not an error; the sign-in page sends you on into the app.
If not: describe exactly what you saw to the assistant, for example "I signed up, landed on the dashboard, but credits show zero", and fix one thing at a time. Do not let it change payment code as part of this step.
### 6. Merge when every test passes
Merge the clerk-signup branch only once every test above has passed. Use your code host's merge button for the branch, or ask the assistant to explain where it is.
You should see: the branch merged, and Netlify building your main site with Clerk in it.
If not: if anything failed above, do not merge. Go back to the failing step and fix it first.

chunks.title: Test sign-up and merge — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test sign-up and merge / Check yourself.
 [ ] A fresh test sign-up works, appears in Clerk and has correct credits.
 [ ] Sign-out and sign-in returns me to the same account and credits.
 [ ] The edge cases behave as described.
 [ ] I only merged after every test passed.

chunks.title: Test sign-up and merge — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test sign-up and merge / Common mistakes.
 Merging before testing a fresh sign-up. Existing sessions hide problems.
 Putting the Clerk secret key in code or chat.
 Forgetting to redeploy after adding the keys.
 Using the production instance too early.
 Letting the assistant change payment code as part of this step.
Next: lesson 10, Stripe keys and the webhook.

chunks.title: Stripe keys and the webhook
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Stripe keys and the webhook.
# Stripe keys and the webhook
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: your Stripe test keys and a webhook endpoint connected to your Netlify site.
---

chunks.title: Stripe keys and the webhook — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Stripe keys and the webhook / Before you start.
You are not adding payments. The app already creates Stripe checkouts for credit packs and already has a webhook that listens for completed payments and adds credits. All you do is connect your Stripe account to your deployment: keys, then a webhook that points at your address. If you did Modules 7 to 9 of the Reseller Setup Walkthrough for Vercel, this is the same set of steps on a different host.
How a payment flows:
1. A customer clicks a credit pack. Your app sends them to Stripe Checkout.
2. They pay on Stripe's page (in test mode: a test card).
3. Stripe sends your app a webhook: a message to a specific address saying "this checkout completed".
4. Your app checks the message is really from Stripe (using the signing secret), then adds the credits.
The two things people get wrong are the webhook address and the signing secret. Your workshop page's webhook panel gives the exact path your app listens on.
Stay in test mode. Stripe's test cards never charge anyone, and test and live data are completely separate: a test key cannot see live payments and vice versa. Going live is lesson 13, not now. As always, you paste keys into Netlify yourself and never into the AI chat.
You will need:
 Your Stripe account in test mode and your Netlify site, signed in to in this browser.
 Your workshop page open, showing the variable names and the webhook path.

chunks.title: Stripe keys and the webhook — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Stripe keys and the webhook / Before you start.
 About 18 minutes. Menu names in Stripe and Netlify change from time to time, so look for the closest match.

chunks.title: Stripe keys and the webhook — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Stripe keys and the webhook / Step by step.
### 1. Switch Stripe to test mode
Open Stripe and check that test mode (sometimes called a sandbox) is on.
You should see: a visible test or sandbox indicator.
If not: switch it on before continuing. Nothing in this lesson uses live mode.
### 2. Open the Stripe API keys page
In Stripe (test mode), open the API keys page.
You should see: test keys, beginning with pktest and sktest.
If not: keys beginning pklive or sklive mean you are in live mode. Switch back to test mode.
### 3. Add the Stripe test keys to Netlify
1. In Netlify's environment variable settings, add the Stripe variables named in your workshop page, pasting the test values yourself.
2. If your app also uses a publishable key in the browser, add it the same way.
You should see: each variable saved in Netlify, with test values only.
If not: compare each variable name with your workshop page, letter by letter.
### 4. Add the webhook endpoint in Stripe
In Stripe's webhook settings (test mode), add an endpoint. For its address, use your netlify.app address plus the webhook path from your workshop page.
You should see: the endpoint form with your full address filled in.
If not: a wrong path, or a trailing slash that does not match, is the usual cause of failed webhooks later. Check it against your workshop page.
### 5. Choose the event to listen for
Select the event checkout.session.completed, then create the endpoint.

chunks.title: Stripe keys and the webhook — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Stripe keys and the webhook / Step by step.
You should see: the new endpoint listed, listening for that one event.
If not: open the endpoint and add the event.
### 6. Copy the signing secret into Netlify
After creating the endpoint, Stripe shows a signing secret. Copy it into the Netlify variable your workshop page names for it.
You should see: the signing secret saved in Netlify, and nowhere else.
If not: each endpoint has its own signing secret, so make sure you copied it from this endpoint, not another one.
### 7. Redeploy
Trigger a new deploy of your Netlify site. The new variables are only picked up on the next deploy.
You should see: a new deploy built and published.
If not: if the build fails, copy the error text (never a key) into the chat and ask the assistant to explain it.

chunks.title: Stripe keys and the webhook — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Stripe keys and the webhook / Check yourself.
 [ ] Stripe test keys and the webhook signing secret are in Netlify only.
 [ ] The webhook address is my netlify.app address plus the path from my workshop page, listening for checkout.session.completed.
 [ ] I redeployed after adding them.

chunks.title: Stripe keys and the webhook — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Stripe keys and the webhook / Common mistakes.
 A live key during testing. Test mode only until the go-live lessons.
 A webhook address with the wrong path (or a trailing slash that does not match).
 Using the wrong secret. Each endpoint has its own signing secret.
Next: lesson 11, test purchase and check it from the chat.

chunks.title: Test purchase and check it from the chat
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test purchase and check it from the chat.
# Test purchase and check it from the chat
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a test purchase that adds credits, confirmed by your assistant from Stripe.
---

chunks.title: Test purchase and check it from the chat — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test purchase and check it from the chat / Before you start.
Your keys and webhook are in place from lesson 10. Now you will prove the whole payment path works: sign in, pay, return to the app, and see credits arrive. "It seems to work" is not enough, so you will also ask your assistant to confirm from Stripe that the payment succeeded and the webhook reached your app. Then you will try the unhappy paths, because a payment system that only works when everything goes right is not finished.
Everything here is Stripe test mode. No real money moves, and no live key is involved until lesson 13.
You will need:
 Your deployed app, with the Clerk and Stripe test settings from lessons 7 to 10 (and the signing secret redeployed).
 Your assistant with the Stripe connector working in test mode.
 The test card numbers from Stripe's testing documentation (search for "Stripe testing cards").
 About 15 minutes.

chunks.title: Test purchase and check it from the chat — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test purchase and check it from the chat / Step by step.
### 1. Sign in to your app
1. Open your Netlify address and sign in with the account you made through Clerk in lessons 7 to 9.
You should see: your app, signed in, with your current credit balance. Note the number.
If not: if sign-in fails, go back to lesson 9 and fix sign-up first. Payments need a signed-in user.
### 2. Start a credit pack purchase
1. Choose to buy a credit pack.
You should see: Stripe's Checkout page, showing a test-mode banner or label.
If not: if nothing happens or you see an error, ask your assistant to read the app's logs on Netlify and explain the first error. If the page is not marked as test mode, stop: a live key may be in use. Test mode only until lesson 13.
### 3. Pay with the test card
1. On Stripe's page, enter the successful test card from Stripe's testing documentation.
2. Use any future expiry date and any security code, then pay.
You should see: you return to your app.
If not: if the card is refused, check you copied the number exactly from Stripe's testing documentation and that the page is in test mode.
### 4. Check that your credits increased
1. Look at your credit balance back in the app. Refresh once if needed.
You should see: your credits increased by exactly the pack size.

chunks.title: Test purchase and check it from the chat — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test purchase and check it from the chat / Step by step.
If not: if the payment succeeded but credits did not appear, the webhook failed. Carry on to step 5, where your assistant reads the delivery result. Common causes: wrong webhook address, wrong signing secret, or a variable you did not redeploy.
### 5. Ask the assistant to verify from Stripe
Paste this into your assistant and send it:
text
Using the Stripe connector in test mode, find my most recent test checkout session and tell me whether it succeeded, and whether the webhook delivery to my site returned a success response. Do not change anything.
You should see: an answer that the session succeeded and the webhook delivery returned a success response. That turns "it seems to work" into evidence.
If not: if the webhook returned an error, ask the assistant to read the response and the app's logs on Netlify and explain the first error. Check these four things:
 The signing secret was added to Netlify and the site was redeployed.
 The webhook address has the right path (a trailing slash that does not match also fails).
 You used the signing secret for this endpoint. Each webhook endpoint has its own.
 You are looking at test-mode deliveries, not live.
### 6. Try a declined payment
1. Start another purchase.
2. Use Stripe's test card for a declined payment.
You should see: Stripe shows the decline, and your credits do not change.

chunks.title: Test purchase and check it from the chat — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test purchase and check it from the chat / Step by step.
If not: if credits changed after a decline, stop and ask the assistant to explain how the app decides when to add credits. It should only act on a successful payment event.
### 7. Try cancelling at Checkout
1. Start another purchase.
2. On the Checkout page, choose to go back or cancel.
You should see: you return to the app with no credits added.
If not: if credits were added, or you landed on an error page, ask the assistant to check the cancel address used when the checkout session is created.
### 8. Buy twice and count
1. Make one more successful test purchase.
You should see: the credits went up twice in total, once per purchase. Not once, and not four times.
If not: if credits were added to the wrong person, stop and ask the assistant to check how the checkout session is tied to a user. This usually comes from a mapping error in lessons 7 to 9. If credits were added more than once per payment, ask the assistant to check the webhook handles each event only once.

chunks.title: Test purchase and check it from the chat — What good looks like
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test purchase and check it from the chat / What good looks like.
 Stripe's dashboard shows the test payment as succeeded.
 The webhook endpoint shows a successful delivery.
 Your credits increased by exactly the pack size.

chunks.title: Test purchase and check it from the chat — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test purchase and check it from the chat / Check yourself.
 [ ] A test purchase added the right credits.
 [ ] The assistant confirmed the payment and webhook delivery from Stripe.
 [ ] A declined card added nothing.
 [ ] Cancelling at Checkout added nothing.
 [ ] Buying twice added credits twice.

chunks.title: Test purchase and check it from the chat — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test purchase and check it from the chat / Common mistakes.
 A live key during testing. Test mode only until lesson 13.
 Not redeploying after adding the signing secret.
 A webhook address with the wrong path (or a trailing slash that does not match).
 Using the wrong secret. Each webhook endpoint has its own signing secret; copy the one for this endpoint in the Stripe dashboard, into Netlify, never into the chat.
Next: lesson 12, save your prompts and run the customer test.

chunks.title: Save your prompts and run the customer test
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Save your prompts and run the customer test.
# Save your prompts and run the customer test
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a reusable checklist, your saved prompts and a passing customer test on your Netlify address.
---

chunks.title: Save your prompts and run the customer test — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Save your prompts and run the customer test / Before you start.
You have now built the whole path once. This lesson makes it repeatable and checks it the way a customer would. What changes from app to app is only the facts on its workshop page: the name, the database, the variable names. The prompts stay the same, which is why saving them matters.
Here is the whole path in one page:
| Step | Lessons | You do | The assistant does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Accounts | 1 | Create Netlify, Clerk, Stripe (test) | Nothing yet |
| Connect | 2 or 3 | Approve connectors | Reads your accounts |
| Brief | 4 | Paste the briefing, check the summary | Summarises the app |
| Host | 5 and 6 | Add variable values, deploy | Checks readiness, explains errors |
| Sign-up | 7 to 9 | Add Clerk keys, test a fresh account | Plans and changes the code on a branch |
| Payments | 10 and 11 | Add Stripe keys and webhook, buy a pack | Verifies payment and webhook |
| Launch | 12 and 13 | Domain, live keys, final test | Produces the go-live checklist |
You will need:
 A notes app or document where you keep text.
 Your app on its Netlify address, still in Stripe test mode.
 The Reseller Setup Walkthrough, for Modules 10 and 11.
 About 15 minutes.

chunks.title: Save your prompts and run the customer test — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Save your prompts and run the customer test / Step by step.
### 1. Create your prompts note
1. Open your notes app and make a new note titled "Launch prompts".
You should see: an empty note with that title.
If not: any place you can find again works: a document, a notes app or a file. Keep it private, since it describes your accounts.
### 2. Paste in your five prompts
Copy these from the lessons into the note, in this order:
1. The briefing from lesson 4.
2. The deploy-readiness prompt from lesson 5.
3. The Clerk plan prompt from lesson 7.
4. The Stripe verification prompt from lesson 11.
5. The go-live prompt from lesson 13.
You should see: five prompts in the note, each with a short label.
If not: if you cannot find one, reopen that lesson and copy it from there. For lesson 13, you can come back and add it after you do that lesson. Never save a secret key in this note.
### 3. Learn how to reuse the note
1. Read this rule once and add it as a line at the top of the note.
text
For the next app: replace the app name and the repo address, then go straight down the list.
You should see: a note that works as a checklist for your next app.
If not: if a prompt mentions facts that belong to this app only, replace them with a clear placeholder such as APP NAME so you remember to swap them.
### 4. Finish your branding
1. Open Modules 10 and 11 of the Reseller Setup Walkthrough.
2. Follow them for your app's name and logo.

chunks.title: Save your prompts and run the customer test — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Save your prompts and run the customer test / Step by step.
You should see: your app showing its own name and logo, not a placeholder.
If not: if the logo does not appear, redeploy and refresh the page. Ask the assistant to explain any build error.
### 5. Plan your domain
1. In the same modules, decide on your own domain and note it down.
You should see: a domain name written in your note, ready for lesson 13.
If not: if you do not have a domain yet, you can still finish this lesson on your Netlify address. Connecting the domain happens in lesson 13.
### 6. Run the customer test on your Netlify address
1. Open your Netlify address in a private browser window, so you are not already signed in.
2. Sign up as a new customer with an email you control.
3. Buy a credit pack with Stripe's test card.
4. Use the app as a customer would.
5. Check that your credits show correctly.
You should see: the full journey works in order: sign up, buy, use the app, see credits.
If not: note the first step that breaks and ask your assistant to explain it. Fix that, then run the whole test again from the start. A test that passes in pieces is not a pass.
### 7. Repeat the test on your domain
1. Once your own domain is connected (lesson 13), run the same customer test there.
You should see: the same result on your domain as on the Netlify address.

chunks.title: Save your prompts and run the customer test — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Save your prompts and run the customer test / Step by step.
If not: if it works on one address and not the other, the settings for the new address are missing. Lesson 13 covers them.
### 8. Ask for a weekly health summary
Save this prompt in your note, then paste it into your assistant to try it now:
text
Summarise failed deploys and failed webhook deliveries from the last 7 days.
You should see: a short summary, likely "none" for a new app.
If not: if the assistant cannot see Netlify or Stripe, check the connectors are switched on for this chat (lesson 2 or 3).
### 9. Add your upkeep habits to the note
Add these five lines under the prompts:
 Check Stripe and Netlify weekly for failed webhooks and failed deploys.
 Watch your free-plan limits on Netlify and Clerk as users grow.
 Rotate a key if it was ever exposed. Create a new one in the service's dashboard, put it in Netlify's variables, then redeploy. Never paste it into the chat.
 Back up your database per your host's guidance.
 Never let the assistant change live data without a plan you have read.
You should see: a note with prompts on top and habits below.
If not: keep it short. A note you actually read beats a long one you do not.

chunks.title: Save your prompts and run the customer test — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Save your prompts and run the customer test / Check yourself.
 [ ] I saved my reusable prompts.
 [ ] I ran the full customer test on the Netlify address.
 [ ] I saved the weekly health prompt.
 [ ] I wrote down my upkeep habits.

chunks.title: Save your prompts and run the customer test — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Save your prompts and run the customer test / Common mistakes.
 Skipping the customer test because each step worked on its own.
 Testing while signed in as yourself. Use a private window and a new account.
 Saving secrets in the prompts note. Keep prompts and keys apart.
Next: lesson 13, go live.

chunks.title: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live.
# Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: your app live on your own domain with Clerk production and Stripe live mode, tested with a real payment you refunded.
---

chunks.title: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live / Before you start.
 Warning: this is the only lesson that uses live mode. Live mode means real cards and real money. Everything before this lesson was test. Do this lesson once, slowly, and only when lessons 11 and 12 passed.
Going live changes three things at once, and each has a separate "live" version that does not carry over from test:
1. Your domain. Add it in Netlify and follow its DNS instructions. Netlify serves the site on the new address once DNS settles.
2. Clerk production instance. Clerk's production instance needs your own domain and has its own keys and its own (empty) user list.
3. Stripe live mode. Activate your account (Module 7 of the walkthrough), create live keys, create a live webhook for your real address, and put the live signing secret in Netlify.
The safety rule does not change: never paste a key or signing secret into the chat. Put keys only into Netlify's environment variables. Your assistant can tell you where each one goes.
You will need:
 Lessons 11 and 12 passed in test mode.
 Your own domain name, and access to where its DNS is managed.
 Your Netlify, Clerk and Stripe dashboards open in separate tabs.
 A real card of your own, and a few minutes for a small real payment you will refund.
 About 18 minutes. DNS can take longer to settle; that wait is normal.

chunks.title: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live / Step by step.
### 1. Ask the assistant for your go-live checklist
Paste this into your assistant and send it:
text
Give me a go-live checklist for this app on Netlify with Clerk and Stripe: custom domain, Clerk production instance, live Stripe keys, live webhook, environment variables per environment, and a final test. Mark each item as either "I do this in a dashboard" or "you change this in the code". Do not change anything.
You should see: a checklist for your app with each item marked as a dashboard step or a code change.
If not: if it is vague, ask it to name your app's actual variables from the briefing. Save this prompt in your lesson 12 note.
### 2. Add your domain in Netlify
1. In Netlify, open your site and look for a domain settings area (the label may differ).
2. Choose to add your own domain and enter it.
You should see: your domain listed, with DNS instructions from Netlify.
If not: if Netlify says the domain is taken or cannot be verified, check you spelled it right and that you own it.
### 3. Follow Netlify's DNS instructions
1. Where your domain is managed, add the DNS records Netlify shows you, exactly as given.
You should see: Netlify marks the domain as working or secured once DNS settles, which can take from a few minutes to many hours.
If not: wait, then check the records for typos. Keep going with steps 4 to 7 while you wait.
### 4. Create the Clerk production instance

chunks.title: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live / Step by step.
1. In the Clerk dashboard, find the option to create or switch to a production instance (the label may differ).
2. Enter your own domain when asked and follow Clerk's DNS instructions.
You should see: a production instance with its own keys and an empty user list.
If not: if Clerk says your domain is not verified yet, finish step 3 first. Sign-in that fails only on your domain usually means the production instance does not list the domain yet.
### 5. Put the Clerk production keys in Netlify
1. In Netlify, open the environment variables for your site.
2. Add the Clerk production keys as production values only, using the same variable names as before.
3. Redeploy the site.
You should see: the variable names present for production, and a successful new deploy.
If not: if the deploy fails, ask the assistant to read the deploy log and explain the first error. Do not paste the key values into the chat.
### 6. Activate Stripe and create live keys
1. Complete Stripe's account activation (Module 7 of the walkthrough).
2. In the Stripe dashboard, switch to live mode (look for a test or live toggle) and create your live keys.
You should see: Stripe showing live mode, with live keys available.
If not: if activation is still pending, wait for Stripe to approve it. Do not continue until live mode is available.
### 7. Create the live webhook

chunks.title: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live / Step by step.
1. While in live mode, create a live webhook pointing to your real address, using the same path as your test webhook.
2. Copy its signing secret from the dashboard.
You should see: a live webhook endpoint with its own signing secret.
If not: remember the test webhook does not work for live payments. If you see only your test endpoint, you are still in test mode.
### 8. Put the live Stripe values in Netlify and redeploy
1. In Netlify, set the live Stripe keys and the live signing secret as production values only.
2. Leave preview builds on test keys. Live keys must never reach preview builds, and test keys must not stay in production.
3. Redeploy.
You should see: a successful deploy, with production on live values and previews on test values.
If not: if it worked on the preview but not on your domain, production variables, the Clerk production instance and the Stripe live webhook are separate from test. Check each one.
### 9. Final step: sign up on your domain
 Last chance to stop: from here a real card is charged. If any earlier step is unfinished, go back first.
1. In a private browser window, open your own domain.
2. Sign up with a new real email.
You should see: a new account on your domain, listed in the Clerk production user list.
If not: if sign-in fails only on your domain, check step 4 and step 5.
### 10. Buy the smallest pack with a real card

chunks.title: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live / Step by step.
1. Buy the smallest credit pack using a real card.
You should see: Stripe's Checkout page in live mode, then your app with the credits added.
If not: if the payment succeeded but nothing happened, check the live webhook's recent deliveries in Stripe.
### 11. Confirm everything in Stripe
1. In Stripe (live mode), check the payment.
2. Check the live webhook shows a successful delivery.
You should see: the payment as succeeded and a successful webhook delivery.
If not: ask your assistant to read the live delivery result and explain the first error. Do not change live data without a plan you have read.
### 12. Refund your own payment
1. In Stripe, refund the payment you just made.
2. Check your app behaves as your Module 9 plan says.
You should see: the refund shown in Stripe, and the app doing what your plan says.
If not: if the refund is not handled as planned, note it and ask the assistant for a plan to fix it. Do this once, deliberately, before you tell anyone the app is live.

chunks.title: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live — If you need to roll back
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live / If you need to roll back.
You can undo going live without losing anything:
 In Netlify, set the production variables back to your test values and redeploy. The app is then back in test mode.
 In Stripe, refund any real payment and disable the live webhook.
 Your domain and Clerk production instance can stay; they do no harm on their own.

chunks.title: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live / Check yourself.
 [ ] I have a go-live checklist for this specific app.
 [ ] I understand that domain, Clerk production and Stripe live are three separate switches.
 [ ] My live webhook delivered successfully on a real payment.
 [ ] I refunded my own test purchase.

chunks.title: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live / Common mistakes.
 Going live without a final end-to-end test.
 Carrying test keys into production (or live keys into preview builds).
 Forgetting the live webhook. The test one does not work for live payments.
 Not refunding your own test purchase.
You now have the full process. Next: repeat it for every app you launch, using your saved prompts from lesson 12, and use Module 12 of the Reseller Setup Walkthrough to find and win your first customers.

chunks.title: AI Video Ads & UGC
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Video Ads & UGC.
# AI Video Ads & UGC
 Time: about 2 minutes to read. You will finish with: a clear map of six short lessons that take you from first script to a sold UGC ad service.
---

chunks.title: AI Video Ads & UGC — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Video Ads & UGC / Before you start.
This track turns AI-generated video into ads brands actually pay for. You work inside the SmartVideo GO AI studios: Image, Video, Audio, Lip-Sync, Storyboard / Campaign Planner and AI Influencer. Each lesson is a short guided walkthrough with a Copy button on every prompt. Do them in order; each one builds on the last.
Reusable files (scripts, checklists, pricing sheets) live in templates/.

chunks.title: AI Video Ads & UGC — The lessons
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Video Ads & UGC / The lessons.
| # | Lesson | Time | Requires |
|:---:|---|:---:|---|
| 1 | How AI UGC Actually Works | ~18 min | — |
| 2 | How AI UGC Actually Works, part 2 | ~12 min | Lesson 1 |
| 3 | Character & Face Consistency | ~16 min | Lessons 1-2 |

chunks.title: AI Video Ads & UGC — What each lesson gives you
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Video Ads & UGC / What each lesson gives you.
 How AI UGC Actually Works (parts 1 and 2): the 5-stage pipeline, Script → Avatar/Voice → Video → Captions → Export, ending with a captioned 9:16 ad. Templates: templates/ugc-script-template.md, templates/ad-brief-checklist.md.

chunks.title: AI Video Ads & UGC — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: AI Video Ads & UGC / Common mistakes.
 Skipping the consistency lesson. A face that changes shot to shot gets ads rejected.
 Pitching the AI process. Lead with the finished ad and the business outcome.
Next: How AI UGC Actually Works.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works, part 2
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works, part 2.
# How AI UGC Actually Works, part 2
 Time: about 12 minutes. You will finish with: a captioned, 9:16 UGC ad that passed a sound-off and sound-on ship check.
---

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works, part 2 — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works, part 2 / Before you start.
Part 1 gave you a script, a voice and a talking-head clip. Now you finish the last three stages: Video (b-roll), Captions and Export. Most viewers watch muted, so captions are standard for the format, and b-roll is what hides short imperfect stretches in the avatar footage. Prices for this work run roughly $10-$55 per ad on freelance marketplaces, and agencies retainer it at $1,500-$3,000 a month, so a clean finish matters.
You will need your part 1 clip, script and voice, plus product shots or a screen recording. Use Video Studio and, if your account offers it, a caption option in the editing area (menu names may differ).

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works, part 2 / Step by step.
### 1. Plan where b-roll goes
Mark the pitch and proof sections of your script (roughly seconds 2-25). That is where you will cut away from the avatar.
You should see: a short list of two or three moments, such as "product close-up" and "demo: phone onto mount".
If not: if your script has no visual moment, add one (a tap, a slap, a before/after).
### 2. Create the b-roll
1. Make or collect product shots or a screen recording of the product in use.
2. In Image Studio or Video Studio, generate product shots if you have no real footage.
You should see: two or three short clips or stills of the product itself.
If not: keep them simple, one action per clip, so they cut cleanly.
### 3. Cut b-roll in over the pitch and proof
Place the b-roll over the pitch and proof while the voice continues. Leave the hook on the avatar's face.
You should see: the avatar for the first 2 seconds, then cutaways, then the avatar again for the CTA.
If not: if a lip-sync glitch is still visible, cut away earlier to cover it.
### 4. Add captions
Generate auto-captions and burn them in (permanently on the video). Make sure they match the speech timing.
You should see: readable captions synced to the voice, ideally with key words emphasised.
If not: fix mis-heard product names by hand, and shorten any caption line that wraps awkwardly.
### 5. Export at 9:16

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works, part 2 — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works, part 2 / Step by step.
Export at 9:16 for Reels, TikTok and Shorts. Use 1:1 or 16:9 only if the client asks.
You should see: a vertical video file that plays full-screen on a phone.
If not: if it appears with black bars, re-export with the aspect ratio set to 9:16.
### 6. Ship check with sound off
Watch the finished ad once with the sound off.
You should see: the hook is clear from captions alone.
If not: if the hook only works with audio, rewrite the first caption line or tighten the opening.
### 7. Ship check with sound on
Watch it again at regular volume. Notice every place you pause to work out what is happening.
You should see: no moment of confusion from start to CTA.
If not: a pause you feel is one a client will feel. Fix pacing or cut that moment, then re-export.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works, part 2 — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works, part 2 / Check yourself.
 [ ] B-roll covers the pitch and proof, not the hook.
 [ ] Captions are burned in and match the speech.
 [ ] The file is exported at 9:16.
 [ ] The ad passed both the sound-off and sound-on checks.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works, part 2 — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works, part 2 / Common mistakes.
 Shipping without watching twice. Sound-off and sound-on checks catch different problems.
 Covering the hook with b-roll. The face is what earns the first 2 seconds.
 Unchecked auto-captions. Product names are often mis-heard.
 Wrong aspect ratio. Short-form platforms expect 9:16.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works, part 2 — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works, part 2 / Go further.
 How to price it: gig ads about $10-$55 each; price by deliverable (for example "$150 for 5 ad variants"), not by hour.
 How to position it: lead with the business outcome ("more ad variants to test, faster, without a film crew"), not the AI process.
 Where to find first clients: DTC e-commerce brands running paid social ads (visible in public ad libraries); a sample ad for their actual product beats a generic pitch.
 Real numbers: documented case studies show single brands running AI-UGC-style creative at $600K+/month in ad spend for one product. It shows the format is proven, not that you will match it.
 Template: templates/ad-brief-checklist.md for briefing yourself or a client before a batch.
Next: Character & Face Consistency.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works.
# How AI UGC Actually Works
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: a 30-second UGC script, three voice takes and a first talking-head clip of your avatar.
---

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Before you start.
Brands pay real creators $200-$1,500 per UGC-style ad because it looks like a person talking to camera, not a commercial. Humans are slow to brief and cannot scale to 20 variants on short notice. An AI UGC ad is five stages, each swappable: Script → Avatar/Voice → Video → Captions → Export. The weak link is usually the avatar's face and voice sync, not the script. This part covers the first three stages; part 2 covers b-roll, captions, export and the ship check.
You will need a product you know well (a real or made-up one), a quiet minute to read aloud, and these SmartVideo GO AI studios: Image Studio, Video Studio, Lip-Sync Studio and AI Influencer Studio (exact menu names may differ on your screen). Open templates/ugc-script-template.md to fill in as you go.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Step by step.
### 1. Pick your product and write the hook
1. Choose one product and name one specific surprise or problem it solves.
2. Write the hook, the first 2 seconds: a question, a bold claim or a visual surprise.
Example hook for a $28 magnetic phone car mount ("GripMount"):
text
Okay, I did not expect this to actually hold my phone through a pothole.
You should see: one specific, spoken-sounding line, not "this product is great".
If not: replace any generic praise with a concrete moment (a pothole, a failed old product, a number).
### 2. Write the pitch and proof
1. Pitch (10-15 seconds): name the competing product's failure, as a real person would.
2. Proof or demo (10-15 seconds): add a visual action and a concrete number, like "two weeks, potholes included".
You should see: a pitch that names a real pain, and a proof line containing a number or a demo action.
If not: if it sounds like copy ("Introducing the revolutionary..."), rewrite it the way you would tell a friend.
### 3. Add the call to action and check the length
1. Write the CTA (last 2-3 seconds): state the price plainly, one action, urgency tied to a real use ("before your next road trip").
2. Count your words. Keep the full script under 30 seconds spoken, about 75-90 words.
Here is the full GripMount script (~28 seconds) for comparison:
text

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Step by step.
Okay, I did not expect this to actually hold my phone through a pothole. [holds up phone, taps mount] I used to have one of those suction ones that fell off literally every drive — this one's magnetic, snaps on in like two seconds. [demo: slaps phone onto mount] It's held through every drive for the last two weeks, potholes included. It's $28, link's below — honestly just get it before your next road trip.
You should see: a script of roughly 75-90 words with all four parts: hook, pitch, proof, CTA.
If not: too long means cut the pitch first; keep the demo moment, because it gives the avatar something to do with its hands.
### 4. Read it aloud
Read the script out loud once, at normal speed.
You should see: nothing you would be embarrassed to say to a friend.
If not: rewrite every line where you stumble or sound like an announcer. Fix it before producing anything.
### 5. Generate three voice takes
1. In the Audio or Lip-Sync area of SmartVideo GO AI, turn your script into narration with a text-to-speech or voice option. Match tone to the product (energetic for a gadget, calm for skincare).
2. Generate 2-3 versions, varying pacing and which word is stressed in the hook line.
You should see: three takes that read differently, one noticeably less "read off a page".

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Step by step.
If not: if all three sound alike, change the pacing instruction or the stressed word, not the script. Also check the voice's accent and demographic fit your product's likely audience.
### 6. Pick your avatar
1. In Image Studio or AI Influencer Studio, generate or choose a front-facing character (high resolution, neutral lighting). If you already built an anchor, reuse it.
2. Save it. You will lock its face properly in the next lesson.
You should see: one clear, front-facing character image ready to animate.
If not: regenerate until the face is sharp and neutral; blurry or side-on anchors animate badly.
### 7. Animate the avatar
Choose one path in Video Studio or Lip-Sync Studio:
1. Generate a talking-head clip directly from the script and voice, or
2. Animate your still image with lip-sync driven by your chosen audio take.
Use your hook line as the first test:
text
The woman in the image looks at the camera, surprised, and says: "Okay, I did not expect this to actually hold my phone through a pothole." She holds up a phone and taps a mount.
You should see: a short clip where the mouth moves with the line. Lip movement that is decent but not perfect is normal at this stage.
If not: if the mouth is clearly off, try the other path (direct generation vs. lip-sync on your own audio).
### 8. Save your first pass

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Step by step.
Download or save the clip and the script together, and note which voice take you chose.
You should see: a clip, a script and a voice choice stored in one place.
If not: generated files can expire (one provider's outputs expired after 30 days), so download anything you want to keep right away.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Check yourself.
 [ ] My script has hook, pitch, proof and CTA, and is under 30 seconds.
 [ ] I read it aloud and it sounds like speech.
 [ ] I compared at least 2-3 voice takes.
 [ ] I have one animated talking-head clip of my avatar.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Common mistakes.
 Writing the pitch like ad copy. Read it aloud; if you would not say it to a friend, rewrite it.
 Stopping at the first voice take. The stressed word changes whether the hook reads surprised or casual.
 A generic hook. Specific claims beat "this product is great".
 Skipping the demo moment. A hand action gives the avatar something to do.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Go further.
 Worked example, mapped: hook = a surprised, specific claim; pitch = names the suction mount's failure; proof = slapping the phone on plus "two weeks, potholes included"; CTA = price, one action, road-trip urgency.
 Reference pipeline (one real run): nano-banana-2 portrait ($0.06/image) → uploaded via muapi's uploadfile → seedance-2-image-to-video-fast ($0.75/clip) with the dialogue in the prompt, so no separate lip-sync pass. Total $0.81. These models are examples, not fixed recommendations.
 Which model for which stage: Voice: Gemini TTS or ElevenLabs text-to-dialogue. Avatar/video: Seedance 2.x or Kling 3.0. Lip-sync of separate narration: a dedicated lip-sync model or a Kling avatar model.
 Paths compared: managed API (low setup, high consistency, best for client work); paid all-in-one UGC tools (GUI, often subscription, varies); local ComfyUI with models such as LTX 2.3 (free per generation but expect a weekend of tuning; worth it at dozens of ads a month or for privacy-sensitive clients).
 Exercises: easy, write three 30-second scripts for a product you use; medium, produce one full ad end to end; hard, produce 5 variants with different hooks and predict the winner.
 Template: templates/ugc-script-template.md and templates/ad-brief-checklist.md.
Next: How AI UGC Actually Works, part 2.

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character & Face Consistency.
# Character & Face Consistency
 Time: about 16 minutes. You will finish with: one anchor character rendered in three settings with no visible face drift, and a drift-check result.
---

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character & Face Consistency / Before you start.
If your AI creator looks like a different person in every shot, nobody will pay for the ad. This is the most common complaint about AI-generated content, and for an ad campaign, a faceless channel host or an AI influencer it is disqualifying. The fix is an anchor the model cannot drift away from. Three anchor types, weakest to strongest: prompt-only (re-describing the character in text), reference-image conditioning (passing the actual photo with each prompt), and a trained/locked identity (LoRA or equivalent, usually a local step). A fixed seed helps within a session but is a helper, not the main mechanism.
You will need an anchor image (or the one from lesson 1) and these SmartVideo GO AI studios: Image Studio with an edit or reference option, and optionally AI Influencer Studio. Open templates/character-consistency-checklist.md for the final check.

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character & Face Consistency / Step by step.
### 1. Create or pick your anchor
1. In Image Studio, generate or upload one character: for example a woman in her late 20s, front-facing, neutral lighting, brown hair, freckles across her nose.
2. Use high resolution.
You should see: a sharp, front-facing, neutrally lit portrait.
If not: regenerate until face and freckles are clearly visible; a weak anchor makes every later image worse.
### 2. Use the anchor as a reference, not a description
For every new shot, pass the anchor image as the reference or edit input to an edit-capable image model. Do not retype the face in a fresh text prompt.
You should see: a reference or image-input field accepting your anchor.
If not: if your tool only has a plain text prompt, look for an edit, reference or character option (names may differ) before continuing.
### 3. Render the first setting: car interior
Describe only what changes:
text
Same woman as in the reference image, now sitting in a car, holding a phone.
You should see: the same face, freckles and apparent age, in a car.
If not: if the face changed, check that the reference was really passed to an edit-capable endpoint and that your prompt does not describe facial features.
### 4. Render the second and third settings
Repeat with the same anchor each time:
text
Same woman as in the reference image, now standing at a kitchen counter.
text

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character & Face Consistency / Step by step.
Same woman as in the reference image, now walking outside in daylight.
You should see: three images of the same person in three places, including different lighting in the outdoor shot.
If not: regenerate only the drifted shot, and make the prompt shorter and about the setting only.
### 5. Run the drift check
Line up the anchor and all three renders. Compare facial structure, apparent age, freckle placement, hairstyle and jaw shape.
You should see: no meaningful drift on any of them.
If not: common drift signs are a rounder jaw, vanished freckles or a different age. Tighten the prompt to describe only outfit and background, and lean on the reference image for the face.
### 6. Decide whether you need a trained identity
Ask: will this creator front dozens of ads over months, or just one batch?
You should see: a clear yes/no. For a one-off ad, reference-image conditioning is enough. For a recurring creator, plan a one-time LoRA training pass on 15-20 photos.
If not: if unsure, start with reference images and revisit when you notice repeated drift.
### 7. Save the anchor and the checklist result
Save the anchor under a clear name and complete the checklist from templates/character-consistency-checklist.md.
You should see: the anchor and three approved renders stored together.
If not: if any render failed the checklist, do not deliver it; regenerate.

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character & Face Consistency / Check yourself.
 [ ] I used the anchor image as a reference for every new shot.
 [ ] My prompts described only the setting, never the face.
 [ ] I compared at least three renders against the anchor.
 [ ] I know whether this character justifies a trained identity.

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character & Face Consistency / Common mistakes.
 Re-describing the face in text. This is the most common cause of drift.
 Not passing the reference to an edit-capable model. A plain text prompt ignores it.
 Treating a seed as a lock. It does not survive different prompts or sessions.
 Accepting small drift. Clients notice immediately.

chunks.title: Character & Face Consistency — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Character & Face Consistency / Go further.
 Models that worked: nano-banana-2-edit ($0.06/image) was used with the same uploaded image as imageslist for each of 3 shots; alternatives nano-banana-pro-edit and gpt-image-2-image-to-image. Current image models (for example Nano Banana 2/Pro, Seedream) hold identity better than older ones.
 Paths compared: API reference conditioning (good, low setup, the default for most ad work); other paid tools with built-in "character" features (varies, GUI); local ComfyUI with a trained LoRA (strongest, high setup, worth it for a character used dozens or hundreds of times).
 Pricing idea: consistency is baked into your ad price, but you can upsell a "branded AI character" package, a one-time setup fee of $200-$500 plus per-piece production.
 Positioning: sell "your reusable AI spokesperson", not "an AI-generated photo".
 Exercises: easy, same character in 3 outfits; medium, 5 scenes, noting which details drift first (usually age, facial proportions, hairstyle); hard, a local ComfyUI trained identity compared with the API approach over the same 5 scenes.
 Template: templates/character-consistency-checklist.md.
Next: Building a 10-Ad Batch.

chunks.title: Building a 10-Ad Batch
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a 10-Ad Batch.
# Building a 10-Ad Batch
 Time: about 17 minutes. You will finish with: a filled batch matrix of 5-10 ads and a labelled test plan a client could read.
---

chunks.title: Building a 10-Ad Batch — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a 10-Ad Batch / Before you start.
A single ad is a gamble on one hook and one angle. Brands that run paid social test variants and keep the winner, so the real service is "10 variants I can test", not "an ad". A batch is one product varied along a small number of axes: hook (the first 2 seconds), angle (price, convenience, social proof, novelty) and format (different avatar, voice or b-roll). If every axis changes at once you cannot tell why an ad won, so vary one or two and hold the rest constant.
You will need your script from lesson 1, your consistent character from lesson 2, and these studios: Storyboard / Campaign Planner for the matrix, Video Studio and Lip-Sync Studio for production. Open templates/batch-matrix-template.md.

chunks.title: Building a 10-Ad Batch — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a 10-Ad Batch / Step by step.
### 1. Lock the constants
Write down what never changes in the batch: product, core proof point, CTA and demo.
You should see: three or four fixed items at the top of your matrix.
If not: if you cannot name the constants, the batch will not be readable later.
### 2. Write 3-4 hook variants
Use the script template from lesson 1. Each hook tests a different opening: question, bold claim, before/after or problem-first. For the GripMount mount:
text
1. I did not expect this to hold through a pothole.
2. My old mount fell off literally every drive.
3. POV: you're driving and your phone doesn't fall for once.
4. This $28 thing fixed a problem I didn't know had a fix.
5. Two weeks, every pothole, still holding.
You should see: three to five hooks that open differently but sell the same product.
If not: if two hooks sound alike, replace one with a different opening type.
### 3. Pair hooks with 2-3 angles
Angles: price, convenience, social proof, durability/surprise, problem-first, POV, proof-first. Do not produce every permutation: 4 hooks x 3 angles is not 12 ads.
You should see: a matrix of the 8-10 most promising combinations.
If not: drop the combinations you would not be proud to deliver.
### 4. Fill the batch matrix
For each ad record number, hook, angle and the constant ("same product demo, same CTA").

chunks.title: Building a 10-Ad Batch — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a 10-Ad Batch / Step by step.
You should see: a table in the style of the GripMount example: five ads, each with a single labelled variable.
If not: if an ad changes more than hook and angle, split it into two rows or fix one of the changes.
### 5. Produce ad 1 and check the character
In Video Studio, animate your anchor with ad 1's script. Compare the face with the anchor.
You should see: the same creator as in lesson 2, performing hook 1.
If not: return to lesson 2 and re-check that the reference image is being used.
### 6. Batch-produce the rest
Reuse the same uploaded anchor image for every clip and change only the dialogue line in the prompt (about $0.75 per clip in the reference run).
text
The woman in the image looks at the camera and says: "My old mount fell off literally every drive." She holds up a phone and slaps it onto a magnetic mount.
You should see: the same creator and product in each clip, with only the opening line changed.
If not: if a clip drifts, regenerate just that one rather than the batch.
### 7. Label each ad and write the test plan
Tag each file with the one thing it varies, for example "Ad 2 = problem-first hook". Add a short plan: how long to run, which metric to read first.
You should see: every file labelled, and a plan that says to check hook rate first.
If not: if a label says "different in several ways", it breaks the test; remake it.

chunks.title: Building a 10-Ad Batch — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a 10-Ad Batch / Check yourself.
 [ ] My constants (product, proof, CTA, demo) are identical in every ad.
 [ ] I produced 5-10 combinations, not every permutation.
 [ ] The same character appears in all clips.
 [ ] Each ad is labelled by the single axis it varies.

chunks.title: Building a 10-Ad Batch — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a 10-Ad Batch / Common mistakes.
 Varying everything at once. Results become unreadable.
 Producing every permutation. Pick the most promising 8-10.
 Changing the character between ads. Unless the brief asks for multiple creator types.
 Delivering without labels. The media buyer cannot trace results to decisions.

chunks.title: Building a 10-Ad Batch — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Building a 10-Ad Batch / Go further.
 Reading the test: check hook rate (percent watching past the first 2-3 seconds) first; a weak hook rate is dead whatever the CPA. Compare cost per result (CPA/ROAS) only across ads with a decent hook rate; low CPA on tiny spend is noise. Rule of thumb: a few thousand impressions per variant, roughly 3-4 days at a modest daily budget, before calling a winner.
 Tools compared: managed API (fast, script repeated calls; default for client work); GUI-based paid UGC tools (usually one at a time); local ComfyUI queues (fast once set up, worth it only at high recurring volume).
 How to price it: per batch, for example $150-$300 for a 5-8 ad test batch, with revisions included.
 How to position it: sell the testing capability ("8 variants to find your winner"), and mention faster turnaround than sourcing several human creators.
 Real numbers: agency UGC retainers of $1,500-$3,000/month typically buy ongoing batch production like this.
 Exercises: easy, plan a 6-ad matrix (3 hooks x 2 angles); medium, produce 5 ads; hard, produce 10 and write a one-page test plan.
 Template: templates/batch-matrix-template.md.
Next: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service.

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service.
# Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service
 Time: about 17 minutes. You will finish with: a priced gig listing, a cold outreach message and a draft retainer proposal.
---

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service / Before you start.
Many people who can make good AI UGC ads earn less than they could because they guess prices, undersell or pitch the technology instead of the result. The market already has ranges to anchor to. There are three ways to sell: gig work (per ad, $10-$55, fastest start), project work (a batch, $150-$300, needs your own outreach) and retainers ($1,500-$3,000+ per month, needs trust from earlier work). The path is gig, then project, then retainer, each stage's finished ads being the pitch for the next.
You will need a few finished ads (from lessons 1-3), and the templates templates/outreach-template.md and templates/retainer-proposal-template.md. This lesson is business writing, so you will use the studios only to make a sample ad if you lack one (Video Studio, AI Influencer Studio).

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service / Step by step.
### 1. Choose your stage
Count your finished ads and completed client projects: none, 2-3 pieces, or 2-3 projects.
You should see: one stage to work on now: gig, project or retainer.
If not: if you have no portfolio, start with gigs.
### 2. Set your gig price
Anchor to $10-$55 per ad. Price mid-range ($35) with no portfolio yet, higher once you have 2-3 pieces.
You should see: a single number inside the documented range.
If not: do not invent a price outside the range; $35 is a safe first listing.
### 3. Write the gig listing
text
I'll create a UGC-style AI ad for your product — $35. Includes: script, AI creator/voice, captions, 1 revision. Delivered in 9:16, ready to run. Turnaround: 3 days.
You should see: a listing with deliverables, one stated revision round, format and turnaround.
If not: if it does not state the revision count, add "1 revision round included" before you publish.
### 4. Choose your portfolio
Pick your best 3-5 ads. Use real client work if you have it, otherwise high-quality practice ads for a real product.
You should see: 3-5 ads that look consistent and finished.
If not: make one more sample rather than showing a weak piece.
### 5. Write a cold outreach message
Lead with a finished, product-specific sample. Do not explain your process.
text
Subject: a UGC-style ad concept for [Brand]

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service / Step by step.
Hi [Name] — noticed [Brand] is running paid social ads for [specific product]. I put together a quick AI-generated UGC-style ad using the same product [attach/link the actual sample ad] — thought it might be a useful new angle to test against your current creative. If it's a fit, I can turn around a full batch of variants (different hooks/angles) for testing. Happy to share more examples if useful.
You should see: a short message where the sample ad comes first.
If not: delete any sentence that starts with "I use AI to".
### 6. Price a project batch
Package a batch as $150-$300 per test batch, with revisions included. In the worked example the progression is $35/ad, then $200/batch, then $2,000/month.
You should see: a batch quote with a number of ads and a revision count.
If not: quote per batch, not per hour.
### 7. Draft the retainer pitch
After 2-3 completed projects, pitch ongoing production:
text
Ongoing batch production: 8 ad variants/month across 2 batches, $2,000/month. Includes scripting, production, 2 revision rounds per batch, and a one-page test-plan write-up per batch tying results back to which hook/angle won.
You should see: scope, monthly ad count, price and revision policy in one paragraph, priced within $1,500-$3,000.
If not: justify the price by pointing at your previous delivered projects, not a generic capability claim.
### 8. Write your revision policy

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service / Step by step.
State the number of revision rounds before quoting. One free round is standard, anything beyond is new work.
You should see: a one-line policy copied into your listing and proposal.
If not: add it now; do not wait for a client to ask.

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service / Check yourself.
 [ ] My prices sit inside the documented ranges for my stage.
 [ ] My outreach leads with a finished sample ad.
 [ ] Every offer states its revision rounds.
 [ ] I know what I need before pitching a retainer: 2-3 completed projects.

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service / Common mistakes.
 Guessing prices. Anchor to the ranges, and go to the top only with proof.
 Leading with "I use AI". It invites doubt about quality.
 No stated revision rounds. It leads to unpaid work.
 Implying you will match $600K+/month case studies. Cite them only as evidence the format works.

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling UGC Ads as a Service / Go further.
 Cost basis: API production keeps cost per ad low and predictable; local production only changes the math at retainer-level volume.
 Where to find clients: marketplaces for first gigs and portfolio; direct outreach to DTC brands visible in each platform's public ad library for project and retainer work.
 Honest numbers: when you publish your own results, publish the actual number and how it was measured (see the cross-track "Show Your Real Numbers" module).
 Revision situations: if a client wants something the model cannot do well (a very specific product interaction, a shot-for-shot competitor copy), say so and offer the closest alternative. For vague feedback ("make it pop more"), ask: a faster cut, a different hook or a different CTA?
 Exercises: easy, write a gig listing in range; medium, write outreach to a real DTC brand with a sample; hard, draft a retainer proposal with scope, count, price and revision policy.
 Templates: templates/outreach-template.md and templates/retainer-proposal-template.md.
Next: Case Study Teardown.

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Case Study Teardown.
# Case Study Teardown
 Time: about 16 minutes. You will finish with: a five-layer teardown of one running ad and two reusable structural takeaways.
---

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown — Before you start
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Case Study Teardown / Before you start.
It is easy to produce ads and harder to know which parts of a successful ad actually drove performance. Without a teardown you copy surface style (a trending sound, a creator look) and cannot repeat success for a different product. A teardown splits an ad into the five layers from lesson 1 (script, avatar/voice, video, captions, export) and asks of each, "what choice was made, and why might it matter?". Large, long-running campaigns are good subjects because the surviving ad reflects real performance data.
You will need a platform's public ad library (the example uses the Meta Ads Library, free, no login needed), and templates/teardown-worksheet.md. Optionally, a video-understanding model in SmartVideo GO AI (menu name may differ) for a first-pass read.

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Case Study Teardown / Step by step.
### 1. Find a long-running ad
Search a brand in your target category in the ad library. Look for an ad that has run for a while, since brands cut losers quickly.
You should see: an ad showing a start date weeks back, ideally with several near-identical variants.
If not: try another brand in the category. In the worked example, "started running 47 days ago" with 6 variants was the tell.
### 2. Transcribe the script
Write down every spoken line and map it to hook, pitch, proof and CTA.
You should see: four labelled parts with timings, like the skincare example: hook (0-2s) "I stopped using retinol after this happened to my skin.", pitch (2-12s), proof (12-22s) with a dated before/after, CTA (22-25s) "Link in bio, 20% off first order".
If not: if a part is missing, note it as missing; that is a finding too.
### 3. Explain why the hook works
In one sentence, state what the hook does and why it stops a scroll.
You should see: a reason such as "a relatable complaint before the product is named, creating a curiosity gap".
If not: ask what a viewer would wonder in the first 3 seconds.
### 4. Note avatar, voice and video
Record tone, apparent age/demographic match to the audience, energy, and how much is talking-head versus b-roll, plus where cuts fall against the script beats.
You should see: three or four short notes.
If not: rewatch with sound on, then once muted.

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Case Study Teardown / Step by step.
### 5. Note the captions
Record timing, emphasis (bold or highlighted keywords) and whether captions sync tightly to speech.
You should see: a one-line description of the caption style.
If not: if there are no captions, write that down.
### 6. Write 2-3 takeaways
Write them generically, without naming the brand, for example:
text
A pain-first hook that withholds the product name for the first few seconds, paired with a dated before/after, works well for skincare-category ads — the curiosity gap earns the watch-through.
You should see: two or three takeaways you could apply to a different product.
If not: if a takeaway says "copy this ad", rewrite it as "this kind of hook works for this kind of problem".
### 7. Optional: get an AI first pass
Run a short clip through a video-understanding model (the reference run used gemini-video-vision, $0.004/call) with this prompt:
text
Break this into hook/pitch/proof/CTA, and comment on lip-sync quality and video structure.
You should see: a draft breakdown in seconds. In the reference run it correctly noticed the clip had no CTA and no b-roll.
If not: treat the output as a draft, not a verdict; it can miss brand history and audience context.
### 8. Turn it into an outreach opener
text

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Case Study Teardown / Step by step.
I noticed a running ad in the skincare-serum category using a pain-first hook + dated before/after proof — that structure is why it's still running after 47 days. Here's a sample ad using the same structure for [prospect's product].
You should see: an opener that shows judgment before any pitch.
If not: remove any competitor brand name; describe by category and structure.

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Case Study Teardown / Check yourself.
 [ ] I chose an ad that has been running a while.
 [ ] I filled all five layers in the worksheet.
 [ ] My takeaways are generic and reusable.
 [ ] My opener names categories, not brands.

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Case Study Teardown / Common mistakes.
 Copying surface style. Trending sounds are not structure.
 Trusting the AI read as final. It is a draft.
 Skipping the manual version. It builds your judgment.
 Naming the competitor brand in client material. Describe by category and structure.

chunks.title: Case Study Teardown — Go further
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Case Study Teardown / Go further.
 Manual vs AI-assisted: manual builds judgment and is slower; AI-assisted takes seconds at $0.004/call, good as a check or when doing many teardowns, but can miss context.
 Why the skincare ad likely works: the hook never mentions the product, so viewers watch past 3 seconds to find out what happened; the day-count proof is concrete and checkable.
 Using it in sales: a short teardown plus sample ad is a stronger opener than a capabilities pitch; offer a "structural analysis + sample ad" as a low-cost or free first deliverable.
 Exercises: easy, tear down one ad; medium, three ads in one category and find the shared pattern; hard, apply one takeaway to a new product and note what you borrowed.
 Template: templates/teardown-worksheet.md.

Product: GripMount — $28 magnetic phone car mount
Constants (same across every ad): product demo, proof section ("two weeks, potholes included"), CTA ("$28, link's below")
| Ad # | Hook | Angle | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | "I did not expect this to hold through a pothole." | Durability/surprise | Baseline ad — this is the one from the script template |

| 5 | "Two weeks, every pothole, still holding." | Proof-first (leads with the result) | Tests whether opening with proof beats opening with a question |

chunks.title: Character Consistency Checklist — Filled example
chunks.text:
Academy template: Character Consistency Checklist / Filled example.
Using the real anchor portrait from Module 2's Worked Example (woman, late 20s, brown hair, freckles), fed as a reference into nano-banana-2-edit for 3 actual generations — car interior, kitchen counter, walking outside:
| Check | Car interior | Kitchen counter | Walking outside |
|---|---|---|---|
| Facial structure matches anchor | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Apparent age consistent | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Freckles present | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Skin tone/lighting shift | Matches anchor | Matches anchor | Different (outdoor) lighting, identity still holds |
| Outfit continuity (if same scene) | n/a — different shots | n/a | n/a |
Verdict: no drift across any of the 3, including the outdoor shot with very different lighting from the anchor. This is what reference-image conditioning done right looks like — the reference image was passed to an edit-capable model (not a fresh text-only prompt), and the prompt described only the setting, never the face. If you see drift in your own attempts, check those two things first before assuming the model just can't hold identity.

chunks.title: UGC Script Template — Filled example (GripMount phone mount, $28)
chunks.text:
Academy template: UGC Script Template / Filled example (GripMount phone mount, $28).
Product: GripMount — magnetic phone car mount
Target length: 28 seconds (~85 words)
| Beat | Timing | Line |
|---|---|---|
| Hook | 0-2s | "Okay, I did not expect this to actually hold my phone through a pothole." |
| Problem / Pitch | 2-15s | "I used to have one of those suction ones that fell off literally every drive — this one's magnetic, snaps on in like two seconds." |
| Proof / Demo | 15-25s | "[demo: slaps phone onto mount] It's held through every drive for the last two weeks, potholes included." |
| Call to Action | 25-28s | "It's $28, link's below — honestly just get it before your next road trip." |
Why each beat does its job:
- Hook is a surprised, specific claim ("through a pothole"), not a generic opener ("this product is great") — specificity is what stops a scroll.
- Pitch names the competing product's actual failure mode (suction falling off) instead of just describing GripMount — sounds like a real complaint, not copy.
- Proof pairs a visual demo with a concrete duration ("two weeks, potholes included") — numbers read as more credible than adjectives.
- CTA states the price plainly and ties urgency to a real use case (road trip), one action only.

chunks.text:
Academy template: UGC Script Template / Blank template — fill this in.
Product:
Target length: 25-30 seconds (~75-90 words)
### Hook (0-2 sec)
[A question, bold claim, or visual surprise that stops the scroll — be specific, not generic. "I did not expect X" beats "this product is amazing."]
### Problem / Pitch (2-15 sec)
[What problem does the viewer have, and how does this product solve it — said like you'd tell a friend, not like ad copy. Naming a specific competing failure ("the old way always did X") reads more like a real opinion than a feature list.]
### Proof / Demo (15-25 sec)
[Show it working, a result, or a specific detail that makes it credible. A concrete number ("two weeks," "10 minutes," "half the price") is more convincing than an adjective ("amazing," "life-changing").]
### Call to Action (25-30 sec)
[One clear next step — "link in bio," "use code X," "swipe up." State the price if it's a strength. Tie urgency to a real reason, not just "buy now."]

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 1.1 — What you are launching
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 1 (Welcome to Your AI Application Business), lesson 1.1: What you are launching. Outcome: You can explain in two sentences what you are about to launch.
Each of the 38 applications is a finished web app. A visitor signs in with Google, uploads or types something, and the app asks the MuAPI AI service to generate the result.
You do not build anything. You copy an app's source code to your own GitHub account, publish it on your own Vercel account, connect your own database, MuAPI key and Stripe account, and point your own domain at it.
The apps are multi-tenant: one deployment serves all of your customers. Each customer has their own login, their own credits and their own saved creations.
Customers pay you (through your Stripe account) for credit packs. Spending credits triggers AI work that MuAPI bills to you. Your profit is what customers pay minus Stripe fees and MuAPI usage.
Steps: 1. Open the Reseller Studio. 2. Pick any three app cards and read the title and description on each. 3. Look at the buttons on one card: Try Live Demo, Deployment Guide, Source Code, Deploy on Vercel. 4. Write down, in your own words, one sentence on what the app does. 5. Write one sentence on who would pay for it and how the money flows to you.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 1.1 — What you are launching
chunks.text:
