Check it worked: You can answer: "Who pays whom?" — the customer pays Stripe, Stripe pays you; you pay MuAPI for AI usage.
Common mistakes: Thinking the apps are subscriptions. All 37 web apps sell one-time credit packs. Pointing the app at someone else's database or keys.
Troubleshooting: I cannot open the Reseller Studio. -> The studio requires you to be signed in. Sign in and try again. I do not see all four buttons on a card. -> Button labels and layout can change. Use the card's menu or the workshop page, and follow the current screen.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 1.2 — Accounts you will need and what they cost
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 1 (Welcome to Your AI Application Business), lesson 1.2: Accounts you will need and what they cost. Outcome: You have a list of accounts and know which can cost money.
You will create: GitHub (hold the code), MuAPI (the AI), a PostgreSQL database host such as Supabase or Neon (stores users and credits), Google Cloud (the "Sign in with Google" button), Vercel (hosting) and Stripe (payments). A domain name registrar is optional but recommended.
Recurring costs can include: MuAPI usage (billed by use), a domain name (yearly), and — only if you outgrow free tiers — hosting and database plans. Stripe has no monthly fee on its standard pricing in most places; it takes a per-payment fee. Prices change, so always read the official pricing pages before you commit.
Steps: 1. Open the Stripe pricing page and read what applies to your country today. 2. Do the same for MuAPI, your hosting (Vercel) and your database host, using their official pricing pages. 3. Create a simple notes file and list the accounts you will create: GitHub, MuAPI, database, Google Cloud, Vercel, Stripe, optional domain. 4. Next to each account add the email you will use and where you will store the password (use a password manager). 5. Mark which accounts can cost money: usage-billed, yearly, or only after free limits.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 1.2 — Accounts you will need and what they cost
chunks.text:
Check it worked: You can name which accounts are free to open and which bill by usage.
Common mistakes: Using a different email for every service without writing them down. Assuming free tiers last forever — check the limits.
Troubleshooting: A pricing page shows different numbers than this course. -> Trust the official page. This course deliberately does not quote prices that change.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 1.3 — Your launch roadmap
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 1 (Welcome to Your AI Application Business), lesson 1.3: Your launch roadmap. Outcome: You know the 13 steps from choosing an app to taking real customers.
The path: choose an app → get its source → MuAPI key → database → deploy on Vercel → Stripe account → connect Stripe → set pack prices → name and domain → test everything → go live → find customers.
Do the steps in order. Each lesson ends with a way to check your result, so you always know whether to move on.
Steps: 1. Read the path in the learn section once, from choosing an app to finding customers. 2. Say the first three steps out loud without looking: choose an app, get its source, get a MuAPI key. 3. Open your Academy dashboard. 4. Press Continue Learning whenever you return. The course remembers where you stopped.
Check it worked: The dashboard shows your progress percentage.
Common mistakes: Skipping the database before deploying — the app will deploy but fail at sign-in.
Troubleshooting: My progress did not save. -> Progress saves to your browser and, when available, to your account. Make sure you are signed in and try again. Continue Learning opens the wrong lesson. -> Open the lesson list and pick the lesson you want; progress is kept.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 2.1 — Explore the collection and try the demos
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 2 (Choose Your First Application), lesson 2.1: Explore the collection and try the demos. Outcome: You have tried at least three live demos.
Cards are grouped by category (image, video, text and more). The description tells you the use case. "Try Live Demo" opens a working copy so you can feel the customer experience.
A demo is someone else's deployment. Yours will look the same but will use your branding, your payment account and your domain.
Steps: 1. Open the Reseller Studio and choose three apps that interest you. 2. Press Try Live Demo on the first app. 3. Sign in if asked and make one result, noting how many credits it costs. 4. Write down who would use it and what they would pay for. 5. Repeat the demo, the test result and the notes for the other two apps.
Check it worked: You can name the single result a customer gets from each app.
Common mistakes: Choosing by how impressive the demo is rather than who will pay.
Troubleshooting: A demo does not open. -> Demos are hosted separately and can be slow or paused. Try again later and tell support which app it was. The demo asks me to sign in or has no credits. -> Follow the demo's on-screen prompts. If you cannot make a result, note what the page shows and move to the next app.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 2.2 — Pick one application
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 2 (Choose Your First Application), lesson 2.2: Pick one application. Outcome: You have selected the app you will launch.
Launch one app first. Everything you learn applies to the other 37, so a second app takes a fraction of the time.
Good first choices have an obvious audience you can reach (for example real-estate agents for a staging app), a result people already pay for, and a demo you are proud to show.
Steps: 1. Review your notes from the demos and decide which app has the clearest audience you can reach. 2. On that app's Reseller Studio card press "Learn How to Launch This App", or use the dashboard selector. 3. Open the dashboard. 4. Open the app workshop page and read the requirements: accounts, variables and payment model.
Check it worked: The dashboard shows your selected application.
Common mistakes: Launching three apps at once.
Troubleshooting: I want to change my app later. -> You can change it any time from the dashboard; your lesson progress is kept. The dashboard still shows the old app. -> Refresh the page and confirm you are signed in. Then select the app again.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 3.1 — Create your GitHub account
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 3 (GitHub and Your Application Source Code), lesson 3.1: Create your GitHub account. Outcome: You are signed in to GitHub.
GitHub stores your app's files and is how Vercel receives them. You do not need to learn programming — you only need to copy a repository and keep it in your account.
Steps: 1. Open the GitHub sign-up page. 2. Fill in an email you will keep long term, a password from your password manager and a username. 3. Open the verification email from GitHub and confirm your address. 4. Open your GitHub security settings and start setting up two-factor authentication. 5. Finish the two-factor setup and save any recovery codes in your password manager.
Check it worked: You can sign in to github.com and see your profile.
Common mistakes: Using a throwaway email you will lose access to.
Troubleshooting: No verification email. -> Check spam, then use "resend" on the GitHub page. I cannot find the two-factor setting. -> Menus move. Search the GitHub settings for "two-factor" or check the official GitHub help page.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 3.2 — Get your app's source code
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 3 (GitHub and Your Application Source Code), lesson 3.2: Get your app's source code. Outcome: Your GitHub account has its own copy of the app.
The Source Code button on each card opens the app's repository. To deploy it you need your own copy. The simplest way is a fork.
Some repositories are still being completed. The workshop page tells you exactly which repository holds the app's source today and whether it is complete. If it is not, you will see that plainly — do not guess.
Steps: 1. Open your app's Source Code button from the card or the workshop page. 2. Check the workshop page says this repository holds the complete app today. 3. Make sure you are signed in to GitHub, then click Fork. 4. Keep the default name and create the fork under your account. 5. Open the fork and check it contains a package.json file and a src folder. 6. Open your GitHub profile and its repositories list.
Check it worked: The fork shows under your GitHub account's repositories.
Common mistakes: Deploying the original repository instead of your fork. Deleting files inside the repository.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 3.2 — Get your app's source code
chunks.text: Troubleshooting: My fork has only a README and NOTICE. -> That repository does not hold the app yet. Use the Reseller Studio download for this app if it is available, or contact support — this is listed as an open owner item. The Fork button is missing or disabled. -> Make sure you are signed in. If you already forked it, GitHub opens your existing fork instead.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 3.3 — What is inside your repository
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 3 (GitHub and Your Application Source Code), lesson 3.3: What is inside your repository. Outcome: You can find the three files you will meet again.
You will only meet three places: README.md (the author's setup notes), `.env.example` (the list of settings the app needs — names only, no secrets) and `src/lib/config.js` (the app name and credit-pack prices).
Everything else is the app itself. You will not edit it.
Steps: 1. Open your fork on GitHub (not the original). 2. Open `README.md` and skim the author's setup notes. 3. Open `.env.example` in your fork. 4. Compare the names in `.env.example` with the variable list on your workshop page. 5. Open `src/lib/config.js` and find `plans`.
Check it worked: The variable names in your workshop page match those in .env.example.
Common mistakes: Typing real keys into .env.example. It is public if your fork is public.
Troubleshooting: There is no .env.example. -> Use the variable list on your workshop page, which was read from the app's code. I cannot find src/lib/config.js. -> File layout can differ between apps. Search the repository for "plans" or use the workshop page.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 4.1 — Create your MuAPI account and key
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 4 (Create Your MuAPI Account), lesson 4.1: Create your MuAPI account and key. Outcome: You hold a MuAPI key ready to paste into Vercel.
MuAPI does the AI work. When a customer spends credits, your app calls MuAPI with your key and MuAPI bills your account.
The key is a secret. Treat it like a bank password.
Steps: 1. Create or sign in to your MuAPI account. 2. Open the access keys page. 3. Create a new key and give it a recognisable name. 4. Copy the key straight into your password manager. Do not paste it anywhere else. 5. Check the current billing page and add credit or a payment method if API use requires it. 6. Open your workshop page and note the exact variable name your app expects for this key.
Check it worked: Your workshop page names the variable (for example `MUAPIAPP_API_KEY`) — match it exactly later in Vercel.
Common mistakes: Pasting the key into a screenshot, chat or the GitHub repository. Using the wrong variable name — it differs between apps.
Troubleshooting: Generations fail with an authorization error later. -> The key is wrong, revoked, or in the wrong variable name. Create a new key, update it in Vercel and redeploy. I did not copy the key and the page no longer shows it. -> Keys are often shown only once. Create a new key and delete the old one.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 4.2 — Understand and protect your AI costs
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 4 (Create Your MuAPI Account), lesson 4.2: Understand and protect your AI costs. Outcome: You can estimate cost per generation against what you charge.
Each app charges customers a number of credits per generation (the amount is in the app's code). MuAPI charges you per model call at its own rates. Your margin is the difference.
Protect yourself: set a spending limit or alert on your MuAPI account if one is offered, and check usage weekly at first.
Steps: 1. Open the app README and note the name of the AI model your app uses. 2. Open MuAPI and look up the current price for that model. 3. Find the number of credits the app charges per generation (see the app code or demo). 4. Compare the two: what MuAPI charges you against what the customer pays in credits. 5. Find the MuAPI usage page, and set a spending limit or alert if one is offered; otherwise add a weekly reminder. 6. Do one test generation later (Module 11) and compare MuAPI's usage page with what you expected.
Check it worked: You can state your estimated MuAPI cost for one generation.
Common mistakes: Pricing credit packs without knowing the AI cost.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 4.2 — Understand and protect your AI costs
chunks.text: Troubleshooting: Usage is higher than expected. -> Check for repeated retries or test spam; rotate the key if you suspect it leaked. I cannot find a spending limit. -> Not every account offers one. Use a calendar reminder to check usage weekly instead.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 5.1 — What database your app needs
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 5 (Database and Sign-In Setup), lesson 5.1: What database your app needs. Outcome: You know whether your app needs Supabase specifically or any PostgreSQL database.
The apps store users, credits and results in a PostgreSQL database through a tool called Prisma. They read the address from `DATABASE_URL` (and optionally `DIRECT_URL`).
Supabase is one easy place to get a PostgreSQL database; Neon is another. Only some apps read Supabase-specific keys — your workshop page lists exactly which variables yours uses. Do not force steps your app does not use.
Never connect a reseller app to a database that holds other customers' data. Create a new, empty database for your business.
Steps: 1. Open your app's workshop page. 2. Find and read the "Database" panel. 3. Write down the variable names the panel lists, and note whether it mentions any Supabase-specific keys. 4. Look at the two hosts: Supabase and Neon. Pick one for your new, empty database.
Check it worked: You can name your app's database variables.
Common mistakes: Reusing a database from another project.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 5.1 — What database your app needs
chunks.text: Troubleshooting: The Deployment Center mentions SUPABASE_URL but my workshop does not. -> Follow your workshop page: it is read from your app's code. Only apps that use those variables need them. I cannot find the Database panel. -> Make sure you opened the workshop page for the app you picked, not another app's page; the panel is read from your app's facts.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 5.2 — Create the database and get the connection strings
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 5 (Database and Sign-In Setup), lesson 5.2: Create the database and get the connection strings. Outcome: You have DATABASE_URL (and DIRECT_URL if used) saved safely.
A connection string is one line holding your database's address and password. It is a secret.
Supabase offers a pooled connection (for the running app, `DATABASE_URL`) and a direct connection (for creating tables, `DIRECT_URL`). Neon works similarly. The exact button names change, so use the host's own docs.
Steps: 1. Sign in to your chosen host and start a new project. 2. Name the project, choose a region near your customers, and set a database password. Save the password in your password manager first. 3. Open the connection details (the host calls this "Connect" or "Connection string"; menus move, so follow the current screen). 4. Copy the pooled connection string and replace the password placeholder with your real password. This is your `DATABASE_URL`. 5. Copy the direct connection string the same way (only if your app lists `DIRECT_URL`). This is your `DIRECT_URL`. 6. Store both strings in your password manager. Do not paste them anywhere public.
Check it worked: Each string starts with `postgresql://` and contains your project address.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 5.2 — Create the database and get the connection strings
chunks.text:
Common mistakes: Leaving the "[YOUR-PASSWORD]" placeholder in the string. Special characters in the password that break the string — reset to a simpler password if needed.
Troubleshooting: The app later says it cannot reach the database. -> Re-copy the string, make sure the password is filled in, and use the pooled address for DATABASE_URL. I cannot find the connection strings. -> Look for "Connect" or "Connection string" in the project dashboard; the host moves menus, so check its official docs page linked in this lesson. I lost the database password. -> Reset the database password in the host's project settings, then update both strings in your password manager.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 5.3 — Create the app's tables (prisma db push)
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 5 (Database and Sign-In Setup), lesson 5.3: Create the app's tables (prisma db push). Outcome: The app's tables exist in your database.
These apps ship a Prisma schema but no migration files. The app authors' README says to run `npx prisma db push`, which creates the tables from the schema. You do this once for a new database.
The simplest no-terminal route is to add it in front of the build command on Vercel (Lesson 6.2). The app's README also describes running it on your own computer.
`db push` changes your database to match the schema. Only run it against your own new database.
Steps: 1. Choose your route: the no-terminal route (Vercel build command) or the on-your-computer route. 2. No-terminal route: copy this Build Command and keep it ready for Lesson 6.2. [Vercel build command: npx prisma db push && npm run build] 3. No-terminal route: confirm you will use it only with your own new database from Lesson 5.2. 4. Computer route (Node.js installed): clone your fork and create a `.env` file in it with your `DATABASE_URL` and `DIRECT_URL`. 5. Computer route: run the command below in the project folder. [Create tables from your computer: npx prisma db push]
Check it worked: After the first deployment you can see tables such as User, Account and Session in your database host's table viewer.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 5.3 — Create the app's tables (prisma db push)
chunks.text:
Common mistakes: Running db push against a database that holds other apps' data.
Troubleshooting: Build fails at db push. -> Check DIRECT_URL/DATABASE_URL are set in Vercel, have the real password, and the database is not paused. On my computer, the command says it cannot find a Prisma schema or `npx` is not found. -> Run it from inside the cloned project folder, and make sure Node.js is installed (check the official Node.js page). On my computer, the command cannot connect to the database. -> Check the `.env` values have the real password and no extra spaces or quotes, and that the database project is active.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 5.4 — Set up Google sign-in
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 5 (Database and Sign-In Setup), lesson 5.4: Set up Google sign-in. Outcome: You have GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID and GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET.
Customers sign in with Google. Google needs to know your app's address, so you create an "OAuth client" and list the allowed redirect address.
You do not know your final address until you deploy, so you will create the client now and add the redirect after Lesson 6.3, then again when you add your domain (Module 10).
Steps: 1. Open Google Cloud credentials and sign in with the Google account that will own the app. 2. Create a project if asked, then select it. 3. Configure the consent screen: enter your app name and your support email. 4. Start creating credentials and choose the "OAuth client ID" option (menu names move; follow the current screen). 5. Choose "Web application" as the application type and name the client. Leave redirect URIs empty for now. 6. Create the client, then copy the Client ID and Client Secret into your password manager.
Check it worked: Both values are saved; the Client ID ends in `.apps.googleusercontent.com`.
Common mistakes: Choosing the wrong application type (it must be Web application).

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 5.4 — Set up Google sign-in
chunks.text: Troubleshooting: Google shows "redirect_uri_mismatch" when I sign in. -> Add the exact address `https://YOUR-DOMAIN/api/auth/callback/google` as an Authorized redirect URI, with no trailing slash. Google will not let me create an OAuth client until the consent screen is configured. -> Complete the consent screen step first (app name and support email), then return to creating the client. I closed the dialog and did not copy the secret. -> Open the client in Google Cloud credentials and check the official page for how to view or create a new secret; replace the old one in your password manager.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 6.1 — Create Vercel and connect GitHub
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 6 (Deploy Your Application to Vercel), lesson 6.1: Create Vercel and connect GitHub. Outcome: Vercel can see your GitHub repositories.
Vercel builds your app from your GitHub fork and gives it a web address. Signing up with GitHub is the easiest way to connect them.
Steps: 1. Open the Vercel sign-up page. 2. Choose "Continue with GitHub" and sign in to GitHub if asked. 3. Authorize Vercel, and follow any prompts about plan or team name (check Vercel's current plan terms before choosing). 4. When Vercel asks which repositories it may access, allow your app's fork (or all repositories).
Check it worked: Importing a project on Vercel lists your fork.
Common mistakes: Choosing a "Hobby" plan for a commercial project without reading the plan's terms — check Vercel's current plan terms.
Troubleshooting: Vercel cannot see my fork. -> In Vercel → Account → Git, adjust the GitHub app permissions to include the repository (menus move; follow the current screen). I skipped the repository access step. -> Open the GitHub app settings for Vercel from your GitHub account settings and add the fork there.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 6.2 — Import the project and add environment variables
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 6 (Deploy Your Application to Vercel), lesson 6.2: Import the project and add environment variables. Outcome: The project is imported with every required variable filled in.
On the app card, "Deploy on Vercel" opens Vercel's import page prefilled for the app's repository. You can also import your own fork from the Vercel dashboard. Either way, Vercel detects a Next.js project and suggests settings.
Environment variables are how your keys reach the app. Your workshop page lists the exact names for your app. Values are secrets: enter them only in Vercel.
Use your Stripe TEST keys for now. You will switch to live keys in Lesson 8.5.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 6.2 — Import the project and add environment variables
chunks.text:
Steps: 1. Start from "Deploy on Vercel" on your app card, or use Add New → Project on Vercel and pick your fork. 2. Open Build & Output Settings and override the Build Command if you chose the no-terminal database route in Lesson 5.3. [Build command: npx prisma db push && npm run build] 3. Open the Environment Variables section and have your workshop page's variable list beside it. 4. Add each variable from the workshop list one by one, pasting secret values from your password manager. Use Stripe TEST keys only. 5. Set `NEXTAUTH_SECRET` to a long random string. Generate one with a password manager or with the command below. [Generate a random secret (macOS/Linux terminal): openssl rand -base64 32] 6. Set `NEXTAUTH_URL` and `WEBHOOK_URL` to a placeholder address for now; you set them to the Vercel address after the first deploy (Lesson 6.3). 7. Compare your Vercel list with the workshop checklist name by name and check each is set for Production.
Check it worked: Vercel's variable list shows the same names as your workshop checklist.
Common mistakes: Misspelling a variable name. Adding variables to Preview only instead of Production. Pasting a key with a trailing space.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 6.2 — Import the project and add environment variables
chunks.text: Troubleshooting: I do not know what to enter for STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET yet. -> Skip it for the first deploy. You create it in Lesson 8.3 and redeploy. A variable I added is not picked up by the app. -> Check the exact name and that it is set for Production, then redeploy; changes only apply to new deployments. I cannot find the Build Command override. -> Look in the import page's Build & Output Settings, or in the project settings later; menus move, so follow the current screen.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 6.3 — Deploy and open your app
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 6 (Deploy Your Application to Vercel), lesson 6.3: Deploy and open your app. Outcome: Your app loads at its Vercel address.
Press Deploy. Vercel installs, builds and publishes. A green "Ready" means it published; it does not mean every setting is correct.
After the first deploy, set `NEXTAUTH_URL` and `WEBHOOK_URL` to your Vercel address (for example `https://your-project.vercel.app`) and redeploy so sign-in and AI callbacks know where the app lives.
Steps: 1. Click Deploy. 2. Watch the build log until it finishes. 3. Open the generated URL. 4. Copy the address from your browser. Then, in Vercel → Settings → Environment Variables, set `NEXTAUTH_URL` and `WEBHOOK_URL` to it, with no trailing slash. 5. Open Deployments and Redeploy the latest deployment. 6. In Google Cloud, open your OAuth client and add `https://YOUR-ADDRESS/api/auth/callback/google` as an Authorized redirect URI, then save. 7. Open your app and choose Sign in with Google. 8. Finish signing in.
Check it worked: You can sign in, and a new row appears in the User table in your database.
Common mistakes: Forgetting to redeploy after changing variables. Adding a trailing slash to NEXTAUTH_URL.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 6.3 — Deploy and open your app
chunks.text: Troubleshooting: Sign-in shows a configuration or callback error. -> Check NEXTAUTH_URL, NEXTAUTH_SECRET and the Google redirect URI character by character; then redeploy. The deployment stays on "Building" for a long time or ends in an error. -> Open the build log and read the last lines; see Lesson 6.4 for common causes. The home page shows an error instead of the app. -> Open the deployment's Logs; a missing variable is usually named in the error. Fix it in Settings and redeploy. Google says "redirect_uri_mismatch". -> The address in Google must match your Vercel address exactly (https, no trailing slash); add it again, wait a moment, and retry.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 6.4 — When a build fails (and how to redeploy)
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 6 (Deploy Your Application to Vercel), lesson 6.4: When a build fails (and how to redeploy). Outcome: You can read a failed build and fix the common causes.
Open the failed deployment and read the last lines of the build log; the real cause is almost always there.
Common causes: a variable is missing or misspelled, the database address is wrong or paused, `db push` cannot connect, or Vercel connects to the wrong repository.
Steps: 1. Open your project's Deployments list and click the failed deployment. 2. Open its Build Logs and scroll to the final lines. 3. Match the error to a common cause from the Learn section or the troubleshooting list below. 4. Fix the cause (usually a variable in Settings → Environment Variables) and save it. 5. Go back to Deployments and Redeploy.
Check it worked: A new deployment turns Ready after your fix.
Common mistakes: Changing code instead of checking settings first.
Troubleshooting: Prisma error: cannot reach database. -> Re-copy DATABASE_URL/DIRECT_URL with the real password and check the database project is active. The build fails again with the same error after my fix. -> Make sure you redeployed after saving the change; edits to variables only apply to new deployments. Build works but pages error at runtime. -> Open Logs for the deployment; a missing variable is named in the error.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 7.1 — What Stripe is
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 7 (Create Your Stripe Account), lesson 7.1: What Stripe is. Outcome: You can explain how a customer's card payment reaches your bank.
Stripe is a payment processor. Your customer enters card details on a Stripe-hosted checkout page (your app never sees the card number). Stripe charges the card, keeps its processing fee, and pays the rest to your bank account on a schedule.
Your app is already built to send customers to Stripe Checkout and to listen for Stripe's "payment succeeded" message so it can add credits. You only supply your own Stripe keys.
Availability, fees, payout timing and verification rules depend on your country and business type. This course never assumes one set of rules — check Stripe's pages for yours.
Steps: 1. Open Stripe's website. 2. Read the short overview of how Stripe accepts payments. 3. Find Stripe's official list of supported countries and look for yours. 4. Open the pricing page and note where fees are published. Do not memorise numbers; they vary.
Check it worked: You can say: customer → Stripe → (fee) → my bank.
Common mistakes: Assuming money arrives instantly — payouts follow a schedule.
Troubleshooting: My country is not supported. -> Check Stripe's supported countries. You may need a business entity in a supported country; this is a Stripe policy, not something the app can change.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 7.2 — Create your Stripe account
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 7 (Create Your Stripe Account), lesson 7.2: Create your Stripe account. Outcome: You can sign in to your Stripe Dashboard.
Creating the account is quick. Activating it for real payments is the longer part (Lesson 7.3).
Steps: 1. Go to the Stripe registration page. 2. Enter your email, your full name and a strong password (use a password manager), then register. 3. Open the confirmation email from Stripe and confirm your address. 4. Turn on two-step authentication from the Dashboard's security prompts (menus move; follow the current screen). 5. Sign out, then sign back in to the Dashboard. 6. Look at the Dashboard home page.
Check it worked: You can sign out and back in to dashboard.stripe.com.
Common mistakes: Skipping two-step authentication on an account that will hold money.
Troubleshooting: No confirmation email. -> Check spam and the address you typed; use Stripe's resend option.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 7.3 — Activate your account for real payments
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 7 (Create Your Stripe Account), lesson 7.3: Activate your account for real payments. Outcome: You know what Stripe needs from you and have started activation.
To accept real payments Stripe asks for details about you or your business. Requirements vary by country and by business type (individual / sole trader vs registered company). Typical areas: business type and structure, your legal name and address, identity verification, a business website, customer support contact, a statement descriptor (what appears on card statements) and a bank account for payouts.
Stripe may also ask for policy pages (for example refunds and terms) on your website. What it asks for is shown in your Dashboard and in Stripe's activation guide — follow that, not a generic checklist.
Steps: 1. Read Stripe's activation guide so you know what to expect for your country. 2. In the Dashboard, start the activation / "Activate payments" flow. 3. Choose your business type and fill in your legal name, address and identity details exactly as on your ID. 4. When it asks for a website, use the address of your deployed app (a Vercel address now; your own domain later in Module 10). 5. Add a support email you will actually read, and a statement descriptor if asked. 6. Submit every section Stripe lists, then return to the Dashboard home page.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 7.3 — Activate your account for real payments
chunks.text:
Check it worked: The Dashboard shows your activation status (pending, restricted or active). Do not assume it is active until Stripe says so.
Common mistakes: Entering details that do not match your ID or bank account. Describing the business inaccurately.
Troubleshooting: Why hasn't Stripe activated my account? -> Open the Dashboard notices: Stripe lists what is missing or under review. Review times and extra checks vary; use Stripe support for your case. A section will not accept my details. -> Compare each field with your ID and bank records. Stripe's activation guide and on-screen hints say what it expects for your country.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 7.4 — Connect a bank account for payouts
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 7 (Create Your Stripe Account), lesson 7.4: Connect a bank account for payouts. Outcome: Payouts are configured in Stripe.
Stripe pays out your balance to a bank account you add. Supported accounts, currency, first-payout delays and the schedule depend on your country and account.
Steps: 1. In Dashboard Settings, open the payouts / bank accounts section (menus move; follow the current screen). 2. Choose to add a bank account and enter your bank details exactly as your bank shows them. 3. Save the account. 4. Read your payout schedule and any minimum or delay that applies to you.
Check it worked: The bank account appears in Stripe with its schedule.
Common mistakes: Entering a personal account for a business account (or vice-versa) when Stripe expects a match.
Troubleshooting: My payout is delayed. -> New accounts often have an initial hold. Check the payout page for the reason Stripe gives.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 7.5 — Test mode vs live mode
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 7 (Create Your Stripe Account), lesson 7.5: Test mode vs live mode. Outcome: You can tell which mode you are in and why you test first.
Test mode (Stripe may call it a sandbox) uses fake money and its own keys. Live mode uses real money and a different set of keys. Keys, webhooks and their signing secrets are separate in each mode.
Always complete a full purchase in test mode before enabling live payments. Many surprises (missing webhook, wrong variable) show up only on the first test.
Why is my Stripe checkout still in test mode? Because the app is still using your test secret key. Checkout switches to live only after you replace the keys in Vercel with live keys and redeploy (Lesson 8.5).
Steps: 1. Read Stripe's API keys guide to see how test and live keys differ. 2. Find the test/live indicator in your Dashboard (it may be called test mode or sandbox). 3. Switch to test mode. 4. Open the API keys page and note which keys belong to test mode. Do not copy them anywhere yet. 5. Switch the toggle to live mode and open the API keys page again, then switch back to test.
Check it worked: You can state which key prefix means test vs live: secret keys begin `sk_test_` (test) or `sk_live_` (live). Never write a real key anywhere public.
Common mistakes: Mixing a test key with a live webhook secret (or the reverse).

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 7.5 — Test mode vs live mode
chunks.text: Troubleshooting: I cannot find test mode. -> Stripe's dashboard wording changes (test mode / sandbox). Follow the testing guide.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 8.1 — How your app uses Stripe
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 8 (Connect Stripe to Your Application), lesson 8.1: How your app uses Stripe. Outcome: You know exactly what the app already does with Stripe.
Your app already includes Stripe. When a customer chooses a credit pack, the app creates a Stripe Checkout session (a one-time payment) and sends the customer to Stripe. After payment, Stripe sends a `checkout.session.completed` webhook and the app adds the pack's credits to the customer.
You do not create Products or Prices in Stripe for these apps: the pack names, credits and prices come from the app's `src/lib/config.js` (see your workshop panel). You only need keys and a webhook.
Steps: 1. Open your workshop page and find the Stripe panel. 2. Read the payment model and the credit packs shown there. 3. Find the checkout route shown in the panel. 4. Find the webhook path to register, and keep this page open for Lesson 8.3.
Check it worked: You can name your webhook path from your workshop page.
Common mistakes: Creating Stripe Products and expecting the app to use them — it does not.
Troubleshooting: My panel says it did not find Stripe in the source. -> That app's source could not confirm a Stripe integration. Do not guess; contact support (listed as an owner item).

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 8.2 — Add your Stripe test keys to Vercel
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 8 (Connect Stripe to Your Application), lesson 8.2: Add your Stripe test keys to Vercel. Outcome: Vercel holds your test keys.
The app needs two keys now: the publishable key (`NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY`, begins `pk_test_`) and the secret key (`STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`, begins `sk_test_`). The secret key must stay private.
Steps: 1. Confirm the Dashboard is in test mode, then open Developers → API keys (menus move; follow the current screen). 2. In Vercel, open your project's Settings → Environment Variables. 3. Add `NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` and paste the publishable key as its value. 4. Back in Stripe, reveal the secret key and copy it. Do not paste it anywhere except Vercel. 5. Add `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` in Vercel with the secret key as its value, and select Production. 6. Do not redeploy yet; add the webhook secret in the next lesson first.
Check it worked: Both variables exist in Vercel for Production and show as test keys (prefixes `pk_test_` / `sk_test_`).
Common mistakes: Putting the secret key in the NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable — it would be exposed to every visitor.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 8.2 — Add your Stripe test keys to Vercel
chunks.text: Troubleshooting: Which key is which? -> Publishable keys begin `pk_`; secret keys begin `sk_`. Only the publishable one is public. I cannot see the secret key. -> Stripe hides it behind a reveal option and may ask you to confirm; follow the current screen. Never paste it into chat or a public place.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 8.3 — Create the webhook and add its signing secret
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 8 (Connect Stripe to Your Application), lesson 8.3: Create the webhook and add its signing secret. Outcome: Stripe can tell your app when a payment succeeds.
The webhook endpoint address is your app's address plus the path shown on your workshop page. Register only that path.
The app handles only one event: `checkout.session.completed`. Test and live modes each need their own webhook and signing secret.
Steps: 1. In test mode, open Developers → Webhooks and choose to add an endpoint. 2. Endpoint URL: `https://YOUR-ADDRESS` + the webhook path from your workshop page. 3. Select the event `checkout.session.completed` and save. 4. Open the new endpoint and reveal its signing secret (begins `whsec_`). 5. In Vercel add the signing secret as `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, for Production. 6. Redeploy so the new variables take effect. 7. Back in Stripe, open the endpoint again.
Check it worked: In Stripe → Webhooks the endpoint is listed as enabled for test mode.
Common mistakes: Using the wrong path (an app can contain more than one route). Pasting the live webhook secret while the endpoint is in test mode.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 8.3 — Create the webhook and add its signing secret
chunks.text: Troubleshooting: Stripe shows failed webhook deliveries. -> Open the delivery details: a 400 usually means a wrong signing secret; a 404 means a wrong path; a 500 means a server error — check Vercel logs. Redeploy did not pick up the new variable. -> Check the variable is set for Production and that the new deployment started after you saved it.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 8.4 — Make a test purchase
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 8 (Connect Stripe to Your Application), lesson 8.4: Make a test purchase. Outcome: A test payment succeeds and credits appear.
Use Stripe's test card. No real money moves in test mode.
Steps: 1. Sign in to your app and note your current credit balance. 2. Open the pricing / buy credits page. 3. Choose a credit pack and continue to Stripe Checkout. 4. Enter the test card below, any future expiry date, any 3-digit CVC and any postcode. [Stripe test card number: 4242 4242 4242 4242] 5. Submit the payment. 6. Check your credit balance (refresh once if needed). 7. In Stripe (test mode) open Payments.
Check it worked: In Stripe (test mode) → Payments shows the payment; the app shows the added credits.
Common mistakes: Using a real card while keys are in test mode (it will be declined).
Troubleshooting: Payment succeeded but credits did not appear. -> The webhook is not working. Check Stripe → Webhooks → your endpoint → recent deliveries, then the signing secret and path. Checkout will not open. -> Check STRIPE_SECRET_KEY is set in Production and you redeployed. The card is declined. -> Check the Dashboard is in test mode and the keys in Vercel begin `pk_test_` and `sk_test_`. Re-enter the test card number exactly.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 8.5 — Verify, then switch to live safely
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 8 (Connect Stripe to Your Application), lesson 8.5: Verify, then switch to live safely. Outcome: You have a safe checklist for moving to live payments.
Only switch when: Stripe activation is complete, a full test purchase worked, the webhook delivered, and your domain and redirects are final (Module 10).
Going live means replacing three values in Vercel with LIVE ones, creating a live webhook, and redeploying. Do not mix modes.
Steps: 1. Check your list: activation complete, a test purchase worked, the webhook delivered, and your domain is final. 2. Switch the Dashboard to live mode. 3. Create a live webhook for the same path and event; copy its new signing secret. 4. In Vercel replace `NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` (pk_live_…), `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` (sk_live_…) and `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` (live whsec_…). 5. Redeploy. 6. Do one small real purchase yourself and check your credits. 7. Refund that purchase in the Stripe Dashboard.
Check it worked: Stripe live Payments lists your purchase and your app credited it. This is a step YOU perform on your account; the course cannot verify it for you.
Common mistakes: Leaving the test webhook secret in place after switching keys.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 8.5 — Verify, then switch to live safely
chunks.text: Troubleshooting: Live checkout declines every card. -> Check activation status and that no `pk_test_`/`sk_test_` values remain. Live purchase worked but no credits. -> The live webhook is probably missing or has the test signing secret. Check live Webhooks → recent deliveries.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 9.1 — Costs, fees, revenue and profit
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 9 (Configure Pricing and Customer Payments), lesson 9.1: Costs, fees, revenue and profit. Outcome: You can work out profit per pack.
Revenue is what customers pay. Profit is revenue minus Stripe fees, MuAPI usage, and your fixed costs (domain, hosting if any).
Stripe's fees depend on your country and payment type; read the current pricing page. The AI cost depends on the model your app calls and how many generations each pack buys.
Steps: 1. Pick one credit pack from your workshop panel and write down its price. 2. Open Stripe's pricing page and write down the fee that applies to that price for your country. 3. Work out the AI cost for that pack's credits from your MuAPI usage. 4. Subtract the Stripe fee and AI cost from the price. 5. Use the monthly expenses worksheet in Module 12 for fixed costs.
Check it worked: Your profit per pack is greater than zero after fees and AI cost.
Common mistakes: Forgetting the Stripe fee on small packs, where fixed fees weigh most.
Troubleshooting: I cannot find my AI cost per credit. -> Run a few test generations (Module 11) and divide MuAPI's usage charge by credits spent.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 9.2 — Set your credit-pack prices
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 9 (Configure Pricing and Customer Payments), lesson 9.2: Set your credit-pack prices. Outcome: Your packs show the prices you chose.
Pack names, credits and prices are defined in `src/lib/config.js` in your fork (shown on your workshop page). Prices are in cents (500 = $5.00). Changing them is a configuration edit in your own repository; Vercel redeploys when you save.
These apps sell one-time credit packs. They do not offer subscriptions, and this course does not add that.
Steps: 1. In your fork on GitHub open `src/lib/config.js`. 2. Click the pencil (edit) and change only the `price` (and `credits` if you wish) numbers, in cents. 3. Commit the change. 4. Open your project in Vercel and wait for the new deployment. 5. Open your pricing page and hard refresh.
Check it worked: A test purchase (test mode) charges the new amount.
Common mistakes: Entering dollars instead of cents. Editing anything other than the numbers.
Troubleshooting: Price on the page did not change. -> Wait for the deployment to finish, hard refresh, and check you edited the file in the repository Vercel deploys.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 9.3 — Failed payments, refunds and disputes
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 9 (Configure Pricing and Customer Payments), lesson 9.3: Failed payments, refunds and disputes. Outcome: You know how to handle money problems.
Failed payments happen at Stripe Checkout (declined card); no credits are added and the customer can retry.
Refunds are issued in the Stripe Dashboard. Important: the app handles only `checkout.session.completed`, so a refund or dispute does NOT automatically remove credits from the customer's balance. Decide your policy and handle it manually.
A dispute is a bank-initiated reversal; Stripe asks for evidence and may charge a fee. Keep records of what each customer bought.
Steps: 1. Open the Payments page in the Dashboard. 2. Open one payment and find where a refund is issued. Do not issue one unless it is a test payment. 3. Read Stripe's refund guide. 4. Read Stripe's dispute guide. 5. Write your own short refund policy, including what you do about credits.
Check it worked: You can explain what happens to credits when you refund (they stay unless you remove them).
Common mistakes: Promising automatic refunds in your marketing.
Troubleshooting: A customer says they paid but have no credits. -> Check Stripe → Payments, then Webhooks → recent deliveries for that time. Fix the webhook if needed and contact support for the app's credit adjustment process.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 10.1 — Name your business and set the app name
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 10 (Add Your Business Name and Domain), lesson 10.1: Name your business and set the app name. Outcome: Your chosen name appears in the app.
The only branding settings these apps expose are the ones in their own configuration: `appName` in `src/lib/config.js` and, in some apps, the `NEXT_PUBLIC_THEME` variable. Your workshop page shows which exist for your app. This course does not add a branding editor.
Pick a name customers can remember and that you can get as a domain.
Steps: 1. Write down two or three name ideas you could live with. 2. Search each name at a registrar you trust to see if a matching domain is free (you buy it in the next lesson). 3. Pick one name and open your fork on GitHub, then open `src/lib/config.js`. 4. Change the `appName` value to your business name and commit the change. 5. If your workshop lists `NEXT_PUBLIC_THEME`, check the repository README for its allowed values before changing it. 6. Wait for Vercel to redeploy, then open your app.
Check it worked: After the redeploy your app shows your name where it previously showed the default.
Common mistakes: Using a trademarked name.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 10.1 — Name your business and set the app name
chunks.text: Troubleshooting: The old name still shows in some places. -> Some text may be set in pages rather than config. Do not edit code beyond the documented settings; ask support. The name did not change after the commit. -> Check the commit is on the branch Vercel deploys and that the latest deployment finished; then refresh without cache.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 10.2 — Buy a domain and connect it to Vercel
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 10 (Add Your Business Name and Domain), lesson 10.2: Buy a domain and connect it to Vercel. Outcome: Your domain opens your app over HTTPS.
A domain is bought from a registrar (many exist; compare current prices and renewal costs). Vercel then tells you which DNS records to create. Changes can take from minutes to hours to spread.
Vercel issues the HTTPS certificate automatically once DNS is correct.
Steps: 1. Buy your domain from a registrar of your choice (check current prices and renewal cost on its page). 2. In Vercel, open your project, then Settings, then Domains, and add the domain. Menus move; follow the current screen. 3. Read the DNS records Vercel shows for the domain. 4. Open your registrar's DNS page and create exactly those records, removing old conflicting ones for the same name. 5. Wait, then refresh the Domains page in Vercel until the domain is valid. This can take minutes to hours. 6. Open `https://your-domain` in a browser.
Check it worked: Vercel shows a valid configuration and the padlock appears in the browser.
Common mistakes: Adding the records to the wrong domain or leaving old conflicting records.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 10.2 — Buy a domain and connect it to Vercel
chunks.text: Troubleshooting: Vercel says invalid configuration. -> Compare each record with what Vercel shows; check for typos and wait for DNS to spread. The browser shows a certificate or not-secure warning. -> Vercel issues the certificate only once DNS is correct; wait for the domain to show valid, then reload.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 10.3 — Update every address that mentions your old URL
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 10 (Add Your Business Name and Domain), lesson 10.3: Update every address that mentions your old URL. Outcome: Sign-in, AI callbacks and Stripe all use your domain.
Moving to a domain changes your address in four places. Missing one breaks sign-in or payments.
Steps: 1. In Vercel environment variables, set `NEXTAUTH_URL` to `https://your-domain` (no trailing slash). 2. In the same place, set `WEBHOOK_URL` to `https://your-domain` (no trailing slash). 3. In Google Cloud, open your OAuth credentials and add `https://your-domain/api/auth/callback/google` as an Authorized redirect URI. Keep the old one until you have tested. 4. In Stripe, edit your test-mode webhook endpoint to use your domain with the same path. 5. Switch Stripe to live mode and edit the live webhook endpoint the same way. 6. In Stripe activation settings, update your business website to your domain. 7. Redeploy in Vercel so the new variables apply. 8. On your domain, sign in with Google and run a test purchase.
Check it worked: Sign-in works and a test purchase credits the account on your domain.
Common mistakes: Updating test but not live webhook endpoints.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 10.3 — Update every address that mentions your old URL
chunks.text: Troubleshooting: redirect_uri_mismatch after the change. -> The Google redirect must exactly equal your NEXTAUTH_URL plus /api/auth/callback/google. Sign-in works but a test purchase adds no credits. -> Re-check the Stripe webhook endpoint address and path in the mode you tested, and confirm you redeployed after changing variables. Generation hangs after the move. -> Confirm `WEBHOOK_URL` is your new public address and redeploy.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 11.1 — Run the full customer test
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 11 (Test and Launch Your Application), lesson 11.1: Run the full customer test. Outcome: Every part of the customer journey works.
Act as a brand-new customer using a second Google account. Use test mode until the very last step.
Steps: 1. In a private browser window, open your domain and sign in with a second Google account (not your admin one). 2. Run one real AI generation with a small input. 3. Open the result and download it. 4. Open MuAPI usage and find the generation. 5. In test mode, buy a credit pack with the Stripe test card. 6. Check the credit balance in the app and the payment in Stripe, Payments. 7. Open your Vercel deployment logs for the time of these steps. 8. Use up the remaining credits, then try one more generation.
Check it worked: All boxes are your own observations. Nothing here is verified by this course — keep screenshots of your own results for your records (never of secret keys).
Common mistakes: Testing only with your admin account.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 11.1 — Run the full customer test
chunks.text: Troubleshooting: Generation hangs on "processing". -> The app relies on MuAPI callbacks to `WEBHOOK_URL`; check that variable is your public address and redeploy. Purchase succeeded in Stripe but no credits appear. -> Check the Stripe webhook delivery for that payment and compare its endpoint and signing secret with Lesson 8.3. The second account cannot sign in. -> Check the Google consent screen setup (test users, if your app is still in testing) and the redirect address from Lesson 10.3.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 11.2 — Live payment readiness
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 11 (Test and Launch Your Application), lesson 11.2: Live payment readiness. Outcome: You are confident to accept the first real customer.
Live readiness is a short list. Stripe controls whether live payments are allowed; your Dashboard shows its status.
Steps: 1. Open your Stripe Dashboard in live mode and check the account status. 2. Confirm the live keys are installed in Vercel and the live webhook endpoint exists (Lesson 8.5). 3. Write a refund and support policy and a contact email, and publish them on your site or sales page. 4. Make one small live purchase yourself on your domain. 5. Find that payment in Stripe live-mode Payments and refund it.
Check it worked: You saw your own live purchase in Stripe and the credits in the app.
Common mistakes: Launching before the live webhook exists.
Troubleshooting: Live purchase did not add credits. -> Compare the live webhook endpoint, path and signing secret with Lesson 8.3. Stripe still asks for information before live payments. -> Follow the requirements Stripe lists on the activation page; they vary by country, so check the official page.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 12.1 — Find your customers and make an offer
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 12 (Start Selling Your Application), lesson 12.1: Find your customers and make an offer. Outcome: You have a target niche and a simple offer.
Choose one niche where people already pay for the result your app gives (for example real-estate agents for staging, small shops for product photos). Talk to five people in that niche before you promote broadly.
Explain the benefit in the customer's words: what they get, how fast, and how much it costs per result.
Steps: 1. Write one niche where people already pay for the result your app gives. 2. Write the single result you sell in the customer's words: what they get, how fast, cost per result. 3. Talk to five people in that niche and note what they say. 4. Fill in the sales offer and app description templates from the next lesson. 5. Show the live demo of your own domain on a call or in a short screen recording.
Check it worked: A prospect can say back to you what they would pay for.
Common mistakes: Selling to "everyone".
Troubleshooting: Nobody replies. -> Narrow the niche and message people individually with a specific result.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 12.2 — Templates you can copy
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 12 (Start Selling Your Application), lesson 12.2: Templates you can copy. Outcome: You have your sales and support wording ready.
Edit the bracketed parts. Keep claims honest: only promise what your app does today.
Steps: 1. Basic sales offer. [Sales offer: Hi [Name], I run [Business], an AI tool that [one result] in [time]. You buy credits once — [pack name] gives [credits] credits for [price] — and each [result] uses [N] credits. No subscription. Try it here: [your-domain]. Reply with questions and I will help you get your first result.] 2. App description. [App description: [Business] helps [audience] [result] in minutes. Upload [input], choose [options], and download [output]. Pay only for what you use with simple credit packs.] 3. Launch announcement. [Launch announcement: Launching today: [Business] — [one-line benefit]. It is live at [your-domain]. Try it and tell me what you think; early feedback will shape what I improve next.] 4. Customer welcome email. [Welcome email: Subject: Welcome to [Business]

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 12.2 — Templates you can copy
chunks.text:
Hi [Name], thanks for joining. Sign in at [your-domain] with Google, buy a credit pack on the Pricing page, and create your first [result]. If anything goes wrong, reply to this email at [support-email] and I will help. — [Your name]] 5. Customer support response. [Support reply: Hi [Name], thanks for letting me know. I am checking [issue] now and will reply within [time]. Could you send the email you signed in with and roughly when you paid or generated? That helps me find it fast. — [Your name]]
Check it worked: Each template has your business name, address and support email filled in.
Common mistakes: Promising refunds or features you have not set up.
Troubleshooting: I do not know which numbers to put in the brackets. -> Use the pack names, credits and prices shown in your own app and Stripe; do not guess or copy another business.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 12.3 — Monthly expenses worksheet and ongoing operations
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 12 (Start Selling Your Application), lesson 12.3: Monthly expenses worksheet and ongoing operations. Outcome: You know your monthly costs and what to monitor.
Ongoing costs: MuAPI usage, domain renewal, any paid hosting or database plan, and Stripe fees on each payment. Monitor payments, MuAPI usage and errors weekly, answer support promptly, and handle refunds per your policy.
Steps: 1. Copy this worksheet into a spreadsheet. [Monthly expenses worksheet: Month: [ ]
Revenue (credit packs sold): [ ]
Stripe fees: [ ]
MuAPI usage: [ ]
Domain (monthly share): [ ]
Hosting / database plans: [ ]
Other tools: [ ]
Refunds: [ ]
Profit = Revenue - all costs: [ ]] 2. Fill in this month's figures from Stripe, MuAPI and your registrar and hosting bills. 3. Put a weekly reminder in your calendar to check Stripe payments, MuAPI usage and Vercel logs. 4. Repeat the worksheet at the start of each month.
Check it worked: You can state this month's profit using real figures from Stripe and MuAPI.
Common mistakes: Ignoring MuAPI usage until the bill arrives.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 12.3 — Monthly expenses worksheet and ongoing operations
chunks.text: Troubleshooting: I cannot find a figure to fill in. -> Use the billing or usage page of that service and menus move; follow the current screen. Leave a note rather than guessing. Costs exceed revenue. -> Raise pack prices (Lesson 9.2), reduce free test usage, or limit generations per customer if the app supports it.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 13.1 — Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 13 (Build Your App with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe), lesson 13.1: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe. Outcome: You have free Netlify, Clerk and Stripe accounts (Stripe in test mode) plus GitHub, and know what each one does.
Four accounts, four jobs. GitHub stores your copy of the app. Netlify builds it and puts it on the internet. Clerk handles people signing up and signing in. Stripe takes the payments (the apps already include Stripe — you only connect your own keys).
All three services have a free plan at the time of writing, but limits and prices change. Open each pricing page and read the current free limits before you rely on them.
Use the same email you will use for your business, and turn on two-step sign-in for each account. Stripe stays in test mode until you decide to go live later in the course.
The AI part (MuAPI) and the database (Supabase or Neon) are already set up from Modules 4 and 5. If you skipped them, do those first, because hosting needs the database address.
"Free" means a free plan with limits, not free at any size. Typical limits are build minutes, bandwidth and monthly active users. Write the limits you see, with today's date, so you can notice when you are getting close.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 13.1 — Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe
chunks.text:
Protect each account like the keys to a shop: a strong unique password in a password manager, two-step sign-in, and your business email so the accounts never depend on a personal address.
Steps: 1. Create or sign in to GitHub (you should already have it from Module 3). 2. Create a Netlify account. Choosing "Sign up with GitHub" makes connecting your repo easier. 3. Create a Clerk account. 4. When asked, create a Clerk application. Name it after your business and keep Email and Google as sign-in options. 5. Create or sign in to Stripe. 6. Stay in test mode (look for the Test mode / Sandbox indicator in the dashboard; menus move, so follow the current screen). 7. Open each pricing page and note the current free limits, with today's date, in your own notes. 8. Turn on two-step sign-in in each of the four accounts, using the security or account settings of each service (menus move; follow the current screen). 9. Save the recovery codes somewhere safe, away from the chat, such as your password manager. 10. In Clerk, find the API keys page and look at it without copying anything. You will use the keys in lesson 13.8.
Check it worked: You can open all four dashboards in separate browser tabs.
Common mistakes: Skipping the pricing pages and being surprised by a limit later. Switching Stripe to live mode before the test purchase works.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 13.1 — Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe
chunks.text: Troubleshooting: Clerk asks me to choose a plan. -> Choose the free plan if one is offered on the current pricing page. If it is not, check the page again before paying for anything. I cannot see a Test mode or Sandbox indicator in Stripe. -> Dashboards move things around. Look for a test or sandbox switch near the top of the Stripe dashboard, and check the official Stripe page on test mode before continuing. A service does not offer two-step sign-in where I looked. -> Search that service's help page for two-step or two-factor sign-in; the setting is usually under account or security.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 13.2 — Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe with connectors
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 13 (Build Your App with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe), lesson 13.2: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe with connectors. Outcome: Claude can see your Netlify sites, your Clerk application and your Stripe test data, with your approval each time.
A connector (sometimes called a plugin) lets a chat use another service for you. You sign in to the service, approve access, and from then on you can ask the chat to do things there — like listing your Netlify sites or checking a Stripe test payment.
Netlify, Stripe and Clerk each offer a connector for Claude. Where the buttons are and what they are called changes, so you will follow each service's official page rather than a screenshot.
The safety rule: sign in with your own accounts, approve only what you understand, and never paste a secret key into the chat. The connector signs in for you, so you do not need to.
A connector changes what a chat can do from "explain" to "act". The safety comes from you approving access narrowly: one team, one Clerk application, your test-mode Stripe account.
Connectors are removable. You can disconnect each one from the chat's settings and from the service's own list of authorized apps. If you ever approved the wrong account, remove it and reconnect.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 13.2 — Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe with connectors
chunks.text:
A new account will show zero sites and zero payments. That is a good test result: it proves Claude reached your account, not someone else's.
Steps: 1. Open Claude and sign in. Open its settings and find where connectors (or integrations) are managed. 2. Add the Netlify connector and sign in to Netlify when asked. Approve access to your own team. 3. Add the Stripe connector and sign in. Pick your test-mode account. 4. Add the Clerk connector and sign in. Select the application you created in 13.1. 5. Start a new chat. 6. Send this read-only test message. [Test message: Using your Netlify, Stripe and Clerk connectors, list my Netlify sites, my Clerk application name, and my five most recent Stripe test payments. Do not change anything.] 7. Check the answer matches your dashboards (empty lists are fine). If it shows the wrong account or live Stripe data, disconnect, sign out of that service in your browser, and reconnect with the right account. 8. Send this once to set the rule for the whole project. [Working rule: Do not ask me for secret keys. If a step involves a key, tell me the variable name and which dashboard page to paste it into.]
Check it worked: Claude answers with real names from your own Netlify, Clerk and Stripe accounts, and changes nothing.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 13.2 — Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe with connectors
chunks.text:
Common mistakes: Connecting a work or client account by mistake. Asking the chat to change things before testing with a read-only question. Approving a connector for a client or employer account. Ignoring a connector that stays in an "authorization needed" state.
Troubleshooting: A connector says it needs authorization. -> Open its entry in the connector settings and complete the sign-in. The tools only appear after you approve. I cannot find where to add connectors. -> Your plan or workspace may restrict them. Check the official page for your plan, or ask your workspace admin. The answer shows the wrong account or live Stripe data. -> Disconnect the connector, sign out of that service in your browser, and reconnect with the right account in test mode.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 13.3 — Connect ChatGPT the same way
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 13 (Build Your App with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe), lesson 13.3: Connect ChatGPT the same way. Outcome: ChatGPT can use the same three services, or you know exactly what your plan does not allow.
ChatGPT can also use connectors built on the same standard (MCP). Whether you can add them, and where, depends on your plan and on settings OpenAI changes from time to time — so check OpenAI's current help page before you start.
Everything from 13.2 still applies: your own accounts, approve only what you understand, test read-only first, never paste secrets.
You do not need both assistants. Pick one for the build and keep the other as a second opinion for hard problems.
Pick one assistant for the build, because one conversation that knows your app beats two that each know half. Use the other as a second opinion: paste an error message (never a secret) and ask for an independent explanation.
If a feature is missing in ChatGPT it is usually a plan or workspace setting, not something you did wrong. Check OpenAI's current help page for what your plan allows.
Even when connectors are unavailable you can finish the whole module: ask the assistant to explain each change, and make the dashboard changes yourself.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 13.3 — Connect ChatGPT the same way
chunks.text:
Steps: 1. Open ChatGPT and look in its settings for connectors or apps. If your plan does not show them, read OpenAI's current help page for what is available. 2. Add the Netlify connector, sign in and approve access to your own team only. 3. Add the Stripe connector, sign in and choose your test-mode account. 4. Add the Clerk connector, sign in and choose your application. 5. Start a new chat. If your ChatGPT version asks you to enable connectors per chat, switch on the three you added. 6. Send the same read-only test message you used in 13.2. [Test message: Using your Netlify, Stripe and Clerk connectors, list my Netlify sites, my Clerk application name, and my five most recent Stripe test payments. Do not change anything.] 7. Compare the answer with the same facts in your three dashboards. 8. Read every confirmation before approving an action that changes something. Approve only what you expect.
Check it worked: The answer matches what you see in the three dashboards.
Common mistakes: Assuming a menu name from a video is still current.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 13.3 — Connect ChatGPT the same way
chunks.text: Troubleshooting: ChatGPT will not let me add a custom connector. -> It may be limited to certain plans or need a setting turned on. Follow the current OpenAI instructions, or do this module with Claude. The connector is added but ChatGPT does not use it in my chat. -> If your ChatGPT version asks, switch the connector on for the conversation you are using, and check OpenAI's current help page.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 13.4 — Give the assistant your app and your plan
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 13 (Build Your App with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe), lesson 13.4: Give the assistant your app and your plan. Outcome: Your assistant knows which app you are building, what it already includes and what you want changed.
Your assistant knows nothing about your app until you tell it. Give it three things: where the code is (your GitHub copy), what the app already has (the workshop panel below lists its database, sign-in, payments and variable names), and what you want changed.
What the apps already include: Stripe payments, a PostgreSQL database through Prisma and Google sign-in through NextAuth. Netlify hosting and Clerk sign-in are changes your assistant makes in your own copy — this module walks you through them.
Work in small steps and ask the assistant to explain each change before it makes one. You approve every change, and you can undo any step in GitHub.
A good briefing has four parts: where the code is, what the app already includes, what you want changed, and how you want to work. Most failed AI builds fail because one of these is missing.
You do not need to understand every line of a change. Check three things: does the explanation match what you asked for, is the change on a branch, and is there a test you can run ("open this page, you should see this")?

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 13.4 — Give the assistant your app and your plan
chunks.text: Steps: 1. Open your app's workshop page and keep its panels open: they list your app's real variable names. 2. Start a new chat with your assistant and paste the briefing below, replacing the two placeholders with your app name and repo address. [Briefing: I am building my own copy of a reseller app called <APP NAME>. My code is in my GitHub repo <YOUR REPO ADDRESS>. It already uses Next.js, Prisma with PostgreSQL, Stripe payments and Google sign-in through NextAuth. My goal: host it on Netlify, replace sign-in with Clerk, and keep the existing Stripe credits flow working in test mode. Work in small steps. Before each change, tell me what you will change and why. Never ask me to paste secret keys into this chat; tell me which dashboard setting to use instead.] 3. Send the briefing and wait for the reply. 4. Ask it to read the repo and summarise the pieces: the sign-in code, the payment code and the build command. 5. Compare the assistant's summary with the workshop panels: same sign-in system, same Stripe webhook route, same variable names, and the place where users and credits are stored. Correct anything it got wrong. 6. Send the working rules message. [Working rules: For the rest of this project: always show me a plan first, change one thing at a time, tell me how to test each change, and tell me exactly which dashboard I must visit for anything involving a key or a setting.]

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 13.4 — Give the assistant your app and your plan
chunks.text:
Check it worked: The summary names your app's real sign-in and Stripe webhook code, matching the workshop panel.
Common mistakes: Pasting secret keys into the chat to "help" the assistant. Letting the assistant make many changes at once. Skipping the summary check: a wrong assumption now becomes a broken build later.
Troubleshooting: The assistant cannot see my repo. -> Make sure the repo is yours, and use its GitHub connector or paste the files it asks for. Do not paste anything secret. The summary does not match my workshop panel. -> Tell the assistant which part is wrong, ask it to look at the repo again, and confirm the corrected summary before any change.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 13.5 — Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 13 (Build Your App with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe), lesson 13.5: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site. Outcome: Your app is checked for Netlify and a Netlify site is connected to your GitHub repo.
Netlify builds your app straight from your GitHub repo every time you push a change. The assistant checks what the app needs (the build command and the environment variables), and you add the values in Netlify's dashboard.
Netlify builds your app each time you push. If a build fails, the previous working version keeps serving, so a failed deploy does not take your site down.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 13.5 — Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site
chunks.text:
Steps: 1. Ask the assistant to check your app builds on Netlify and to list any change it needs. [Prompt: Check this Next.js app is ready to deploy on Netlify. List the build command, the Node version, and every environment variable the code reads (names only). Tell me about any change needed before I deploy.] 2. Review the answer: compare the variable names with your workshop page and ask about anything missing or extra. 3. If the assistant proposes a configuration change for Netlify, ask for it on a new branch (for example netlify-setup) and have it explain the change first. It should not change how the app behaves. 4. Create the Netlify site from your GitHub repo: ask the assistant to do it through the connector, or do it yourself in Netlify with "Add new project" and choose your repo (menu names move; follow the current screen).
Check it worked: Your Netlify dashboard lists the new site connected to your repository.
Common mistakes: Skipping a check at the end of the lesson.
Troubleshooting: Something did not match what the lesson says you should see. -> Stop, copy the exact message or describe what you see to your assistant, and ask it to explain the first problem before changing anything.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 13.6 — Add variables, deploy and fix failures
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 13 (Build Your App with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe), lesson 13.6: Add variables, deploy and fix failures. Outcome: Your app builds on Netlify and opens at a netlify.app address, with every secret in Netlify and none in the chat.
Secret values — the database address, Stripe keys, MuAPI key — go in Netlify's environment variable settings, never in the chat and never in the code. The assistant tells you the names; you paste the values yourself.
After you add or change a variable, trigger a new deploy so the app picks it up.
The assistant lists the variable names; you paste the values into Netlify. After adding or changing any variable you must redeploy, because the app reads them when it is built or started.
Two values need care: the variable holding your site's own public address (it must match the real netlify.app address, so set it after the first deploy and redeploy), and the database address (use the application connection string your host gives you).

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 13.6 — Add variables, deploy and fix failures
chunks.text:
Steps: 1. In Netlify, open the site's environment variable settings. 2. Add each variable from your workshop page. Paste the values yourself, never into the chat. 3. Trigger a deploy and wait for it to finish. 4. If the deploy fails, ask the assistant to read the log and name only the first error. [Prompt: Read the failed deploy log through the Netlify connector and tell me the first error and what causes it. Do not change anything yet.] 5. After the first deploy, set the variable that holds your site's public address to the real netlify.app address, then redeploy. 6. Open the netlify.app address Netlify shows for the site.
Check it worked: Your netlify.app address opens your app's home page.
Common mistakes: Changing variables and forgetting to redeploy. Putting a secret in the repo.
Troubleshooting: The build fails. -> Ask the assistant to read the deploy log and explain the first error. Fix one error at a time and redeploy. The page loads but sign-in or the database fails. -> A variable is missing or has a typo. Compare Netlify's list with the workshop panel and redeploy.

chunks.title: Reseller Setup Walkthrough 13.7 — Plan the Clerk change
chunks.text:
Reseller Setup Walkthrough, Module 13 (Build Your App with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe), lesson 13.7: Plan the Clerk change. Outcome: You have a reviewed plan for replacing NextAuth with Clerk that keeps every person's credits.
Your app ships with Google sign-in (NextAuth). Clerk replaces it with ready-made sign-up and sign-in pages, email and Google options, and a user dashboard. This is a code change in your own copy, so you and your assistant do it together in a separate branch and test before merging.
